paragraphs.text: NOTES OF LEONTIUS, TAKEN DOWN FROM THE LECTURES OF THEODORE, THE MOST GOD-BELOVED ABBA AND MOST WISE PHILOSOPHER, WHO STUDIED BOTH DIVINE AND SECULAR LITERATURE. LECTURE ONE. Since we are about to discuss heresies, we must first deal with four terms used by the Fathers. They are these: essence, nature, hypostasis and person. It must be understood that for them essence and nature are the same thing, and likewise hypostasis and person are the same thing. By essence, or nature, they mean what the philosophers call a species, and a species is what is predicated of many things that differ in number. What they call hypostasis, or person, the philosophers call an individual essence. We were right to add the words "individual essence", for church writers call the individual instances of accidents neither person nor hypostasis. With these points established in advance, our faith is that there is one Godhead, understood in three hypostases. There is one hypostasis of the Father, one of the Son,

and one of the Holy Spirit. These three differ from one another in nothing except their properties: the one is Father, the other Son, the other Holy Spirit. For the three have one essence, one power and one will. They differ only in this: the Son is begotten of the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from him. How the Son is begotten of him, or how the Holy Spirit proceeds, we must not pry into. We must also understand that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not to be thought of as they would be among human beings. Holy Scripture gave them these names simply, as best it could find a way to teach and speak about them, and as we would be able to take it in. This Holy Trinity, then, one Godhead, made all things out of what did not exist in any way at all, both the visible and the invisible. Whether the invisible things came into being first we shall learn later. But this we must know: God made all things in six days, and on the last he made man; and having made him, he placed him in paradise. What paradise is we shall learn later. Then God took flesh from one of his ribs and made a woman, who was named Eve by Adam. He gave them a commandment, saying: "If you keep it, you will be saved; but if not, you will die." They did not keep it, and they were driven out of paradise, and God cursed the human race. After they had been driven out, Adam knew Eve, and they had three sons, Cain, Abel and Seth. Once these were born, the human race multiplied and began to provoke the Lord. In his anger he sent the flood upon them, from which only Noah was saved, with his wife, his three sons and their wives, eight in all. After these were saved, the human race multiplied once more and again began to worship idols. Then God looked upon Abraham, a Chaldean from the land of Mesopotamia, and said to him: "Go out from your kindred and from your land, and come into a land that I will show you." He went out, and God showed him the land of Canaan, that is, Palestine, saying to him: "I will make you heir of this land." In that land Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot twelve children, one of whom was Judah. These were the twelve patriarchs; they were called patriarchs because the twelve tribes were named after them. These people were called Israelites, Hebrews and Jews. They were called Israelites after Jacob, for God said to him, "You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel," which means "a mind that sees God." So from Jacob, who was named Israel, they were called Israelites. They were called Hebrews after Eber, Abraham's forefather. Strictly speaking, not all of them were called Jews, but only those descended from the tribe of Judah;

but in a looser sense they were all called Jews, because the kings came from this tribe, and so the name came to prevail for all of them. Among these twelve was Joseph, whom the other brothers envied, until they sold him to men who were going down to Egypt. When he came to Egypt, he found favour with Pharaoh the king and with the people there. When a famine came upon Palestine, Jacob, having heard that there was plenty of grain, came to Egypt with his sons and his sons' children, seventy-five in all; and when Joseph made himself known to them, they stayed there. After Jacob and Joseph had died there, the Israelites were oppressed by the Egyptians. Then God remembered the promise he had given to Abraham, and he brought them out of Egypt through Moses the prophet, six hundred thousand of them, not counting children and women. They stayed in the wilderness forty years, during which God gave them the law through Moses; yet they did everything contrary to the law, as Scripture says. After forty years, Moses having died, they came out of the wilderness into the land of promise. But even when they had entered this land they did not turn back, though many prophets appeared and gave them much exhortation; they stayed the same. And then the Son and Word of God, dwelling for our sake in the Theotokos and putting on a body endowed with a soul, with mind and with reason, in a word a human body, was united to the human body without confusion, truly and without division: truly, because one hypostasis was formed from God the Word and the human body; without confusion, because after the union the things united were preserved, neither of them changing anything of its essence; and without division, because their hypostasis is one. We confirm all this from Holy Scripture, for it speaks of the works of one and the same person as proceeding from different natures, sometimes those of God, sometimes those of man. He endured everything a human being must endure: he was born, nursed with milk and brought up; he grew, and at thirty years of age he was baptized; after his baptism he began to work signs and to teach the Jews; in his thirty-third year he was crucified, and having been crucified he rose on the third day, and was taken up into heaven with his body. Now he sits with it at the right hand of the Father, and it is he who will judge the living and the dead at the resurrection. This is the faith of Christians. Since these things are so, let us in the present study call to mind four heresies. Two of them concern theology, and they are diametrically opposed to each other. Sabellius said that the Holy Trinity has one nature and one hypostasis with many names. Arius, on the other hand, spoke of three hypostases and three natures foreign to one another. He said that the Father came first, and that the Son and the Holy Spirit were his creatures, brought into being by him to serve the things he would go on to create. While these two

were fighting each other in this way, the Church kept to the middle path between them. It did not, like Sabellius, hold one nature in such a way as to hold one hypostasis as well, nor, like Arius, three hypostases in such a way as to hold three natures as well. (For Sabellius, led astray by the one nature, held one hypostasis too, while Arius, because of the three hypostases, spoke of three natures too.) Keeping the middle path between them, then, the Church speaks of one nature of God in three hypostases. And this is the unity in Trinity and the Trinity in unity. Next, concerning the incarnation of God the Word, Nestorius and Eutyches fought each other as if from opposite ends. Nestorius spoke of two natures but did not say that they had received a union. Rather, he said that the man had so close a relation to the Son that the Son worked through him whatever he wished, and for this reason he said that the man was also called Son. If someone asked him, "Then why do you speak of one Son and not two?" Nestorius would answer: "The love and relation of God the Word toward the man was so great that the two were called one Son." Eutyches, for his part, spoke of one hypostasis, and said that the union of God the Word with the man was so complete that one nature was formed from the two. Again the Church kept to the middle path between them. It did not speak of two natures as Nestorius did, so as to say that no union had taken place; nor did it say, as Eutyches did, that the union was of such a kind as to require speaking of one nature. For Nestorius, because of the two natures, denied that a union had taken place, while Eutyches, because of the union, spoke of one nature too. The Church, however, holds one hypostasis in two natures. And so the doctrine of the incarnation is the reverse of the doctrine of theology, as the divine Gregory says: "There we ascribe the oneness to the nature and the distinction to the hypostases; here, on the contrary, the oneness to the hypostasis and the distinction to the natures." Here the lecture ends.

After what has gone before, the next step is to deal with certain heresies. There are eighty-four in all, as listed by Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus. But before we take them up, let us first list the books of the Church. Of the books of the Church, some belong to the Old Scripture and some to the New. By Old Scripture we mean the Scripture written before the coming of Christ, and by New the Scripture written after his coming. The Old has twenty-two books. Some of them are historical, some prophetic, some hortatory, and some were composed to be sung. Even if each kind is found in each book, each is named after what predominates in it. The historical books are twelve. The first of them is Genesis;

this book covers events from the making of heaven and earth to the death of Joseph. The second is Exodus. It covers the period from the death of Joseph and the exodus of the Israelites up to what happened before they reached Mount Sinai: how they crossed the Red Sea, what happened in between, and how they received the law from God through Moses. The third book is the one called Numbers, in which the tribes of the Israelites and their leaders are counted. The fourth is Leviticus, in which it is prescribed how the priests are to perform their worship; that is why it was called Leviticus, for the priests came from the tribe of the Levites. The fifth is Deuteronomy, in which the events from the Exodus up to Mount Sinai are recounted in summary, and the law is set out at length; that is why it was called Deuteronomy. For what is written briefly about the law in Exodus is handed down more fully in Deuteronomy, together with other material. Everyone agrees that these five books are by Moses; as for the books that follow, no one knows whose they are. These five are called the Pentateuch. Sixth, after Deuteronomy, is Joshua son of Nun, which tells how Joshua, who had been Moses' disciple and was his equal in power, led the Israelites out of the wilderness into the land of promise. The seventh is the book called Judges. When the Israelites came into the land of promise, they appointed judges for themselves to judge the people. They had no kings, and called God alone their king. Since this book recounts everything the judges did up to the time of the kings, it was called Judges. The eighth book is Ruth. It is called Ruth because it tells how Ruth, a Moabite woman, came over to the Israelites. She was the wife of David's forefather. After these come two books which contain the Kingdoms; for there are four books of Kingdoms, carried in two volumes. The Jews came to have kings for the following reason. Samuel, the last of the judges, was a great man and a prophet, who judged the people of Israel with complete righteousness. He had two sons, who became judges when Samuel grew old, but they did not judge the people according to their father's righteous ordinances; instead they took bribes and betrayed justice. So, since their father was old, the Israelites gathered together and asked him to appoint a king for them. When he prayed to God about this, he heard: "Make them a king. For it is not you they have rejected, but me, by asking for a king for themselves." Having heard God, he made Saul their king, a man of the tribe of Benjamin. Saul ruled forty years but did not keep God's commandments. Then God made David, of the tribe of Judah, king in his place. And from then on the tribe of Judah went on reigning,

son succeeding father in the kingship, until Nebuchadnezzar came and enslaved Jerusalem. So the ninth and tenth books contain the Kingdoms. The eleventh is Paralipomena. They were called Paralipomena, "things left out", because they go through what the writers of the Kingdoms left out. The twelfth of the historical books is Ezra, which covers what happened after the captivity of the Jews, down to their return from the Assyrians, which took place under Cyrus. These, then, are the historical books. The prophetic books are five. The first of them is Isaiah, the second Jeremiah, the third Ezekiel, the fourth Daniel, and the fifth the book called the Twelve Prophets, which contains the prophecies of twelve prophets. Then there are the hortatory books. The first of them is Job; some have thought this to be a work of Josephus. The second is the Proverbs of Solomon, the third Ecclesiastes, the fourth the Song of Songs. I say that the Song of Songs is now placed after the hortatory books because its contemplation is loftier. These three books are by Solomon. After these comes the Psalter. These are the twenty-two books of the Old. The New has six books. Two of them contain the four evangelists: one has Matthew and Mark, the other Luke and John. The third is the Acts of the Apostles. The fourth is the Catholic Epistles, which are seven: the first is by James, the second and third by Peter, the fourth, fifth and sixth by John, and the seventh by Jude. They were called catholic because they were not written to a single nation, as Paul's were, but to all universally. The fifth book is the fourteen epistles of Saint Paul. The sixth is the Revelation of Saint John. These are the canonical books in the Church, both old and new; of these the Hebrews accept all the old ones. This being so, it is fitting to set out first the doctrines of the Hebrews, beginning with those about theology. The Hebrews say that God has one hypostasis and one nature. They nowhere hold a Trinity, nor do they speak of Father, Son or Holy Spirit, except, they say, that we might call God Father, since he is the father of all human beings. They maintain that God is one hypostasis on the basis of Moses' words: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one." We answer them that Moses said this with a view to the essence, not the hypostases. For we too speak of one God, in three hypostases. That there is a Trinity can be shown from many passages. First, from God's words in Genesis, "Let us make man": he would not have said "Let us make" in the plural unless others shared his power with him. Second,

from what he says again in Genesis: "Behold, Adam has become like one of us." That there is a Holy Trinity, then, can be shown from many passages. Let us now move on and show what they hold about the incarnation of Christ. Three questions are asked about Christ: whether he is coming, whether he has already come, and third, whether the one who came is God. About the first, whether he is coming, there is no need to say anything, for they themselves admit that he will come. About the other two, we must show that they are wrong. We say that he has come, and we show this from many proofs: first, from the signs he worked; second, from the fact that the idols were overthrown by him (for Isaiah says: "Behold, the Lord sits on a swift cloud and will come into Egypt, and the handiwork of Egypt shall be shaken before his face"); third, from what Daniel says, for the seventy weeks of years that the angel tells him of, along with the point from which they are to be counted, end in the times of Christ. The starting point of the count is the twenty-fourth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus. When we show them these things, they insist that he has not come. For the psalm, they say, declares: "In his days righteousness shall dawn, and abundance of peace"; and they bring forward other such passages from Holy Scripture. "But now," they say, "we see none of this; on the contrary, we see injustice abounding and many sins committed." To this we reply that Christ's coming is twofold. One is in glory, which Daniel describes when he says: "I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming on the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days, and to him were given dominion and honour and authority; all the nations shall serve him," and so on. The other is in humility, of which Isaiah says: "And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, and inferior to that of all men." So when the psalm says that righteousness shall dawn in his days, it is speaking of the glorious coming that is still to come. That sins must necessarily occur at Christ's first coming is quite clear from the following. I ask them: "Will the Christ who comes die a natural death, or will others kill him?" They answer, of course, that others will kill him. "Well then, does not whoever kills so great a man sin greatly?" They will certainly say yes. So if this is the case, sin must necessarily occur at Christ's first coming, and therefore the psalm is speaking of the second. Besides, elsewhere the psalm says: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." This shows that he had enemies. And where there is enmity,

there is no peace. As for the claim that Christ is not God, which was the third question, they base it on Moses' words: "The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among our brothers, like me." "See," they say, "he did not call him God but a prophet." To this we reply that Christ was all of these: he was man, and prophet, and God, so that he could be called by any of these names. Once it has been shown that he has come, it would be easy to prove from the New Scripture that he was God. But we shall show it from the Old [?] as well. For Jeremiah says it openly somewhere: "This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterwards he appeared on earth and lived among men." These, then, are the teachings of the Hebrews and the arguments against them. Let us now move on to the doctrines of the Samaritans. But first let us learn some history: where the heresy of the Samaritans comes from. After Saul had reigned forty years, God set up David, a man of the tribe of Judah, as king of the Israelites in his place; and David's line went on reigning, son succeeding father in the rule, down to Zedekiah. When King David died, his son Solomon received the kingdom. He did everything with righteousness, and so God granted him great wisdom and power. But in his old age he worshipped idols, persuaded by his wives. So God in his anger said to his servant Jeroboam: "If you do my will, I will make you king over ten tribes of your master; the other two I will leave for the sake of David his father. This will happen after his death." When Solomon died, his son Rehoboam was about to inherit the kingdom. The Israelites gathered and said to him: "Your father made our yoke heavy; lighten it for us, and we will serve you." He answered them: "Give me three days, and I will tell you my decision." He went away and first consulted the elders among his father's friends. They said to him: "Treat Israel well, and they will serve you." He also laid the matter before the young men. They told him: "Say to them: 'My little finger is sturdier than my father's loins. He disciplined you with whips; I will discipline you with scorpions.'" Persuaded by them, Rehoboam gave this answer to the Israelites. The Israelites replied: "Tend your own house, David, and let each of Israel go back to his tents." With these words they all broke away from him, except two tribes, Benjamin and Judah. These two held Jerusalem and the country around it, while the ten that broke away held the region around Neapolis. The ten tribes were called [?]

Israelites, taking their name from the larger part; the two were called Jews. So the ten set over themselves Jeroboam, the servant of Solomon, and made war continually on the Jews. Now since there was a law that the Hebrews should worship before the ark in Jerusalem every year, Jeroboam was afraid that they would desert to the other side if they kept going there. So he made two golden heifers and said to them, “These are the gods who brought you up out of Egypt; worship these.” From Jeroboam's time, then, both the Israelites and the Jews practised idolatry under many kings, until God in his anger brought against them Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians. He carried the ten Israelite tribes into captivity; the Jews he did not even attack. Having taken the Israelites captive, he settled others there in their place to guard the land, and these were called Samaritans, since among the Hebrews a guard is called a “samarite.” But while they lived there in place of the Israelites, lions kept killing them, until they sent word to the king of the Assyrians, saying, “Lions are destroying us, because we do not know how to worship the God of this land.” When the king heard this, he sent them one of the captive priests to teach them how the God of that land must be worshipped. When he came, according to outside historians, he taught them nothing but the Pentateuch, which is why the Samaritans accept it alone. This is as far as Scripture tells the story. And it is from these people, they say, that the Samaritans descend. Their heresy is as follows. On the doctrine of God they hold the same views as the Hebrews, for they believe in one hypostasis and one nature. On the incarnation of Christ, their position is this: they do not believe that he has come, but that he is yet to come, and that the one who is coming is not God but a prophet. They do not believe in angels, or in an immortal soul, or in resurrection. Nor do they agree with the Hebrews that Christ will judge the living and the dead. That angels exist, however, they are refuted from the Pentateuch itself, for there it says, “Behold, my angel goes before your face”; and that “the angel of the Lord called Hagar”; and that “the angel of the Lord called Abraham”; and that “the angels came into Sodom”; and other such passages. And that the soul is mortal and not immortal, they say, Moses testifies when he says, “You shall not eat blood, but pour it out on the ground; for the blood of every living creature is its soul.” To this we reply, first, that the blood is not the soul of living creatures; rather, because when the blood is poured out the soul also perishes, he was speaking about the blood of beasts, which we too acknowledge to be mortal, not about human beings. And from history

we also show that the soul is immortal and that there is a judgement of the dead. Cain and Abel were two brothers; one was a farmer, the other a shepherd. Both offered sacrifice to God, and he accepted Abel, as a righteous man, but not Cain. From that time Cain envied Abel, until he killed him. Now since the Samaritans say that each person receives the reward of his deeds in this present life, what are we to say about Abel, to whom God bore witness that he was righteous? As far as this present life goes, he received evil instead of good. From this, then, it is clear that the soul is immortal and that we must believe in a resurrection. For if there were none, and a man were to receive the reward of his deeds only in this life, such a man would not have died unjustly. This is the heresy of the Samaritans. It should also be known that Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, came to Jerusalem in the reign of King Zedekiah, took the Jews captive, and carried them off to Persia; among them were Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Ezekiel and Ezra. After seventy years, in the reign of King Cyrus, they returned to Jerusalem, Cyrus having permitted their return because they had foretold to him much of what he was going to do. Ezra wrote an account of their return; and when he came to Jerusalem and found that all the books had been burned when they were taken captive, he is said to have written out from memory the twenty-two books which we listed above. Here ends the survey.

Since our discussion concerns Christian doctrines, it is necessary to make a division of the periods of time, so that from them we may know which teachers and which heresies there were, each heresy accepting the Fathers who came before it but not those who came after it. Of the periods, then, some are before Christ, and these we have already treated in the preceding sections; others are after Christ. The periods after Christ are divided as follows. Some run from the birth of Christ to the reign of Constantine; others from the beginning of Constantine's reign to the present. The period from the birth of Christ to the reign of Constantine is further subdivided into three. The first runs from the birth of Christ to his ascension; the second from the ascension, the period which the Acts of the Apostles covers; the third from the travels and death of the apostles to the beginning of Constantine's reign. This last period is covered by certain church writers, Eusebius son of Pamphilus and Theodoret, whom we are not bound to accept, for it has been laid down as a rule that we accept writings only as far as the Acts of the Apostles. The period from the beginning of Constantine's reign to the present is divided thus: one part runs from the reign of Constantine to the beginning of the controversy over the Council of Chalcedon; the other, from

the controversy over the Council of Chalcedon to the present. In the period from the birth of Christ to the reign of Constantine there were the following teachers and fathers: Ignatius the God-bearer, Irenaeus, Justin the philosopher and martyr, Clement and Hippolytus, bishops of Rome, Dionysius the Areopagite, Methodius bishop of Patara, Gregory the Wonderworker, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria and martyr. All of these are accepted by the heresies that arose after them. Many heresies arose in this period, but only the notable ones need be mentioned. First, then, there arose the heresy of the Montanists, which we shall discuss elsewhere; then that of the Manichaeans, which picked out the worst elements of every heresy and has nothing good in it. No one can speak about it accurately unless he becomes part of their way of life. It does not even shrink from idolatry, nor from any kind of evil. Their reckless errors concerning the Godhead and concerning the humanity are these. Concerning the Godhead they hold the following: they speak of two principles and two gods, one good and one evil. The better things they ascribe to the good god, the worse to the evil one. For instance, they ascribe light to the good God and darkness to the evil one. Again, in composite living beings they ascribe the matter to the evil God and the form to the good God. They also ascribe certain books of the Old Testament to the evil God, such as the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. For it is not the work of the good God, they say, to drive them out of Egypt and afterwards do them many harms. They also invent certain new books for themselves, for they speak of a Gospel according to Thomas and one according to Philip, which we do not recognize. It was because of them that the holy Fathers laid down which books we must accept. Concerning the incarnation they hold this: they do not confess that the incarnation of Christ was real, but say it was in appearance only, and that in the passion he substituted another man in his place and himself escaped. They tried to support the idea of mere appearance from certain words found in the Gospels, from which they say that while on the mountain he was transfigured and became invisible; and again, that when a great crowd stood around, Jesus slipped away. But this is not enough to prove that the incarnation took place in appearance only. For human beings too have been transfigured and have become invisible. Moses was transfigured with a glorious face, so that the Jews could not look at him, and he spoke to them with his face veiled. Philip too vanished, and from the hill country suddenly came to be

Another heresy also arose in this period, that of Paul of Samosata, who erred both concerning the Godhead and concerning the incarnation. Concerning the Godhead, he said that there is only the Father; concerning the incarnation, he said that Christ was a mere man (b) [? note: for “humanity” read “incarnation”, a little further on, within.]

and that the Word of God came to be in him—though he is not to be thought of as holding the same views as Nestorius. For Nestorius, although he called Christ a mere man, nevertheless said that the self-subsistent Word of God, the Son, came to be in that man; for Nestorius did not err concerning the Trinity. But Paul of Samosata did not say that the self-subsistent Word came to be in Christ; by “Word” he meant the command and the order. That is, God commanded through that man whatever he wished, and did it. Nor concerning the Godhead did he hold the same views as Sabellius. For Sabellius said that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the same, and he called God a single thing with three names, no longer believing in a Trinity. Paul, on the other hand, did not say that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the same; rather, he called God, who created all things, the Father; the mere man, the Son; and the grace that came upon the apostles, the Spirit. In this period the heresy of Sabellius also arose, concerning which, in the preceding sections

In the period from the beginning of Constantine's reign to the controversy over the Council of Chalcedon there were the following teachers and fathers: Sylvester bishop of Rome, Alexander bishop of Alexandria, Eustathius of Antioch, Athanasius of Alexandria, Julius of Rome, Alexander of Constantinople, Hilary of Poitiers, a city of Gaul, Ambrose of Milan, Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory of Nazianzus, Amphilochius of Iconium, Antiochus of Ptolemais in Phoenicia, [?] of Caesarea in Palestine, Nectarius, Atticus, John, Proclus and Flavian of Constantinople, Severian of Gabala, Epiphanius of Cyprus, Augustine of Hippo, a city of Africa, and Theophilus and Cyril of Alexandria. All these bishops are accepted by the heresies that came after them, but not by those before them. Right at the start of Constantine's reign the heresy of Arius arose. He erred both concerning the Godhead and concerning the humanity: concerning the Godhead, in that he said the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures of God; concerning the incarnation,

Hebrews: “Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Jesus, who was faithful to the one who made him.” And the Lord himself says in the Gospels, “The Father who sent me is greater than I.” The holy Fathers refute him, first by bringing forward texts that say the opposite, and then by explaining the very texts he adduced. As for the opposing texts: John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And again in the Epistle to the Hebrews the Apostle says of the Son, “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being.” If Christ were a creature and not the offspring of God, he could not be the imprint and radiance of God. And the Lord himself says, “I and the Father are one.” So by the opposing texts they refute Arius; and they explain the texts he adduced in this way: the Son of God, having consented to endure everything as a man, did not disdain to say that the Father was greater than he. So when the Apostle calls him a thing made, he does not call him so with a view to his Godhead, but with a view to his humanity. For insofar as he is God, he is the offspring of God, not a thing made; but insofar as he is man, he is a thing made, and an apostle, and all such things. And it should be known that it is the doctrine of our Church that refutes Arius. For unless we speak of two natures in Christ, and ascribe these lowly expressions to the human nature and the others to the Godhead, Arius is not refuted. That is why the doctrine of Arius said that the body of Christ was without a soul: so that we would no longer ascribe such lowly expressions to Christ as man, but as Son of God, and so, according to his doctrine, the Son would be found inferior to the Father. But that the body of Christ also had a soul, Christ himself testifies when he says, “My soul is troubled,” as do many other passages. Against this Arius, who was a presbyter of Alexandria, a council of three hundred and eighteen select bishops was convened at Nicaea in the reign of Constantine. They deposed him and set out against him a creed, that is, a statement of teaching, which is in circulation and may be read by anyone who wishes. Here ends the section.

After the heresy of Arius—or rather while it was still flourishing, for it prevailed for a long time—two other heresies sprang up: that of Macedonius, who was bishop of Constantinople, and that of Apollinarius, who was a presbyter. The heresy of Macedonius was as follows. He erred concerning the Godhead, [?]

[?] sharing in the impiety of Arius; for while he said that the Son was the offspring of God, he said that the Spirit was a thing made. He supported his doctrine on the grounds, he said, that it is not stated plainly in holy Scripture that the Holy Spirit is God. But he is refuted by many texts, for holy Scripture does speak of the Holy Spirit as God. First, in the Acts of the Apostles, Saint Peter says to Ananias, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours, and after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? You have not lied to men but to God.” See how plainly he called the Holy Spirit God. Then again in the Acts of the Apostles it is said, “While they were fasting and ministering to the Lord, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them.’” By the words “Set apart” he showed his own authority, that he speaks as being himself God. For if he were a creature of God and sent by him, he would have said, “The Lord said, ‘Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas’”; for this is how holy Scripture usually speaks when the Lord speaks through someone lesser. The Lord too says in the Gospels, “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father”—which indicates something produced from the essence of God; nowhere does holy Scripture appear to use this word of a creature. Again, elsewhere the Lord says, “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” If the Holy Spirit were a creature, he would not have been counted together with the uncreated, so as to be worshipped and glorified together with them. As for Apollinarius, he does not appear to err concerning the doctrine of God, though the Gregories convict him of erring on this point too. He does not, they say, call them creatures, but he speaks of a slight subordination of the Son and the Spirit to the Father. Concerning the economy, however, he plainly went astray. He said that the body which God the Word put on had a soul but no mind whatever; he said it had something like an irrational soul. He supported his doctrine not by any text of Scripture but by his own reasoning. For he said that the mind is something prone to sin, and that it is utterly absurd to suppose that the Word of God was united to something prone to sin. But we say that, on the contrary, we ought rather to suppose that he was united to what is prone to sin, since that is what needs salvation. For he saved that to which he was united. While these doctrines were being stirred up, the council of a hundred and fifty men met at Constantinople, which included great men, the Gregories and Amphilochius. When they had assembled, they deposed Macedonius and Apollinarius and set out a definition, that is, a statement of faith, which we recite.

Around that time there were two great men, Diodore bishop of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, who contended against the Arians, Macedonius and Apollinarius, and wrote commentaries on the rest of Scripture. They died held in great honour; no one in their lifetime attacked either of them, and many wrote encomia on them. Basil praises them, and so does John Chrysostom. Later, however, when the Nestorian doctrine was being stirred up, Cyril, who had formerly praised them, was compelled to write against their works, since Nestorius supported his doctrine from them. For in commenting on holy Scripture they did not stop where they should have, but in their wish to divide the expressions in holy Scripture, assigning some to the Godhead and others to the humanity, they were found to introduce two hypostases of Christ and a division. And for this reason Cyril was compelled to write against them, since Nestorius supported his doctrine from them. No one contradicted them in their lifetime because the struggle against the greater heresies kept such doctrines hidden. A short time after the deaths of Theodore and Diodore, the heresy of Nestorius arose. Nestorius himself was bishop of Constantinople, Cyril of Alexandria, and John of Antioch. What the doctrine of Nestorius was we have already said in the preceding sections, but let us now go over it briefly. He did not speak of a union of the Word of God with the man, but spoke of two hypostases and a division. Hence he did not call holy Mary the Mother of God, but the Mother of Christ. And although he called Christ both man and God, it was not as we do, but by relationship and affinity, just as we say of two friends who love each other very much that the two have one soul, in the sense that the same things please both of them, because of the greatness of their friendship. Cyril opposed this Nestorius and wrote to him repeatedly, urging him to turn away from this doctrine. He wrote him a first and a second letter, and did not persuade him. Later he wrote him a third letter, in which he set out twelve chapters on the faith, and after that he wrote, “If you accept these, you are our fellow minister and friend; if not, you will be anathema.” Even so he did not persuade him. As this conflict went on, the emperor—it was Theodosius the Younger—ordered that a council be held at Ephesus, and that John, bishop of Antioch, be judge between Cyril and Nestorius. So Cyril came to Ephesus on the appointed day with his whole synod, and likewise Nestorius with his. But John was slow in coming and overran the appointed time by sixteen days. Cyril, thinking he was no longer coming, gathered the bishops who were present, read before them the writings of Nestorius, and then texts from the holy Fathers opposing them; and since Nestorius did not come—

[?] … but when people told him to wait for the judge, he went ahead with Nestorius's deposition. Sixteen days later John arrived and found that Nestorius had been deposed without him. He was angry and hurt, because Nestorius had been deposed without him, to his dishonour. So he did not join the church that Cyril had gone up to. He went up to another one instead, where he fought against Cyril, and they anathematized each other [?]; but he did not accept Nestorius. With John was a certain Theodoret, a learned man, bishop of Cyrus in the East. Speaking against Cyril, he also attacked the twelve chapters that Cyril had written in his third letter to Nestorius, and tried to refute them, saying that Cyril was an Arian and held the views of Eunomius and Apollinarius. For Cyril, in fighting against Nestorius, who divided the economy [of the union?], had taken care [to stress the union?]. So Cyril somehow seemed to Theodoret to speak of one nature, as the Arians and the followers of Apollinarius do. Yet Theodoret is never found accepting Nestorius. He only found fault with Cyril, because of the dishonour that had befallen John. It should be known that a letter of John, bishop of Antioch, written before this council, is extant. It was addressed to Nestorius, refuted his doctrine, and was signed by all the members of John's synod. It should also be known that certain letters of Theodoret and Nestorius are in circulation in which they approve of each other. But these are forgeries: the heretics forge them so that they can use them to fight against the council. If anyone wants to know that Theodoret actually hated Nestorius intensely, let him read the book on heresies written by Theodoret himself. Once Nestorius had been deposed and these disputes had been stirred up, the council broke up, and each man went back to his own place. Cyril went to Alexandria and John to Antioch. From this arose a quarrel between the Easterners [and the Egyptians?]: [?] … that the Easterners held the views of Nestorius, while the others [?] … [?]. The emperor Theodosius writes to Cyril and to John, [?] … And when John received the emperor's letter, he wrote a letter to Cyril setting out what he believed, and [sent it by?] Paul, [bishop?] of [Emesa?] [?] …

[?] … of Cyril, the quarrel between the Eastern bishops and the Egyptians was resolved. After a short time had passed, the affair of the council at Chalcedon began to stir. At that time the bishop of the church of Alexandria was Dioscorus, of Constantinople Flavian, of Rome Leo, and of Antioch Domnus. In Constantinople there was a man named Eutyches, a presbyter and archimandrite, who held that the body of [Christ] was not …

[?] … the surpassing nature of the union, and because he spoke of one nature, he would not say that after the union the body was consubstantial with us. Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, knew this Eutyches. When he learned of this doctrine from Eutyches himself, he reported it to Flavian, saying: "You must rebuke Eutyches for bringing in such a doctrine, so that our faith is not perverted." When Flavian heard this, he assembled the bishops of his synod, about thirty of them, and questioned Eutyches in their presence: "Do you confess that the body of Christ is consubstantial with us, or not?" He answered: "Until today I did not confess it, but because of you I confess it." He said this ironically. Flavian answered him: "It is not we who tell you to confess this, but the Fathers. If you confess it, then anathematize those who do not believe this." Eutyches said to him: "As I said, until today I did not confess this, but I say it because of you. I do not anathematize anyone. If I anathematize anyone, I anathematize my fathers and the holy Scripture. For it is Scripture that says the body of Christ is not consubstantial with us." When Flavian heard this, he deposed him from the priesthood and from his office of archimandrite, saying that faith is not a matter of compulsion. After the deposition Flavian wrote to Leo, bishop of Rome, about it, and Leo wrote back that he had been right to depose him. This letter is called the Tome of Leo. The Dissenters dispute it and say it is wrong. After his deposition Eutyches kept appealing to the emperor, saying that Flavian had wronged him. Then the emperor Theodosius ordered an ecumenical council to be held at Ephesus to judge whether Flavian had been right to depose Eutyches or not. He entrusted the whole judgment to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. When the council met, Dioscorus first did something improper. He read only the proceedings of Flavian's synod, and did not allow Flavian to speak in their defence or to ask about anything he thought was in doubt. Second, he did not even let Eusebius, Eutyches' accuser, come before the court. Instead he voted against Flavian and deposed him, received Eutyches, and made him a presbyter and archimandrite again. When this was done, the council broke up. Flavian died, and the legates of the bishop of Rome (for the bishop himself never attended a council) went back and reported to him what had happened. When he heard it he was angry, and he went to Valentinian, the emperor in Rome, to obtain redress. At that time there was one emperor in Rome and another in Byzantium. So Valentinian, pressed by Pope Leo, wrote to Theodosius the Younger asking him to allow a council to be held to find out whether Dioscorus had judged rightly or not. Theodosius wrote back to him, saying:

"I am not holding another council, for Dioscorus judged rightly." When Theodosius died, Marcian became emperor. He at once allowed an ecumenical council to be held at Chalcedon to judge the proceedings of the council at Ephesus, and whether it had judged wrongly the things done in Byzantium concerning Flavian. This council of six hundred and thirty men met, and on the first day Dioscorus sat with them. Then evening came and the session broke up. On the next day they met and sent for him twice, and then a third time, but he refused to come. Since he did not come after being summoned a third time, they deposed him according to the canons and exiled him to Gangra. They also set out a teaching on how one must believe: that there is one Christ in two natures, without confusion and without division. And so the council broke up.

SESSION V. After the council at Chalcedon had broken up and Dioscorus had been exiled to Gangra, the whole populace of Alexandria and Egypt broke away along with him. Proterius, who accepted the council's doctrine, was made bishop in his place. But not one of the Alexandrians would communicate with him. They hated him so much that they were stirred up and burned him. The evils that the emperor Leo brought on them for murdering him cannot be told here. When Dioscorus died in Gangra, Timothy succeeded him. So Proterius was bishop in Alexandria openly, and Timothy in secret. This Timothy anathematized both the council and Eutyches: Eutyches because he would not say that the body of Christ is consubstantial with us, and the council at Chalcedon because it spoke of two natures of Christ. He also defended Dioscorus, saying that Dioscorus believed as he himself taught. After Proterius had been burned, Timothy succeeded him. And there were two Timothys, [?]

[?] … of the council, he did not explicitly anathematize it. But he wrote this: "If anyone of those at the council at Chalcedon, or at those held earlier elsewhere, does not believe rightly, let him be anathema." When this Henoticon arrived, Peter Mongus accepted it, but John fled to Rome. At this time Peter the Fuller was also appointed bishop at Antioch by Zeno. When the union took place, Peter was clearly the man the Alexandrians preferred. So Peter accepted the Henoticon and also received the throne of Alexandria, and he was now bishop openly instead of in secret. But some people hated the council at Chalcedon so much that they split off from Peter and would not communicate with him, because although he had accepted the Henoticon he did not openly anathematize the council. Such people were called Acephali ("Headless"), because they did not follow their patriarch but held communion on their own. Then Peter, seeing that the people were badly divided, was forced to anathematize the council openly. So he accepted the Henoticon, but also openly anathematized the council. [?] Even so the Acephali did [not?] communicate with him, because he had accepted the Henoticon in the first place without anathematizing the council. Athanasius succeeded Peter. He too accepted the Henoticon and anathematized the council. Yet the Acephali would not communicate with him either, because he accepted Peter. After Athanasius came John, and then another John, then Dioscorus, and after him Timothy. All of these accepted the Henoticon and anathematized the council. When the emperor Zeno died, Anastasius succeeded to the throne, and then the doctrine opposed to the council gained even more ground. For Anastasius was one of the Dissenters. In his time Severus also became bishop at Antioch, holding the same views as Timothy of Alexandria. When Anastasius died, Justin I became emperor, and after about a year and a half Justinian directly followed. Justinian, once he was emperor, was one of the supporters of the council. Severus was afraid and fled to Alexandria, taking with him a certain Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus. On their arrival they settled at the Ennaton. Once, when a discussion arose between them, they disagreed about the corruptible and the incorruptible: was the body of Christ corruptible or incorruptible before his resurrection? Julian followed the ancient opinion and said that the body of Christ is incorruptible. "For if we do not call it incorruptible but corruptible, we introduce a difference between it and the Word of God. And once a difference is introduced, two natures are found in Christ. Then why are we fighting the council for no good reason?" To this Severus said [?]
that one can call the body of Christ incorruptible [?], introduce a difference, and [still speak of] one nature [?] …

So these men went on fighting each other and putting out statements. Timothy took the side sometimes of one and sometimes of the other. Timothy was about to go to the emperor when he died. The emperor had summoned him, meaning either to persuade him to become a supporter of the council or to depose him. At that time there were two men, Gaianus and Theodosius. Gaianus was Timothy's archdeacon, and Theodosius was a secretary. When Timothy died, the clergy and the leading men of the city ordained Theodosius bishop. After he was ordained, the populace came in and saw him sitting on the throne. They were so angry (for they hated him) that someone immediately threw him off the throne. Theodosius fled, and Gaianus was made bishop in his place by force. The city also split according to the two men: the great men of the city were with Theodosius, and the populace with Gaianus. So the city came to be divided not only over persons but also over doctrines, for Gaianus followed the doctrine of Julian, and Theodosius the doctrine of Severus. When the emperor Justinian heard what was happening, he sent Narses to find out which of the two ought to be bishop. Narses came and asked which of the two had been made bishop first. He learned that it was Theodosius, so he exiled Gaianus (who has not been seen from then until today) and seated Theodosius on the throne. A little later Justinian sent and deposed Theodosius too, and brought him to Byzantium. In his place he ordained Paul, who accepted the council's doctrine. Paul was deposed for consenting to a murder. After Paul's deposition Zoilus succeeded him, and he too was deposed, as we shall relate later. After Zoilus came Apollinarius, after Apollinarius John, and after John Eulogius. All of these, from Paul on, were supporters of the council. This, then, is the succession of the …

While Theodosius was living privately in Byzantium, the doctrine of the Agnoetae arose. The Lord says that no one knows the hour of judgement, not even the Son, but the Father alone. So the question was raised whether Christ was in fact ignorant, as a man perhaps. Theodosius said that he was not, and wrote against the Agnoetae. Others said that he was ignorant, just as we say that he suffered toil. Over this the so-called Agnoetae split off from the Theodosians. They formed their own church and held communion on their own. While Theodosius was still living in Byzantium, the doctrine of the Tritheites arose, and its heresiarch was Philoponus.

For the Church had been challenged in this way: "If you speak of two natures in Christ, you must also speak of two hypostases." The Church replied: "If nature and hypostasis are the same thing, we would have to admit the absurdity [?]. But if nature is one thing and hypostasis another, what compels us, when we speak of two natures, to confess two hypostases as well?" The heretics answered the Church: "Yes, nature and hypostasis are the same." Then the Church replied in turn: "If nature and hypostasis are the same, then we must also speak of three natures in the Holy Trinity, since it admittedly has three hypostases." When the Church said this, Philoponus answered: "Then let us say that there are three natures in the Holy Trinity." He said this taking his starting point from Aristotelian teaching. For Aristotle says that among individuals there are particular substances and one common substance. So Philoponus likewise said that in the Holy Trinity there are three particular substances and one common one. In these matters the [?] … SESSION VI. [?] … of certain [arguments] that all the Dissenters commonly raise against the Church; let us discuss them briefly. Let us divide them into three groups. Some of them are historical, drawn from what was done at the council at Chalcedon. Others come from syllogisms and ingenious reasoning, and others from citations. But first let us discuss the historical ones. There are four arguments we are going to mention. The first is this: the council at Chalcedon must not be accepted, because the men who took part in it were turncoats and inconsistent. For they both deposed Eutyches in Byzantium, and then went to Ephesus, received Eutyches along with Dioscorus, and rejected Flavian. To this we say, first, that we must make allowance for human weakness. For elsewhere too some of the approved holy Fathers are evidently found to have often fallen into this. Second, even if five, or thirty, or more of those six hundred and thirty were shown to be turncoats at the council, that is no reason to reject a council of six hundred and thirty men. The second argument on this subject is that this council at Chalcedon, as one can learn from its acts, is evidently on record as saying: "Dioscorus was not deposed on account of the faith." So, they argue, Dioscorus believed rightly and the council rejected him wrongly, and how can we accept such a council? Since another absurdity also seems to us to follow from this, it is worth explaining what prompted this statement. It should be known, then, that after the six hundred and thirty had assembled at Chalcedon and deposed Dioscorus, they then decided to draw up a definition of faith and a teaching.

So their leading members met by themselves and drew up the definition, which Asclepiades read out to the council. This definition contained the phrase "from two natures." When it was read, a great dispute broke out among the bishops. The officials whom the emperor had sent to keep order saw them disputing and said to them: "Dioscorus said 'from two natures,' but the most holy Leo said that Christ is in two natures, without change, without confusion, without division. Whom do you follow, Dioscorus or Leo?" They all stood up and said: "We believe as Leo does. Anathema to Dioscorus." After these and some other things had been said, as the acts record, the patriarch Anatolius said: "Dioscorus was not deposed on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated the blessed Leo, and because he did not come when the council summoned him three times." Given this, the Dissenters raise two difficulties against the Church. The first is: "If this council said that Dioscorus was not deposed on account of the faith, why does it reject us? For we believe as he did." To them we say that, if one looks at the truth, Dioscorus was not rejected on account of the faith, and that was not the cause of his deposition (for he did not even come into the council to be judged on that point). The cause was that he was in fact summoned three times and refused to come. Had he come, he would have been rejected on account of the faith as well. It was with this in view that Anatolius said Dioscorus was not deposed on account of the faith. The second difficulty is why the council rejected the definition that contained "from two natures," when the holy Cyril speaks of "from two natures" again and again. To this we say that the council did not reject it because it contained "from two natures" (for both we and the Dissenters accept this, and so does Eutyches), but because it was deficient. It did not contain what overturns the doctrines of Eutyches, but only what he believed in common with us. The council was so far from opposing "from two natures" that in the second definition, which overturns Eutyches at every point, it nowhere mentioned "from two natures," evidently because it accepted it. The fourth difficulty (for the second divides into two) is that the council at Chalcedon received heretics. It received Theodoret and Ibas. Theodoret is the one who spoke against the twelve chapters of the blessed Cyril, as one who held the views of Nestorius. Ibas too was a Nestorian, as his letter to Maris the Persian shows, in which he praises Theodore again and again, and it was from Theodore that Nestorius drew support for his own doctrines. Regarding Theodoret, then, we say that the council did not receive him until he had anathematized Nestorius and his views. But they press us again: "And why did it not require him also to anathematize his own writ-

-ings against the twelve chapters of the blessed Cyril?" To this we say that they ought to bring this charge against the holy Cyril rather than against the council. For when Cyril entered into communion with the Easterners, and with Theodoret himself, he did not require him to anathematize his own writings against the twelve chapters. Should the council be blamed for not doing what the holy Cyril himself did not do? In fact, the council did what the holy Cyril did not do: it compelled Theodoret to anathematize Nestorius aloud in front of everyone. Regarding Ibas, we say that the council did not receive him either until he had first anathematized Nestorius and his views. But they object again: "And why did it not require him to anathematize Theodore, but accepted his letter to Maris, in which he praises Theodore at length?" We answer that this too they ought to have charged against the holy Cyril first, rather than against the council. For Cyril himself, now among the saints, is found writing to Proclus, when some were already seeking to have Theodore anathematized, that he must not be anathematized. "For all the Easterners," he says, "regard Theodore as a great teacher, and if we anathematize him we will cause a great schism in the church of the Easterners." Ibas was one of these Easterners, and he would not consent to anathematize Theodore. How could the council do what the holy Cyril forbade? Even if we grant that these men were openly heretics, that still would not be a reason to reject the council. For look: the council at Nicaea also received seven heretics, who held Arian views before it and persisted in them afterwards. And yet we do not for that reason call it the council of three hundred and eleven, but of three hundred and eighteen. Moreover, Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, and some others who had taken part in the second council at Ephesus, which the Dissenters accept, were present at Chalcedon. That being so, another difficulty has arisen for us from the time of Justinian. Justinian saw the Dissenters denouncing Theodoret and Ibas and, so it seemed, turning away from the council because of them, so he anathematized these two. Now they object to us: "Why do you anathematize them? They were either good or bad. If they were good, why do you anathematize them? If they were bad, why did the council receive them? Even if you now anathematize them as bad, what about the council at Chalcedon, which received them and which you accept?" To this we say that Justinian did this as a kind of concession for the sake of peace. For he saw, as we have said, that the Dissenters were turning away from the council because of these men, and he thought that if he anathematized them he would get the council accepted. So he judged it right to anathematize two persons (even if they ought not to have been anathematized) in order to bring about the union of all. That is why he anathematized them. And yet even so the Dissenters did not accept the council.

After the arguments drawn from historical events, let us move on to the arguments that they put to us on the basis of syllogisms. The first of these is this: "If you say," they say, "that there are two natures in Christ, you certainly also say two hypostases. If two hypostases, then also two persons, two Christs and two sons; and you will be found to hold the same views as Nestorius." We resolve this difficulty by objection and by counter-argument. By objection, in that you raise the difficulty wrongly, so much so that the same absurdity follows for you as well. For if you say that Christ is from two natures, then there are two hypostases, and two persons existing on their own and individually circumscribed; and on your view the humanity once existed without the divinity, which is absurd, and which not even you will consent to confess. For what you say was united, we say exists after the union. If, then, you say that the natures were united as anhypostatic, we say this too; but if as enhypostatic, it is absurd to confess, yet we say it too, though only because you began the absurdity first. But in order to resolve the difficulty by counter-argument as well, let us take up another difficulty that they bring forward, similar to the former but woven in a somewhat different way; when it is resolved, the earlier one will be resolved too. It runs like this: "If you say two natures," they say, "they are either enhypostatic or anhypostatic. If they are enhypostatic, you introduce two persons, two Christs and two sons. If they are anhypostatic, then they are not among the things that exist; but to say that the natures of Christ are not among the things that exist is absurd." Against this difficulty in turn we fight by objection and by turning the argument around. By objection, in that you raise the difficulty wrongly. For if you say that Christ is from two natures, these natures are either enhypostatic or anhypostatic. If they are enhypostatic, you introduce two persons, two Christs and two sons. If they are anhypostatic, you are saying that Christ is from natures that do not exist. But so that we do not remain resolving one difficulty with another difficulty (for there is nothing noble in that), come, let us turn the argument around and expose the faultiness of the difficulty. One must know, then, that "enhypostatic", or "hypostasis", has two meanings. It means what simply exists; in this sense we call even accidents enhypostatic, although they have their being in other things. It also means what exists by itself, like the individuals of substances. So it happens that what is enhypostatic by itself is called enhypostatic in two ways: insofar as it exists, and insofar as it exists by itself, that is, Peter and Paul. But "anhypostatic" too is twofold. For what in no way exists is called anhypostatic, like a goat-stag or a hippocentaur. And again, what is called anhypostatic is not what does not exist, but what has its hypostasis in another and does not

subsist by itself, like accidents. This being so, when they ask us, "If you say Christ has two natures, do you call them enhypostatic or anhypostatic?", we ask them in return, "In what sense are you using 'enhypostatic' here?" If they say, in the sense that signifies simply what exists, we reply that we speak of two natures of Christ in this sense, and no absurdity follows for us such as introducing two persons as well; for we did not take "hypostasis" in that sense. To make what is said clear, let us substitute the terms, present the argument syllogistically, and put it thus: If Christ has two natures, it follows that they are enhypostatic; but "enhypostatic" means what exists; therefore the two natures of Christ are among the things that exist. But if they say, "We use 'enhypostatic' of what exists by itself," we say that in this sense the two natures of Christ are not enhypostatic but anhypostatic. And no absurdity follows for us: for we call them anhypostatic not because they do not exist, but because they are among the things that do not exist by themselves. And again, to make what is said clear, let us substitute the terms and present the argument syllogistically. If Christ has two natures, it follows that they are anhypostatic. But "anhypostatic" means not what does not exist, but what does not exist by itself. Therefore the two natures of Christ do not exist by themselves. And if we speak in this way, we neither introduce two persons nor place them among the things that do not exist; for here we took "anhypostatic" as meaning what is not by itself, no longer what does not exist. That the usage of the Church knows two meanings of hypostasis, both the one that signifies what simply exists [?], St Cyril shows. He speaks now of what simply exists, now of what exists by itself: "that the hypostases, therefore, have remained unconfused, we shall know from this"; and again, "If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ…"; and "Whoever assigns the sayings in the Gospels to two persons, that is, hypostases, let him be anathema." So it has been shown that they want to mislead us by playing on an equivocal term. They raise another difficulty for us, which runs like this: "If you say two natures, you introduce division; for you introduce number, and number belongs to discrete quantity." To this again one can say what was said above: the same absurdity follows for you too. For if you say that Christ is from two natures, then since "two" introduces number, and number falls under the discrete, you will be found to be introducing division. But so that we too may argue as philosophically as they do, one must know that number is not confined to discrete quantity; one can also find it

said of continuous things, as when we speak of a five-cubit piece of wood, and as Aristotle says that time is the number of motion. For he called time a number, though it is admittedly continuous. Number, then, is twofold: it is said both of discrete and of continuous quantity. But if we must be precise, we ought not to speak of the dyad in Christ as continuous number; for the continuous is that whose parts are joined by a common boundary. To conceive of parts in the divinity, so that a common boundary might join them to the body, is not easy even to imagine; for "continuous" is said only of magnitudes. Rather, we must take number here in the sense of discrete quantity. For the discrete is not necessarily what is altogether divided; it can also be what is united while preserving its own distinct principle. Thus we call a body both continuous and discrete: continuous insofar as it simply has dimensions, discrete insofar as there are three dimensions. And yet the dimensions are not scattered away from one another; we call them discrete because each of them has its own principle. But since some people are altogether uneasy at hearing the word "discrete", come, let us leave this solution aside, sound as it is, and offer another. One must know, then, that just as "one" is said in many ways — one in number, like Socrates; one in species, like man; one in genus, like animal — so too with "two". Things are called two in number, like Socrates and Plato; two in species, like man and horse; and two in genus, like substance and white. This being so, when we say "two" of Christ, we do not say that he is two in number, but one in number and two in species. That we may speak in this way, Aristotle also shows, when he says plainly of matter and form that they are one in number but two in species. And St Gregory, speaking of Christ, says, "so that the two together are one, not by nature, but by their coming together." To this they raise a further difficulty for us: "By saying 'one' and 'two' of the same thing, you introduce a contradiction; and either what you say will be false, or the contradictory statements will be true together." To this we say that it is not true in the same respect, but in [?]

One must know that none of these difficulties is the Dissenters' own; they stole them from the Nestorians and pose them to us. For the Nestorians, holding two persons and two Christs, used to pose these difficulties to all alike who say two natures, whether they say the natures were united or exist after the union: "If you say two natures, you also introduce two persons." Indeed, it is for this reason that the absurdity followed from these difficulties both for us and for the Dissenters. For the Nestorians, however, no such thing follows; on the contrary, as far as these difficulties go, their position is actually strengthened.

They also raise another difficulty for us, which is their own, but which ends up in the doctrine of the Nestorians. For the Church says to them: "If you say that the things united are unconfused, and that one is passible and the other impassible, visible and invisible, circumscribed and uncircumscribed, mortal and immortal, and so on, you necessarily introduce two natures." They reply that there is nothing absurd in confessing that the things united are unconfused, one passible and the other impassible, and yet saying one nature in their case; and then they bring forward the example of man as proof. "Look," they say, "soul and body were united in man without confusion, one visible and the other invisible, mortal and immortal, and the rest; and yet we do not speak of two natures, but of one nature of man." To this, again, those of the council reply: "In the same way that you say the things united in man are preserved after the union, one mortal and the other immortal, and all the rest, so we speak in the case of Christ; but all these things belong to two nature[s] [?]

To this the followers of Gaianus can find nothing to say. For while they confess that the things united are unconfused, they will not tolerate speaking of any difference at all, or naming "two" at all; instead they say that the things united are some one thing after the union. But the Theodosians, that is, the followers of Severus, have found themselves a defense, and they say: "We confess that the parts are different, but the result is one, just as in man too the parts, soul and body, are different, but the result is one." For they want to apply the example of man to Christ in every respect. Then, when they realized that they had fallen into the council's doctrine, they shift the argument onto something else and say: "We speak of different natures of the parts, but of one nature of the result. The council, however, was speaking about the result." To them we say: You are lying. For the council was speaking not about the result but about the parts, and this is clear from many things. First, from the Gaianites. For they, guarding the ancient doctrine, are now fighting the council on the ground that it says the parts are two; for they want even the parts to be some one thing after the union. But perhaps the Theodosians will reply to this: "No; it is not the Gaianites who guard the ancient doctrine, but rather we." But to this again we say: Even if you are not convinced of this by the Gaianites, you must at any rate be convinced of it by the Acephali. For they, who are plainly older than both you and the Gaianites, fight the council on the ground that it says the parts are two. Then we are also assured of this from Eutyches. For the council was addressing Eutyches, who was disputing about the parts, since he did not say that the body was consubstantial with us. So, as it was addressing him [?]

[?] …but not two, as we say Christ has? To this we say: precisely because we speak of one nature of man, but of two natures of Christ. For the relation that the one nature has to the hypostasis of man is the same relation that the two have to the hypostasis of Christ. To make what is said clear, we must go back over the difficulties stated earlier. When the Church said, "If you say that the things united are unconfused and that their natures are preserved after the union, one mortal and the other immortal, and so on, you necessarily introduce two natures," they replied that there is nothing absurd in saying both that the things united are unconfused and that their natures are preserved after the union, and in speaking of one nature. "For look," they say, "we speak of one nature of man, and yet the things united in him are unconfused." Hard pressed by this example, those of the council said, "In man too we speak of two natures." Then the Theodosians: "Well then, if you speak of two natures of man, we must speak of three of Christ." Then the conciliarists said to them in turn: "If you force us to say that Christ is in three natures, then you too say that he is from three. For you say that he is from humanity and divinity; and humanity has two natures, and divinity one." One should note that it does follow for the council to speak of three natures, but it does not follow for the Theodosians to speak of "from three". For they, while saying that Christ is from humanity and divinity, speak of one nature of man, whereas we speak of two. So it follows for us, not for them, to speak of three natures; for we speak of two of man and one of the Word. But we do not say this without qualification; rather, we say that man has one nature and Christ two. And one must know on what grounds. We say that there are certain principles in Holy Scripture, acknowledged by all, which both we and they accept. Let us therefore examine each doctrine against these, and whichever we find to agree with the principles is plainly sound; whatever is opposed to them is clearly unsound and must be rejected. It is agreed, then, that the same one was God and man; that the same one is properly God and properly man; that the same one is by nature God and by nature man; that the same one is consubstantial with the

Father and consubstantial with us; that the same one is one of the Holy Trinity and one of us; that God the Word deigned to become man; and we shall find many other such things in Holy Scripture. Let us therefore examine each doctrine against these, first the doctrine of one nature: if it holds up, let us accept it; if not, let us reject it. Let three things be posited: souls in general, bodies in general, and completed men. Taking from these one soul and one body, let us complete a particular man, Peter, say. He will clearly not be found to have the nature of those, but is consubstantial with men. Peter, then, once completed, is consubstantial neither with souls nor with bodies, and is neither properly a soul nor properly a body. For whatever definition one gives of the soul or of the body, one does not give the same definition of Peter; rather, he is consubstantial with men (for he admits their definition), and he is something other than the soul and the body. Let us come to Christ; for in their view the divinity corresponds to the soul and the humanity to the body. Then Christ is neither consubstantial with the Father nor consubstantial with us, just as Peter is neither consubstantial with the soul nor consubstantial with the body. Then Christ too is neither properly God nor properly man, neither God by nature nor man by nature, neither one of the Holy Trinity nor one of us, just as Peter is neither one of the souls nor one of the bodies. But to say such things of Christ is to destroy the principles we have agreed upon, which is absurd. If, however, we posit that Christ has two natures, we destroy none of these principles, but find them all in agreement. For the same one is both God and man; the same one is consubstantial with the Father and consubstantial with us; properly God and properly man; God by nature and man by nature; one of the Holy Trinity and one of us. For the same hypostasis admits the definitions of the two natures: whatever definition one gives of the divinity, one finds the same in Christ; and whatever definition one gives of the humanity, one finds the same fitting the substance of Christ according to substance. So there are necessarily two natures of the one hypostasis of Christ. They raise a difficulty, saying, "And how can two be found in one individual?" We answer the "how" by appeal to the paradox: it is not absurd that something paradoxical took place in Christ; what is absurd is to speak falsely and to contradict the principles. One must know that those who hold one nature in Christ are necessarily forced to speak of either two hypostases of the Godhead or four, but no longer of three, as all confess. For if they tell us there is one nature in Christ, where do they give us the three hypostases of the Godhead? We have one of the Father and one of the Holy Spirit; but the other

they can no longer name, when they speak of one nature in Christ. For if he is one nature, he is no longer God by nature, as we have already shown. And if he is not God by nature, how could he be said to have a hypostasis of the Godhead? So they are forced to speak of two hypostases. But if they say that the third hypostasis is that of God the Word, so that the first is the Father's, the second the Holy Spirit's and the third God the Word's, they necessarily introduce four: one of the Father, one of the Holy Spirit, one of God the Word and one of Christ. On every side, then, it has been shown that one must hold two natures, not one.

It remains to go through the arguments they bring against us from citations of the holy Fathers. Of these, some concern what the council did not say; some they bring forward in support of their own doctrine; and some concern what it did say. On the basis of what it did not say, they attack it on three counts: that the council did not speak of the hypostatic union, nor of the one incarnate nature of God the Word, nor of "from two natures". Yet St Cyril said all these things. It is worth explaining why he speaks of the hypostatic union. Its sense is twofold. When Nestorius said that the union of God the Word with the flesh came about by relation, and spoke in a relational sense of one person of God the Word and the flesh, St Cyril, opposing him, says that the union came about hypostatically, that is, in actual existence and of the realities themselves, and no longer speaks of it as by relation. And here again one should note that "hypostasis" is used also of things that simply exist. The second sense is that he said the union came about hypostatically, that is, in one hypostasis. Each sense is opposed to Nestorius, but the first is the truer. So they say: "Although St Cyril said these things, the council rejected them and said nothing about them." We overturn all this with a single argument: the council passed over these things as common and agreed; for it was addressing Eutyches, who, fighting diametrically against Nestorius, obviously confessed these things too. And what is agreed need not in every case be stated; it is sometimes permissible to leave it out. The earlier councils show this, having left out many agreed points in many places. Further, we find the council in many places speaking of one hypostasis and one person, which is nothing other than speaking of the hypostatic union. These, then, are the arguments concerning what it did not say. In support of their own doctrine they bring forward many citations, and first that St Cyril clearly [?]

[?] said, "one nature of God the Word incarnate." To this we reply that we acknowledge that Saint Cyril said this, but it is in no way opposed to our doctrine. For he did not say "one incarnate nature of Christ," but "one nature of God the Word incarnate," and in this way he indicated the other nature.
