That he means to indicate the other nature by saying "incarnate" is clear from his own explanation in his second letter to Succensus, where he says: "If, after saying 'one nature of God the Word,' we had fallen silent without adding 'incarnate,' and had, as it were, set the economy aside, perhaps their argument would not be implausible when they pretend to ask: Where is the perfection in humanity, or how has our substance come to subsist? But since both the perfection in humanity and the indication of our substance have been brought in by saying 'incarnate,' let them stop propping themselves up on a staff of reed. For those who throw out the economy and deny the incarnation could justly be charged with depriving the Son of his perfect humanity. But if, as I said, in saying that he was made flesh there is a clear and indisputable confession that he became man, nothing any longer prevents us from understanding that Christ, being one and alone, is himself both God and man, perfect in Godhead and likewise perfect in manhood. And most rightly and very wisely does your Perfection set out the account of the saving passion, firmly maintaining that the only-begotten Son of God himself, insofar as he is conceived to be and is God, did not suffer the things of the body in his own nature, but rather that he suffered in his earthly nature. For it was necessary, clearly necessary, that both be preserved in the one who is truly Son: both that he does not suffer as God, and that he is said to have suffered as man; for it was his own flesh that suffered." It should be known that Saint Cyril was the first among the orthodox to say "one nature of God the Word incarnate." We say "among the orthodox" because Apollinaris often said it; and that is why Saint Cyril was thought by the Easterners to be an Apollinarian, though he was not. For we need not reject absolutely everything that heretics say, but only cast off what is bad. They also bring forward another citation, supposedly from the blessed Julius, found in the letter to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, which begins, "I am amazed to learn about certain people." The citation runs as follows: "For those who speak of two natures must worship the one and not worship the other, and be baptized into the divine but not baptized into the human"; and many other such things are found in this letter. But we prove on many grounds that this letter is not by the blessed Julius but by Apollinaris. First, if one examines the matter carefully, nothing by the blessed Julius is in circulation; indeed, even the seven letters which they say are his are by Apollinaris. Second, because in this very letter, though he mentions the body,

he nowhere calls it rational or ensouled. Yet the Fathers of that time had the custom, wherever they mentioned the body, of saying "rational and ensouled"; and this is so true that, being wary of this very charge, they later added "rational" and "ensouled," and one cannot find any books of later writers that lack this addition to what the ancients said. That the letter is also shown on this ground to be by Apollinaris and not by the blessed Julius himself is evident, for Gregory of Nyssa, in his treatise against Apollinaris, clearly mentions many of the things in this letter and refutes them as wrong. It can also be shown on other grounds not to be by the blessed Julius. For they say that it is found in the acts of Ephesus under the blessed Cyril, and they are plainly lying. Nothing of the kind is found there; the letter found there as being from Julius is a different one, and it is not by Julius either but by Timothy, as one can learn from many copies. But since it does not oppose us in any way, even if they say that this one is by Julius, we need not trouble ourselves about it. They also bring forward another citation against us, supposedly from Saint Gregory the Wonderworker, from the Detailed Confession of Faith: "Not two persons, not two natures; for we must not worship four," and so on. To this too we reply, first, that this work was also doubted by older writers as not being by Saint Gregory; second, that Gregory of Nyssa, writing a funeral oration on the Wonderworker, says that no writing of his is in circulation except the creed alone, which he saw in a vision. They also bring forward yet another citation, supposedly from Saint Athanasius, from the discourse On the Incarnation. It runs as follows: "And that the same is Son of God according to the Spirit and Son of man according to the flesh; not that the one Son is two natures, one to be worshipped and one not to be worshipped, but one nature of God the Word incarnate." To this we reply, first, that it does not oppose us at all. For we do not hold two natures, the one to be worshipped and the other not to be worshipped; rather, we hold one nature of God the Word incarnate. Second, it is not by Saint Athanasius either. For when we ask them where it is found, and they are at a loss to show it, under pressure they bring forward a short treatise of about two leaves in which this citation is found. But it is clear to everyone that all the writings of Saint Athanasius are very long. But what do we have to say, given that they cite the blessed Cyril adducing it against Theodore as from Saint Athanasius? To this we reply that it is indeed found in what the blessed Cyril wrote against Theodore, but it is an old corruption. For Dioscorus, having become the successor of the blessed Cyril and having come into possession of his writings, would perhaps not have hesitated to insert whatever he wished. One may even conjecture that the blessed Cyril did not

adduce it against Theodore at all, as is clear from the following. Theodoret, speaking in defense of Theodore and refuting all the citations from the holy Fathers that Saint Cyril had adduced against him, nowhere mentions this citation. But they reply to this that Theodoret passed over it maliciously: since he could not face it, so plain was it, he deliberately left it out. To this we reply that he was so far from passing it over while it stood there that, when the blessed Cyril had said elsewhere, "But one nature of God the Word incarnate," he would not, had he known that this citation stood in the blessed Cyril's work as adduced from Saint Athanasius, have spoken so ignorantly as to say: "Which of the Fathers told you 'one nature of God the Word incarnate'?" But they say again that he knew perfectly well it had been said by Saint Athanasius, since he said: "As the Fathers have said." To this we reply that everyone is eager to show that what he says has been said by the Fathers, if not word for word, then in substance. They also bring forward another citation from Erechthius, who was never heard of as one of the Fathers; so much so that when Timothy wrote against the council and adduced a citation from Erechthius, Cyrus, his own priest, wrote to him about it: "I wish you had corrected this, for Erechthius was never heard of as one of the Fathers." So much for this examination.

Since they also seize on certain expressions in the council's definition and attack it on that basis, come, let us set these out as well, state how they attack them, and then bring forward the refutations of their attacks. The council, then, said: "This wise and saving creed of divine grace would indeed have sufficed for a full knowledge of true religion; for it teaches the perfect doctrine concerning the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and sets forth the Lord's incarnation to those who receive it faithfully." But the objection is very feeble. In the first place, the council is so far from holding the views of Nestorius that a certain John of Aegeae, a Nestorian priest, attacking the council, says that this council is Cyrillian and holds Cyril's views. If it were Nestorian, John could not have said this. Next, if they attack the council on the basis of such expressions, why do they not attack the holy Fathers as well? For they too have said many such things. For the blessed Cyril, in his commentary on the prophet Zechariah, which begins "The holy Zechariah prophesies," says the following: "We must, then, depart from such things and, as from a foreign land, move out of the cold and dead disposition of mind into Zion, that is, into what is

true (so that we understand the Church of Christ); and having come to be in it, we shall behold what pleases God, and survey the teachings concerning the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and we shall find Christ himself gathering us together by every means and binding us spiritually into unity of soul." See, having said "what pleases God," he added, "and we shall survey the teachings concerning the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and we shall find Christ himself gathering us together." So, to judge by what they say, the blessed Cyril too glorifies a quaternity. And we find many other such things in the holy Fathers, which there is no need to set out now, to avoid lengthiness. They also attack the council again for saying "in two natures." But that this too has been said by the Fathers is easy to show from many passages.

After all that has been said, it is fitting also to go through the opinion of the Gaianites and of certain others. The Gaianites, then, confess that God the Word became man from the Virgin perfectly and truly; but they confess that from the moment of the union the body was incorruptible. For they say that he underwent every kind of affliction—he hungered, he thirsted, he grew weary—but that he did not suffer these things in the same way as we do. For they say that we hunger and thirst out of natural necessity, whereas Christ underwent everything voluntarily. For he was not enslaved to the laws of nature; otherwise we would be confessing that his sufferings were involuntary, which is absurd. That is the opinion of the Gaianites. To this we reply that we too confess that his sufferings were voluntary; but we do not therefore say that he suffered out of necessity in the same way as we do. Rather, we say that he voluntarily submitted to the laws of nature and willingly allowed the body to suffer what was proper to it, in the same way that we suffer. And the Fathers bear witness to this: Saint Gregory, who says, "He allowed nature, when he wished, to perform its own operations"; and the blessed Cyril, who says that "through the taking in of food and its passing out he sustained the subsistence"—that is, of the body. And again, from the dialogue That Christ Is One, that he allowed his own flesh to proceed according to the laws of its own nature. And again: "Since he permits the bodily to suffer what belongs to it by nature, as proof that he really and truly bore flesh and became man according to the Scriptures." And Saint Athanasius, in the discourse Against Apollinaris: "That is why the Lord said, Now my soul is troubled. And this 'now' means: when he willed. Yet he shows what really was; for he did not name what was not as though it were present, as if the things spoken of happened only in appearance; for by nature and in truth all things

took place." And again elsewhere: "Even if the things spoken of did not happen through weakness of nature, yet the things that happened happened as a demonstration of real existence." Hence, if he suffered in the same way as we do, we cannot call his body incorruptible, any more than we can call ours so. And we put this difficulty to them: if you call the body of Christ incorruptible, it is not consubstantial with us, since Christ's is incorruptible while ours is corruptible. But they in turn might reply to this: "Just as you, while calling the body of Christ incorruptible after the resurrection, say that it is consubstantial, so we too, while calling it incorruptible before the resurrection, confess that it is consubstantial with us." We, however, say: even if we confess it to be incorruptible after the resurrection, we do not call it incorruptible by nature, but by grace. And if they say, "Then let it be incorruptible by grace before the resurrection too," we reply that what is said about Christ does not allow this; for before the resurrection he is said to have hungered and to have thirsted. And how could what suffered these things be incorruptible? After the resurrection, on the other hand, he suffered nothing of the kind; so it is clear that before the resurrection the body was corruptible, and after the resurrection incorruptible. For even if he is said to have eaten after the resurrection, he did this by way of accommodation—not because he was really hungry, but to show his disciples that he himself was the one who had risen from the dead—just as he is also said to have shown them the marks of the nails. And yet we shall not rise bearing any of the afflictions we had before the resurrection; but Christ is the firstfruits of our resurrection from the dead, and nevertheless he was found to bear them. So it is clear that this was done by way of accommodation. Indeed, Scripture does not say that he hungered, but that he ate. It should be noted that they bring forward certain citations from the Fathers calling the body of Christ incorruptible—for example, the blessed Cyril saying that "the flesh of the Word did not admit corruption." When they bring forward such citations, bear in mind that the word "corruption" is equivocal. "Corruption" means the complete dissolution of the body into the elements of which it was composed; and "corruption" also means these human afflictions, that is, hunger and thirst and everything of that sort. So when one of the Fathers says that the body of Christ did not undergo corruption, he means that it was not utterly dissolved; and that this is so is clear from the statements that seem to contradict it. For in many places they call it corruptible before the resurrection and incorruptible after the resurrection. So much for the Gaianites. The Agnoetae confess everything that the Theodosians do, but disagree with them on this point: the Theodosians do not say that Christ's humanity was ignorant, whereas the Agnoetae say that it was. For he resembles us in everything, they say; and if we are ignorant, clearly he too was ignorant.

"And he himself says in the Gospels: 'No one knows the day or the hour, not even the Son, but the Father alone.' And again: 'Where have you laid Lazarus?' For all these expressions," they say, "are expressions of ignorance." But the others answer them that Christ said these things by way of accommodation, to deter his disciples from learning from him the hour of the end. Indeed, they say, when he was asked by them again after the resurrection, he no longer said, "not even the Son," but "none of you." We, however, say that one should not inquire too precisely into these matters; and that is why the council did not concern itself with any such doctrine. Nevertheless, it should be known that most of the Fathers, indeed nearly all of them, clearly say that he was ignorant. For if he is said to be consubstantial with us in every respect, and we too are ignorant, [?] clearly he too was ignorant. And Scripture also says of him that "he advanced in stature and wisdom"—clearly by learning what he did not know. It is fitting also to speak of Origen and his doctrines. Origen, then, was a man of early times, one of those who lived before Constantine; he was great and learned in the holy Scripture, and he was also a grammarian. His father was martyred, and he himself was brought to martyrdom. But he was compelled to sacrifice, for the following reason. While he was undergoing his martyrdom, they brought an Ethiopian before him and tried to force him either to commit an indecent act with the Ethiopian or to sacrifice to the gods. He chose rather to sacrifice to the gods, and taking the incense he threw it on the sacrifice; but afterward he deeply repented and lamented over it. As regards doctrine, he was of the following kind. He spoke of a subordination of the Son, as the Arians did later. People defend him by saying that the early Fathers were not concerned with precise language: since the heresies had not yet appeared, they used words rather loosely, and only when the heresies appeared did each of the Fathers begin to guard himself. We, however, say that he did not hold subordination merely because he used words loosely, but that he really clung firmly to this doctrine. For in a letter of his he is clearly contending vigorously for it, saying: "The Son is either greater than the Father, or less, or equal. If, then, I show that he is not greater, [?]"

pure: the demons, the souls, and the angels, serving God and doing his commandments. But the devil, who was one of them, since he had free will, chose to oppose God, and God thrust him away; and all the other powers revolted along with him. Those who sinned very gravely became demons; those who sinned less, angels; those who sinned still less, archangels; and so on in order, each received according to its own sin. There remained the souls, which had neither sinned so gravely as to become demons, nor again so lightly as to become angels. So God made the present world and bound the soul to the body as punishment. For God, he says, is no respecter of persons, such that, though all these beings are of one nature (for all immortal beings are rational), he would make some demons, some souls, and some angels; rather, it is clear that, punishing each according to how it had sinned, he made one a demon, another a soul, another an angel. For if this were not so—if souls had not existed beforehand—why do we find some newborns blind, though they have committed no sin, while others are born with nothing wrong with them? Clearly, then, the souls had certain prior sins, in accordance with which each receives what it deserves. Concerning the restoration, he holds the following: that there is a resurrection of the dead, and there is punishment, but not without end. For as the body is punished, the soul is gradually purified, and so is restored to its original rank. And he says that the demons and angels too are restored. Let us refute all of this, beginning with pre-existence. Since, from saying that God is no respecter of persons, he concludes that, souls being rational and immortal just as the angels are, God bound some to the body and allowed others to dwell with him in heaven, it should be known that "rational and immortal" is equivocal. The rationality and immortality of the angels is one thing, surpassing human nature, and ours is another; for we also call God rational and immortal, yet we do not say that he is of our nature. As for their saying, "And how is it that some are born blind and others with nothing wrong with them?", we reply that these are the judgments of the Lord, and we must not inquire into them. For we in turn put this difficulty to them: why is it that horses, which are of one nature, some toil in bakeries while others live in luxury with great men? And yet they do not confess that the souls of horses pre-exist. The Platonists, hard-pressed by this difficulty, said that the souls of irrational animals too pre-exist. As for their saying that punishment is not endless (for they say that the word "age" is used of a limited time, and that when Scripture says that punishment is eternal, it means nothing more than for a limited time), it should be known that the word "age" is indeed, both among outside writers and in Scripture,

often used of a limited time; but in the case of punishment it cannot be taken in that sense. For Christ himself says: "These will go away into eternal life, and those into eternal punishment." So either we take the life as limited, which is absurd, or we take both as endless. These things, for the demonstration of orthodox doctrines and the refutation of heterodox heresies, Christ our God, the giver of good things, has supplied to us in the opening of our mouth. To him be glory and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and to the ages. Amen.

OF LEONTIUS THE MONK, AGAINST THE NESTORIANS AND EUTYCHIANS. Certain God-loving men, eager for the divine doctrines, having welcomed the public discussions that we have often held, urged us to hand over to them in writing some outlines of the objections and solutions that have often been discussed, so that these might be able to serve them, as someone has said, as a remedy for forgetfulness and a kindling of memory, and as a solace against time, by which all things are buried. But we, though pressed [?], kept putting it off, for a great many other reasons, but chiefly for two. The first is that we are not sufficiently practised in writing, since we have had no share in secular learning, and we do not yet possess the spiritual teaching which divine grace bestows on the pure in heart; for I am not ashamed to acknowledge my own littleness, of which now

[?] utterly turning themselves away from the ancient labours of the holy Fathers: their ingratitude made my mind very reluctant to obey the command of love. For if they have not been persuaded by treatises set forth with such great grace and wisdom of God, and with the height of secular philosophy and of all other learning besides, how could this brief discourse, coming from a small mind and tongue, persuade them? Nevertheless (for we have been charged not to take on those already held fast, but to provide for the safety of the healthy), we have now learned, if not before, to obey a friendly command. We have composed three treatises in all. The first gathers in one place, in summary form, the objections and rejoinders of the mutually opposed and falsely so-called knowledge of Nestorius and Eutyches, enclosing almost all their difficulties in a few words. We have arranged this treatise in chapters, each chapter containing the matters that can be referred to it. Its title has been aptly chosen for the purpose at hand: A Refutation and Overthrow of the Contrary Illusions of Nestorius and Eutyches concerning the Divinity and Humanity of Christ. For under fair-sounding names, and as each sees fit, the one teaches that the divinity exists only in appearance, the other that the humanity does. The second is directed against those of our own side who have attached themselves to the corrupt notion of the Aphthartodocetae. These especially one might justly refute, since they acknowledge the difference, the properties and the operations of our one and only Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ. As for those who set themselves against the natures, deny their difference after the union and lawlessly confuse the properties and operations in them, we do not so much laugh at their lack of education as pity their impiety, since they puzzle over the mode of natures that they neither confess nor regard as existing. They ought first to have posited that the nature of Christ's divinity and the nature of his humanity both exist and are preserved after the union, and only then to busy themselves with the relation of these to one another and the mode of their existence. This treatise is cast in the form of a dialogue, and leaves out, I think, nothing that is useful or relevant to the inquiry before us. So that the speakers may not be confused, we have marked the one who raises the difficulties with an asterisk, and the one who brings the solutions with the sign of the cross. Nor have we done this without reason: by the star we have hinted at his dim and unclear knowledge, while we have armed the champion of truth with the trophy of the cross. This treatise, then, is entitled: A Dialogue against Those of Our Own Who Have Attached Themselves to the Corrupt Opinion of the Aphthartodocetae.

The third and last treatise contains the overthrow of those who pretend to accept the great and ecumenical council of Chalcedon while championing the doctrines of Nestorius. For these, like the other initiates of the heresies, appear to accept the divine Scriptures and the earlier holy councils. They do not think in accordance with them, however, but make them a cloak for their own impiety in order to deceive the simpler sort. So Apollinarius and Macedonius did with the council of Nicaea; Nestorius, besides that one, with the council of Constantinople; and Eutyches, besides the others, with the council of Ephesus. In the same way these men feign acceptance of the holy council of Chalcedon, at once covering their impiety with the credibility of its members and paving the way for their own attack on the truth. Wishing to uncover their villainy, together with the impiety woven into it, we have carried the refutation back to the first Fathers of their impiety, bringing the principles and sources of their godlessness into the open. In this way we strive to stop up those sources once and for all, and to cut off the godless flow by the simple refutation of the truth. For thus the rest of the stream of impiety will vanish too, since the effects of evils naturally perish together with their principles. We have divided the treatise of refutations into chapters, writing a number at the head of each so that they may be easily remembered. The treatise is entitled: The Exposure of and Triumph over the Secret and More Primordial [?] Impiety of the Nestorians and of Its Fathers. We ask those who read this modest work to pardon us wherever we have not struck our opponents fittingly, or if we appear to have fought for the truth more weakly than we should. For all of us alike fall short of the dignity of the subject, but in zeal for piety we differ from one another, and each will plainly have the measure of grace that corresponds to his own preparation. We also urge the reader in love that, if anything we have said seems unclear to him, whether because of the depth of the subject or because of the altered meaning and peculiar use of certain words, he should not condemn it at the first reading. If he applies his mind to what has been said twice or many times, he will find its meaning becoming clear to him. And the discovery of truth is itself sufficient reward for the labour of inquiry. Beneath each of the treatises we have also set citations that support what we have set forth, confirming the truth of what has been said by the testimony of the ancients as well.

A REFUTATION AND OVERTHROW OF THE CONTRARY ILLUSIONS OF NESTORIUS AND EUTYCHES CONCERNING THE DIVINITY AND HUMANITY OF THE LORD. I have set out to clarify and explain the account of hypostasis and essence, that is, of person and nature (for the two are not the same), which among the wise men of today is confused and obscure in both respects. I also intend to resolve certain other questions that follow from the first inquiry, with God's help, as he supports the weakness of our reasonings through your prayers; trusting in these, I have committed myself to the examination of this subject. We are not unaware that those who have now risen up against us, united only in their opposition both to the good and to the men who spoke of God, spit upon us, who have emulated and championed those men's teaching, just as they spit upon the men themselves; and without realizing it they have honoured us by this partnership in dishonour. For the same people make sport of divine things and insult the theologians; so what great thing is it if they also despise us, who are nothing? The only thing about them worth wondering at is this: they diligently neglect every virtue that shows itself in deeds, yet command themselves to be wise. They are intelligent as if by decree, and their mere wishing has made them well educated, so that one of the wittier sort gracefully named them 'Acrophilosophers'. But their wicked disposition must not make us give up any of our boldness or our struggles. On the contrary, we should let the contests of the blessed men sharpen us to courage as much as possible, and fare like the hottest iron, which is tempered when it meets cold water. So we too are strengthened for the contests by their struggles. Well then, let us cut through their opposition and battle line against the truth on either side with a most cutting word, as with a two-edged sword, and overthrow it, beginning our subject from this point. The disciples of Nestorius's man-worship and of Eutyches's phantasy, or rather the disciples of the phantasy on both sides (for a pious and [?]

divine man rightly called them so, naming both 'Contrary-Docetists'): for the one party says that the divinity, the other that the humanity, exists in the Saviour only in appearance. Each, however, puts something forward in its place: the one puts forward the good pleasure and the dignity in place of the illusory divinity, the other an ineffable flesh in place of one that is by nature also ours. With fair names and auspicious words, as with painted-on colours, they try to dignify the ugliness of an impiety that is opposite but equal. It is as though our concern were to cultivate beauty of names, and not to gaze upon the truly golden face of truth, than which nothing is lovelier, even when fair and brilliant diction is absent. Truth needs no cosmetic adornments, for it shines with natural beauty, and it needs nothing of the deceptive shaping that words lend, like rouge. These men, then, fighting both against themselves and against the truth, have divided the war against it between contrary positions, each using the same premises for his own aim. As a result, their agreement through contraries is overthrown by a single refutation from the friends of truth, and the agreement of wickedness becomes a surplus of victory. For whatever arguments overthrow one of the pair entwined in impiety overthrow the other along with it. It must be understood that Eutyches stands in the same relation to Nestorius concerning the economy as Sabellius did to Arius concerning theology. Those two fell into an equal evil through contrary positions: the one, because of the essence, confused the hypostases into one hypostasis; the other, because of the hypostases, divided the essence along with them. These two do the reverse: the one cuts the natures into hypostases, the other mixes the natures into a single nature. The one makes the hypostasis into hypostases; the other pours the natures together into one nature. For we find the economy confused by the later heretics with the same arguments by which one can see the Trinity divided by the earlier ones; and the arguments by which the present ones divide the economy are those by which the former confused the Godhead. Come then, let us bring their sophistical propositions into the middle of the discussion and, as in a court, give room to their charges against us, and so try to dissolve their vain notions against the truth. For they say: 'If you speak of two natures in the one Christ, and there is no nature without a hypostasis, then there must also be two hypostases.' The contest is one and the same against both, as I said, even if their aims differ. The one party uses this same argument in order to bring in hypostases along with the natures; the other, in order to abolish the natures along with the hypostases. But let those of Eutyches's party also hear from us; for one contest is common to us against both, and another is particular to us against [Marginal scholion: He is speaking of Abba Nonnus.]

these. What do you say? Do you speak simply of one nature? 'No,' they say, 'but of one incarnate nature.' Nothing prevents us from engaging with you more pleasantly. The one nature of the Word of which you speak we accept from you and hold. Let the battle be over the other one, which we call a nature other than that of the Word, but which you like to call flesh. What do you say about this flesh? Does it have a nature, or an essence, or at least part of a nature? How large a part, you may decide: whether you wish to call it a half, or a third, or some other fraction. And, to use the same form of argument as you: is there flesh without essence, or flesh with no share in nature? How then will you escape your own difficulty? If there is flesh without essence, or outside nature, show what it is and how it comes to be so, and we will accept it. But if it is the height of ignorance to posit flesh that is not what it is called, or is not called what it is, how will you escape the proposition you yourselves put to us? For if there is no flesh without essence, that is, without a nature, and there is no nature without a hypostasis, then there will be no flesh without a hypostasis. It is time, then, for you either to strip away the nature of flesh entirely, or to grant the Lord two hypostases, according to your own law, which says, 'There is no nature without a hypostasis.' For if there is no nature without a hypostasis, and you speak of a nature of the Word, then you will also grant the Word a hypostasis. What remains in question, then, is the flesh: whether it too, having its own nature, is deemed worthy of the name, and, having obtained it, also has the hypostasis; or whether, lacking it, it will lose both the hypostasis and the nature. So you are caught in your own difficulties, and this cunning has done nothing to free you from the charges you brought against us. Resolve just one more of these difficulties and you will seem worth a great deal: if there is no nature without a hypostasis, and you confess that the Lord is from two natures, then he will also be from two hypostases. Who, then, has become liable to the charge of Nestorius's division, we leave you to consider. With these arguments, then, we have dismissed you as well. To those who have missed the truth in the direction diametrically opposite to yours, we shall speak as follows. Hypostasis and enhypostatic, sirs, are not the same thing, just as essence and what is in an essence are different. Hypostasis signifies 'someone', whereas enhypostatic signifies the essence. Hypostasis marks off a person by its characteristic properties, whereas enhypostatic signifies that something is not an accident, which has its being in another and is not seen in itself. Such are all qualities, both those called essential and those called adventitious. Neither kind is an essence, that is, a subsisting thing; each is always seen in connection with an essence, as colour is in a body and knowledge in a soul. Therefore whoever says 'There is no nature without a hypostasis' speaks the truth, but does not reason correctly when he infers from 'not without hypostasis' that it is a hypostasis. It is as if someone said that there is no body without shape, which is true, and then incorrectly concluded that the shape is a body,

rather than something seen in a body. A nature, that is, an essence, could never exist without a hypostasis. Yet the nature is not a hypostasis, because the terms are not convertible [?]: a hypostasis is also a nature, but a nature is not also a hypostasis. Nature admits the definition of being, while hypostasis admits the definition of being by itself as well. The one holds the definition of a species, while the other indicates 'someone'. The one signifies the character of a universal thing, while the other separates the particular from the common. To put it briefly: things that are consubstantial, and whose definition of being is common, are properly said to be of one nature. A hypostasis, by contrast, is defined either as things that are the same in nature but differ in number, or as things composed of different natures that possess communion in being together and in one another. By 'sharing in being' I do not mean that they complete each other's essence, as one sees with essences and with what is essentially predicated of them (these are called qualities). I mean rather that the nature and essence of each is not seen by itself, but together with that which is joined and has grown together with it. One could find this in other things too, but not least in soul and body, whose hypostasis is common while the nature and definition of each are its own.

'But man,' they say, 'even if he is composed of things of different kinds, nevertheless neither of them had being without the other. The Word, however, exists even before the humanity. Moreover, man is composed of incomplete parts, whereas Christ has complete parts, and for this reason they could not reasonably even be called parts. How, then, can you apply the compound of man to the Word and the incarnation, when there is nothing [?]?' So say some, the advocates of the contrary doctrine and of division. For the other party, too, is fond of the example, but they take it, not appropriately, but quite ignorantly, in a way worthy of the archetypal confusion, as though it were a vivid image of it. That this example is not our own invention, but that we have received it from of old, 'son from father', as the saying goes, is attested by the treatises of the God-wise men, in which they used the example of man to illustrate the union. Yet our opponents do not handle the example well when they force it to correspond in every respect to the archetype. [Notes: 'of being by itself' [?]. Coinsita: 'grown together'.]

For the example shows that the Word was united in his very essence to the body taken from us and was never seen without it, even if he preserves the difference within the union, just as ordinary man does. In neither case do the properties appear confused. Our soul has not become visible and mortal instead of invisible and immortal, nor has the Word become visible or mortal, although both our soul and the Word have come to be in a visible and mortal body. Each of them preserves its properties without any deficiency: ordinary man, who is from soul and body, and the Saviour, who subsists from divinity and humanity. Our opponents, however, take the example not where it resembles but where it differs, and spitefully nitpick in their questions. It is as if, when we use the radiance of the sun to illustrate the Word and the Father because of their conjunction and co-eternity, they were to slander us as thereby making the Son without hypostasis. That man too is not composed of incomplete parts, at least according to the definition of how each part exists, even if, with respect to the definition of the whole man, the parts do not admit the definition of the whole as whole, you may learn as follows. What would the soul lack for being an incorporeal, self-moving essence, since it has a life that is separable and its own? This very fact shows its immortality and indestructibility. And what does the body lack for being a body? They give its definition by saying that a body is that which has three dimensions, or that it is a natural, organic body potentially possessing life; and both definitions fit our body properly. These things, then, are not incomplete when taken by themselves, although again they are called incomplete with respect to the hypostasis of the whole of which they are parts. Using this same reasoning, one would not go wrong in interpreting the mystery of Christ as well. For [?] even if he is taken as God alone or as mere man; so that the definition of completeness is twofold: one is stated absolutely, the other is seen in relation, as the great Gregory teaches. For the Word is complete and full, and the bestower of completeness; and the soul of man is also complete with respect to the definition of its existence. But neither is the Word [?] complete [?] unless the humanity is ranged with him; nor is the soul a complete man, even if it has a complete essence, unless the body is conceived together with it. This too must be noted: times are not included in the definitions of things, any more than places are, for they hold only the status of necessary conditions. Furthermore, every definition is a definition of the thing as it is now,

not of what will later come of it. Otherwise nothing that comes to be could admit a definition of being what it is, since it does not remain; all things that are subject to coming to be and passing away change into one another. Even all rational essences, since they admit more and less in respect of virtue and are now in one state and now in another, are seen to be in motion. For to stand fixed in the same state is not proper to created nature, since 'But you are the same' is said in the proper sense of God alone. 'But the soul,' say the champions of division, 'is circumscribed in the body, receives passions and endures pains. If the Word is united in this way, it is time for you to subject him to the same things as well, and to make him passible and circumscribed.' What then? Are you not the ones, I would say, who are establishing the very things you charge us with? For you are afraid to join him to flesh and to a whole man, as though he would of necessity be circumscribed and suffer. If the Word is passible by nature, or admits circumscription in place, these things will be in him because of himself, not because of his union with a circumscribed and passible body; and he will then be passible and circumscribable even if he has neither suffered nor been circumscribed. But if by nature he is immutable, uncircumscribed and impassible, then even when he comes to be in a body he preserves [?] the principle of impassibility and immutability that is his own. For neither when he created the world, bringing it into this form when it did not exist before, does he appear to have fallen from what is above the world into what surrounds the world or is within it, or to have passed from his own uncircumscribedness into being circumscribed by it. So he was not circumscribed earlier, when he brought forth the world and everything in it, nor later, when he fastened around himself man, the great world in a small one. And what wonder is that? Even the soul of man suffers these things, not simply because it is in a body, but because it is by nature apt to suffer even without a body; otherwise it would also be seen, and would suffer all the other things that belong to the body. But it has not suffered these, since it possesses what it has essentially, having received it from God. It suffers, however, because it has passible powers, which also go with it when it departs from the body. This is shown by the souls in Hades and their bonds, on account of which Christ's presence there also took place, when, as Peter says, he preached release to the spirits in prison. It is shown too by the unclean demons, who are punished now and will be punished hereafter, although they are free of human bodies. The soul, then, suffers in the simple sense because it has received passible powers fitted to it for its own benefit [?]; but it also suffers bodily passions, beyond the

…the temperament of the body to which it is bound, and the particular character of the places in which it may live. Since by nature it is simply capable of being affected, it can also receive this kind of affection. It is circumscribed by the principle of its existence, and it is said to be circumscribed in a secondary sense because it lives its life in a circumscribed body. It may also experience divine things in a godly way. This happens least of all through the body, for how could it, when the body often even resists? It happens through the soul itself and its own nature: the desiring part is stretched up toward God in love, the spirited part is braced manfully and stretched out without swerving together with the desiring part, and the reasoning part receives the immaterial impressions without shadow and is illumined in a unified way. A certain God-wise man before us said it well (e): "The one who longs for true knowledge is one good and eternal desire." When the soul defiles these powers, it falls into vice and ignorance. It does not get its vices from the body, even if some of them are carried out through the body. The Word of God could never take on any of these, since he is unchangeable and unalterable in nature. Yet the impassibility of his nature will not make him refuse to be joined essentially to human nature. Otherwise the refusal would itself be a real passion, namely the fear of coming to be among those things in which the souls of earnest people, with him as their helper and assistant, have received no harm from the body. Instead they have grown rich toward God, using the body as a fellow worker for virtue and not as an adversary.
— "If," they say, "the hypostasis of the Word is perfect, and that of the man he assumed is also perfect, and the Word has remained unchangeable while the flesh has been preserved without alteration, how is it not pious to speak of two hypostases, with neither of them confused?"
— They seem to me to put their questions most maliciously and most ignorantly. We have already set out what "perfect" means and how it can be said, namely in two senses, and we have also explained the proper meaning of "hypostasis." Yet they act as if we had not. They shift from "the nature of the Word," a phrase that signifies the common element of the nature together with what is particular to the hypostasis. (We said "nature of the Word," not simply "nature," because the phrase refers to its proper meaning as hypostasis.) Then they say the hypostasis of the Word is perfect. By this they mean the self-complete nature of the Lord, which is no other than that of the Father and differs only by the distinguishing mark of the property of generation. So they predicate the property in place of that in which the property exists, and the relation to one another in place of the things of which it is predicated. For some names indicate the nature of the underlying subjects, while others make known the relation between things. Between things of different kinds and things of the same kind one can find the sharing of relations criss-crossing. (e) Scholion: Concerning Evagrius. (17) Contemplations. By "immaterial impressions" he means the contemplations of invisible things, that is, of things that are not seen.

For in the respects in which things of the same kind share with things of different kinds, they are divided from one another, and in the respects in which they are divided from things of different kinds, they are joined to one another. They are distinguished from one another by number and joined to one another by definition, and in this way they are distinguished from things of a different kind. Two relations, then, are observed with respect to the same Word. By one the Son is identical with the Father, and by the other the Son is distinguished from him. The first is made plain by the term "nature," and the second is made known by the name "hypostasis." But these people switch the relations around and assign to the flesh the relation that distinguishes him from the Father. They do not know what [?] hypostasis is: the whole essence of the Word is the nature of God, perfect from perfect, but the property of generation has caused it to be called hypostasis and Son. In the same way, in the case of the Father, the property of being unbegotten and of being cause has shown him to be hypostasis and Father. The same must be understood of the Holy Spirit as well. The nature is not something that completes Father, Son and Holy Spirit, so that it would be no more in the one than in the three. By nature the Trinity is exactly what any one of those contemplated in the Trinity is. It is not one perfect thing made of three imperfect ones. Out of three perfect ones it is one thing that is more than perfect and prior to perfection, as the great Dionysius says somewhere. So we contemplate six relations. Two are of the Father to the Word and of the Word to the Father. Two are of the Word to the flesh and of the flesh to the Word. Two are of Christ to us and of us to him. These make three general pairs. The relation in the first of these pairs is the same as in the third, but the second, the middle one, is different. In the respects in which the extremes are akin to each other, they are opposed to the middle. The middle is the reverse: in the respects in which it is opposed within itself, it is akin to the extremes, and in the respects in which it is akin within itself, it is opposed to the extremes. I have said this briefly, so I will try to make it clear with an example. Let us posit three things: soul simply, body simply, and a man composed of soul and body. Let us also posit their relations to one another, such as soul to soul, soul to its own body, and man to soul simply. One soul is united with another by identity of essence and distinguished from it by difference of hypostasis. This is what the first and last relation of the pairs preserves. A soul is distinguished from its own body by difference of nature but united with it by the principle of hypostasis, which their shared life in each other has produced. This is what the second and middle relation preserves. A man, however, stands in relation to body simply and soul simply as a whole that is entirely distinct from them,

and because of his first relation to his own parts, he forms a second communion with them. In the same way Christ, as a whole made of parts, stands in relation to us and to the Father and mediates between the extremes through his own parts. He is wholly a hypostasis in relation to us [?], with the Godhead through the humanity [?]. The relations of distinction and union alternate: there are those he is known to have toward himself through his own parts, and those he has toward the Father and toward us through the kinship of the parts with the extremes. But "parts" must be understood charitably. I do not call them parts as if they were imperfect in nature. I call them parts because they complete the person of the hypostasis of Christ. This is how Gregory and Cyril spoke both of "the whole" and of "not one nature," and of the imperfect and the perfect, both absolutely and relatively.
— What, then, do they say? "Do we not speak of one nature of man, even though we know that the things that have come together are different? So what harm is there if, just as here we call the natures a nature without abolishing the distinct character of the parts, we appear to do the same in the case of Christ? Yet you revile and disparage us for supposedly conceiving a confusion in Christ, because we signify the parts by the name of the whole."
— If you wanted to call the parts by the name of the whole, you certainly ought also to have made the whole known by the name of the parts, and then we would have had no grudge against you. If you had preferred to call the Lord flesh or man, you would have signified the whole by a part, but you would not have called the two natures one nature. Failing to speak properly often produces disagreement in doctrine as well. That is why we, following the divine Scriptures and the contemplations handed down from the fathers, often call the whole by a part and the parts by the name of the whole. We name the Word "Son of Man" and confess that "the Lord of glory" was crucified. Yet because of this exchange of properties we do not abolish the proper principle of what is distinctive to each within the same subject. Moreover, these things are made known to us by proper terms: we see the exchange of properties in the one hypostasis, and we recognize what is distinctive within what is common in the difference of the natures. You, however, have used the example of man and destroy the example together with the prototype itself. We do speak of one nature of man, but not, as you would claim, by making the nature of the flesh identical with the essence of the soul, or the reverse. Nor do we say that the two together have produced something that is neither of them. When we call this a nature, we are not looking at the relation of the parts, for no principle damages their difference of nature, even in the union. Instead we predicate what the universal and the species signify of the particular and individual. Those who sort out logical questions teach that particulars share in universals and universals are predicated of particulars, and that individuals share with the species according to

[?], while universals share with the parts according to the name. As I said, we have not refused to call the part by the name of the whole. The one nature represents the whole of the human species, and none of those counted under the same species is of a different essence. So the particular is fittingly named by the name of what is common. One cannot find any individual man who differs in kind from man in general. But in Christ no such order of relation is found. There is no species of Christs, as there is of men, in which one of them would be called Christ in a particular way alongside a universal and common Christ. Only then could he be said to be one nature with them and from them, and only then could we call him both one nature and two natures, having the one through what is common and the other through his own parts, as we see in our own case. Since the cause is not found, and from that [?] which is in our case, it is not possible to apply to him what is properly said only of us. Here it is clear in what sense man is called one nature and two natures. He has the one through sharing in the species, and he has the other through the unchangedness of the parts. But since there is no species in Christ's case, how could the two be called one? We find three ways, and only three, in which something is called one nature. It is either the species itself, or it shares in the same species, or something of a different kind has been produced by confusion out of things of different kinds. Such a thing shares in each but is purely neither, and those versed in these matters call it a hybrid. Besides, you put forward such objections in order to do away with speaking of two. You do not do it in order to say both two and one, as in this case, but in order to say one only. That is why the affliction of confusion surfaces in your position even against your will. Nor does the affliction of division go away. For one nature need not be one in number. On the contrary, it may well be many, as many in number as the hypostases that complete it. (22) Let us also look at it this way. Things equal to the same thing, they say, are also equal to one another. Let an equilateral right-angled triangle be drawn in a diagram. As the first side is to the second, and the second to the third, so too is the first to the last. Draw the three sides, assign three persons, one to each side, and you will find that as the first is to the middle, and the middle to the

last, [so is the first to the last]. This is why I say: if you grant that the Word and the flesh are said to have one nature, and you also confess that the Word and the Father have one nature, then you will have to grant that the flesh and the

— But, they say, we do not say that each pair has one nature in the same way. In the case of the Father and the Son it is by identity of nature, but here it is by the principle of union.
— Then what is called one by union is not the same as what is one by nature. And if it is not the same, one is so in one respect and the other in another respect. The same thing will therefore be one and two: one by union, two in natures. If not, the same thing in the same respect will be both consubstantial and of a different substance, both one nature and not one nature. What could be more absurd than that? So the one nature you speak of has not escaped division, which a nature has in the many persons who share in it (25). It has also brought in confusion through the identity of the composite nature, since after the union it presents neither of the things united. We, God willing, have kept both truths safe. The difference of the things united is proclaimed even in the union by speaking of two natures. The identity of the person is summed up as the united natures come together into one hypostasis.
— As you saw fit, you established beforehand that in the case of each individual man both two natures and one nature are spoken of. What follows from this? That in Christ one must confess not only two natures but three. So how can you confess the one and deny the other? The force of the argument has compelled you to say this even against your will.
— What, then, do we say to this? Only what suits them: that, as Scripture says, "wisdom is [beyond?] a fool" [?]. Theirs are unexamined arguments. It is as if they do not chew their own arguments and so do not digest them either. From the bad food of ignorance they belch up at us vapours that are, how can I put it inoffensively, not sweet-smelling. Every inquiry examines what is in doubt and draws its conclusion from what is agreed. These people, however (for they are not wise, to say nothing of their lack of education), set out what is agreed as though it were doubtful and needed examining, and they reason about what is obvious as though it were obscure. According to the common notions of everyone, the nature of man indicates soul and body, and, as I have often said, it signifies the parts together with the whole. Yet they treat what everyone concedes as a puzzle, as though one of us were declaring that man is a double thing, or body alone, or soul alone. For this reason they demand that we speak of three natures in Christ as well, as though human nature were not enough to bring its parts along with it. We speak of two natures, not of God and flesh, nor (23) In the margin: that is, of whole men.

of God and soul, but of God and man. The nature of a part is not properly the nature of man. So whoever says "man" or "nature of man" has indicated the natures. But whoever names Christ has named neither a term that is agreed upon and falls within our notions, nor a reality

This is shown by the different opinions about him among Christians. They are many and varied, they fight with one another, and they would not have arisen if the name "Christ" had signified the truth of the underlying reality straightaway. The name "man" is common and known to everyone, not least to Christians. But the name "Christ" resembles a technical or scientific term. Such terms are known only to those who have received the same training. In the same way, the truth hidden in this name has been made clear only to those who are wise in divine things. Our opponents themselves bear witness to the truth of this argument. They always affirm that Christ is from two natures and never say that he is from three, even though they too grant a rational soul to the flesh of Christ. Or else let them take the lead in this lack of education and confess him to be from three natures, and we will go along with it, confessing that the things from which he came to be are preserved in that in which they are known. But then they will be forced to say that he is from more than three, as we shall show again. A simple and general grasp of things gives us a comprehensive but unarticulated notion, while dividing them in thought leads us to exact knowledge of the things of which they are composed. That is why we distinguish the whole into its parts. But after the first division, trying to cut the parts into parts of parts is ridiculous, for the inquiry does not stop there but goes on to infinity. What I mean is this. The parts of man are soul and body. The parts of his parts, in the case of the soul, are rational essence and incorporeal quality. Of these, one is the ruling part, another the spirited part, and another the desiring part. Of these in turn, one is conceptual and discursive, remembering, deliberating and forming opinions; another is appetitive and averse [?]; another is defensive and active. And they are subdivided into many others besides. Let us leave aside for now the question whether these are in the soul as parts or as powers, and which are one and which the other, for that is not part of the present inquiry. Again, the body is divided into parts that are uniform and parts that are not. These are further divided into head, hands and feet; these into bones, flesh and sinews; these into the four elements; and these into matter and form. The sons of physicians also philosophize at length about the natural faculties, which they call attractive, retentive, alterative and excretive. They say much too about sensation and imagination, and about the vital and instrumental [faculty] that holds the living creature together

It is enough, then, to present all these by saying "flesh" or "human body," and it is enough again to indicate by "rational soul" the parts into which the soul is divided. Technical hair-splitting is neither welcome nor customary among the faithful. In the same way, whoever has said "man" or "nature of man" has presented and indicated everything of which man is composed and in which he is known. Our opponents, however, devise such sophistries not to show that man is perfect, but to slander the Lord and to make him a stranger to our nature. They would have him either not assume what is ours at all, or not keep safe what he received from us, the unfailing pledge of salvation for the whole of our nature. Let them learn, then, that confessing the parts, as I said, is a mark of the salvation of the whole. But subdividing the parts into further parts does not belong to the conciseness of doctrine, nor to the word "cut short" according to the Gospel. It belongs to a [?] kind of speculation and to technical analysis that most people find superfluous and hard to grasp. The parts of Christ, unconfused, are Godhead and humanity. Soul and body are not parts of Christ but parts of the part. They are already indicated by the complete meaning that belongs to the nature of the humanity, so subdividing the parts into natures is superfluous. Unless, that is, our opponents mean to add to these subdivisions the further division that we used earlier in the case of man in general. They would then proclaim not merely three natures of Christ, as they hold, but even more. What could be more laughable than that?
— Since the whole war has been stirred up because most people do not know the mode of the union, and so everyone disputes it, you must examine this question philosophically. Then we can know whether we disagree about the mode itself, or whether we agree on it and our inquiry concerns the result of the union. We can also know whether it concerns the realities themselves or the words that signify them. Once the inquiry has been made clear in this way and the truth of the matter has come to light, anyone who contradicts out of ignorance or impiety will be exposed, either to be corrected or to be justly blamed.
— Some have declared that the union of the Godhead with the humanity came about by essence, others by activity, and others by will. Some, having or feigning excessive scruple, have attached themselves to none of these views. They declared instead that the union came about in a way that is ineffable and cannot be named. Whether or not they really held this, they did so because they feared being refuted for impiety. Even now we have seen some who hold a quite expressible and well-worn notion of the union and yet call it ineffable. They do this not only to establish one thing by its opposite, that is, the expressible by the ineffable, but also to dodge refutation. In just the same way others too, in the case of the flesh of the

…of the Lord, to strengthen the fantasy, being eager for confusion, "He became flesh," they say, "as he willed, and as he alone knows." For it is not to establish these things that they resort to this truly irreverent reverence (otherwise the truth would have led them to its own light). Rather, so that they may freely indulge their impiety, they take refuge in the solemn names as in some strong and impregnable fortress. Truly ineffable and inconceivable is the union according to essence, the essential and enhypostatic union, and it alone. For how did things so different in nature, and so far apart from one another, come together, and how were they mixed without being confused? Yet it is one and is known as two. It is neither blended together in the singleness of the person, nor divided into hypostases because of the properties of the natures. Faith alone can grasp these things, together with divine reason, which makes them plain not by spoken words but by illumination of the mind, and initiates the worthy through ineffable [?] teachings. Now those who are sick in their reverence, so long as their aim remains unclear, do not deserve even a word. They neither openly embrace the light, if they happen to have it, nor are they troubled that their souls are wrapped in darkness. As incurable, let them be spat out by us too. With the others, however, let us argue as follows. Those who have taught that the union is not according to essence but according to operation, or good pleasure, or some other such relation, come nowhere near the truth. They would have divided the many-branched lie among themselves, each snatching off a different portion of it, and they come together as one only in missing the truth. For what kind of union would this be, and how would it deserve the name of union (that supernatural union, unique after the unique and first one), if it does not bind the realities together and bring them into one and the same? Hence it occurs to me to wonder that, while they champion such a union, they throw in the words "unconfused" and "unchanged." For what sort of change is it fair to suspect them of in this division of the realities, when they confuse the dignities into one dignity (for dignities could never become one dignity without confusion, any more than natures could become one nature without change), but separate the essences? A union of dignity is not a union of realities. Otherwise we would by this reasoning bring all who have received divine dignity into identity with the divine essence, and teach two natures in each of the saints. For the amount of dignity does not wholly separate things that differ in dignity. However great it may be, to that extent it will also join the natures, since it will certainly not wholly separate them from what joins them, not being wholly separated itself. For as far as they share in the dignity, so far must they also share in the nature of the Word. [?] He has also made use of the [?] …

But if they wish to join the other saints besides Christ to some other member of the Trinity, let that be left to their impiety. For the saints have been called gods, and sons of God, and holy spirits, according to the text, "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." How is it, then, that when all rational and blessed creation, whether among angels or among men, has been filled with the deifying and adopting grace of the Spirit, he alone who appeared from the Virgin is called God and Son of God, in word and in truth, and is worshipped by every rational nature? The godless ought to know this: if the higher do not enjoy some special privilege in the varied distribution of gifts over the lower, but the gift of operation and the bestowal of dignity are common to all, then they must do one of two things. Either they must join those saints too into two natures with God the Word, or with whichever member of the Holy Trinity they please, or even with the whole venerable Trinity, and divide two or three or four hypostases. Or else they must not join any of them to the nature of God the Word, and must either combine this man with the Word into one Son, or make him a son only in name, alongside the archetypal Son, and stop thinking one thing while saying another. For since natural sonship is one, and all other sonship comes from it by participation, the man they have improvised must share either in the natural sonship or in the sonship that comes by grace. So they must either join him to the Only-begotten, since the essential union exchanges what belongs to the one nature with the other, or, if they cannot bear to be pious, openly set him apart and rank him with the rest. But they do not avow their impiety openly (for evil by nature cannot speak openly), yet they do not love the truth, nor do they fear the wages of a deceitful tongue. Let them be driven out of the divine choir, together with the fathers of impiety, Nestorius and all who became his initiators and initiates. But let the truth of the union according to essence be proclaimed aloud, and let us reason about it as it itself sees fit. For there is no small danger that those who turn aside from it fall into the opposite but equal evil, by which I mean confusion. So that we may recognize the difference between things united according to essence without being changed and things that by nature are changed by the union, and what the form of the first is and what the result of the second, let us now make the division. All beings are joined to one another by universal common features, and again divided from one another by specific differences. Nor do they separate what is united by these unions [?]. Rather, if one may speak paradoxically and with the Fathers, they are united while divided and distinguished while joined. Unions and distinctions are of two kinds. Some things are united in species but divided in hypostases; others are divided in species but united

in hypostases. Of those united in species but divided in hypostases, some have a simple union and distinction, others a composite one. Let us leave aside for now those whose twofold relation is simple. Their detailed [?] does not belong to the present inquiry, and in any case it lies beyond the knowledge and learning of most people. But we must speak of things joined by composition (that is, by interweaving, or mixture, or union, or whatever one likes to call it), the essential relations of things of different species. We leave to the word-fighters the meanings they consider more expressive or more proper, for we have no time to pick words when we are pressing on to understanding. Of things that exist essentially and are united according to essence, some keep their own principle of existence even in the union. Others are confused and, by damaging them, make the extremes that were united vanish. In the former, the relation observed between them and within them produces one thing out of both, and shows them to be, as one might say, one in number, while preserving the difference of existence within the sameness of the unity. An example of this among living things is our own human being, and among simple or natural bodies, a certain relation to one another of things that subsist in themselves and are able to exist on their own. One may observe this in a lamp. The wick is one thing, and the flaming substance of the fire is another, but being together and in one another, both have made one lamp. And, to force the expression, one might say it is fire made wood and wood set on fire. The one has shared in the brightness of the fire, the other has partaken of the earthy thickness of the torch, and they have exchanged their properties with each other while remaining in their own lasting and unconfused property. Let no malicious person seize on the example again if it has some point of unlikeness, bringing up the oil that mediates their union, or the underlying oily quality, or the fact that it does not last over time but turns to ash. Let him remember what we said earlier about examples and their definition. The same would be found in the blending of fire with air, and of air with water. For the mixing of water with earth touches on the confusing kind of union. It opens the way for liquid and fine-grained things, which differ in the variation of their qualities, to undergo the change and alteration that come from the extremes acting on each other. I pass over the qualities, which often come to be in one another and are joined without mixing even when their substances are separate. In the same way the gleams of the light-bearing stars mingle with each other and with the air and keep the property of quantity within quality. Art, which imitates nature, shows this. If, as the great Dionysius says, someone lit many torches and shut them in

one house, and then detached one from all the rest and took it out of the room, it would carry its light out with it, and leave nothing of its own behind for the others. In general, none of the things united undergoes change or confusion unless each of them has passive qualities. Where this is not so, the active one would act and not be acted on, and the passive one would be acted on and not act. But things that share a common principle of acting on each other are acted on and act on one another, more or less, according to whether the causes of affection prevail or are equally balanced. So it is with all fusible things, with metals, and with whatever physicians or craftsmen have contrived by their art to mix or melt together. With these distinctions made beforehand, one must know the following. Things that alter and change one another, made up of many forms and different substances, keep none of their components pure after the composition. The composition mixes and confuses the properties of all of them and produces out of them all a new, wholly mixed form, different from them all. In the mixing there arises a blending and confusion of many hypostases and natures, which preserves neither the particularity of the hypostasis nor the common feature of the nature. It produces something else, which has come from these but is identical with none of the things from which it came. If, then, divinity and humanity, united according to essence, do not keep their own natural property even in the union, they are confused. Neither divinity nor humanity has remained, but the union has produced another kind of essence, which came from them and is not them. What could be more impious or abominable even to imagine, let alone to hold and to teach as doctrine? It remains, then, from our examination of the principle of the union according to essence, to take the unconfused property of divinity and humanity after the manner of the earlier examples. From them all we gather a dim image of the truth that is beyond them all. It shows that the result of these is one thing, whether one likes to call it person, or hypostasis, or individual, or subject, or anything else; I do not quarrel about it. As for those who separate the natures by joining them through dignity, or authority, or some such dividing relation, our argument has already struck them down and driven them off. It has refuted them for dividing the natures into hypostases, and for making them have no communion or exchange or

Having said these things according to the small measure of understanding given us by God, we refer the reader to the teachings of the God-inspired Fathers. From them we too have drawn these things, and with the account of our lowly mind, as from a small mixing bowl, we have tried to give the lovers of truth something to drink. And you who long for the truth, may you have these pages as a remedy against forgetfulness, and after our final departure as a memorial of love, so that the beauty of love may not flow away with time [?] and be

gone. Muzzle the more audacious, and lead the simpler by the hand to the pure and clear radiance of the truth that shines out through these things in the holy Fathers. And pray for us, who, as our conscience bears witness, have undertaken to write these things out of love, even against our inclination. To God be thanksgiving for all his gifts in all things, forever. Amen.

PREFACE TO THE CITATIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS. As I am about to set out the citations of the holy Fathers to confirm our arguments, I ask the reader to pay close attention. The instruction of the wonderful counselors of the Spirit needs an intelligent hearer, for a word labors when it sounds in ears weighed down with the filth of ignorance. "As a golden earring and a precious sardius are set together, so is a wise word in an obedient ear," as wise Proverbs has declared. Let us therefore cleanse our hearing, which perceives divine things, of every burden that comes from prejudice and deafens the mind. And now we shall bring forward "the cloud of witnesses," as the Apostle says, in the hope that the disobedient may yield to witnesses so great. Because of their inherited love of quarreling, we have brought forward no ambiguous or doubtful citation, nor have we called more obscure Fathers as witnesses. We have called on the most illustrious, who shone brightly throughout the world, and have brought in the clearest and most indisputable testimonies, shutting off every scheme of theirs against the truth. We have not used citations with "out of which," or "from which," or "by which," or "before the union," as they like to say, or "in the union" but not also "after the union" (if indeed, by their wisdom, the union has an end). Rather, we have shown the saints proclaiming "in which" and "through which," "both," "through both," and "the two," natures and essences that exist and are preserved in the union, and remain undivided forever in the essential hypostatic union. Someone may not respect their number or the trustworthiness of their persons, like the impious man in Scripture ("For impious," it says, "is he who has not respected the face of an honored man"). If he brings forward obscure and unknown citations, said to be from these Fathers or from others, that contradict these, let him first show that ours are not really theirs, and then we would accept his. But as long as ours carry weight through the brilliance of the writings and the renown of the Fathers, we should either not accept at all the citations that campaign against them, or, if we accept them, interpret them as having a meaning that agrees with ours and conflicts with it in nothing. For trying to drive the theologians into contradiction, and claiming that they disagreed with one another, is an undertaking not against us but against their glory [?]

—or rather against the glory of Paul, and indeed against the authority of the Holy Spirit and of Christ who speaks in him. For after the apostles and the prophets, God has set teachers in the Church, according to the unsearchable dispensation of the Spirit, "for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ." So whoever does not accept the Fathers who are illustrious and renowned in the Church of God openly resists God's ordinance. How essence differs from hypostasis, that is, nature from person, can be learned from the great luminaries Basil and Gregory. They brought what we are now investigating under rule and definition. They taught clearly what essence is and what hypostasis is; that nature is the same as essence, and hypostasis the same as person; how these terms are used and of what; and their interchange, and the reverse interweaving that theology has with the economy through the combining and exchanging of these names. After setting out their words, we shall bring forward the other holy teachers too, with one or two citations each that present to us the whole mind of these divinely wise men. These are enough to put the fair-minded to shame. Those who are not so would not be persuaded even by the whole choir of saints, even if we drew out all their teachings and poured them out at once. Of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, on "A child is born to us." The same is truly God and without falsehood man: consubstantial with the Father in what he was, and of my race, without sin, in what he became. The divine nature is uncreated; the nature assumed from me is unadulterated. And he is one Son, not because the natures are divided into two hypostases, but because the awe-inspiring economy has united the natures into one hypostasis. Of Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and
