For as the ark was overlaid with pure gold within and without, so too the body of Christ was pure and translucent: within, adorned by the Word,

[?] and without, made radiant by the Spirit, so that from both the splendor of the natures might be displayed. Of Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, from [?]. Of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria and martyr, from his work On the Coming of the Savior. And to Judas he says, "Do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" These sayings and others like them, and all the signs that he worked, and the miracles, show him to be God made man. Both together, then, are shown: that he was God by nature and became man by nature. Of Saint Cyriacus, bishop of [?] and confessor, from the discourse on the Theophany; he too was one of those at Nicaea. "Who, being in the form of God," he says, "did not count equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave." If the form of God is equal to God, and he was perfect God, then the form of the slave is also perfect man (for this is what divine Scripture teaches). Christ is perfect in both essences: consubstantial with God the Father, and consubstantial with the Virgin Mother; without a mother above, from the Father, and without a father below, from his mother. [?] Ambrose, bishop of Milan and [?]. Of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan and confessor, from the work Against Apollinaris [?] and confessor, from the work Against Apollinaris.

For he is one in each, that is, in the divinity and in the body. For it is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin, but the same one, having one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin. And neither does one birth take precedence over the other, nor the flesh over the divinity.

So, while remaining in the perfection of the divinity, he emptied himself and took what is perfect, human nature in its entirety. Just as he lacked nothing as God, so he lacked nothing in his human makeup, so that he might be perfect in each nature. Of Gelasius, bishop of Caesarea, who also belonged to the synod of the 150, from the Interpretation of the Creed. But human tongue alone could not accomplish this, for the nature was weak. So God and man came together into one, so that the body might serve and God might supply the working through it. Everything is twofold, everything is true, everything is perfect. Let every heretical mouth be muzzled: God is with us; he who is with the Father is with us; he who is from us is with us. "My flesh," he says, "is from them." But the one is always, the other is for our sake. The divinity is always, the humanity is for our sake. Of the same, from the same discourse. But let us, lit by the divine Word, keep the nobility of the Only-begotten free from insult. Let us neither reject the Word because of the lowliness of the flesh, nor disregard the flesh because of the loftiness of the divinity. Rather, let us honor the Word as God and the flesh as the temple of God. Of the great Ephrem, from the discourse on the pearl.

The precious pearl shares in two natures, to show forth Christ: that, being the Word of God, he was born a man from Mary. He did not have a partial nature, for then he would have been some other kind of creature. He has the twofold nature complete, so as not to lose the two. He neither appeared on earth as a demigod, nor ascended to heaven as half a man. He is perfect from the perfect, man from man, God from God, Christ from the Virgin. Of Saint Flavian, bishop of Antioch, from the discourse on the Gospel according to John [?]. For he who took our nature upon himself showed himself through the cloud of the body, so that we might be taught both his natures: the man who was seen, and the divinity working through the body.

Of Antiochus, bishop of Ptolemais; the blessed Cyril mentioned this citation. Do not confuse the natures, and you will not be bewildered about the economy. Hold to God, and give what befits God; receive what is human, and give what befits humanity. Scholion of Leontius. In addition to all the foregoing, we have been careful to set out also citations of the blessed Cyril that confirm the Fathers before him and explain his whole mind. In this way they may know that neither he nor any other of the Fathers said "from two" or "from both" in order to do away with "in two." For [?] in fighting against the division of Nestorius, he not only used "from which" but also applied the preposition "in" to both, as can easily be learned at once from the citations of his that we have appended. And in all of them we have been careful to set out only the indisputable citations, which not even madmen will be able to misinterpret.

TO THOSE OF OUR OWN WHO HAVE JOINED THE CORRUPT SECT OF THE APHTHARTODOCETAE. In what we said earlier we have, with God's help be it said, refuted as well as we could the objections and counterarguments of the knowledge falsely so called. Those of the opposite Docetism use them against us (for I will never stop calling them this, since it would not even be right to stop), and they suppose they can lead the simpler away from the straight path. Now I will try once again to unfold and clarify the study of another question and problem. Let Christ lead the discourse, he who is God and Word, and light, and life,

…and truth, breathing understanding into us, so that with grace and the wisdom from above we may rightly understand what bears on our subject and be able to express it. Now if I saw that the infighting which has now broken out among our opponents stayed among them, and did not strive to cross over to us as well, I might perhaps even have counted the battle and mutual opposition of our adversaries a gain. As they were struck down and overthrown by one another, they caused us no trouble and gave us only the bare spectacle of the war. We would have grieved over one thing only: the ruin of those who dared to rebel against the house of David, as the oracle says, and who then despised even concord with the house of Jeroboam and did not keep even that, but were split and divided from one another and against one another. So the more discerning may recognize the tree by its fruit, as the Saviour's saying has it, since their many-branched factions show most clearly the turbulent spirit at work in them. For a love of enmity and a delight in war are somehow bound up with impiety by nature. But now the enemies' hostility toward one another has turned out to our harm. O the ignorance! [?] We have become more wretched than those who rank second among them in wickedness [?], unable to watch over and guard our own affairs even as well as our enemies do. For the father of one party in the schisms recognized what was needed and shrank from open war against the truth, while we have made their recognition a provision for ignorance and have become even more foolish than our enemies. Severus and Julian, the two leaders of the one impiety, fell out with each other, foolishly with regard to their own principles but sensibly with regard to the truth itself, and fought over the corruptible. Those of Severus's party, to speak truthfully, profited from the wickedness of their enemies, for what no one could have persuaded them to say before this, their present hostility toward their own people compelled them to confess. But when they began to lift their eyes toward the rays of the truth, some of our own took their lifting up as an occasion for blindness. These joined the worse side, came by means of a single word to the same position as our opponents, and for the sake of a seemly name threw away, together with them, the whole economy. For while those men, as I said, were inquiring foolishly with regard to [their own principles, but sensibly with regard to] the starting points of the truth whether one must call corruptible and passible the body which our Lord bore from us and for our sake and accepted, Severus came to his senses, late but nonetheless. He profited from the war against his own people, being compelled to confess and proclaim difference and properties. Yet it would be just like his wisdom, and that of those who emulate him, to predicate difference and properties of no underlying realities, or, while refusing to confess two natures, to speak of two

properties, of the corruptible and the incorruptible, and now to be not in the least wary of the division into a duality, which he used to attack in the past, turning everything upside down and throwing it all into confusion. How could anyone not marvel at the learning of this man? He proclaims participation in a loud voice, yet he not only guards against that from which participation is derived but even hastens to make war on it. For if he says that the body is passible by nature, and grants it natural passions, and that after the union, then let the wise man answer us whether natural things do not come from nature, just as things made by art come from art. But we have reserved what concerns him for longer discussions, or for those of our people who have the most leisure. And what would you say about those who always proclaim these things in a loud and piercing voice, and who also confess one operation of the flesh and another of the Godhead, passion in the body and impassibility in the Word? They have granted that these interpenetrate and are predicated each of the other in turn, because the property of the one passes over into the other. But now, as if on purpose, they fall foul of their own teachings and have gone over to incorruption. I do not know what one ought to say of them, whether I should marvel at their firmness or praise their fickleness, swept off toward the plausibility of the deception by a single seemly word, a bait for the greed of the soul [?]. We know that others too, both long ago and now, have suffered the same. Some in earlier times went over to the deception of the Encratites and were dragged by the elegance of the word into the pit of Mani. Others were defiled with the uncleanness of the so-called Cathars, the 'Pure', and were corrupted by nothing other than that charming name. And many, both new and old, whose names it would be most laborious to list, have fallen into the pit of Nestorius through their impassioned advocacy of the impassibility of the Word. In short, we know of whole fleets of souls seized and sunk, as if by some Scylla or by the opposite Charybdis, because they stumbled in their ignorance over the humbler words and deeds of Christ our God, which come from his condescension to what is ours. For what else [?] drove the countless tribes of the nations, and the Jewish phalanxes, to madness against us, but what Paul called the foolishness of the preaching? And who would not marvel at the learning of the new dogmatists? If it had been possible, as their nonsense would have it, then all the celebrated martyrs and all the confessors could have received the crowns for piety without any tortures, by means of these two words, had they only happened to learn them. But the martyrs had no share in this great wisdom of theirs, so they departed this life as a mere by-product of a deception and never became monuments of courage for the world. For none, I think, even of the bitterest and most hostile persecutors would have exacted any penalty from Christians

if they had confessed at the tribunal that the one born of the Virgin, crucified, buried and raised, was only a man. What envy would have come over the persecutors at the proclamation of a man's resurrection? They were not seized with jealousy over any of the many others who are said, whether in fables or in true history, to have come back to life. Nor would they have been, if, as those schooled in the new wisdom say, the very body of Christ were also impassible, immutable and unalterable. [?] Their same licence leaves them free also to blaspheme that body as invisible, intangible and impalpable, without quality and without quantity, in short bodiless, for they conceive all these things together with this marvellous name of incorruption. For what is this arbitrary allotment, to give the body some of the names fit for God but deprive it of others, and to cut away a large part of the dignity and honour of what they, to its dishonour, imagine to be a superessential, supernatural and bodiless body? And which of the unbelievers would be angry with us if we said that the Lord's body was not by nature seen, did not take food and drink, did not sleep or suffer, and did not undergo all the other things of human weakness that it was not ashamed to endure without sin? It is surely plain to everyone that many such things have already happened by the law of miracle and not by the principle of nature. The populous Jewish people would never have been driven to such a frenzy if any argument had suggested to them that the body they crucified, which accepted suffering and was buried by his acquaintances, was not like us in every respect and truly of human nature. Since the holy Scripture is filled with many appearances of God, one can see that the good providence of our God toward us, for the benefit of those it was caring for, lowered itself into human forms and actions, operations and words. Yet none of these things led them to form human notions about the Divine, even though he managed these things in a human way. But their own outrages convince them that the Lord is a man subject to the same passions as everyone, even if the miracles have not convinced them that he is also God, raised above all things by the pre-eminence of his nature. So the 'impassibility of the only-begotten Word' that the godless set against Christ, and the 'incorruptibility of the flesh' that the sophists of today set against our salvation, are both seen to be truly passionate and corruptible. The first does not let him who is above us be with us, and the second does not let him who is with us remain as we are. [?] …as the time of healing requires, and the ascent [?] and resurrection of what is ours toward what is above us, taking place in due order and sequence. For how shall we gain the likeness to God unless we suffer with him who suffered? And how did he suffer, unless he suffered as we do? Yet he did not suffer as we do unless he remained as we are. And he was in no way glorified unless he received according to the flesh what he always had according to the spirit.

But recently I met one of those who are wise in such matters, and he said that the Lord's becoming man was enough for our salvation.
Orth. 'Then why,' I said to him, 'would his will alone not have been enough for salvation?'
Aphth. 'It is enough,' he said.
Orth. 'Then how is it,' I said, 'that he did not save us by willing alone?'
Aphth. 'Because,' he said, 'it pleased him to use toward me not his authority but rather his love for humankind and his justice. The one would have been a master's compulsion, the other a father's care. The one would have been force alone, the other also a voluntary condescension. The one would have been his alone, the other ours as well. For it befits God not simply to will, but also to do the things by which he persuades and puts to shame the one he saves.'
Orth. 'Well said, my admirable friend,' said I. 'It seems to me that this is why the new mode of his kindness toward us was introduced, after the frequent and manifold providence he had shown toward humankind from the beginning, as the only remedy for salvation that remained. We could find nothing more effective for turning people to the better than the economy in the flesh. In this way the only wise physician of our souls took the passions of men upon himself and healed the disease of all.'
Aphth. 'Then those of sound mind,' he said, 'may not confess anything other than that the wondrous and great mystery of the divine incarnation is entirely sufficient for our complete salvation.'
Orth. 'Nor would I myself say,' I replied, 'that it is otherwise. But we would most gladly learn the manner of the incarnation, uncovering it more clearly by a diligent inquiry of the mind.'
Aphth. 'Examine it with me,' he said, 'if you like.'
Orth. 'Well then,' I said, 'since God had not only to will but also to do something for us, what he did surely had to be such that nothing could surpass it in wisdom.'
Aphth. 'You are right,' he said, 'since there could be nothing more fitting. Otherwise that other mode, and not this one, would have been needed to achieve perfectly what he intended.'
Orth. 'You say this rightly, my dearest friend,' I said… [?] …no surpassing. 'Such that nothing could surpass it in wisdom': there would have been a surpassing of wisdom if [?]

Aphth. 'You speak divinely,' he said.
Orth. 'So by assuming in essence a whole man, I mean one composed of a body and a rational and intelligent soul, he worked the salvation of the whole man, cleansing like by like.'
Aphth. 'You put that most excellently and most perfectly,' he said.
Orth. But I said to him, 'Then suppose that he took a soul but did not assume mine. Or suppose that he took mine, but not one that existed in its essence just like mine in every respect. Then what was saved would certainly be something other than my soul.'
Aphth. 'Clearly,' he said, 'for the salvation would surely belong to that soul which his own soul exactly resembled…'

Orth. 'In the same way,' I said, 'suppose he took flesh, but not mine. Or suppose he took mine, but altered in some way so that it had some difference, and was not subject to the same passions and in agreement with ours in every respect. Then the salvation would surely belong to that flesh which he made the flesh united to him resemble.'
Aphth. 'And who,' he said, 'has gone so far into madness that he does not confess these things to be true, and does not count those who think otherwise among the condemned?'
Orth. 'Surely those,' I said, 'who define the body as impassible and incorruptible.'
Aphth. 'We do not say,' he said, 'that the body is impassible and incorruptible by nature, but by its union with God the Word.'

Orth. 'The second view is no different from the first,' said I, 'and has just as much power for harm, if the Lord's flesh renounced altogether its kinship with our body in being subject to the same passions.'
Aphth. 'What do you mean?' he said.
Orth. 'I mean,' I said, 'that the question is not whether it became incorruptible by the union or by the constitution of its nature, but whether it kept the marks of our nature unchanged, except for sin…'

Aphth. 'It did, as far as its first constitution is concerned, and in having its beginnings from the Theotokos, who is our sister by nature and shares in every property of the human make-up.'
Orth. 'Your answer,' he said, 'needs a clearer explanation, one that sets the question before us more plainly. For from what you have said one cannot simply know…'

Aphth. 'What have I said so unclearly?' he asked.
Orth. 'Do you mean,' I said, 'that the Virgin's body was changed in its elements and left its own nature through the power of the Word, so that our nature was united to him already in a different condition, straight from the womb itself? Or that the Virgin remained in the properties of her nature, while these first beginnings, I mean the virginal blood, were transformed, and so the flesh became incorruptible?'
Aphth. 'Some of the simpler folk, I think,' he said, 'even hold the first opinion, extolling'

the Virgin more than is fitting. They do not foresee the absurdity that follows from it: if anything of the kind had happened to the Virgin, she would have lost her very capacity to give birth.'
Orth. 'Very true,' said I. 'What has been made incorruptible could never become capable of carrying a child and giving birth in the flesh. Yet the coming of the Spirit did not take away or hinder the Virgin's capacity to bear. On the contrary, it brought her supernaturally to a conception that came about without seed. And something else occurs to me to consider: if, as they say, the Virgin became incorruptible at the coming of the Spirit, then she would surely be the root of our race's incorruption, and not the divine shoot that came forth from her.'
Aphth. 'Excellently said,' he replied. 'Nor is the rest of the Virgin's life ever recorded to have undergone any transformation of her natural state. The coming of the Spirit gave her purity of soul and holiness of flesh, but did not bring about in her any change of substance or nature.'
Orth. 'Add this too,' I said, 'to what has been said: that the Spirit, if [?] what is above nature to exist for nature, to bear an unploughed ear of grain and a branch springing supernaturally from a virgin root.'
Aphth. 'Well said, my good friend,' he said.
Orth. 'Now it is time, my dear friend,' I said, 'for us to examine what follows together, lovingly and gently. Since we agree that the Virgin always remained the same in her nature and did not pass into any state other than the one she had from the beginning, did not the one born from her, the pledge of our nature, go through the stages of gestation by the way and order of nature?'
Aphth. 'Certainly,' he said.
Orth. 'For little by little he grew in the virgin womb by the law of gestation until he was a fully formed infant, as one can hear from the voice of the gospel, which says, The days were fulfilled for her to give birth. There, at the birth, as at the first conception, a strange new wonder is worked, the birth neither [destroying] the virgin'

…and what was assumed was being transformed into incorruption. For how could it fail to put off its corruptible nature once it was united to the incorruptible Word?'
Orth. 'You seem to me, my good friend,' I said, 'rather to be forgetting your own words. Earlier you agreed that the Virgin Theotokos remained unchanged, and that the Creator of the ages did not refuse to dwell in the virgin womb for the appointed time of human gestation while he was being formed there. He consented to dwell in a mother's womb and completed the times of gestation, and the Virgin in no way surpassed us except in her holiness alone. How then, as though he had changed his mind, does he disdain the nature of his own body, and that when it agreed unvaryingly in every respect with the one who bore him…'

Aphth. 'Everyone will agree with that,' he said. 'But that, having taken from the womb the Virgin's corruptible body, he at once changed it into incorruption, is one of the views we consider correct…'

Orth. 'Then where,' I said, 'is the measure and time of his living among us, which we needed most of all? On your view he showed his likeness to us in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, and quickly changed it. Yet we needed not only this, but also that the Lord should live among us and pass through all the stages through which human nature begins, proceeds through those in between, and comes to its own…'

Aphth. 'What was there to prevent it,' he said, 'even though the union had made the body impassible?'
Orth. 'And how,' I said to him, 'could he either have lived among people at all, or have accepted the sufferings on our behalf, if from the first moment of the union he had refused to share our passible and mortal condition?'
Aphth. 'He did suffer,' he answered, 'but surely not by necessity of nature. He suffered by reason of the economy, because the Word permitted him to suffer.'
Orth. 'What you say,' I replied, 'is nothing short of a riddle. How could the flesh have a nature above passions, and yet in turn be permitted to suffer, contrary to its nature, the things that belong to the nature of flesh? If the union with the Word had granted the flesh impassibility, he would not have taken from it what God had given it and once assigned to it. Moreover, if it gained a share in incorruption from its union with the Word, it is time for you to dare, against all law, to split apart that supernatural and wondrous union. What is impassible because of the union could not suffer unless the union were first abolished, just as darkness could never exist unless the cause that gives light withdrew. To put it simply, nothing that derives from a sustaining cause can by nature remain in its effects unless the cause is present. Consider this too [?]: if he endured to be with the body while it suffered, he would also have endured to be united to the body while it was passible.'
Aphth. 'Was it not, then,' he said to us, 'by his willing'

Orth. 'And who,' I answered, 'would say that any of the natural accidents befell the flesh without the Word willing it? Who would deny that he rather permitted the flesh, which is passible by nature, to undergo without sin what is natural to it? It was not that the flesh, being by nature above passions, became passible because of the Word. On the contrary, there were times when it rose even above the natural passions, because the Word granted it, as he often did, mastery over the passions. So the Word's natural union with the flesh is inseparable and unbroken for ever, while freedom from passions did not always remain with the body. The body did not have impassibility from the union, but from the will of the one united to it, who arranged this at the right time and for some useful purpose. If this were not true, one would have to confess one of two things: either that the flesh did not suffer anything at all, being impassible by nature because of the union, or that by suffering it was wholly cut off from the union.'
Aphth. 'If, then,' he said, 'as your argument has it, the flesh had a passible nature and underwent death, as well as everything else, on its own account, then our boasts are gone and have perished, the boasts we have had from that flesh as having suffered for us.'
Orth. 'That the Lord's flesh suffered for us, my good friend,' I said, 'is said in two senses. First, the suffering befell it with the Word's consent, for though he was able to prevent it, he did not, as the great Athanasius says. Second, having shown itself superior to all sin, it did not owe death on its own account. For death entered in the beginning through sin and passed through all human nature, because, as Paul says, all have sinned. There is not and never has been, in all the ages, a human soul pure of sin, whether voluntary or involuntary. Indeed, I would say that even the souls of the saints have taken in some small stain of wickedness, if not in act, at least in thought. One can hear the Lord teaching this clearly where he says, The ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me. By saying "in me" and "nothing" he showed expressly that he alone remained free even from sin in thought. Therefore the condemnation of sin, finding no room in him, came to a halt, was confined, and from then on withdrew from those who were liable to it. For death died when it tasted sinless flesh. But to think that the flesh, being impassible and immortal by nature, voluntarily accepted what was not natural to it, first of all belongs to people who do not know that willing and not willing are not a property of the flesh but of the rational soul. It is in the soul that free will and the will's inclination in either direction are found. Next, they make the flesh out to be culpable, the'

…wills what is contrary to nature, and chooses what is not natural to it. This is the ultimate definition of sin. We should not leave this unremarked either: three causes are observed from which every activity comes about. One comes from natural power; another from a deviation from the natural state; and the third is seen in the ascent and progress toward what is better. Of these, the first is natural, the second contrary to nature, and the third is, and is called, above nature. The one contrary to nature, as its very name shows, is a falling away from natural states and powers, and it damages both the essence itself and its natural activities. The natural one comes about from an unhindered cause, established according to nature. The one above nature leads up and exalts, and empowers toward more perfect things, even things it could not have done had it remained within what is natural. So the things above nature do not destroy the things according to nature. They lead them on and urge them forward, so that they can do both what is natural and also gain the power for what lies beyond it.

A. Make what you are saying clear with a more familiar example, for my mind has not yet grasped it.

O. Consider, then, I said, what can be seen in things made by art. Art rearranges its product, carries the natural formlessness of the underlying matter over into a more seemly shape and form, and calls it forth to greater usefulness, for art bestows what nature did not have. Thus flutes and lyres and similar instruments were made to sound by the compulsion of art. Thus sculpture transforms gold and other materials into countless kinds of irrational animals, and into human forms as well. Mechanics in turn has devised astronomical spheres, timepieces and the like. It would take long to list them all by kind. In all of them the reasoning of art adds the beauty and usefulness of art, while nature remains within its own bounds and suffers no harm at all. In the same way (if we may take lowly things, which bear only a faint echo of the truth, as an example for things divine and higher), conceive with me that the Lord's flesh too kept the laws of nature unharmed even after the supernatural and wondrous union, and yet also received what is above nature. Neither is separated from the other or hindered by it. For things above nature have no place unless nature keeps to what is natural. And if nature changes into what is above nature, it is no longer even a miracle, and generosity becomes an outrage that tyrannizes over the truth.

A. I think so too, he said. But only in this sense: the sufferings happened to the Lord's flesh by way of miracle, while its impassibility and incorruptibility rest on the unfailing laws of nature.

O. And where, I said, did you get this, my good man? Who has been your interpreter of this strange wisdom? Do you not know that a law of nature is not

what is rare, but what is observed and persists always, or at least for the most part? For thirty-three whole years our Lord lived among us in the flesh. By being no different from us in what is ours, he ennobled the human: he ate and drank and slept, and naturally accepted all the other things that establish the truth of the body he had assumed. He did not begin to work miracles before he was thirty. Let no one put forward to me, out of a childish mind, the Lord's childhood miracles. This age is the full test of virtue and the time for teaching. It was then that he preached to us the gospel that truly is, and, bringing faith to his divinely inspired teachings, he sealed his words with the extraordinary character of his miracles. Yet even then he clearly made such use of the natural and blameless properties of the body that he got the reputation of a glutton and a drunkard, filling the measure of need just as we do. And what could you say about his always being seen in our form, going about with the crowd, and in no way differing in appearance from the many? The crowds pressed upon him, as Peter says. And the one who betrayed him gave a sign by which he might be recognized by the God-slayers, because, as one of our own writers has said, the Lord resembled his disciples in appearance. These things went on in sequence and natural order from his first birth until his going up on the cross, and indeed his burial of three days and nights. But to reveal the divinity, which had not yet been made known to the many, he rarely (compared with the whole course of his life) brought about new divine signs in his body. He did so, as I said, to reveal his own divinity, not to abolish the truth of the body. That is why he is made light upon the sea and transfigured on the mountain. Before these, he remained without food for forty whole days and forgot his natural need. He blossomed from a virgin womb while the flower of virginity was kept uncorrupted. He worked these wonders to reveal the treasure of the divinity, not to abolish what he had assumed or change its elements. To put it briefly: the ineffable divine works he put forward as tokens of the transcendent divinity. But the sufferings, and before them the conception and the swaddling clothes, the growth in stature, and every other thing that happened to his body by the law of nature, showed it to be true humanity, [?] with us. But I will also add something that nearly escaped my mind.

A. Say it, then, he said.

O. I have been reflecting, I said, on what everyone considers right and pious. Just as the Lord, while imparting all that is his own to the flesh, remained without departing from himself and keeps his firm abiding according to his nature, so too his humanity stands in what is according to nature, having the body's

natural powers and activities and never lacking the common and blameless passions. It possesses in its essence the full measure of our perfection, and it has shared in all the good things that come from the Word. Or rather, since it has the Word himself as the source of good things, it pours forth from itself all that belongs to the Word, because of the Word. Let us not suppose that we are saying something great about the Lord's flesh when we grant it what did not honor it and deprived it of the honor that is ours. It was not the Word's part to strip it of what is ours while it remains with us. Nor was it the part of the humanity, which has kinship with us, to disdain sharing our passions, if we are not to fall away from the very imitation of God. Nor should we throw at the Lord's flesh, as though it were something great, what will belong in common to the righteous and the unrighteous after the resurrection: I mean immortality and incorruption, and before these, not hungering or thirsting or craving sleep. Here one can truly say that the glory is in the shame of those who, by honoring, dishonor both us and the Lord's flesh: the flesh by depriving it of what is ours, and us by our falling away from what is its. For the flesh that glorifies through suffering will not glorify us unless it suffers with us.

A. Look now, he said, even against your will you have distinguished the corruptible from the passible. The bodies of sinners suffer in punishment together with their souls, yet surely, though they suffer, they will not fall into death or corruption. So it is clear from this that the corruptible is not the same as the passible, since those bodies suffer but are not corrupted.

O. No, my good man, I said. I do not say that every suffering always corrupts what suffers, but that sufferings of this kind corrupt a subject of this kind. Of the punishments in Hades, and the bitter feeling that comes from them, we would not say that it is their property to corrupt the underlying nature. Indeed, if one may dare to say it, they even contribute something to the lasting endurance of those punished. One might see this very thing happen with medicines too: they revive and warm nature, stinging it to the depths; they do not let it wither into insensibility but keep it alive through the pain, and by their burning they bring it tension and vigor. But the human and natural passions of the flesh which the Lord accepted naturally tend to wither the flesh, to tire it and distress it and at last to dissolve it, as we know happened on the cross. And as far as nature is concerned, corruption follows upon dissolution. So human passions naturally grieve nature, damage its composition, bring about its end and separation, and [?] corruption. In all of these the Lord, like us,

shared, according to the Apostle's great teaching of the mystery.

A. What else, he said, have you been striving to persuade us of and prove by all this, except that since Christ was passible, and that by the nature of his body and not by the will of his divinity, he will also of necessity be corruptible? You have not hidden that this is what you are building up to. We would never accept it, even if you added ten thousand arguments. We must rather believe Peter, the chief of the apostles, and also the one chosen by God among kings and chief of prophets [?], when they declare that his flesh did not see corruption.

O. Since, I said, you have at last given up human reasonings and plausible arguments and taken refuge in the divine Scriptures, I too have remembered a prophetic saying which seems to contradict what you say. This, I ask you, [?] now for us

A. Tell me, he said, which saying you mean.

O. That of Jeremiah, who spoke for God, I said in reply. He uttered it in Lamentations, foretelling the one who would deliver us from lamentations: "Christ the Lord," he says, "was taken in our corruptions." And another such saying can be found, proclaimed in the person of the Lord through the prophet, when he says: "What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to corruption?" Both the title of the psalm and the whole sequence of its words lead us to understand it of the Lord, who is mystically prefigured in the psalm, as the theologians interpret it. Moreover, Peter himself is found saying most weightily to those who did not believe in the Savior's resurrection that God raised him up, no longer about to return to corruption. Does not "no longer about to return" show that the one he was speaking of had been subject to corruption? Do you not think, then, that these sayings oppose what you have put forward and tie us up in even greater bonds of perplexity?

A. By the truth, he said, these sayings are full of obscurity, unless they find an interpreter who aims at the truth and straightens out the apparent disagreement in them.

O. Come then, I said, my excellent and noble friend, lay open straight to the mark what is shadowed in their meaning, and uncover the truth for us, whether you have it from yourself or have received it from another.

A. The pretext you seem to me to have found, he said, is not at all fine or respectable. You have wrapped the truth in greater obscurity with contradictory sayings, so that perplexity might bring in doubt for you, and doubt might bring in the confession of a falsehood. As for me, whether some explanation resolves for us the difficulty of these sayings or not, I would never abandon my own view, since the divinely inspired Scripture plainly cries out

that his soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption.

O. Did it not see corruption, I said to him, while being by nature capable of being corrupted? Or, if not, answer me.

A. While not being by nature capable of it, he said at once, without any hesitation.

O. Then, I said, you are bound to confess exactly the same about the soul as well. For the prophet, giving thanks in the person of the Savior, spoke of both together, proclaiming that his soul was not abandoned to Hades nor did his flesh see corruption.

A. Indeed, he said, I would say the same about the Lord's soul: it was not of a nature to be left in Hades.

O. Shall we then grant, I said, that it did not even go down into Hades?

A. This I would not deny, he said, but it was not at all of a nature to be held fast there.

O. Does the Lord's soul, then, I said, differ by nature from our souls?

A. Not that it differs, he said, but since it was mingled with the Lord, it was higher than the grip of Hades and stronger than it.

O. So then, I said, it was not because of its own nature (for in nature it was like all other souls) but because of the divinity of the Word, with which it went down into Hades, that it was not only exempt from being held there, but also loosed the bonds of those held there who believed in him.

A. He said that this was so.

O. Something similar, I said, may be understood about the Lord's flesh too. As far as his flesh shares the same nature as the bodies of other men, just as it died, so it could also have been corrupted. But the fact that it was not corrupted shows, not a difference in nature, but the almighty and effective power of the divine influence. Likewise, walking on the sea did not reveal the nature of the body; it was a token of the divinity. So dying is proper to the nature of the body, while not being corrupted signifies the power of the divinity.

A. I think so too.

O. Why then, I said to him, do you offer rightly but not divide rightly, as the oracle says? Assign to the flesh what belongs to nature, and what is above nature to the ineffable and superessential power of the Word. In this way you will resolve the disagreement between the sayings quoted above and hit upon the truth. You will say that he was taken in our corruptions, meaning his natural capacity, and that he went down into corruption, having come to be in corrupting

places and circumstances; but that he did not see corruption, because the Word prevented him from experiencing it, so that, along with the other things, this too might belong to the resurrection [?]. Incorruption began from him and in him, and it has passed, and will pass, through the whole human lump, of which he became the firstfruits and so leavened the whole lump into himself.

A. We have heard the divine Scripture say, he said, that Christ suffered, and Paul's great mind proclaims that Christ is passible according to the flesh. But no Scripture has handed down so plainly and in bare words that Christ is corruptible. His being taken in corruption does not by any means show this.

O. Did Scripture, then, I said to him, declare only that he suffered, or also that he was born in the flesh of a Virgin?

A. This too, he said, is among the things agreed on. For how else could we understand "The book of the genesis of Jesus

O. Then, I said, besides his suffering, Scripture also proclaims his birth?

A. I agree, he said.

O. What next? I said. Have we not also received from Scripture his bodily growth?

A. Certainly, he said.

O. And what outside philosophers call alteration, I said to him: do you think it arises from a capacity for being acted upon, or not?

A. And where in Scripture have we found such a thing?

O. We are taught this mystery, I said, by the saving Word himself, who says outright, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." And again the divine Apostle says of him: "For though he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by power." What else is weakness than an alteration and change in the power one normally has? And the great Isaiah says: "A man under a blow, and knowing how to bear sickness." And a little later: "And we saw him, and he had no form nor glory; but his form was without honor, and failing beyond the sons of men." Is there anything else one could call failing and sickness than the alteration caused by suffering, which his body underwent? It lost its color and did not keep the hue that naturally blooms on a body, because the heat withdrew into the depths, and the surface, as the blood drew in, grew cold and turned pale.

A. You speak very rightly, he said. And in this you seem to me to be imitating the great Basil, who gave a natural explanation of the body's passions.

O. Nothing of what I have said is my own, I said. I have taken it all from the Fathers. But let us consider together what comes next, if you wish.

A. What is that? he said.

O. Since birth and growth [?] and al-

-teration have been clearly granted from the divine Scriptures, let us look for the remaining pairs too, and see whether these can also be found in the divine oracles.

A. I see what you are building up to from here, he said. Since you have it agreed that there is locomotion, the Lord's movement from place to place, you are trying to prove diminution and corruption. But as it seems to me, you will not reach that conclusion.

O. You speak rightly, I said, if you look at our weakness. But truth, when it is fought for, fights for those who fight on its behalf. Do you think, then, that hunger and thirst are a desire for food and drink?

A. I do, he said.

O. And have you understood, I said, that desires arise where there is lack?

A. Yes. For what else is appetite than a desire for what is lacking, to replenish what has flowed away

O. You have defined appetite very well. Indeed the great Basil says that the Lord hungered when the solid food in his body had been dissipated, and you clearly know what he says after that. We say that the onset of sleep is nothing other than a slackening of the sensory spirit. In these things nature runs short and is diminished. It needs sleep to recover its vital and sensory power, and rest, so that the strain in the feet, or the hands, or the whole body may be relaxed when it is worn out by a journey or by the effort of other labors. Nature seeks food and drink when the solids and liquids we are made of have been dissipated and need to be replaced, once what was there has been emptied and has flowed away.

A. That is how it is with our bodies, my good man, he said. But it is not so with the Lord's flesh.

O. But if these things were not so with the Lord's flesh too, I said to him, and did not happen in the same way, I would boldly say that he was not born at all. Otherwise, show us the other way it could have happened. For you would never say it was mere appearance.

A. May I never be so mad, he said. These things truly happened, but because the Word willed it and allowed it to the flesh.

O. Well said, I told him. May no one obtain the better change who does not say and believe that the natural passions came upon the flesh by the Word's permission.

A. That is what we too believe, he said. For God is beyond the grasp of men, if he so wills.

O. Then, my admirable friend, I said, since birth, alteration, growth and locomotion have been granted to the Lord's body, tell me, what prevents us from granting it the remaining pair as well?

A. Then by your arguments, he said, also

O. God forbid, I answered him. A. Why do you say that? he asked. O. Because it is not even lawful, I said. A. For what reason? he asked. O. Because, I said, he had to taste our sufferings, even to the point of experiencing death itself, but not to pass into actual corruption. Just as in everything he had what is ours and also what is above us, so too in the case of death itself. To have died is ours, and it heals our mortality. Not to have been corrupted belongs to the higher power of the Word, who prevented that experience and did not allow the flesh to be corrupted in the least, so that incorruption might pass from it to us as well and become the firstfruits of our own incorruption. So the fact that corruption did not occur belongs to his invincible power: it happened by way of miracle, not by the law of nature. A. But surely, he said, the Lord was also called the new Adam. How could this be said unless he bore the body of the first-formed man? And the first-formed man was incorruptible before the transgression. Therefore the Lord's body was also incorruptible, for it certainly remained entirely sinless. O. I replied: Whether the body of the first-formed man was incorruptible or not, I will not yet say, unless they are shamed by the fact that the immortality of the first-formed man is not ascribed to the Lord. They will certainly grant that he died, unless they want to bring the whole charge of illusionism down on themselves. But I would maintain with great confidence that the Lord took up a body not only like that of the first-formed man but also like ours. Since the disease is common to all, it would be quite absurd for him to resemble one man but be unlike all the rest, who needed his likeness in every respect in order to be healed. And where do you get the idea, my good man, that the body of the first-formed man was incorruptible? He did not have immortality as part of his constitution, much less incorruptibility. Otherwise, I think, he would not have needed the tree of life, from which the transgression cut him off, since, as the Fathers say, he would have been made immortal by eating its life-giving fruit. But this is not the time to discuss these matters, since the question about Adam is not a matter of dogma. What is now under inquiry is this: the Lord united to himself hypostatically the same kind of flesh that the condemned man was seen to have after the transgression, and that all of us have who come from the same lump. For he did not come to save a sinless Adam, so as to be made like him, but the Adam who had sinned and fallen, so that, having suffered with him, he might also raise him up with himself. Otherwise, how could he have paid the debt on our behalf, or reversed the defeat, or become a pattern of virtue and set forth in himself his most perfect life as the standard of the best conduct for everyone? A. And how, he asked, could anyone imitate the life of the Lord,

O. The exact likeness of the Lord's flesh to ours, I said, has made it possible for us to become like him. That is why Paul and those like him can say, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ," and the Lord himself can say, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." Nor would Death, which died through the Lord's being put to death, ever have kept away from the people who came after, had it not attacked him exactly as it had attacked the one who fell long ago. When it tasted him, its teeth were set on edge, as the saying goes, so that it no longer dared to touch those like him, and even vomited up those it had swallowed before. The effect, I think, clearly shows the nature of the drug, for it forced the devourer to vomit up everything of the same nature. And how would the law of the wrestling match have been kept in the trial that was brought against him, unless the nature being tried bore a natural likeness to the one who had fallen? Grappling against the rules of the contest is not winning but cheating. The rule of the contest is to throw the one who had already conquered by means of the one who had fallen long ago, and in this way to reverse the earlier defeat. And how could we imitate someone who has a superiority in virtue because of the difference of his instrument, when we are required to become like the incorruptible while living in a passible and corruptible body? That seems much like someone decreeing that the smith's craft be carried out with a carpenter's tools. Indeed, if that were so, even failing to imitate God would be entirely blameless. For the model would not be close to us, and those who imitated it would have ended up surpassing their teacher, since they lived and struggled in a weaker nature. I pass over the point that one cannot even find the laws of practical, human virtue in an incorruptible body. Since such a body lies above human passions, it knows no hunger, and so no self-control; no toil, and so no endurance; no insult, and so no humility; nor anything else of that kind, not to linger by going through them one by one. It is no great claim to say that there is not even any display of virtue to be seen in a nature that is incorruptible and lacks nothing. A nature free from pain has no contest; without a contest there is no victory; and without a victory there are no crowns. This is the enormous absurdity to which the elegant name of incorruptibility has led you. A. Then, he said, it utterly confounds the great mystery of the union if the Word did not give incorruptibility to his own body from the beginning, but, just as with us, reserved incorruption for it until later. O. It would be worthy of greater reverence, I said, to say that the Lord's ascension and his seating at the right hand took place at some later time, and not

from the first union. For it is not lawful for me to magnify him in any other way. A. But even if this had happened, he said, we would gain nothing more from it. O. Why so? I asked. A. Because, he said, even so we are not provided with either natural incorruption or that of baptism, nor is the kingdom of heaven given to us. O. Then grant me on the same grounds, I said to him, that the mystery of incorruption holds as well. For what need was there for him to take up the life that followed, if we already had in him, from his first formation, the completion of the whole mystery? For if these things are not so, we find that it was not the whole economy that took place for our sake, but only the prelude to the mystery. A. What do you mean? he asked. I do not understand what you said. O. That on your arguments, I said, he became incarnate for us and for the incorruption that came to us from it, but lived, suffered and rose again for what purpose I do not know. His aim was to raise up the fallen one, to redeem him from death, to call him to life and new life, and to make him radiant with an incorruptible body. And these things came to us in no other way than by the Lord displaying each of them in his own flesh. But if, as you hold, everything was accomplished by the Lord from the first union, when he changed his own body into incorruption, then we have the whole of the mystery from its very first beginning, and the rest of the economy is superfluous. If a patient were restored to perfect health by the first medicine, any later effort the physicians spent against an illness already conquered would be superfluous. In the same way, if the good of incorruption was instilled in us by the union with the flesh, the whole remaining course of the mystery is superfluous. But I think this happens to you because you do not know that the principle of the body's [formation?] is one thing and the mode of the union another. The first came to it from the presence and indwelling of the Spirit, who fashioned it as Creator. The second came not from the activity of the Word but from the [total?] and essential union with him. For the power of the Spirit gave the Virgin the power to conceive, as one of our writers has said, and very well. The body was brought into being by the Holy Spirit and was constituted by his creative activity, but the matter of its substance was taken from the Theotokos. And the Word dwells in the temple being built for him by the Spirit from its very first formation. He did not wait, as someone somewhere has rightly said, for the temple to be finished, but was joined to it at the very first beginning of the ineffable economy, in the workshop of nature, and put on the whole building

around himself. It was not that, once the body had come into being, he then entered it from outside. Rather, he moulded himself around it and bears our image as a statue does. So the particular character of the body is to be recognized as coming not from the union of the Word but from the power of the Spirit, who fashioned and formed it without the usual primary instruments of nature. But its sinlessness and [?], its total union and blending with the whole of the one who assumed it, its being one Son and being called one Son, and the shining forth in it of the brightest marks of everything that belongs to the Son, were brought about by the natural union of the Word. Their blessedness cannot be taken away, since the union also cannot be divided. So we have learned that the [?] that belongs to the body's particular character came about through the activity of the Spirit, and the union came not from the bare activity of the Word but from the [?] blending of the Word himself. This is what we argued with the man who met us recently, resolving as far as we could the difficulties that seemed to him unanswerable. We ask those who read this modest treatise of ours to go back to the holy works of the Fathers, from which we too took our starting points in writing these things. We have also appended the citations to confirm what has been said. May the Lord grant to both sides, as they seek and search out the truth lovingly and according to his will, to find it revealed to them. The truth is Christ, God over all, to whom be glory and might for ever. Amen.

Preface to the Citations against the Aphthartodocetae

By the grace of Christ we have refuted, as far as we could, the plausible arguments drawn from their propositions. We also promised to add the credibility of the ancients' testimonies to what we have said. So receive at once this swarm of testimonies, harmonious and musical, striking up the melody of truth. Someone who has learned to trample on his own conscience may reject the testimonies we have set out and bring forward others from the same Fathers that, as he thinks, conflict with them. To him we have this to say first: by setting the Fathers against one another and trying to make them contradict themselves, he has openly

declared war on them. He has no more overthrown our position than he has confirmed his own. Next we have this to say: the true Fathers of the Church, who received the word of the teaching gift in the same Spirit, disagreed neither with others nor with themselves. It is no great claim to say that they did not disagree in other matters, and they disagreed least of all on the problem now raised. It may seem otherwise to those who have drained the whole undiluted cup of ignorance and dare to pin the dizziness of their own drunkenness on the firm and sober truth of the Fathers. For we must be convinced that it was not they who were speaking, but the Spirit of their Father speaking in them. Those who are not like this deserve to be called teachers falsely so named. The very fact that they fight and quarrel among themselves convicts them of having not the spirit of peace but that of the adversary, who loves discord. "How is it, then," someone will say, "that we find them calling the body both corruptible and incorruptible?" I would say it happens in only two ways. First, following the idiom of Scripture, they were accustomed to use "incorruptible" in place of "sinless," "pure" and "free from every stain of wickedness." Second, they called the same body both corruptible and incorruptible without distinction and without spelling out the times. When they named it corruptible, they had in view the time of the economy in the flesh. When they named it incorruptible, they had in view the time from the resurrection onward into the endless age to come. And if anyone should say that, as a pledge of incorruption, the body already had the incorruption of the Word, and that because of this it was not allowed to be corrupted, even though its nature was corruptible, I do not disagree. The testimonies set out below will show that these things are true. They do so not vaguely or confusedly, but very clearly and distinctly, marking out for us the times at which the Fathers said the Lord's body had become passible and corruptible, and showing how after the resurrection we have been enriched in him with both the reality and the name of incorruption.

From Saint Ambrose, Against Apollinaris

If you do not acknowledge the passible at all, you have overturned the Master's [piety?] and denied your own salvation. That is why such people must be considered senseless.

From Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, Book 1 on Matthew

How then did he die, though he was immortal, so that he might also be raised and put death to death, unless he took on a body subject to the laws of death? Or how could he have destroyed corruption and rescued from it the race that lived and lay under it, unless he took what is by nature corruptible and shaped it into his own life?

From the same, Book on the Epistle to the Hebrews

For he allowed his own body to suffer death

for the sake of the economy, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. And since, as a body of life, it immediately came back to life, having conquered corruption, let us show our reverence by attributing the accomplishment of such holy things not to the nature of the flesh but to the power of the Word.

I am composing this third discourse after my two earlier ones, as a thank-offering to God and as a monument and triumph over the impious. I pray that the Lord may be present now too, to help our thinking and to direct our discourse by his Word, in grace moved by the Spirit. For if God helps us as we take up all other things and the subject at hand, that help will be a full reward for our labours. And for those on whose behalf and because of whom these words are written, it will be a pledge of benefit, measured, if not by its true worth, at least by our ability. In another sense, too, the present work discharges a duty for us. We are paying an old debt, the most just of all debts to repay. It was owed long ago, but because of a great and long poverty it is being paid only now, and barely, and not in the full measure it deserves, but only in its beginnings.

I have just chosen to raise a monument to God against certain people and to lead them in triumph, so that they no longer hoard their impiety in secret and lure many by staying hidden and unknown, but can be seen from far off and so be shunned as accursed. There was a time when I myself belonged to their company. When I was young they had captured both my time and my reasoning, setting every instrument of wickedness in motion to that end. For I had set my heart on precision in doctrine, and once I had tasted

it with the tip of my finger, as the saying goes, I became greedy for it, and my zeal knew no measure. But they took hold of me, like a blind man looking for a road, and tried to drag me down into the pit of their impiety. But a grace appeared to me from above and snatched me from between their teeth, when I had already become the readiest of prey, and it kindled in me a most ardent longing for virtue and for the exile that is worthy of it. How could he who guided Israel in the desert not also become my companion on my journey abroad? He carried me and did not [let me go?] until he had placed me in the hands of godly men. They not only cleansed the eye of my soul of all that discharge, but also [armed?] it with holy light from the books of the God-wise, in which truth and every other virtue are found, and so purified my hands and my mind. Would I not then justly have been indicted by fair-minded people for utmost impiety, had I let all this pass in complete silence? That I did not compose this thank-offering from the start, at the very hour, so to speak, when I was granted to see again, I ask God to forgive, and each of those whom God loves. It was not out of ingratitude. Rather, I reined in my speech out of fear, so as not to seem to be using thanksgiving for these things as a pretext for rash writing. But now a just cause has stirred us, one that will not even allow us to keep quiet, and so I have hastened to discharge both the debt and the longing. I would be the most credible witness of all, both for gaining belief in what will be said and for putting the godless to shame, if they are willing, for experience, they say, is surer than words. Let Christ be my witness, and his Father, that I shall not speak about them out of hatred for some or to please others. First, I pity those very people, and there is no time when I do not lament them. And third, I have endeavoured to mix this discourse like a preventive medicine, as a protective aid for those who are on the point of falling in. Besides, I fear judgment, if even what we suffered has not made us compassionate. So, if nothing else, I shall bear this fruit for the one who redeemed and saved me: the protection of others. And let them not be angry with us if I have dared to speak out what they themselves did not shudder to think. Come, then, let us drag into the open the schemes they use against the truth and against those who are beginning to be caught, to their misfortune, in their murderous nets.

1. Here, then, is their first trick, worthy of their wickedness. Though they do not accept at all the holy and God-given teachers of the Church, they pretend in words not to accept even Theodore and Diodore, the first sources of their impiety.
2. Moreover, they hold out the great and numerous council as bait, in place of any other lure, to the

simpler people, though they do not think in accordance with it. Indeed, I do not know whether they yield first place to anyone else in thinking against it. Yet by slipping it on like a solemn mask for their play-acting, they go unnoticed in the first stages of their attempt. Once they have persuaded someone to accept the council, supposedly, or have got hold of someone who does accept it, they ask him which of the Fathers he is accustomed to study and likes best. If the person happens to name John, the great eye of the Church, or the two great luminaries, the Cappadocians I mean, or Athanasius, that most brilliant morning star, they immediately change countenance, for they cannot bear even to hear the names spoken. Still, so as not to shock their prey at the first meeting and drive him off, they say, "These Fathers are good too, but they are not better than ours." And if he asks for the names, they say, "Read first, and then you will know who they are and how great they are, you poor wretch who have not yet even learned what they are called."

3. They also promise many other gifts and kinds of support: access to the emperor, should he need it, the highest honour among officials, and the company of the learned among them. What boundless evil! They do not let go until the man falls into their hands, whether through ignorance, need, flattery, or any of the other things that can ensnare those who do not guard their own hearts with all vigilance.

4. Then, once they have him in hand and find him obedient in whatever they want, if their prey is a monk, they urge him toward pagan learning, should he prove suited for it. They mock the simplicity of the monastic order at length and say that fasting, vigils and withdrawal from the world are nothing. Indeed, they slander the practical life and are annoyed even at its very name. They urge him to change his habit, since it supposedly stands in the way of philosophy in civic life, and they promise to enrol him in the clergy or advance him in some other way, if only he becomes a partner in their impiety. If he is a layman, they promise him gifts suited to him. These promises are not sincere, for that is their "blessedness in evil"; still, they beguile him with hopes and make him gape after them. But though the refutation of these things is brief, time is pressing.

5. Having mentioned one or two of their practices, I shall turn to their great teacher of ignorance. They see the just hatred growing day by day among the faithful against their godless doctrines and against the prime author of their impiety, and they regard it as something bitter, a threat to their own life. So, as a piece of play-acting and a mask, they say to us, "Away with Nestorius!" But the father of those same doctrines will be the one who was also his father,

Having settled these things among themselves and adopted this as their best plan, they put Theodore forward to the faithful in his place.

6. But there is something more astonishing than this, and though I would like to pass over it, I am not allowed to. They have imitated the knavery of the Manichaeans (for they could not live any other way). Just as the Manichaeans divided themselves into the so-called elect and the indifferent, these men too have divided themselves into two groups. Some are devoted to Nestorius himself and set great store by communion with him. Others anathematize him but put on a show of communion with the Church. The overseer of hidden things is my witness that I have not invented this. One of the genuine believers was being pressed by them both to take communion with them and to be enrolled in the clergy of the Church. When he seemed rather hesitant before so dreadful a venture, they said: "What harm is it to you if you use the Church as a headquarters and the clergy as an army, while you hold our faith and embrace communion with us?" He was perplexed at this and said it was impossible to be in communion both with them and with the Church. Then they said: "You should not be troubled by an arrangement of this kind. The bread set out as a type of the body of Christ has received more blessing than the bread sold in the market, or than what the Philomarianites offer in the name of Mary."

7. It is now time to go through the praises of their great teacher Theodore. They say that he is the man whom the great John tried to draw up with two letters, as with strong, long ropes, after he had fallen into the abyss of licentiousness, abandoned his resolve and forsworn his vows.

8. They say that when he was eighteen years old and no more, he behaved like a drunkard toward the sacred Scriptures. I could call his interpretations of the divine Scriptures nothing else.

9. They also say that he wanted to seize Tarsus, the eye of Cilicia, when Diodore, the originator and father of his evils and his impiety, departed this life. Theophilus of Alexandria prevented the attempt, because the people under his tyranny sent an embassy to Theophilus.

10. This loathsome man was preaching in the great church of the city once called Antioch's and now called the City of God. There, among many other things, he dared to slander the word Theotokos, so that he turned the whole populace against himself.

11. This foul man never stopped, in all his misinterpretation of the divine Scriptures, mocking and disparaging the labours of the holy teachers who had toiled over them. But I now seem to be doing what the great

Basil spoke of: correcting a murderer with a slap. But come, "change your theme and sing" of the inner adornment. Look into what they keep secret and what is inaccessible to the many: I mean the inner sanctum of their impiety. I will not, as the saying goes, profane the mysteries, but I will uncover the abominable doctrines of their godlessness. Let no one be annoyed with us for what is said. We are not the originators of these evil things, and we have not given occasion for what is about to be said, for many books contain their godless mysteries. I myself would pray to God that such mysteries of impiety might be covered in silence and darkness. But as it is, I have let myself into this discussion not to make you disciples of evil but to deliver you from terrible things. I myself flee from them headlong and cry aloud to everyone: Flee, all of you, flee! Flee far from the cliffs and pits! Flee the books of these godless teachings, defiled with every heresy!

12. This wise man, as his admirers would put it, this great Theodore, found the struggle against human beings too small a thing. So he sets his hand to attack the very glory of the Spirit and dares to do so. He takes in a lowly sense all the lofty Scriptures that the God-inspired writers wrote under the Spirit's inspiration, and he excludes some of them from the God-appointed number of the sacred books.

13. Take the great servant of God Job, the living pillar of courage inscribed for all ages. In about two thousand lines (manuscript A has ten thousand) Theodore abuses the book that the Spirit wrote about him and strikes it out. Yet the great James confirmed that book in his catholic Epistle, saying: "You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord." We have heard of his patience and learned of his end from nowhere else than from the Scripture about him.

14. That is the reason, I think, why he rejects the epistle of the great James itself, and the other catholic epistles that follow it. It was not enough for him to attack the Old Scripture, in imitation of Marcion's impiety. He had to fight against the New as well, so that his struggle against the Holy Spirit might be all the more conspicuous.

15. He threw out entirely the titles of the most sacred Hymns, Psalms and Odes, and in Jewish fashion he attributed all the psalms to Zerubbabel, Hezekiah and their circle, [?] only three to the Lord.

16. Then there is the Song of Songs, the holiest of the holy songs. All the God-wise and all Christians sing it, the churches throughout the world know it, and even the Jews, the enemies of the cross of Christ, admire it. This bold man, whose daring knows no limit, interpreted it according to his own whorish mind and tongue, and cut it out of the holy books.

LEONTIUS OF BYZANTIUM

17. And what was he not going to do, when the inventor and [?] of impiety was at work in him? So, adding evil to evil, he likewise threw out Chronicles, both the first and the second book, and Ezra as well as the books already mentioned.

18. Does he then attack the divine Scriptures and carry off the glory of the more brilliant contests against the Spirit, while keeping away from the lesser ones and leaving the wrestling and the victory in those to others? Not at all. When, as he supposed, the contest against the God-inspired Scriptures had been fought to the finish, he began a second double lap, equal to the first. And so as not to tire himself by attacking details, he takes his stand against the first elements of Christianity. He strikes out the creed that deifies those who are born again, I mean the faith of Nicaea. He does not merely mutilate it; he discards it wholly and completely and hands down another one beside it. He took no account of such great luminaries and did not shudder at the daring of the attempt. As I said, he sets out another creed of faith, or rather of unfaith. After faith in God the Father, the only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, he wrote that one should also believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. In this way he introduces a fourth person into the Holy Trinity and divides into two persons what belongs to our one Christ and God. To the true Son he assigns the divine attributes and the birth from above. To this Christ of his own he assigns what is human and befits a man, and above all the birth from the Virgin.

19. He dares another evil, second to none of those already mentioned. He improvises another anaphora besides the one handed down from the fathers to the churches. He did not respect the anaphora of the apostles, and he did not think that of the great Basil, written in the same Spirit, worth any consideration. He completed the rite with an anaphora of blasphemies, not of prayers. Could any other Antichrist still deserve to be expected, when this man so hates the things of Christ and tries to overturn them? I do not think so. This man, I say, is enough to fill that one's place and play that one's part in every respect.

20. But hear his other teachings too, which it would have been good and most desirable never to hear. Take the judgement of God, proclaimed in all the holy Scriptures. Even those far from the divine wisdom of Christians have not failed to hear of it. It alone keeps those who stand firm, raises up those who have fallen, heals those who have sinned, and is the fitting end for the devil. Not even the devil and the demons dared to deny it, when they said to the Saviour: "What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?" The wretch laughs at it, and at Gehenna, the darkness, the gnashing of teeth, and all the other things threatened against the impious and sinners. He does not expect that judgement himself, and he

urges others not to be afraid of a terror that, as he supposes, is only a threat. But experience will convince him, since the threat did not frighten him. The impious man, truly without fear, dared to put these things into writing. He truly laughs at "the fire-bearing earthquake"; like the devil, "the judgements of God are removed from his sight."

21. That is why those of your party love you, you wretch. You have mixed this for them as a drug to remove the fear of God, a truly bitter drug and one worth weeping over. This is the impiety of Eunomius, which you imitated. What was said about him seemed incredible until (would that it had never happened!) these things were set down in your books. Eunomius said one should give the passions room and not trouble the mind, but your teaching has gone even further than his.

22. Your disciple is Barsauma, who corrupted the way of life of Persia with doctrines of godlessness and with moral indifference. He made it a law that no one, not even a member of the clergy, let alone a layman, should abstain from unlawful intercourse and from taking many wives. As for drunkenness and revels, he considered them gifts of God.

23. Those who belong to your faction, which shares the impiety of Arius, translated your treatises into the speech and language of the Chaldeans and the Armenians, and so handed down to those nations a heresy even more godless. The members of Arius' bands had been eager to do the same thing, except that the Arians brought the western barbarians into their own impiety and your followers brought the eastern ones into theirs.

24. These are small matters to you. But add, if you please, the fictitious transgression of Adam. According to you, God imposed it on him and he suffered it, so that the world might have a plausible beginning for God: the most unjust punishment and exile of a man who had not sinned but had been slandered. For according to you, Christ did not come because of this root of evils and the impiety and wickedness of mankind that followed from it. He did not come as the good shepherd to save and bring back Adam, the sheep that went astray when it was separated from the flock of a hundred.

[?] 25. Add also, if you like, the angels created together with that darkness of yours. In your eyes the sacred psalmist is not a reliable interpreter of their nature, though he strikes the lyre to God in the Spirit: "Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire." "Makes" is a present tense, but by a scriptural idiom it indicates the past, as he teaches at once when he adds: "who founds the earth", that is, who founded it. Nor are you put to shame by the other appearances of angels in the Scriptures, which appear as light and flash like lightning.

26. Add also the substantial darkness of the Manichaeans. According to you, it is the first thing in visible creation, and either it exists alongside God without having come into being, or it was made by God.

27. Then there is another clever piece of unwise sophistry: you say that the devil's Antichrist will not be punished but will be destroyed and dissolved into non-existence. Supposedly this lets the fear of God come to souls as a good thing from a good thing, since they were to have it from nowhere else. For in your view the judgement has been abolished. The fear of God is not to come from the enjoyment of good things or from the natural and ineffable longing for God, but only from the complete destruction of the Antichrist and his dissolution into non-existence.

28. You also hold that not everything in creation and providence comes from God. Many useless consequences have crept in, by-products of what has come into being. They do not happen because God wills them; they follow from the nature of things and are not prevented. But time would slip away from us unnoticed if we went on endlessly about each of the grape clusters of your Sodomite vine. And you never tire of reveling in impieties, you most fertile source of evils. You do not believe that God is good in his very essence, or that he is the source and principle of everything beautiful and good, from which these flow forth essentially. Tell us, then: where has goodness been supplied to him from? For according to you he is not goodness itself. And what is the principle of that goodness? So you yourself are the principle of such evils, falling little or nothing short of Marcion's boastfulness and his principles.

29. Our discussion has now reached the very crowning point of your impieties.
