Where did you invent the man who came into being as a counterpart to the Trinity, to be its living idol, measured alongside the infinite life of all that exists [?]? You grant that he is to be worshipped instead of the Trinity by all creation, visible and invisible, now and hereafter. Were you not convinced by the legislation of Moses, who decreed that one should worship the Lord God and serve him alone? Nor by the Saviour himself, who put this forward against the tempter?

30. But you, as I said, invent the idea that Christ was created by the Trinity itself as another living idol, and you slanderously accuse the Trinity of teaching creature-worship. You are no different from the old error by which man slipped away from God and served the creature rather than the Creator. Indeed, you make this error even worse than that one. You teach that not only human beings will be led into it, but all the creation that came into being after the Trinity and through the Trinity. You herald of these evil Gospels, you proclaim that worship is to be offered for ever, not to God made man, but to a man honoured with the title of God. You explain this by saying that the worship that all beings offer to your Christ is referred back to the Trinity, just as honour passes from an image to the king. I would gladly ask you about this

Christ of yours: how and to whom do you say he offers worship? If he worships himself, that is utterly absurd. If he worships the Trinity through some intermediary, [?]. If he worships through himself, then he alone of all beings is found to have this privilege of serving no one. Since he alone has not had your mediator, what limit [?] is there in place of God, or [?] the one you grant to Christ? You present the one who has been so honoured as alone being honoured, but not honouring.

31. How charming you are! You weave for this man a dignified and refined birth and upbringing, as much as a prophet's and a little beyond it. You say that God the Word, by foreknowledge, granted him union by his good pleasure in the very formation in the womb, because he knew that this man's purpose to do good would never fail.

32. You cover him in the gloom of ignorance, as knowing nothing except what seemed good to the Word united with him according to merit. How is it that you present him as filled with ignorance and not with sin as well? For sin flows from ignorance as a river from a spring. Or perhaps you will decree that ignorance is to his advantage, since what is done irrationally out of ignorance is usually thought to deserve pardon, unless it is very grave. You say he was so ignorant that even when he was being tempted he did not know who was tempting him. You do not allow that even the Lord himself, let alone the saints, was free from sin in thought, and you do not even think that this is sin.

33. Nor do you shudder to decree that he was troubled more by the passions of the soul than by those of the body. You say plainly: "and by better reasoning he overcame pleasures."

34. You claim that he was purified little by little through progress in the virtues, and became more fit every day to receive the goods that were to come to him from God as to a man.

35. You baptize him so that from then on (and not before), having been perfected in the virtue of the law, he might be called Christ, perfect, and might take up the gospel way of life and fulfill it. Then why do you not also say that his time was cut short for this reason? He would have grown weary over so long a span, and so he found the cross as a short road to salvation.

36. You present him going to die even unwillingly, both for himself and, not least, for the whole world, as though the glory of the ascension and of sitting at the right hand would not have been his in any other way unless he had been perfected through martyrdom. I do not know who among men, or from where, this man is, to whom you entrust so great a work, an economy so great and so exceptional that it surpasses not only human nature but every created nature.

37. He feared death, not in order to form us in himself as a model and to undo our cowardice in himself, but because he himself was fleeing from it headlong. He would never have agreed to undergo it willingly, had he not

received your long admonition of many lines, which you invent and attribute to the angel. For you do not refrain from slandering angels either. The angel sang a theological hymn and a song of victory to Christ as to God, who was on the point of freeing human beings, through this marvellous and supernatural drama of fear, from the truly real fear of death and from the bitter tyrant of mankind. But you [?] it as said by the angel to the Saviour by way of encouragement and consolation, as if to someone cowardly, unmanly and altogether self-centred. You even brought forward, in support of this interpretation, what was said in the great song by the God-wise Moses: "Let all the angels of God strengthen him." But according to your impious claim, the soul of Christ had fallen in grief and was [?] by the fear of death, and needed the angel's long consolation, as the angel hurried to raise it up. For it was in the utmost danger, and the whole universe was shaking along with it.

You say that this is false? I would have given a great deal for that. But as it is, your marvellous and brilliant contests against the incarnation of God the Word proclaim these things. So do your wars, supposedly fought against opposing heretics but really waged against the truth. You set out to fight the truth, but since you knew the attempt was beyond you, you headed your war against it with the title "Against the Heretics". Your nonsense against the Magusaeans proclaims these things too, and so do your other misinterpretations of the Scriptures. There is no place where these products of your marvellous labours are not noised about. They began with Paul of Samosata and came down through those in between to Diodore, who became your leader in these evils. You cultivated them so well that they grew to such a size that your abundant river covered over its godless source.

38. Your channel and narrow ditch was Nestorius, who could not hold the whole stream of your impiety. And even if he had been able to hold it, he could not also speak it boldly and pour out your streams of blasphemy to everyone. That was not because of any laziness of will (for I will speak in his defence), but because the crowds hemmed him in. You kept company with impiety in quiet and drank its whole channel dry. But he picked up just one piece of refuse from your sins and put it forward in public, forbidding only the word Theotokos. He was cunning to take his stand at the very beginnings of the truth, and by

denying the first birth of our God according to the flesh he did away with the whole sequence of the mystery that follows from it. Nevertheless he was caught and paid the ultimate penalty. He was driven out of the divine choir together with the impieties he had cultivated from you, and he paid the penalty your teachings deserved.

These things are enough to show the whole impiety of the man, revealing the lion from its claw, as they say. If anyone disbelieves them, they truly deserve disbelief, and I do not blame that reaction, since it is entirely just. Not disbelieving such evils is not without fault, for it convicts the person who believed too easily. Someone who is ready to agree is also most ready to be tested [?]. But experience does not allow us to disbelieve, even though we would like to: both what we have gathered from his books and what we have heard from his admirers. And how could I disbelieve, when I came close to experiencing these evils in myself?

39. But they are not wise either, except at doing harm. Since they cannot defend these things, they put forward to us the great Basil, who wrote to Diodore and approved one of his treatises on the Trinity. For they cannot point to one on the incarnation. They also wheel in certain other Fathers who either wrote to him or mentioned him.

40. But they do not admire Origen, though Gregory, named for his wonders, went through countless rounds of praise for him when he composed his farewell address. And why do I mention Origen? Even Apollinarius, who strayed diametrically from the truth, boasts that countless letters were written to him by the great Athanasius, by Serapion, and by the other brilliant luminaries and champions of the truth of that time. If anyone takes up the whole ecclesiastical history composed by Timothy, the disciple of Apollinarius, he will find that all this labour had no other aim than to commend Apollinarius. Timothy assembled that commendation from countless letters written by him and to him, and from the replies to them. These same people, it seems to me, would perhaps commend Demas to us too, because Paul commended him to the Romans. They would rank Judas in the choir of the apostles, because he often ate with the Saviour. But let them hear this from us as well: if they intend to revere letters written to some of the Fathers above the truth, they will be forced to accept not only Theodore or Diodore but many others too, including some they themselves do not want.

41. Here is another of their arguments: "For the very things for which you call Theodore or Diodore to account," one of them says, "we find the other Fathers guilty as well." And they bring forward

…to us: from Serapion, "God clothed himself with the man"; from Basil, "the God-bearing man"; [?] "'God' would be said not of the Word but of what was seen"; [?] of the one who says [?], and "the stripes of the servant, around whom the Master [?]"; and from the rest of the Fathers they pick out such things as these with their fingernails, scraping off little phrases, such as

And what need is there to speak of the union in essence and by essence, and of the one hypostasis of the two natures, than which nothing is more unified or more naturally joined? First, then, it is worth considering that our dispute is not about words but about the mode of the whole mystery of Christ. And this cannot simply be accepted or rejected on the basis of this or that word, or of certain expressions, but from the first principles. For it is over these that every heresy splits off, since, once past the principles, everyone agrees with everyone about words, so that they even appropriate the words of the Scriptures themselves, fitting them to their own purpose. And what are the principles in these matters? Clearly, the mode of the union, which came about essentially and not relationally; and that the Word is in the perfect humanity as the inner man, according to the Apostle, is in us, subsisting together with it and contributing to the definition of the whole after the union, just as the Fathers who publicly denounced the Samosatene also [said] [?]

But we neither pay heed to those who stand diametrically opposed to the truth when they bring forward passages which, as they think, suit them, so that we should on that basis champion with them seeming and phantasm, or change and confusion; nor do we accept from you yourselves, as you might suppose, things brought forward as coming from the Fathers in support of a phantasm with respect to the Godhead, or of your vain hope in a mere man. For, as I said, our battle is not about words but about the realities themselves, and about their union and natural conjoining with one another, which the Fathers held to have come about essentially, whereas you introduce it as relational and a matter of will, and through it you strive to establish the worship of a man. What could be more impious than this? For to think such things belongs only to the impiety of Paul and Marcellus, of Photinus, Nestorius and Theodore, who flatly defined Christ as a mere man—men whom the God-speaking mystagogues of the

Church, each individually and all in common, condemned and anathematized with unanimous verdicts; and above all the last of all the synods, which became the seal of the holy synods before it, namely the one at Chalcedon. It utterly overthrew the champion of your impiety; it confirmed the Creed of the faith and proclaimed with brilliant acclamations the destroyer of your impiety; and they crowned with fitting glories the one who was truly a Leo, a lion, who rose up justly against the crafty fox Eutyches and tore apart and killed his hidden impiety with words of refutation. [?]. "But those men," they say, "were condemned, whereas none of these was condemned." This, my good sirs, they obtained not from any blamelessness of their own but from taking great pains to escape notice. For they did not dare to display their impiety to many, since they knew this was not safe for them. Besides, the heresy of the Arians, which was then raging and devouring the churches like a wild flame, gave many people leisure, and especially Apollinaris, and later Macedonius too, to escape notice in their blasphemies. The medical saying may fittingly be quoted here: when two pains prevail in a body, the more violent obscures the lesser. In this way Apollinaris too, like a spleen, grew (to speak in the manner of your own expounder, and to grant you something even in my refutations), acquiring an unnatural size while the whole body was in a bad state. By the same example I can explain your case too. For the zeal of the Fathers for the most necessary and especially urgent matters let your forebears in impiety escape notice, above all because they feigned a common struggle and battle alongside them in matters concerning the Trinity, and so stole their goodwill and used the pretence of agreement to escape notice. For wickedness is hard to detect when it is hidden under the mask of goodwill. [?]. And yet in the anathema against the most unfortunate Nestorius (for he is truly unfortunate, being the only one to pay the penalty for the murder, having received the sword, as they say, from others) they too were cast out along with him. For in the disciple who, as Scripture says, is fully trained like his teacher, they reaped the fruit of their own labours. And indeed, if anyone should look into this, he will find that they too were indicted by many others, and by those most zealous against your [?] impiety, Cyril and Proclus. The first of these composed an entire treatise against them, even if some ventured a defence that introduced a case worse than the accusation against them [?]; while the other, writing the synodical letter to the Armenians, appended to it chapters of Theodore's blasphemies in refutation of his impiety. And what need is there to speak of the holy Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, a man who, as they say, was a prophet? Since the zealots of Theodore's impiety at that time could not endure his frankness and his refutation, after those countless

LEONTIUS OF BYZANTIUM

dangers they pursued him by guile, entrusting the deed to one of those inside. If, then, we persuade you by these means, and you change your minds, however late, preferring the truth to persons, that is better, and thanks be to God. But if not, we will at least weep for you, since you deserve laments and lamentation; and we ourselves will hang upon God, and, holding fast to the blessed hopes, we will never let go of those which our Fathers held and which, in their great kindness, they handed down and passed on to us through those in between, teaching us only this: to keep their deposit unharmed. This the holy Church of God continues to keep, neither diminished nor added to, and will continue to keep until the great appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the might for ever.

From the blasphemies of Theodore we have been eager to set out a few out of many, to show his whole perversity in doctrine, so that from these we may also give assurance about the rest, that we have told no lies against him or against those who think as he does. For if it had been possible to find all his treatises easily, we would not have hesitated to make him his own witness on every one of the heads on which we have indicted him. But since only with difficulty, with much labour and countless devices, have we been able to find his book against the Incarnation (for they dare to hand out his works to the uninitiated only with great caution), for this reason we have been able for the present to collect only what he said against the Incarnation of the Saviour. If anyone disbelieves us, and has plenty of leisure and the will for it, let him look up his vain labours on Genesis, his book against Job, the misinterpretation he has made of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and indeed of those to the Corinthians and Galatians, what he wrote against the Magians themselves, the blinding preface on the holy Psalms, and his writings for Eunomius against the great Basil (for that is what I call his defence of Eunomius, which is full of every accusation); and the muddied

expositions and blasphemies on Matthew, John and indeed Luke, and the arrogant and audacious censures against the holy apostles and evangelists themselves, and his other treatises, not to list them one by one: he will see a depth of impiety, a mind and an enterprise more abominable and more godless than all that of Marcion and Valentinus, and also, I say, of Mani, the fountain of evils. But we, as we said, so as not to seem to leave the charges against him wholly without witness, have used, as I said, many devices and methods, and were able to find only what he composed against the Incarnation, from which we have been eager to set out these quotations. If God permits, and time does not fail us, we shall compose another treatise against him, collecting at leisure each of his impieties from his own words, and we shall show to which of the quotations of those men [each corresponds] [?]. And indeed we shall demonstrate from his most "sacred" works his whole derangement and the opinion, contrary in everything, which he holds against all the holy Fathers; and on these points we shall use refutations to rebut him. For the present I shall be content with the more summary indictment that has been made against him, so that he may not harm the simpler folk by escaping notice altogether. And let those who have emulated him know that they think fit to commend a man whose impiety not even the most eager could easily match. [A. MAI, Script. …] These are the blasphemies that the impious Theodore uttered in his rage against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, saying that God the Word is one and Jesus the Christ another; that the one is the benefactor and the other the beneficiary, the one saving and the other saved. Whoever says this plainly denies the salvation that has come to us through Christ the Master. For how can one who received benefit from another, that is, who was saved, save others? Those, then, who think this way—whose body and blood do they think they partake of? The benefactor's, or the beneficiary's? If the benefactor's, God the Word's, how can they say this, when they do not confess that he became flesh and became man? But if the beneficiary's, their hope is vain, since they champion the worship of a man; and having their hopes in a man, they are accursed, because they worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen. I thought it necessary also to set out a few quotations from the one who was the first leader of their impiety, through which one can see that they are bound together in impiety. From Diodore, from the first discourse Against the Synousiasts: "We urge you to make yourselves secure in the exactness of doctrine. The Son is perfect before the ages; the Son of God took up from David a perfect son of David. You will say

to me: 'Then do you preach two sons?' I do not speak of two sons of David, for I did not call God the Word son of David; nor do I speak of two sons of God by essence, for I do not say there are two from the essence of God when I say that God the Word, who is before the ages, dwelt in the one from the seed of David." From the same, from the same discourse: "The man from Mary is Son by grace, but God the Word is Son by nature; the one by grace and not by nature, the other by nature and not by grace. Let it suffice for the body taken from us—the sonship by grace, the glory, the immortality—that it became the temple of God the Word; let it not be raised above its nature, and let God the Word not be insulted in place of the thanksgiving we owe him. And what is the insult? To compound him with the body and to think that he needs the body for perfect sonship. God the Word himself does not wish to be son of David, but Lord. But that the body should be called Son of David he not only did not begrudge; he even came for this reason." And after other things: "And when there is talk of births according to nature, let no one suppose that God the Word is the son of Mary. For by nature a mortal begets a mortal, and a body one of the same essence. And God the Word did not undergo two births, one before the ages and the other in later times." From the same Diodore, from the same discourse: "If anyone wishes, using the term loosely, to call the Son of God, God the Word, son of David as well, because of the temple of God the Word that came from David, let him call him so; and let him call the one from the seed of David Son of God by grace and not by nature, neither ignoring the natural fathers, nor overturning the order, nor saying that the incorporeal one is both from God before the ages and from David, both having suffered and impassible." From the same, from the same discourse, 4 [?]: "The Son of God is Son on account of no one, for he is Son by nature; the flesh is Son on account of the Son. And why do I say 'on account of the Son'? The flesh is on account of us. And do not think the saying blasphemous, but demand the proofs. If men had not stumbled, there would have been no need of a law; for the law is not laid down for the righteous. If they had not increased their sin

[?] to bring. This Paul is the devil's bitter tare that sprang up from Samosata. But it is right also to expose to public view the destructive fruit of Nestorius, the last and most godless shoot of the first root, so that between the two extremes the notorious and blasphemous pair in the middle—I mean Diodore and Theodore—may be recognized as joined to them. Perhaps they will be able, however late, to sober up from their drunkenness, once they learn to what fathers of evil, and how great, their first kinship goes back, and how from them, through those in between, this last branch of impiety grew—whose fruit they hasten to strip off wholesale and gorge themselves on. The refutation of both, I mean of Paul and of Nestorius, that is set out here comes from the Protest posted publicly, as they say, by Eusebius, who was at that time distinguished in the legal profession and was later entrusted with the helm of Dorylaeum. Having, as is attested, a divine zeal, he was the first to detect and refute the heresy of Nestorius himself, and indeed of Eutyches, amid countless dangers on behalf of true religion. Hear, then, with what collections, and how many, of the blasphemies of the Samosatene he matched those of Nestorius, and showed that the utterly senseless mind of both was one. And whether the deadly song of Theodore and Diodore is at all out of tune with these Siren melodies, we leave to those who can listen without danger to judge.

Protest, posted in a public place and displayed in church: "I adjure whoever takes up this paper, by the Holy Trinity, to make it known to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers and laypeople living in Constantinople, and further to give them a copy of it, for the refutation of the heretic Nestorius, showing that he is of one mind with Paul of Samosata, who was anathematized one hundred and sixty years ago by orthodox bishops. What was said by each of them is as follows. Paul said: 'Mary did not give birth to the Word.' Nestorius said in agreement: 'Mary, my good man, did not give birth to the Godhead.' Paul said: 'For she did not exist before the ages.' Nestorius said: 'And they set a mother in time over the Godhead that created time.' Paul said: 'Mary received the Word, and she is not older than the Word.' Nestorius said: 'How then did Mary give birth to one more ancient than herself?' Paul said: 'Mary bore a man equal to us.' Nestorius said: 'The one born of the virgin is a man.' Paul said: 'But better in every way, since the grace upon him is from the Holy Spirit, and from the promises, and from what is written.' Nestorius said: 'For I have seen,' he says, 'the Spirit descending like a dove

and remaining on him'—the Spirit that granted him the ascension. 'Having given commandment to the apostles,' he says, 'whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit'—this very Spirit that granted Christ such great glory. Paul said: 'So that neither should the one anointed from David be a stranger to Wisdom, nor should Wisdom dwell in another in the same way. For it was in the prophets, and still more in Moses, and in many lords [?], but still more in Christ, as in a temple.' And elsewhere he says that Jesus Christ is one and God the Word another. Nestorius said that it is not possible for the one who is before all the ages to be born a second time, and that as Godhead. See, the transgressor has been clearly shown to say: 'The one begotten of the Father was not born of Mary.' See, he agrees with the heretic Paul, who says that the Word is one and Christ Jesus another, and not one, as orthodoxy proclaims." Thus far the Protest.

From Paul of Samosata: "A man is anointed; the Word is not anointed. The Nazarene is anointed, [not] our Lord. For the Word was greater than Christ, since Christ became great through Wisdom. For the Word is from above, but Jesus Christ is a man from here below. Mary did not give birth to the Word, for Mary did not exist before the ages. Mary is not older than the Word; rather she bore a man equal to us, but better in every way, since he is from the Holy Spirit." From the same, from the dialogue with Malchion: "So that neither should the one anointed from David be a stranger to Wisdom, nor should Wisdom dwell in another in the same way."

"The one who appeared was not Wisdom; for Wisdom could not be found in a form, nor in the appearance of a man, for it is greater than the things that are seen." "It is a great thing for the Christ-bearing Virgin to have borne a humanity, the instrument of the Godhead of God the Word; it suffices her for surpassing honour to have given birth to a mediator joined to the dignity of God." These few out of many we have set side by side, wishing to show the agreement in evil between these men and the ancient fathers of heretics. Anyone who wishes may read the encyclical letter written against the Samosatene by the holy synod that deposed him, and also the dialogue that the presbyter Malchion held with him. He will learn with certainty that Theodore and his circle are genuine disciples of that man; for they proceed almost through the very same words, so that their treatises seem to be not compositions but rather transcriptions, as they transfer his words into their own. How the holy Fathers from the beginning thought

about the union, and the most holy Churches governed by them, can be clearly known from the holy synod held against the Samosatene and from their encyclical letter, in which, among other things, they accuse him of the following in these very words: "[?] then in the memoranda, as if speaking of Paul, to preserve the dignity of Wisdom." And after other things: "But if it was conjoined in the constitution and generation, this happens to the man." And again: "For Wisdom was not born together with the human essentially, as we believe, but also according to quality." And after other things: "And what does it mean to say that the constitution of Jesus Christ is different from ours? We hold that his constitution differs from ours in this greatest respect: that God the Word is in him what the inner man is in us." And after other things: "If he means that Wisdom dwelt in him as in no other—for this indicates the same mode of indwelling, but surpassing in measure and quantity, say double, or in any way more or less than double, he knowing more from Wisdom than the others—this the catholic and ecclesiastical canons do not allow. Rather, they hold that those others partook of Wisdom breathing into them from outside and being distinct from them, whereas Wisdom itself, through itself, came to dwell essentially in the body from Mary." And after other things: "And yet he says that two sons do not subsist. But if Jesus Christ is Son of God, and Wisdom too is son, and Wisdom is one thing and Jesus Christ another, then two sons subsist." And after other things: "Understand the conjunction with Wisdom differently, as by learning and participation, not as an essence made essential in a body." And after other things: "Neither was the God who bore and put on the human primarily without share in human passions, nor was the human in which he was, and through which he did these things, primarily without part in divine works. He was formed primarily as a man in the womb, and secondarily he was God in the womb, united in essence with the human." From the proceedings against him by Malchion, a rebuttal: "Did I not say this long ago, that you do not grant that the only-begotten Son, who exists eternally before all creation, was essentially present in the whole Saviour?"

(62) "Secondarily": κατὰ δεύτερον λόγον. Turrianus.

BY THE ALL-WISE MONK, LORD LEONTIUS OF JERUSALEM: AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT THERE ARE TWO HYPOSTASES OF CHRIST AND DO NOT CONFESS ANY KIND OF COMPOSITION IN HIM. From this quarter the divided opinion rises up against us, or rather the cloven tongue. Its portion will be set with the unbelievers when the Master and Judge of all comes to convict them of all that ungodly sinners have spoken against him, as it is written, unless it should resolve in its heart to turn to the Lord and to declare its own fault among men. For these are the charges brought against us from the other side by those who divide the ineffable and God-befitting union of the Word with the flesh, and who in turn reject the economy wrought on our behalf. Denying the God who redeems them, they say, first, that we are wrong to hold a composition of the divine and human natures. Second, that since Christ's hypostases are two, we are wrong to say that a union according to hypostasis took place and to acknowledge his hypostasis as one. Third, that since there are two sons, we wrongly confess Christ to be one Son. Fourth, that we falsely call the holy Virgin Theotokos, Mother of God. Fifth, that we know Christ to be by nature not a mere man only, but God as well. Sixth, that we know the Word not as a God-bearing man, but as God made man.

Seventh, that we unlawfully proclaim that one of the Holy Trinity suffered in the flesh. In the eighth point of their impiety, denying the hypostatic union, they conjure up certain other unions that cannot hold together. Whatever objections they might reasonably raise against those who say that there is one nature as well as one hypostasis in Christ, we shall not defend these. But we who confess one hypostasis and two natures of Christ our Lord shall meet, in the power of Christ our God himself, the things they say against us in particular under each of the chapters listed above. By overturning these we shall refute the whole premise of their most impious doctrine. As was said, then, they accuse us first of all over our confession of the composition of the natures in our Master Jesus Christ, God, and they say:

CHAPTER ONE. "Everything that is composed with another is composed either whole with whole, or part with part, or part with whole; otherwise it is impossible to speak of composition. But whole and part are not said of the uncircumscribed. Therefore God the Word, being uncircumscribed, was not composed with the man taken from us. If he was composed, he is both made of parts and circumscribed, which is impious." First, then: these people limit every mode of the compositions God brings about to their own knowledge, so how can they say that everything composed is composed either as a whole or as a part? This whole sensible universe, that is, the visible world, is plainly a composition. What then do they say? Is its composition made from certain pre-existing wholes or parts, or was it rather compacted out of what did not exist at all? If they think that in the beginning it came to be from certain pre-existing wholes or parts, let them make their opinion known to us. If that is what they say, we may then argue with them as with pagans, and not as with people who differ from us only about the mode of the economy. But if they prefer piety to contentiousness and say that the composite world came to be out of what did not exist, they will hear that what does not exist is neither whole nor part. How then did the composition of this whole world come about, when neither any whole nor any part existed beforehand? If every composite necessarily comes about when some whole is composed with a whole, or a part with a part, or a part with some whole, as you say, then the universal assertion of your very first premise is false. Answer us another question as well. Every body is said to be composed of quality and quantity. Are these said to be composed as wholes or as parts? If as wholes, where and how did they exist as wholes, since they are not substances that exist separately before the body? And then, if the whole of quality and quantity was composed in the one first body among individual things, how did any second body come to be from quality and quantity after the first? Nothing would have been left over uncomposed, once the wholes of quality and quantity had been composed. But if they are composed with one another as part with part, first:

of what whole is quality, as quality, a part? If of a whole made of like parts, it differs from its own whole only in quantity, so it is a part in respect of quantity. And if it is composed in the respect in which it is a part, then in a body quality too is composed with quantity in respect of quantity. But if these belong to a whole made of unlike parts, then whole and part do not have the same form. In such cases, if the whole is a quality, is its part a quantity or something else [?]? And again, if the whole is a quantity, is its part a quality or something else? To put it another way: if they are composed as part with part, we must still inquire into the composition of each of their wholes, whether it is from wholes or from parts. This goes on to infinity, until we find something that came to be neither from wholes nor from parts, though it is one of all the composite things (for only the divine is altogether simple). In this way it will certainly be shown that not every composite is formed by some whole being composed with a whole, or a part with a part, or a part with a whole. These, then, are the inconsistencies of your first premise. Then there is the assertion of your second premise: that everything composed by any kind of composition whatever must be made of parts and circumscribed, and that nothing whole and without parts can ever be composed. Let someone come forward and answer this. Look: the point is indisputably without parts, yet when composed it produced a line. How then was something without parts composed? By common consent the point is granted to be without parts. Likewise the ultimate instants of time, which are without parts, produce time by being composed. Then, what do you tell us about the soul? Does it seem to you that it too is made of parts, since it is composed with the body? Or, being without parts, is it by nature incapable of composition with the body, according to your axiom, if everything composed is made of parts? If you hold that the soul is without parts and uncircumscribed, and for that reason incapable of composition with the body, we will not cut you short with many arguments. Instead we will put a burning wick to your flesh, if it can still be called yours, and ask you: does your soul, which is debating these matters with us, feel nothing at the burning, or does it? It is not the body we are questioning. If you say that the soul suffers nothing at the burning, we will go away in silence, as men convicted most plainly by your impassibility of ignorance about these matters. But if you say that you are in extremely violent pain at this and cannot even bear to discuss these things because of the burning, you will hear from us that we will not stop or take the wick away until reason persuades us of the cause of this shared suffering. A great difficulty arises for us. We are burning a body made of parts, not you, that is, not your soul, to which we are speaking and which is without parts and incapable of composition with the body. And yet that very soul says it is impeded in its natural activity. If, as you hold, the soul or any other nature whatever is truly without parts, it will in no way be composed with anything. And what is in no way composed with anything, but always exists absolutely and by itself, is not struck along with something else when that is struck,

nor is it beaten along with it when it suffers, nor does it rejoice with it when it is pleased, nor, in short, does it share in the same experiences. No one will share an affection that is numerically the same as what befalls another. Indeed, when the rich man feasted in luxury, Lazarus did not rejoice; likewise, when the rich man was burning in Gehenna, Lazarus felt no pain. Nor did we just now feel pain with you when you said you were in pain from the wick, since we are admittedly not composed with you. Their own mischief has turned back on them, and these things clearly show that those who want to push natural philosophy too far, even into divine matters, are fighting against sense-perception. Will they perhaps choose the other branch of the dilemma, then, and say of the soul that it is made of parts as well as circumscribed, and for this reason is composed with the body, which is made of parts and circumscribed? If you say this, we in turn would say: consider the consequences. First, the soul would grow with the body, shrink with it and be cut up with it. Otherwise it will not give life to the body once the body has grown, since it has not come to be in the added part as well by composition. Nor would it fit the diminished body, unless it somehow contracted along with it. Then what would you say next, since everything made of parts and circumscribed is in a place? What is in a place is either a body or an inseparable accident of a body, so the soul too must necessarily be an inseparable accident. In that case one can no longer think the soul immortal, or self-subsistent, or a substance. Or else one must say that it is a body, contained by a body. But if the soul is a body, it will not pass through the body without dividing it or being divided by it, if it is true that one body does not pass through another without one of them being divided. Moreover, if every body added to a body increases its bulk, ensouled bodies would necessarily appear bulkier than dead ones. Further, if the soul is a body, it too has continuous quantity and shape. Having received body throughout its whole self in the composition, it too will come to have greater bulk, for whatever one body does to another as a body, it will also undergo from the other. There is a host of other absurdities besides, which we must pass over for now because they would lead us far from the questions at hand, and what has been said already shows well enough how weak your hypothesis is. All this has been said because of your second premise, the assertion that whatever is composed must be both made of parts and circumscribed, the premise on which your whole fine argument was built. What has been said is enough to demolish your house built on sand, so we will pass over the countless other absurdities that follow from your hypotheses. Indeed, you simply suppose that the intellectual and spiritual thing, equal to the angels, and still more the thing made in the image of God and breathed from the glory of the Almighty, is made of parts because it is admitted to be composed. If this is granted, then by your reasoning it must follow either that its kindred, archetypal

and productive principles, those of the soul, must also be reckoned made of parts like it, since the soul is their image and inbreathing [?]. Or else, if you say that those principles are without parts, you must free the soul too, along with them, from the division into parts that belongs to bodies. Whether you overlook the truth willingly or unwillingly, we will show it to you in the power of Christ, and what we say will serve either for your understanding, if you are willing, or for your condemnation. The whole does not always signify, simply and absolutely, what is complete with respect to its parts or made of parts, as you suppose. If it did, all simple things would have to be called incomplete, since they are without parts and do not have a wholeness of their own composed of parts. Or else, if they were called whole and complete, they would be composed of parts and no longer simple, so that nothing simple would be complete or appear entire. If this is granted, your own words will turn against you. You do not allow even the Divine itself simplicity without a wholeness made of parts. In representing it too as necessarily needing composition and parts for its completeness and wholeness, you would be forcing this whole Divinity, which is without parts and more than perfect, to lose one of the two, either its simplicity or its perfection. But in truth, gentlemen, what is properly whole is what is complete according to its own principle, whether it is simple and without parts or composite and made of parts, provided only that it is seen to possess its own principles without deficiency. That this is so, and that a subject's being without parts does not hinder the notion of wholeness, is plain: we say that the point is something complete and whole, and so is the unit, and the partless and instantaneous "now" of time, and the divine, and all simple things. We do not attest their wholeness because they possess their own parts without deficiency, for we have already admitted that they are without parts. Rather, each of them possesses the full principle of the partlessness proper to its form, preserved, unimpaired and complete, and so, according to its own nature, bears the distinguishing mark of its form. This, then, shows concerning the whole that something can be composed whole with whole, and that what is called whole need not be made of parts as a result of the composition. As with what was said about what is without parts, the uncircumscribed too must be, and be called, whole. By the principle of the uncircumscribed, it is whole with all the properties of uncircumscription, and as such it is complete; otherwise it will not be uncircumscribed. If, on their hypothesis, the whole is conceived solely as the completeness of its parts, then God, being without parts and uncircumscribed, will not have wholeness. And if he lacks wholeness, then even though he is freed from composition, he will be charged with imperfection instead. But if he is something whole, he can also be composed. If, then, he possesses both his uncircumscribedness and everything that belongs to the uncircumscribed without deficiency, he could, as uncircumscribed, [?] even on this basis, as their own assertion holds. And so he can be composed, being something whole, complete in the principle of uncircumscription and partlessness. We have examined these things at length because you do not rightly know what the whole is. You think it exists only in bodies, or rather only in continuous quantities,

as a local juxtaposition of certain parts joined together and positioned relative to one another. It seems, my fine sirs, that the natural philosophy you pursue so zealously through the senses has dragged you down into this great senselessness. Still, let us look more closely at how you say the uncircumscribed cannot be composed with what is made of parts. First, to call something uncircumscribed is to speak rather superficially, in terms of relation to place. Is uncircumscribedness, then, an obstacle to union by place? But such union is juxtaposition, not composition. You may think the union of the Word with the flesh is of this kind: that one of the things composed extends beyond the other, and that things united and juxtaposed in this way must be like the double soles of sandals, where one sole must not jut out, hanging beyond the other and exceeding it. If so, you have made it plain from this as well that you imagine both the union and uncircumscribedness not in a way befitting God, but as a bodily magnitude. You picture something ten thousand cubits long, or simply of infinite size, joined to some other, smaller body by a certain arrangement of parts. Yet even if you think this, on your own terms nothing would prevent their juxtaposition. You granted that composition can also occur between a part and some whole, so there is also juxtaposition of the small with the great. And if you say, "This juxtaposition is not really of a whole with a part, but of a part of the whole with the whole of the part [?]," consider even so: when the parts of something are circumscribed, so is its whole. So even if not with this particular thing made of parts, then with another, larger one, the whole of the divine part that is juxtaposed would by nature be capable of juxtaposition. Nothing, therefore, will be shown to be uncircumscribed by nature on the basis of being uncircumscribed in place. We must ask you further: does this uncircumscribed one, that is, God, circumscribe the world or not? If he does not circumscribe it, then the world is not in him, nor will it necessarily be shown to be truly smaller than he is, and the other blasphemies will follow. But if he does circumscribe it, then, since everything made of parts, if it is circumscribed, is circumscribed either as part by part, or as whole by whole, or as part by whole, or as whole by part (we shall use your own terms), God, who circumscribes what is circumscribed and made of parts, must certainly be made of parts too. And again, how do you say this happens? Suppose God circumscribes things as a larger body does a smaller one, the way people shut beetles up in balls of wax. Then he is merely the place of the things in him, and God is a continuous quantity, a body of bodies, made of parts and composite. Far from being free of composition, he is necessarily of a nature to admit composition. But if these ideas are senseless and utterly loathsome, then God must be said to circumscribe the world in another way than bodies circumscribe. For in truth it must be said that he circumscribes all things, bodily and bodiless, but not as a body does. And he is uncircumscribed, not as a body that has no larger body to circumscribe it, nor as though he left some of his parts hanging somewhere in an empty

region of the universe, but because in power he surpasses every nature and extends beyond every place and time. So when he is composed, he will not be composed as a body or as some divisible nature, so as to be thought divisible because he is composed as part or whole. The principle of body and of division into parts did not necessarily attach to him in order for him to circumscribe things made of parts. In the same way, his composition with man does not bring any such suspicion in its train. Otherwise, it would be no great thing for the uncircumscribed not to be contained by the circumscribed, for that belongs even to an uncircumscribed body, namely the heavenly one. But if, even in something smaller that he himself circumscribes, he can be contained without hindrance, whole and uncircumscribed, cramped by nothing, this is truly the uncircumscribedness of a natural power that no force shuts in or circumscribes from doing what it wills. This is what was said, as something exceedingly wonderful, by the one who said of Christ according to the flesh, "In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." So, you wretched men, you are wrong to claim that in God's case too everything composed is composed either as a part or as a divisible whole. Refuting just one of your premises would have been enough to demolish your whole argument, since once one absurdity is granted, all absurdities are conceded. Yet see: we have gone through all your premises, even if we have drawn out the refutation at greater length, and the conclusion of your whole syllogism has been shown to be utterly false. In the first premise you wrongly claimed that everything composed is composed as a part or as a divisible whole. It was shown that things are not so, since this universe, fitted together by the divine will, is composed out of what did not exist. Bodies too are constituted in their essence from quality and quantity, and for the reasons given above, neither of these can be called whole or part before their composition. Your second premise misled you in asserting that "whole" is not said of things that are without parts or uncircumscribed. It was shown that the point, the unit, the "now," the soul, all simple things and the Divine are called whole by their own principles and are without parts, even if their partlessness is not the same in each case. But even if we granted you that all simple things, being without parts, can necessarily neither be called whole nor ever enter into composition, I would gladly ask you: how, then, could it be granted that all composite beings did not come from composites? And the regress will go on to infinity if composites do not come from simple things, since by your account they cannot come from things without parts. The first composites will then have been composed from I know not what, unless you come forward and show us. Furthermore, that the uncircumscribed is whole by the principle of the uncircumscribed, just as the circumscribed is whole by the principle of the circumscribed, must [?]

[?]…has been shown, and so it can also be composed, if indeed this is what you think prevents composition. It has also been shown that just as what has no parts is not prevented from circumscribing what has parts, so it is not prevented from being composed either, though in the way proper to itself and not part by part. So even to young boys the weakness of your impious conclusion is obvious, the one that says: "Therefore God the Word was not composed with the man from us." In this way all your sophisms have been poured out and scattered like chaff before the wind, because they were put together in unbelief and in ignorance of the power of the divine will. But, sirs, even if there were no argument to refute your absurdity, do we not shudder to think this way? God found out all these existing things when they did not exist, together with all their various compositions, and made them both to be and to be such as they are. Could he then not bring forward here some newer and more necessary composition than those known to us, and devise it for himself, when he wished, for the sake of existing things, to compose himself with one of them, and so to reveal a composition not yet set in order among existing things? If we doubted this, how could we not reasonably suppose that all the other existing things also came from things that existed before them? For no composition of existing things was yet known to anyone when, in the beginning, it was devised by God. And yet, though none of them existed before, we confess that God afterwards made all composite things. When and where did another world come into being, or did such a Christ appear to the world? It is clear, then, that both in the beginning and out of things that are not, God makes what he wills, according to the piety of Christians and according to the belief of the Hebrews. Since he is himself the Maker of nature, how could he not also be an unseen innovator of natural things?

"Everything that is composed with another is circumscribed and has parts, as was taught above. And everything circumscribed and having parts is of a different essence from what is simple and uncircumscribed. If this is so, God the Word was not composed with the man from us, since he is consubstantial with the simple and uncircumscribed Father. Or, if he was composed, he is of a different essence from the simple and uncircumscribed Father, which is impious." But it is not true, as you declared, that anything whatever composed with another by any composition whatever is circumscribed and has parts. We truly demonstrated this above, and you assure yourselves in vain about uncertain things. When you try to build further arguments on what has been conceded in order to prove your own positions, the same thing happens to you as to those who want to build in the air or to lean on a reed of papyrus. Since we have demonstrated the contrary of what you proposed, it is clear that the contrary of your conclusions will also follow. For if something follows from one of two contraries, its contrary will certainly follow from the other.

[?]…from the simple and uncircumscribed Father. And everything of a different essence from the simple and uncircumscribed Father is not properly Son of the simple and uncircumscribed Father. Therefore everything composed with another is not properly Son of the simple and uncircumscribed Father. And if everything composed with another is not properly Son of the simple and uncircumscribed Father, God the Word was not composed with the man from us, since he is properly Son of the Father. Or, if he was composed, God the Word is not properly Son of the Father, which is impious." Since we are dragged around again by your repetitions, we too say: But, sirs, not everything composed with another is of a different essence from the simple and uncircumscribed Father. So your present syllogism is also entirely destroyed, because its first premise has been overturned. Nothing of a building is left standing once its foundations have been torn out from the base. Those who are wise only in their own eyes, and who often insist on uncertain things, seem to do nothing but write on water, card wool into the fire, and beat the air.

"Anything whatever that is composed with another is called Son of the simple and uncircumscribed Father only in some loose sense, if it is called so at all. And everything called Son of the simple and uncircumscribed Father in some loose sense is properly a creature of the simple and uncircumscribed Father. Therefore everything composed with another is properly a creature of the simple and uncircumscribed Father. If this is so, God was not composed with the man from us, since he is Creator of all and not a creature of the Father. Or, if he was composed, he is a creature of the simple and uncircumscribed, and not properly Son, which is impious." It is no labor for an opponent always to set against your undemonstrated axioms simply their negation when you affirm, and their affirmation when you deny. But you ought to have put forward your first premises soundly, so that you would not add your later ones on a rotten basis. Since your positions have been overturned from the roots in the first arguments, it would seem foolish to answer you at length about the later ones, because all your syllogisms up to now rest on the force of your first argument. Besides, since the uncircumscribed Father has only one true Son, the very one who was composed, how can anyone show by a universal negation that the proper sons of the uncircumscribed are not composed, or by an affirmation that every Son of the uncircumscribed who is properly so is also incomposite? Suppose unique things, of which there is no species or genus, had to be shown through universals. Then, since every body is in a place, heaven too would be in a place, and so on to infinity. And since no star is seen by day, neither is the morning star, although it has been seen by day on several occasions. And since no point lies exactly in the middle of a circle in every direction, neither does the center. And what connection, most sagacious sirs, would you have composition bear to sonship, whether proper or loose? For quality is composed with quality, and quantity with quantity, and [?] with [?], and stone is composed with wood.

Was he composed, then, because he is Son of the uncircumscribed in a loose sense? Or is it neither because of the loose sense nor because of the proper sense? If things are composed for none of these reasons, then neither would they remain incomposite for any of these reasons, but for other reasons that are proper and necessary to composition.

"Every uncircumscribed essence exists everywhere, and in each thing, and in itself, in the same way and alike, beyond comprehension, insofar as it is essence, since this is proper to what is uncircumscribed. And everything that exists in all things in the same way and alike cannot be in something in one way and then another, insofar as it is essence, for 'alike' excludes 'in one way and then another.' Therefore no uncircumscribed essence can be in something in one way and then another, insofar as it is essence. If this is so, we must ask whether we say that the essence of God the Word is circumscribed or uncircumscribed. If we say circumscribed, the blasphemy is obvious. If we say uncircumscribed, then either the essence of God the Word is composed with all things or it is composed with nothing, because it cannot be in something in one way and then another insofar as it is essence, since it is also uncircumscribed. But it is agreed that it is not composed with all things. Therefore it is not composed with anything, and those who say that the essence of God the Word is composed with the flesh from us, which he took for his own manifestation, are impious." Truly the sinner is caught in the works of his own hands, and his mischief returns upon his own head. Consider what you have just said. You say that the uncircumscribed essence exists in the same way and alike everywhere and in each thing, that is, in each and every circumscribed thing, and in itself, that is, in the uncircumscribed. You say that this is proper to an uncircumscribed essence: not to be one way in the circumscribed and another way in itself, that is, in the uncircumscribed. And you have already supposed that it cannot be in different ways in the things in which it is, even if those things differ, for it is alike both in circumscribed things and in itself, since it is uncircumscribed. Then how can it be impossible, because it is uncircumscribed, for it to be in some circumscribed thing, whether formerly or now? Following your premises, it would not even be able to be in itself, if indeed it is alike in itself and in things other than itself. If it is alike in all things as in itself, it would rather follow necessarily that nothing prevents it from being in a circumscribed thing, and that, just as it is in the uncircumscribed and simply in itself, so by your own account it is also in the circumscribed. So both in this argument and in the preceding ones the opposite of what you want has been demonstrated against you: you wanted to show that the uncircumscribed cannot be composed with the circumscribed. Now suppose that, because the uncircumscribed cannot be in things in one way and then another, you insist that it is in Christ just as it is in all things. Then, because it appears alike, as you say, both in itself and in all things, it will be in water, stone, plant, ant, fish, horse, man and angel, and in all things, just as it is in itself. But if it is not alike in itself and in an ant, your 'alike' has been dissolved, and it will be in Christ differently from

all other existing things. You say: "Since it is agreed that it is not in all things, it is not in anything either." But you who said that it is in all things just as it is in itself will hear the opposite. It is agreed by all, even more firmly than that, that it is in itself. So it would be clear that it really is in all things too, for your own words say that it is in all things alike, just as it is in itself. Either, then, it is not even in itself, but outside itself and separated from itself, or it is in itself, and in something, and in all things. It follows that no composition can any longer exist or be conceived as unique. Instead, you who wish to set aside the truly most glorious union of the Word with the flesh end up attesting every kind of composition to the uncircumscribed.

"Anything whatever that is composed with another so as to complete one living nature or hypostasis turns out to be a part of this nature or hypostasis. And every part of one living nature or hypostasis suffers, by natural necessity, together with the part with which it completed such a living nature or hypostasis. The soul suffers with the body even when it does not will it, so that it sometimes ceases from its own activities when the bodily members through which it acts are harmed. Likewise the body wastes away by natural necessity along with the griefs and cares of the soul. But it is not right to say that God the Word suffered by necessity together with the ensouled flesh from us. Therefore God the Word was not composed with the man from us so as to constitute one nature or hypostasis. And if he was composed, he also suffered by necessity, which is impious." Before anything else, I would gladly learn from you whether you too think that nature and hypostasis are the same, as the champions of one nature do. If you too say this, we will catch you without effort in sophistry, blurring things that have different names and different meanings by assuming that they are just several names for one thing. Meanwhile we will refute you on this point. First, from the doctrine of the Trinity: if you take these to be the same, you must think either that there are three essences or that there is one divine hypostasis. Second, when we speak of two natures, you demand that we also speak of two hypostases of the Lord, as though in your opinion the duality of nature were not fully stated unless the doubleness of hypostasis were added. The other things said on this subject in the chapter devoted to it will also lead you in triumph. There you, together with the followers of Eutyches, plotted against us by saying that nature and hypostasis mean the same thing: "So either speak of two hypostases as well, or do not speak of two natures." But these matters have been dealt with elsewhere, for you and for them.

But perhaps you are now ashamed to say this, and take each term as different. The conjunction "or" seems to bear witness to this for you when you say "so as to complete one living nature or hypostasis." You did not say "one nature, that is, hypostasis," but brought in the second term with an additive conjunction.

In that case we could say this to you. If you were directing this argument only against those who say that one nature is completed from the composition, it would carry some weight. But you have dared to bring the same charge against us, who confess that one hypostasis, and not one nature, results from the composition. So first let us hear how you can call everything composed to complete it a part of a hypostasis that has an essence. The description of a hypostasis is made up of certain properties, beyond what it shares in common with things of the same essence: properties that are essential or supervenient and accidental, and that either exist inseparably or come later. The essences of composite things are not parts of their hypostases, for the parts of essences are essences, not parts of hypostases. Nor does any accident that comes and goes without destroying its subject exist as a part in a hypostasis. Nor are even the natural properties themselves parts of the hypostases whose essences they belong to; rather, they are particular characteristics. For suppose the properties were parts of the hypostasis. A whole is of the same kind as its parts and identical with them, and is no kind of thing apart from all its parts. Then the whole of the hypostasis would also be nothing but a property, universally without essence. Not only this: since every property would be the whole of the hypostasis, then, if it is truly a property, either it will be a property of something else, and that again would have to be sought to infinity, or, if it belongs to nothing else, it will not be a property, and so not a hypostasis either. Therefore neither essences, nor accidents, nor essential properties are parts of a hypostasis that has an essence. Rather, they are certain things contemplated particularly in this particular thing: arising from the essence, or concerning the essence, or coming from elsewhere and existing in it and around it. Yet even if we grant you this (for it is not worth contending about it now), and say that God the Word is a part in his own hypostasis, it will follow that each of the three holy persons must be conceived as a whole greater than the essence of the whole Godhead. So much for this. Again, how is your second premise secure, which says that everything called a part of a hypostasis must suffer together with the other, and this always, in every respect, without qualification? The horse and the vulture both belong to the hypostasis and nature of the world. Yet not only does the one species not suffer with the other, but vultures thrive when horses are killed. And the lion kind has its very existence only through preying on cattle and the like, perhaps, since it is a destroyer of animals and an eater of flesh. What would one say birds suffer if the foxes that prey on them fall sick? On the contrary, one can see that when one part of the things in the world suffers, another flourishes, and when one thrives, another fares badly. And even within one single man, as one of our teachers says, though the outer man is wasting away, the inner man is renewed day by day. For in the same individual, numerically one, the spirit desires against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit. And the very many parts of one being, though entirely of like nature, are opposed

to one another, and one part thrives through the affliction of another. When we lie down on our right side, we rest the left, and when the left hand is tired, the right hand gets its rest. Moreover, in one particular hypostasis, when fat melts away in exercise, the flesh grows firm. When the skin is whipped, the bones and cartilage feel nothing, although they are in the same single composite body. And certain parts of the body that were sick before have not only not suffered along with other parts of the same body when those suffered, but have even been freed from the affliction they had before. One can see this in people with headaches or inflamed eyes when they get gout in the feet, and in those whose hand is cauterized for ailments of the mouth, or the crown of the head for leprosy [?]. Even if these things happen through a certain sympathy, still the affliction that destroys one part plainly preserves another, just as was said a moment ago about carnivorous animals. And as for fire composed with water into one nature and hypostasis of a body, it would be surprising if it suffered with the water as a part. Is it not rather said to increase and grow stronger as its opponent is weakened?

But perhaps you call parts of hypostases not the essences themselves or their parts, but the things that surround the essence. Then how, for example, has a snub nose suffered with grey eyes, or baldness with thinness? You will make us laugh heartily, though we are not joking but in earnest, you who are so clever at speaking and who always follow the facts of nature! Why then do you simply assume that every part of a hypostasis suffers with the other? So that, when we say the Word came together with the flesh into one hypostasis, you may prove that he suffers with it by nature. You ought rather to understand that the afflictions that come upon something composed of different things arise in each of its parts as befits that part. Fire does not melt the soul as it melts flesh. So if one of the components were entirely incapable of receiving the affliction that falls on the composite, it is clear that it will not suffer with what is passible, even though it is composed with it. Asbestos mixed with hay will not be burned along with it, nor will fire be beaten along with the iron. These things are seen through the senses and among sensible things. What, then, should we reasonably say about the clear impassibility of more immaterial things, which is preserved even after they are interwoven? Consider that. So much for this. Your other point, crafty as it was, did not escape us. We do not know where you got it from, but you said that all sympathy of one component toward another is involuntary. Stated universally, this is false, just like your preceding premises. For look: when the body is passively subject to pleasant objects of sense, the soul willingly shares such passions with the body. That is why, in the more licentious, it longs for them, runs after them, and does everything to obtain pleasurable passions. What necessary, or persuasive, or even merely possible premise, then, have you put together from which you could prove that we are forced to concede that God the Word suffered together with the ensouled flesh from us, which is what you thought

you were proving? If you examine your own arguments and look at what we have now said, you may perceive the truth and know this. No hypostasis has more than one nature; it exists in one composite nature made from different powers. Such a natural composition is natural in every respect, and so it shows its natural parts suffering together. But if a hypostasis were made from several natures or hypostases, the sympathies among them within it must necessarily be only in proportion to their likeness to one another, for that is also how it holds their natural unions. Nothing is joined to another entirely without some likeness and kinship, and so nothing suffers with another without them either, not even among inanimate things. This is precisely why the so-called simple elements, that is, the primary qualities, do not actually exist subsisting by themselves. Even if they did, they would be useless for composing the bodies of the world, because, differing entirely from one another, they would have no way of being joined. Fire and water, earth and air, by contrast, are mixed with one another through one of the qualities they have, when that is needed, and separated through the other, when that is needed. Hence fire is not composed directly with water, nor earth with air. Likewise one can see the unions of soul and body, and of all things, ordained by the creating Word. For in all creatures there is a likeness and a difference fully known to him, though often hidden from us. Since, then, God was not united to flesh naturally out of likeness and natural kinship, he does not suffer with it by necessity either. He assumed it out of good and beneficent will, by his good pleasure. And so that through the likeness his union with it might be firm, and the benefit to us through the union might be firm as well, he did not change himself to conform to it, since he cannot, and since acting in that way would not serve his own purpose. On the contrary, he makes it impassible together with himself, and changes it, though changeable by nature, once for all by the better change and into the better nature, that is, into his own unchangeability. The one who is unchangeable by nature was not changed and made like it in the worse nature. He has devised for himself an everlasting natural composition. The beginning of this union was the will and good pleasure of the Good. Its end, completion and confirmation is the assimilation to him of the nature composed with him. By the good pleasure that springs from his natural goodness, he grants his whole self in supreme goodness even to those unlike him in nature. At the beginning of creation he joined himself, the one who is, in some way known to him, even to what is wholly opposed to him, to what is not. Now he is united. He presented to himself all things that exist in any way, and that once were. Having now brought them forward into being and leading them into a higher being, he made them subsist in himself. He who is embraced all things and gathered them around himself, so that nothing of his own might ever again turn back through corruption into non-being, but that the whole might remain incorruptible with the incorruptible, all creation being set fr—

…[creation] set free from its bondage to corruption in Christ. For through the … from the beginning [?] … the things of the same kind as the firstfruits, and then all the things akin to these, and the kinds that first came into being to supply the fitting gladness of those set free, are made rich in God [?], and God will be all in all.

"Anything whatever that is compounded with something else to constitute one living nature and hypostasis is shown to be a part of the nature or hypostasis thus completed. Every part of a living nature or hypostasis necessarily needs the part with which it was compounded for its own benefit. The soul needs the body, and the body needs the soul, each needing the other for its own benefit: the soul for learning the divine commandments and pleasing God, the body for living with the soul and for holding an honour greater than all visible things. But it is not lawful to suppose that God the Word needs anything for his own benefit. Therefore he was not compounded with the man taken from us to constitute one living nature or hypostasis. If he was compounded, then he also needs that man for his own benefit, which is impious."

This present argument has the same force as the syllogism you set out before, or rather the same weakness, since that was really a paralogism. Clearly, then, it meets the same downfall. You have swapped some of the words and drawn the second argument from the consequences of the first, so as to show us how many arguments you have and how readily they come to you. For whatever admittedly suffers along with something surely also rejoices along with it in some respect, and therefore needs it for its own pleasure. If gaining such pleasure is counted as a benefit to the one who enjoys it, then you have raised the same difficulty against us with both arguments: first from shared suffering, and now from benefit. But look: in the earlier discussion it was shown that things compounded into a hypostasis are not necessarily natural parts; that things so compounded do not necessarily suffer together; and that things which do suffer together do not necessarily do so involuntarily. So it is not clear what part of your first argument survived unrefuted, that you were so bold as to move on to the second. And this example of yours, that the soul needs the body for learning the divine commandments and pleasing God: how did you come to say it? You did not put this forward well either, although in some sense it can be said. The body does not guide the soul toward learning true and divine things or help it to do so. On the contrary, at times it does it the greatest harm, overshadowing the intellect's contemplation of intelligible things with the images of sensible things. You yourselves fall into this failing quite often when you investigate certain mysteries that befit God. For among the

material and bodily things, which are the objects of learning through the senses, are stones and wood and animals, heaven and sun, water and fire. It is plain to all that these were the cause of the fall of the impious and the idolaters, who imagined nothing beyond visible things as objects of worship. Nor, I think, do even you doubt that the soul, not trusting only the sense that comes through the body, found the invisible Creator of this universe by reason and not by sense, and came to know him fully, although he has never been seen by sense and does not exist bodily. And how you could rightly say that what lusts against the Spirit helps the soul to learn the divine commandments and please God is unclear, unless perhaps you think that the Spirit assists what is opposed to these. When the one who says, "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" pleads to be delivered, is he pleading to be delivered from something useful for learning the divine commandments and pleasing God? Then how is he distinguished among the holy, the God-taught, the lovers of God? And what should we say about the spiritual learning and practice that are dulled in us every day by our cares for the body? In truth one can see the very opposite. Or do you want to show that the soul gains through the body? It does win a reward for itself by fighting against the body and disciplining it. It takes care of the body only so far as to keep it from being in pain and so hindering the soul's own activities, or from dying through the soul's neglect and so charging the soul with willfully loosing the bond that ties it to the body. That is why, though we live in the flesh, we have been commanded not to walk according to the flesh.

"Anything whatever that is compounded with something of a different essence to constitute one nature or hypostasis is shown to be a part of the nature completed from them. No part of one nature or hypostasis that differs in essence is called by the name of the thing with which it is compounded. In the case of man, the parts are indeed called by the name of the whole, but with some addition such as 'inner' and 'outer'; they are not so called without such an addition. And even if the whole is sometimes signified by a part, the parts are still not given the names of the other parts: the soul is not called flesh, nor the flesh soul. Therefore anything compounded with something of a different essence to constitute one nature or hypostasis is not given the name of the other part. If this is so, then either God the Word, who is called Son of Man, was not compounded with the man taken from us; or, if he was compounded, neither is he himself called Son of Man nor is what was taken from us called Son of God, which

Now, as though you had stopped caring about inquiring into the realities, you have moved on to an investigation of names. Through this whole argument of yours you have taught us something remarkable: that a thing which is entirely separated

from another would sooner be called by the other's name than a thing which is in some respect compounded with it. And yet we do not even claim that, if one part of a compound is called by the name of the other, it is called so in the same way. But let us examine your construction in order. You say: "Anything whatever that is compounded with something of a different essence to constitute one nature or hypostasis is shown to be a part of the nature completed from them." We have already said earlier that you could fairly bring arguments about things that make one nature by composition against those who speak of one nature of the Lord, but not against us.
