We have also shown that, where things are compounded so as to present only one hypostasis, one cannot properly call certain properties of essences "parts of a hypostasis," even though these properties are never observed apart from their own essences. It is their aggregate that presents one hypostasis, since by themselves, apart from the natures, they can neither exist nor come together with one another. Things that have no existence or coming together of their own, because they are referred to other things, cannot be conceived as having a wholeness of their own. Even when these properties change in individuals, provided they do not all change at once, the hypostasis is said to remain numerically the same. But a whole must never be supposed to remain numerically the same when it, or some of its parts, has changed. Suppose you call the natures of the properties within the hypostasis its parts. Then there are two possibilities. Perhaps you regard the whole as a nature just as its parts are, and so you regard every hypostasis as a nature formed by confusing the natures compounded in it, and as the generation of another nature besides those that came together in the hypostasis. Or perhaps you say that the whole of the hypostasis is unlike its parts. Then, if the parts are essences, you think of the whole as something without essence, and from a composition of things that exist you conclude to something that does not exist, for there is no middle ground between essences and things without essence. Or suppose you call both the essences and the inherent properties parts of the hypostasis. Then again, since the hypostasis cannot be at once and in the same respect both essential and without essence, its whole will reasonably resemble only one of its parts and differ from the other. So, first of all, it will be another thing to be counted. If it comes partly from essence, it is baffling how it could be without essence; if it comes partly from accident, it is unclear how it could be an essence. Besides this, if inherent properties are themselves parts of the whole within the essences, just as the essences are, then the parts of the whole exist within its parts to infinity and are not simply seen in the whole. Furthermore, when one part, namely the essence, perishes, the other parts in the whole, namely the inherent parts, all the accidents, must perish along with it, and so the whole is also destroyed together with this one of its own parts. What could one reasonably call more absurd than all this? For if the essence is a part and the accidents are a part, and there is nothing in the whole beyond these, and the accidents are inherent in the essence, then when the essence, which is one part of the whole, is removed, all the other parts are removed with it, and so the whole perishes because of one of its own parts. What, then, are these things that you have seen fit to call parts of a hypostasis in arguing against us, if neither the essences nor the natural properties nor the accidents

are in the hypostasis as parts? Whatever is in something is not necessarily in it as a part, for things are said to be "in" something in many ways. Moreover, you have argued against us, who believe the composition of the natures to be solely into the union of one hypostasis. How, then, could you declare that things compounded into a hypostasis are parts of a nature, cleverly misleading us, as you suppose? If you say this because you regard nature and hypostasis as the same, you have already been refuted by what was said on that very point, namely that they are not the same. But perhaps you consider nature to be one thing and hypostasis another, and yet still say that everything compounded is shown to be part of a nature, whether it is compounded into the wholeness of a nature or into the constitution of the definition of a hypostasis. (Not every composition and gathering together belongs to a natural wholeness.) Then clearly you also count fairness of hair, whiteness and grey eyes, for example, as parts of human nature. These too belong to the hypostasis, and even if they are natural parts, they are partial principles of what is in it. Then gypsum, gold and the sea will be akin in essence to the human species by nature, since in such features they partly share this kind of essential likeness with it. But your absurdity does not lie only here. You also said, without qualification, that the parts of a whole are not given the names of the other parts that are with them in the whole: "the flesh is not called soul, nor the soul flesh." Yet holy Scripture called the whole "flesh" when it said, "My spirit shall not remain among men, because they are flesh." In the whole, that is, in man, the soul is clearly present as a part, and it is above all the soul that is here accused of having become flesh. For the flesh did not become flesh by corrupting itself, nor would God charge it with having become flesh, since it was made so by him. How, then, is one part not given the name of the other, especially when God is accustomed to call them so? Admittedly, you could have said that the name is not applied in the same way, nor by nature, if you were willing to examine the matter properly; and we would have agreed with you on that. For we do not say that the same one is Father of the Word and of the flesh by nature in the same way, or that the same woman is mother of the Word and of the flesh by nature in the same way, as far as the mode and principle of nature are concerned. But we know that the same one is Father of one of the parts in Christ (so to speak) by nature, and of the other by grace, through its union with what is his by nature. And conversely, the same one woman is mother of the one by nature and of the other by grace, through its union with what is hers by nature. But consider your conclusion, which says: "Either, then, God the Word, who is called Son of Man, was not compounded with what was taken from us" (as though the composition were cancelled by the name), "or, if he was compounded, neither is he himself called son of man nor is what was taken from us called Son of God." This conclusion above all

shows that you have fallen into the greatest neglect of your own positions. It is astonishing that you say the same one is both Son of Man and God the Word, and again that what was taken from us is Son of God (which you have now proclaimed it impious not to believe, if you would only listen to your own words). You attach the same two names to each of the parts, with the utmost and most futile cunning and with an intention that is not right. Your aim, so he says, is to show from the exchange of names that the things which came together as parts did not come into a composition as a whole. This follows your irrational assertion set out above, that "what is compounded into one hypostasis is not given the name of the part that is with it," whereas in fact the flesh is given the name of the Word, and the Son of Man the name of the Son of God. If, sirs, it is truly given the name, there is no need to inquire any further about the composition. For since through the composition each part was made the other's own by nature, it also came to share in the other's natural names. But if it is not truly so named, then, on your own terms, it is not truly prevented from composition with the other either. So if God should ever move you to confess this, that the same one is truly named both Son of God and Son of Man, we will resist you no longer, but will embrace you as friends and brothers. But suppose you say that, because God the Word is not compounded with the man, you are free to call one part by the other's name, since the parts are uncompounded and distinct. Suppose you hold that if they had been compounded, both of the things that came together would be deprived of such an exchange of names. Then clearly you are drawing this conclusion: the further apart things that are distinct in their wholes stand from one another, the more readily they can share one another's names; whereas things that have come together and been compounded in their natures into one whole must on no account share names. What could be more ridiculous? It is as if someone thought that the coming together of things produces a separation of their names, and that the separation of things produces a coming together of their names. Yet we see the very opposite. When iron has been fired by fire [?], it is then also called fire. When the ark is overlaid with gold, it is called golden. In other cases too we see that whatever is in whiteness is called white. But on your view, when something is fired, it ought rather to be called water; when someone is self-controlled, he ought then to be called licentious; and when he does wrong, just. For at those moments these things stand furthest from their opposites. Yet every derivative name has taken its name from participating in a thing and being united with it. But you really seem to suffer the derangement of the gravely ill, who often strike themselves violently without feeling it.

"Anything whatever that is compounded with something else so as to complete one nature or hypostasis is shown to be a part of the

one nature or hypostasis completed in it. No part of one nature or hypostasis knows how, where or when it was compounded with what it was compounded with, much less learns it dimly afterward. Therefore anything compounded with something else so as to complete one nature or hypostasis does not know how, where or when it was compounded with what it was compounded with, much less learns it dimly afterward. If this is so, then either God the Word, who knows all things and never learns anything, was not compounded with the man taken from us; or, if he was compounded, he does not know how he was united to our man, which is impious."

Your first premise in this argument too serves as a kind of keel for both the earlier syllogism and the present one, and it has already been shattered in our earlier replies. Still, let it be granted for the sake of argument that the constituents of the hypostasis are parts and do not know how, where or when they were compounded. Even so, sirs, no one who shares even a small spark of rational nature would understand all this to mean that these things must happen in this case as well. Once it is agreed that the one who is compounded is himself the maker of the composition, how could he be ignorant of his own composition, since he is the maker of every composition? To put it another way: every part that is perfect in knowledge and exists before its own composition must surely know where, how and when it was compounded, even if it is said to have been compounded by another, unless it either fell away from its own perfect knowledge after the composition or was deprived of it before the composition. So either God the Word is not perfect in knowledge; or, on your view, he will not have existed before his own composition; or he will certainly know his own composition. What necessary conclusion, then, can be drawn for us from the chaff of these statements that would securely prove the claim that, if God the Word was compounded, he does not know how or where he was united to the man taken from us?

"If the Lord Christ is composite, as they say, then God the Word is a part, as the law of composites requires. But every part is in some respect less than its own whole. God the Word is therefore in some respect less than something, for he would not be a part if he were not less than the whole. If this is so, then God the Word is not true God either, since true God cannot be called less than anything: God is utterly beyond comparison and without equal. So let them either openly admit that they are opposed to those who know God the Word to be true God, or stop introducing to us a composite essence made of God the Word and our flesh endowed with a soul."

Your universal affirmations and the proofs drawn from them will now be shown to be truly useless to you. We tell you prophetically that you will be defeated by the very things in which you thought your strength lay. For you have missed the decisive point of what is under discussion, since you did not consider its nature. It does not follow that, because every part is less than the whole, God too, as a part … [?] of the Word … [?] of the whole,

in the composition that concerns him, will be thought less than what is called the whole composite in his case. Quite the contrary. All other beings, when compounded, are seen as parts and as less than their own whole. But God is not one among all things; he is around all things and transcendently above all things. It follows, then, that even when compounded he would not stand in the same relation as all other things, nor be reckoned a part of some whole. You should consider that the universal statements made in premises carry the necessity needed for a proof only when the argument concerns something of the same genus or the same species as the things covered by the qualification. When it comes to the nature of things of a different species or genus, even universal statements contribute nothing to a proof, unless they include the thing under inquiry as being of the same species, and show that it either falls under the principle that governs its kindred things or departs from it. For example, if we ask whether Paul the man is an animal, the universal affirmation about the species, which says that every man is an animal, will be useful for establishing what is sought. Likewise, if we are examining whether this Paul, the animal, is a substance, the universal affirmation "Every animal is a substance" will be relevant. But if the inquiry concerns something of a different genus or species, then all affirmations and negations that do not say something about things of the same species or genus are idle and useless for the question. For example, if it is asked whether Paul is not rational, and someone eager to prove this, namely that he is not rational, says, "Every stone and every blackness [?] is irrational," he has inferred nothing at all relevant to the question. He will rightly be laughed at, since he affirms irrationality universally, but of something of a different species. So we too say, "Every part is less than its own whole." Now if you say that God the Word is of the same genus and the same species as all the parts that are compounded and whose whole is known to be greater than they are, then you are right to apply to him the same predicate that comes from the universal affirmation. In that case, having become a part just like all things of the same genus and species, he too will be reckoned to relate in the same way to his own whole. But if you will not dare to belch out this godless claim, because you cannot bear the refutation of your impiety that winnows you and would immediately fall upon you, then clearly you are not arguing reasonably. You see this rule holding universally in other natural things, and you seem to think it rightly applies [?] also to the Word, who is above nature and, in his principle, beyond all other things. Hence you, who pretend to free the Divine from composition out of reverence, have already dishonoured it most lawlessly, by supposing that its nature has nothing exceptional about it compared with the other things that can be known. On your view, therefore, since he is subjected to the same principles as all things, he too could enter into composition with something else. Then where are the prohibitions of his composition that you set out earlier, on the grounds that his nature is beyond comparison and without equal among all things? But it is clear that

And where God, who is above us, is said to do or to suffer something, this is not to be understood in the same way as it is with us, even if it is expressed in the same terms we use, when certain things take place through his economy for our salvation. It happens in a different manner, one proportionate to his own nature. He is said to beget and to be begotten as we are, yet not in altogether the same way, but in a way above us. In the same way, when he is compounded, it is in a higher sense than anything that applies to us. Even among corruptible things, though composition is predicated of all of them, there is not one and the same principle and manner for every composition; each is proper to its own nature. But you now suppose that God has the same essence as created things, and so you think that he too is subject to the same things that befall them. On your view, then, the blessedness of the divine nature will have to be understood only as its avoiding and declining states that seem meaner, more wretched and more dishonourable. It will not be its natural and essential power of being above such things and free from them, nor its essential inability to share in such humiliations or be subjected to them. In that case it is time for you to suspect that his invisibility, too, comes not from his nature but from some concealment that screens him from every sight. And likewise his incorruptibility will come from his not entering, but keeping away from, the corrupting places among us, and from qualities, passions and activities, and simply from every attack against him. This, then, is what you need to understand, and it is plain even to boys: where natures differ, their compositions and whatever accompanies those compositions differ too. If you do not deny that the divine nature differs from us, how can you demand that its composition be like ours? We truly shudder at how easily you slide into impiety, and we think it necessary to remind you of this. When grammarians claim that some word has been noted in their own general rules, we concede it and put up with it, but we do not set the rule above usage. Usage comes first: they discovered the rule of analogy from usage, and usage was not taken from the rule. Likewise we subject the laws to the king, not the king to the laws. And do we then think that God, who invented all creation and all composition before they existed, cannot, when he so wills, be compounded otherwise than by the ancient laws of composition? Or that he cannot lay down some newer and more particular law for the composition that concerns him? How will these views not shut you up again in the atheism mentioned earlier, that of refusing to believe that the Creator of the universe, the Word who was also incomprehensibly made flesh, makes things even out of what does not exist? And why have you looked askance at this one marvel, the composition befitting God, if you believe nothing that is above our reason and nature? For we proclaim to you other doctrines still more paradoxical, concerning this same supernatural divine union. We say that our God Jesus Christ was conceived without seed. And if you think he is a mere man, that will be all the more incredible, for by natural reason what human being was ever conceived without seed?

What then shall we say [?]? Since this is not possible by nature, can it not have been done by God either? Or must we instead reflect piously and see the opposite? If it were one of the things that happen by nature, it would not be an act of God but of nature, and what happened would have come about from nature. But whenever something comes to be directly by the design of the divine nature, not from anything pre-existing but from what is not, it is newly ranked and acknowledged among the things that exist. Once we have admitted that something paradoxical can be done by God, we must not look for the reasons and credibility of paradoxical things in what has long been known. The laws of nature are very easily set aside by the lawgiver at the right time. If you do not accept these things in this way, it is time for you to refuse to admit that any body at all came forth from a virgin's womb, even if, as you wish, someone says that what was born of her was a mere man. For every body that passes through another body will leave the other visibly divided. Nor would it make sense for a man's body to walk with dry feet on the sea, since that has no natural plausibility either: lighter bodies float on heavier ones, not heavier on lighter. Nor could eyes ever be formed from clay and spittle and made fit for immediate sight in a man blind from birth, nor could the dead rise from the tomb. Nor could one confess that any other such miracle was the power of Christ or of the saints, since their cause cannot be demonstrated beforehand from natural principles. So you will not reasonably accuse the divine perfection of partial imperfection just because it has been compounded. Once God is understood to be called a part of this whole compound, he will not be understood as having some whole greater than himself, as a part does, because the principles that follow from his nature prevail even over those of his composition. Even if the principle of the divine composition requires that the whole be greater than the part, the principle of the divine nature requires that nothing be conceived as greater than it. Of the two opposing principles, then, which is the one that will be overturned by the other? If the composition is destroyed along with the nature, but does not destroy the nature along with itself, why must the composition not give way to the nature? But if that is not so, then clearly the composition would have to prevail over the nature. It is clear, then, from everything we have shown, that though the Word is called a part, he is not said to be one with partial imperfection. When he is compounded, he is not subject, as you claim, to the law of the compound substances among them. Nor is he less than what is called the whole in any sense in which 'compound' is used. Nor does he display his own uncreated, essential perfection after the measure of the smallness and natural relations of created things. So God the Word is not less than anything or in any respect, whether as compounded or as uncompounded. And your sophisms, which you think unanswerable and hard to defeat, vanish and dissolve like smoke. Even so, we do say that the Word is compounded in his essence with our essence, and we distinguish him as a part of the compound whole, Christ. But a compound essence, formed from his essence and ours, we never [?] say. God forbid!

CHAPTER 11 [?]. "Every single nature or hypostasis that is composed of parts of different essences has certain activities that neither of its components can ever perform in any way by itself, without the activity of the other. Soul and body, for example, need each other to fit out a ship, build a house, weave a tunic, and so on. As I said, neither of them can possibly do these things in any way without the cooperation of the other. If, then, one nature or one hypostasis was produced from the composition, as they say, of God the Word with the man from us, there are certain activities of this nature and hypostasis that God the Word could not in any way carry out by himself. (In the divine Scripture and in common usage, 'cannot' is said in two ways. Either it is like 'God cannot lie', because of his unlimitedness. Or it is like 'gifts and sacrifice cannot perfect the worshipper in conscience', because of weakness and an inability to achieve any effect whatever, if they should give [?].) These activities, which God the Word could not carry out by himself, he performed through the activity of the man. This shows either that God the Word is weak, or that he did unseemly things. If the first, then even now the Father lacks the strength to carry out such activities, since he is not compounded with the man from us, and in this respect the Son is greater than the Father, which is impious. If the second, the blasphemy is obvious, for God does nothing unseemly, either by himself or with another. And if it is not pious to grant either, then no composition of God the Word and the man from us has taken place." You seem to us to have suffered something like those clumsy archers who overshoot the target. They show lack of skill rather than good aim, because they do not know at what, how far and how the arrows should be shot. In this argument, as in the one before it, you imagined you were contradicting those who say there is one nature. Now, carried along as if by the momentum of your desire for a quarrel, you also set yourselves against us, who say that in our Lord Jesus Christ there is one hypostasis, not one nature. But we will briefly demolish what you have built. Every activity comes from a power, and every power of composite things belongs to them either from their parts or from the composition itself. Now one part of this composite hypostasis is God the Word himself. He is also the cause of the other part that is with him, and of his own composition with it. And every cause is greater in power and in activities than its own effects. How, then, will whatever composite one might say came to be in Christ have any activity greater than that of the part in it which is also its cause, namely the divine Word? But since the overflowing irrationality of your absurdities has led us to speak about substances, even though things stand as we have said,

we must nevertheless tell you this as well. If you look intently with the eyes of the mind, it is very easy to see that very many striking activities have belonged to the composite. Neither God without flesh nor man without deification could have performed them as they have now been performed. Tell us, by what reasoning will God without flesh pass bodily through an uncorrupted womb, or a body without deification pass through the body of an uncorrupted womb [?]? Who, having fasted forty days, was not hungry, being a man? And what God was ever hungry at all, before forty days or after? Who would say that God ever truly walked with a fleshly foot upon the water? Or that human nature [?] crossed the back of the sea with steps that did not sink? And there are other mighty works like these. The divine nature never performed any of them bodily, and human nature never worked such wonders at all. If, then, you have nothing to say to all this, it would be good for you, now that you know, to do one of two things. Either, seeing what is truly marvellous and extraordinary, speak as spectators of great things. Or, if you see nothing great, stop babbling about trifles. "Anything at all that is compounded with another is compounded either for its own sake or for the sake of another. It is compounded for its own sake as the soul is with the body, and for another's sake as the parts of a house are, for they exist for the sake of man. But God the Word will be compounded neither for his own sake, since he needs nothing, nor for another's, since he is inferior to nothing. For anything compounded with another, not for its own sake but for another's, is lesser than that for whose sake it is compounded. If God the Word will be compounded neither for his own sake nor for another's, then he is uncompounded and never enters into composition with anything." All your shoots spring from one and the same impious root, and all show the same kind of absurdity in mixing, against all reason, God who is above all things with all things. You claim that anything compounded with another is compounded either for its own sake or for another's. And if God is [the maker] of all things [?], as you think, we will show where your error leads from your own universal premise. For we too could reason thus. Everything that makes something makes it either for its own sake or for another's. On your view, what makes something for its own sake needs what it produces, and what makes something for another's sake is, as you say, lesser than that other. So God, in making the world, makes it either out of his own need or in the service of some other, better being. Or, if he makes it neither for himself nor for some other greater being, he will never make it at all. How could you say such things without signing yourselves up for the most extreme heresy? Again, whatever provides for something does so either for its own sake, as the soul does for the body, or for another's, as servants in household service do for their own master. So by your account God, who provides for all things, either does this out of his own need, and will need the things he provides for, or he does it as an inferior, not of one master only but of all. And he will turn out to be lesser than the things he cares for: the ravens, the lilies of the field and the beasts, for whom

he will prepare food and covering in due season. Who will put up with such blasphemies? But this too escaped you. Again you wilfully overlooked it, passing over in silence the chief point of the mystery of the divine incarnation and never even calling to mind the other way in which things come about. That is the way of providence for inferior beings, which comes about through the care that proceeds out of goodness from the Superior. It is by this above all that God is known to be good, almighty and the cause of all. It is for this reason that he is said to have been compounded, since the orthodox truly reckon his own purpose as the truth about him. For the sacred oracles say of him: "He did not count equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." What benefit, then, could come of this, as the goal answering to the purpose of the one who emptied himself [?]? None other than that we, whom he assumed, should be rescued from slavery and be equal to God, according to his good pleasure toward us from the beginning, that we should be in the image and likeness of God. Are you really of the opinion that no help of any kind is ever given to inferiors by those who need nothing? Have you never seen or heard of yourselves or anyone else exposing himself to danger, often, for the sake of a man perhaps, or a dog or some other animal that had fallen into a pit or a ditch, in order to pull it out? This happens every day among those whose intentions are not satanic and who take no pleasure in the ruin of the perishing. What, then, shall we say about such things that plainly happen? That the one who stood in safety shared the danger and was plunged down with the perishing creature for his own sake? Then show us what he gained by it. But if the helper came to the aid of the one helped as of a better being, then this argument of yours often shows the man who saved a dog to be worse even than the dog. It also shows the same of a king who happens to defend a little animal of his own free choice. And the Samaritan who tended the man who had fallen among robbers lifted him onto his own beast, served him, cared for him in every way and spent extra on him. Either he did these things because he himself had suffered what that man suffered, and, as you say, grieved at the man's wounds for his own sake and not for the man's. Or he was serving a better being, and is said to have done these things as a slave. On either account he will be neither virtuous nor reasonably owed any reward or thanks. In this way God, the helper of all, would be worse than all, more than anyone. And on your view he who supplies the needs of all would be suspected of being inferior not just to some one or some few, but to the whole universe. Who will tolerate such madness? So it is clear that our God was compounded with us for our sake and on our behalf.

[…] remains. Some do not remain, like the parts of irrational animals, and some do remain, like those of human beings after the resurrection from the dead. But everything that remains indissolubly in composition with that with which it was compounded, or does not remain, does not remain of itself. Rather, it is dissolved according to the limit the Creator has set in its nature. Nor does it remain by its own power, but by the power of something better and transcendent. Yet it is not lawful to say that there is any power better than God the Word. Therefore God the Word was not compounded with the man from us. And if he was compounded, either he does not remain indissolubly in the composition with that man, or, if he does remain, he remains by the power of something better, which is impious." Now that your bold talk is fading, it is time for us to cry out with David: "The swords of the enemy have failed."¹ What do you mean by this problem, born of perplexity? We would say the opposite. Since all compounded things are either preserved by something greater or dissolved in due time, those who wish to inquire securely must above all ask this very question: what is it that preserves all compounded things? Some say that this happens directly in some cases and in others through intermediaries, such as nature perhaps, or some other power. Yet the divine Word alone preserves and defines all things, since he also brought them into being. So both the intermediaries and the things bound together or separated through the intermediaries are preserved and compounded by his ordering and sustaining power. How is it not foolish, when he is present, to look for some other sustainer of his own composition? Or are you perhaps saying that he can preserve things far removed from his nature, but cannot hold together what is united in a proper sense to his own nature? What could be more nonsensical than that? You think that because his composition is not preserved by another, better being, it is therefore not preserved indissolubly by himself either, or at all. By the same logic, since he did not come into being through another, better being (for everything that exists has come into being through something better), would you then confess that he does not even exist? For nothing is better than God. It would then follow that God does not exist, since he had no better being through whom he came into being. Or else, if he does exist, according to your supposed wisdom he must have come into being through something better. How great the impiety of these views is, we will leave you to measure when you wake from your sleep. But […] ¹ Ps. 9:7.

[…] God the Word is held back from his own activities against his will, just as the soul necessarily ceases from activity when the body turns to sleep. But if God the Word is not compounded with the ensouled flesh from us as the soul is compounded with our body, and yet is compounded in some way, let them give us an example of the composition by which they want God the Word to be compounded with the man from us. If they cannot supply one, let them confirm their claim by the testimony of Scripture, for that is more trustworthy to us than any natural demonstration. If, besides the example, they lack this as well, then their claim is unattested, a bare assertion, and so unproven. For what is neither shown by natural reason nor confirmed by the testimony of Scripture would be the speaker's own fiction, and that is both implausible and impious." Is it really so necessary, O wise men, that what is taken as a likeness of something in one respect must resemble the example in its entire definition? How then could it still be called an example? It too will become an archetype, since the likeness lacks nothing. This is especially so when the likeness is said to concern the properties around the essence, or things that come to be in an essence, and not the essence itself. How, then, can anyone drag the properties of one thing over to the other as though they were its own? They would then be common. If you think this is how things stand, you must presumably reason in cases like this one. Black is seen in Ethiopians just as it is in ravens, so whatever is attested of ravens must also belong to Ethiopians. If, where there is a partial likeness in accidental features, all the other features must likewise be looked for in each of the like things, then consider this: it is said of ravens that sometimes they fly and sometimes they rest from flight and walk. Must we then think that Ethiopians do the same? And conversely, what belongs to Ethiopians must belong to ravens in turn. Again, the people in a theatre and the stones in it are said to be similarly juxtaposed, and it is agreed that they are composed with one another by a similar local union. Then the stones will be able to laugh, and the people able to be hewn, since the juxtaposition appears similar in both, at least by your facile reasoning [?]. What great carelessness! But you have already been refuted on the earlier points, and so that your later absurdities do not escape notice, we must also recall the rest of the argument. How do you show us that the soul necessarily ceases from its own activities when the body turns to sleep? First, sleep does not even belong to the body, since you cannot show that waking does either, unless you also attributed it to other inanimate things. In fact, it will necessarily be reckoned as something proper to the soul, or to the two together, O most expert natural philosophers. But let us grant you this point too. Even so, most people hold that in sleep the vegetative power of the soul is at its most active, so that even in this respect the soul is not idle. But we must put forward what is beyond dispute: that of the imaginative power very much so, but also of the memory

[…] often, and further, much activity of the soul's intellectual power is also put forth during sleep. Countless witnesses to this are the visions seen in everyday dreams, whether they arise from diet, from worry, from study, from some delusion, or from another cause. And though they are rare and few, the worthy acknowledge theophanies and predictions of what will happen, and healings, and the various ways Providence cares for those who sleep. Why then have you declared, so carelessly, that the soul is idle in sleep, and idle of necessity? It is true that the soul does not display all its activities in sleep, nor at all times: for example its vegetative and locomotive motion, its sensory and imaginative [?] activity, its memory and intellect [?], and both kinds of appetite. But it is also attested that even when awake these do not all act at once, nor wholly in the same way. For it is not the soul's nature to put forth all its activities always, since its nature is not wholly simple, such that everything coming from it would be one and belong to a single activity. Rather it acts in some respects, at some times, and with some activities. Only God can put forth all his activity at once, timelessly and always. [?] So you have not reasonably seized on the example. Do you charge those who say that the composition of the Word with the man resembles that of soul with body (resembles it in a certain respect) that the holy [?] must therefore also be [?] in sleep [?]? Those who used the comparison of likeness adopted it for no other reason than to rule out the other known kinds of composition: bare relation, perhaps, or local juxtaposition, or a union by alteration, or a mixture that confuses. From this comparison they presented only the meaning of a natural blending without confusion, and an unchangeable union of differing essences. That is no reason for you to demand that we also say of the Word everything that belongs to the things united in this other union. Otherwise, when the flesh suffered, the Word would feel pain. When it grew, he would somehow grow with it, and be stretched along with it in its activities. When it declined, he would be contracted and hindered, as happens with soul and body. You would also say that he was composed by another and not by himself, and that he shared unwillingly [?], so far as is lawful, in the things of the flesh, either from necessity or for a reward. For these things happen in the case of soul and body. For these reasons we have already shown that what is alike in some respect need not be the same in every respect. But if everything that follows from the soul's composition with the body will follow from this composition of the Word, then do not even consent to say that he is composed. Instead you demand that we either call the union alike in every respect, or name some other union which the Word's composition exactly resembles. You point out to us, as it were, that things are not easily admitted to faith when they are seen not by induction from similar cases but by a principle peculiar to themselves. First, then, we will say to you again: Give us some nature among existing things that is in every respect like the nature of the divine Word,

and we in turn will give you a composition in every respect like the composition in his case. But if there is no nature like his, clearly there is no natural composition like his either. For where no instrument among existing things is like a certain musical instrument, its sound must also differ from that of all existing things. It is time for you, since we cannot point to any other craftsman who brings into being out of nothing the things that come to be, to refuse to accept this about God as well. Nor should you believe in a Father who begets God in this way, or in a Son, God, begotten in this way. Nor should you believe that Christ himself truly came to be, as we hold, or even the Christ you describe, since neither can we show you another like him, nor you us. Unless, of course, you say he was wholly equal to the prophets, as present Jewish opinion holds. In short, all rare things that exceed nature, the miracles, things that not everyone knows, things whose knowledge no rule or principle of art defines, things to which experience bears no witness: all these will be abolished according to you, or, so to speak, because of you. And what worse charge could anyone bring against you than this? But if, deeming yourselves worthy of the teaching of the scriptural word, you are moved to be persuaded, as you have now promised us, and you accept the testimony of the divinely inspired oracles, recognizing at least that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world, then we could put you to shame with countless citations. They show that the natural composition of our Master Jesus Christ came about truly, as of true God with true man. His holy flesh did not exist before its union with the Word; rather its coming into being and its natural union with the

This too must still be considered on our side concerning this matter. Within us there are certain organic parts that serve natural and most proper activities. They should not be thought of as simple instruments worked from outside. Rather they cooperate with what acts in them and through them according to nature, and together with it they produce something. In a human being these are the tongue and the palate and the other parts used for voice and speech, or even for laughter. Now it is acknowledged that the most proper activity of the divine nature is the making of things that did not yet exist, not even potentially, but are brought forth directly from him without any nature as intermediary. Such is the fashioning of human flesh from earth into life. Our Master and God Jesus the Christ displayed this in the case of the man blind from birth, and he did it through his own body: with his fingers he made clay and formed the man's eyes, although he could have done this by word alone. Clearly, then, he does these things in this way to show that his flesh is composed with him according to nature, because he puts forth through the body, acting in a human way, the things most proper to his own nature. No one, however much he wished, could himself speak or laugh or converse through an instrument not naturally composed with him. In the same way, God could not put forth the most proper activities of God through flesh

unless he were composed according to nature with his own flesh. But truly the divine power alone, with its own body, fashioned eyes of flesh from earth, gave them life, and gave them light. With its own body it also raised man up from the earth and abolished the power of death. For no one else can do these things, which God the Word was made known to us as doing through flesh, to show his own composition.

Chapter 15. "Anything whatever that is composed with another into the constitution of one nature, or of one living hypostasis, departs in some respect from the condition it was in before the composition. And everything that departs in some respect from its former condition becomes either better or worse than itself in that very respect in which it departed. But it is not lawful to say that God the Word became better or worse than himself. Therefore God the Word was not composed with the man from among us, since he did not become better or worse than himself. If he had been composed, he would have progressed either toward the better or toward the worse, which is impious." It is true that the divine nature does not admit what is worse. Indeed it surpasses anything whatever, since it supplies every good thing and needs nothing. If something belonging to the composite Word, whether after the composition or before it, were alien to him or greater than him, then perhaps his voluntary composition, making him depart in that respect, would have put him in a better state. It could not have put him in a worse one, since it is acknowledged to have come about by his good pleasure, and no one takes pleasure in what is worse. But if all things are from him and through him and to him, and he is the one above all things both before his composition and after it, what else can be conceived in which he might, after the composition, become better or worse by departing from his former condition? You will not be allowed to testify that the nature of composition changes and alters the things subject to it, while we are forbidden to recognize unchangeability and unalterability in the nature of him who causes all composition. If you do not forbid us this by mere fiat, we could not show it to you more plainly than by this very fact. Though his essence was subjected to a composition that, on your view, alters, displaces and changes, it preserved its own unchangeability. Beyond circumscription and beyond reason, it remained within its own bounds and principles, and never departed toward anything alien to itself. So truly, most wretched men, you lean on this argument too to no purpose at all.

"Anything whatever that is composed with another either leads that with which it is composed, as the soul leads the body; or is led by it, as the body is led by the soul; or neither leads nor is led, like the parts of a house. And everything that in a composition is led, or neither leads nor is led, is wholly irrational and mindless, like the body and the parts of a house. If then God the Word was composed with the man from among us, he either leads or is led, or neither the one nor the other. And if he leads, the man from among us will be irrational and mindless,

which is impious, an offshoot of Arius and Apollinarius. If he is led, let the blasphemy that follows be turned back on the heads of those who say that God the Word is composed with the man from among us. But if he does not lead, as in a composition, because the Lord's man is not irrational, and again is not led, because of the acknowledged blasphemy that would follow, then he was not composed with the man from among us at all. For anything whatever that is composed with another either leads or is led or neither, as we said." We marvel at how you invent such methods of compelling syllogisms, and we would pray never to learn the cleverness of such intelligence as yours. Let us consider what bearing your statements have on proving that the Word is not composed with the flesh. For we can turn them around and use your own words to prove the opposite, the composition, by saying this: "Anything whatever that is not composed with another either leads that with which it is not composed, as the helmsman leads the ship; or is led by it, as the ship is led by the helmsman; or neither leads nor is led, as Mount Sinai is not led by the sea. And everything that is uncompounded and is only led, or neither leads nor is led, is irrational and mindless, like the things just mentioned. If then the Word was not composed with the man from among us, he too either leads or is led, or neither the one nor the other. If he leads, the man from among us will be irrational and mindless. If he is led, let the blasphemy be turned back on the head of the dragon who first sounded such impieties in your ears." Seeing, then, how senseless your argument is, you might correct yourselves and begin to build your syllogism from your second premise, saying perhaps: "We know that all things led in a composition are irrational, not simply because they are led, but because they are led while in a composition." To this too we will reply: Do you know these things to be irrational because they are led in a composition, or simply because they are led? Or is it because by their nature they are always things of this kind? Whether they are spoken of and considered on their own or in a composition, they are recognized as irrational, and are carried along both by things composed with them and by things not composed with them, provided these have any power at all to lead them. For you will not show that what is rational by nature becomes irrational in a composition, or the reverse; composition does not make it any less rational. If you do not agree that this is so, but reckon that the body became irrational because it is led in the composition, then clearly you know it to be rational when it is on its own. You think that the body, when not composed with a soul, is rational, but in its composition with the rational soul comes to share in irrationality. And who will put up with such irrationality in those who think this? Further, if composition is the cause of the body's irrationality, and you posit it as the proper cause of irrationality, you would force the soul to be irrational as well, since it too was composed. And if it is irrational, it too is led. And if it is led in the composition, it too

will be led by nothing other than the body composed with it. So you will end up proving the opposite of what you set out to establish: that for the body, composition became the cause not of being led but, on the contrary, of leading something, namely the soul. Since these things are so, the argument is vain. We know that the soul thinks, because it is by nature rational both in the composition and without it, and that it is not led by the things it is naturally fitted to lead, but leads them. And the body, because it is by nature irrational and soulless both in the composition and without it, we recognize as being led rather than leading. These considerations show that it is not composition but nature, being irrational or rational, that causes a thing to lead or to be led. We must now go further and examine whether the nature of rational beings is naturally fitted to lead in every respect and never to be led in any respect at all. Then we will know whether the Lord's man, if he were led by the Word, would really be shown to be mindless and irrational. If rational beings are never led at all, then servants are not led by a master, nor a city by a ruler, nor soldiers by their general [?], nor will they ever be led, though they are seen being drawn even to death at his nod. Nor would the souls of the holy, nor angels, nor Powers, nor anything at all rational or intellectual in the ranks of the holy orders be led by God in any respect, as the products of your sagacity would have it. Otherwise, whatever is led is shown to be wholly irrational. For you have given simply "not being led" as the mark of what is rational, without properly adding "not being led in every respect against its own free will." So these clever syllogistic arguments of yours, my good sirs, make you a laughingstock to those who are truly rational.

"What is by nature impassible cannot be composed with what is passible. For of the things that are seen to happen to the composite, either we will say that the impassible also shared in them, or we must suppose that the passible did not suffer either, but only seemed to. If then the divine nature was in the suffering body, either it did not remain impassible itself, or the flesh did not truly suffer." It would be astonishing if you think as you speak, most wise men. No one, not even the utterly foolish, says that because the soul is composed with the body, it is certainly cut, warmed and chilled along with it. Yet the soul is not attested to possess impassibility to the degree that the divine does; it falls incomparably short of the impassibility of the divine nature. Nevertheless, because the soul is not itself cut in this way, no one would say that its body is not truly cut or chilled. The soul perceives the sufferings that befall the body in another way. The soul does not undergo the cutting or division of its instrument, even if it feels pain over these things. But above all we say this to you. You say that God the Word is not composed with the passible nature because he is by nature impassible, lest some of the sufferings that befall that nature remain in it and the divine undergo them. In saying this you rather insult him

in the very things in which you glorify him. For if the adamant were thought unbreakable because it is not present with the materials being struck, it would not have its unbreakability by nature. Rather its distinction of being unbreakable would be accidental, a matter of fleeing and keeping away from what breaks things. On that basis glass, too, could have this distinction, and every other of the most fragile things [?]. Rather, a thing's impassibility will be recognized as coming from its nature if it is struck along with the things being struck and yet remains unharmed. Tested in this way, the adamant would rightly be admired, offering proof of its own nature in the trial of the matter. Likewise the so-called amiantus is not shown to be incombustible by having no contact with the nature of fire. If that were the test, all matter, even grass itself, could [?] be called incombustible. But because, when combined with burning bodies, it does not burn along with them, we are rightly amazed at it. That the Lord's flesh suffered, the senses, behold, bore witness to the eyewitnesses. But that the Word did not suffer with it, his activity both during the suffering and after the passion of his flesh has given full assurance. For if he himself had suffered and died, he would not have given life to the nature that died, that is, the human nature, and he would not truly be attested to have raised himself. In one of the things in him, then, Christ died; but in another of the things that are his, living and not having died, he raised himself.

Chapter 18. "On your view, the composition of God the Word with the man from among us benefited either him alone, or the man with whom he was composed, or both together, or neither himself nor that man but only us, or [?] us, but not at all the man from among us who was composed with him, or both him and us together, or [?] also the man from among us, but God [?]. If it benefited God, or only the man with whom he was composed, or God and the man together [?], but not us, how is it not false that our Lord Jesus Christ became flesh and died for us and for our salvation? If it benefited us alone, or God and us, but not at all the man from among us, how could we have been improved while the one from among us received no benefit whatever from the economy carried out through him? For the man from among us was not entirely without need either, since he was created, and indeed passible and corruptible, according to the wise. If it benefited God and the man from among us and ourselves, how is God the Word not in need, on your view, as is the man from among us who was composed with him [?]? But if the composition of God the Word with the man from among us, on your view, benefited us and the man from among us, but not God at all, since he is without need, let anyone who wishes come forward and say what the first benefit was that came about: either to the man from among us [?] of creatures from the composition of God the Word and the man from among us. Which

[?] combing out [?] for us, you now spread yourselves out in words. So you should heed the saying: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." Tell us, what need was there for your many-branched division into to whom, to which ones, and to what the benefits of the divine economy came? We proclaim this to you plainly, concisely and openly. The divine nature consented to be composed with ours not for any benefit directed toward itself. May no God-fearing person ever say or think that! Its becoming human came about for its greatest benefit toward us alone. First, then, the wealth of deification passed to the Lord's man as the firstfruits of the human [lump] and the head of the body of the Church. It passed to him first, as first recipient, and directly into his own nature, through the hypostatic union with God that blends them together [?], from his natural union with God. Then the benefits passed to the rest of the lump of humanity, to the other brothers of the seed of Abraham, and to the body of the Church, secondarily, by participation and indirectly. They passed through our natural union with the Lord's man from among us, who was benefited first. For he is of the same lump, even if he is its firstfruits. He is a brother, even if he is only-begotten and firstborn. He is of the same body, even if he is its head. He is the one who mediated for us, being the one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus our Lord. [?] But you say to us: "What need was there, then, for him to be composed with [?] nature, and as a result to be disgraced and dishonored [?]"

[?] goodness and beneficent power he has, having triumphed over the world. More and more is he glorified and [?] by all, our God, composed for us and for our sake. And this [?], according to this madness of yours, neither creat[or] [?]

…seed according to its kind, and living souls of creeping things, and the rest. In the same way, they say, he ought now as well to have entrusted the work of creation to another intermediary, and not have dishonoured himself by making man with his own hands. Nor should he have brought man forth after his own image and likeness, bringing his own stamp down into a lump of earth. Above all, he should not have put a living soul and the breath of life into him by his own breathing, settling himself in the clay from the beginning and laying down, as a pledge of his union with man, something from his own nature for the flesh that came from the earth. For it was not for any benefit to himself that he did these things either. If so, [?] another greater in power to make… For nothing is so characteristic of the divine nature as the creating of rational beings. By this the only Creator of all intelligible and rational things is distinguished from everything created and intellectual. Why then did it seem incongruous to you that he, who had entrusted the creation of man to no other being beside him or beneath him, should now also take on himself, with his own hands, the work of man's re-creation? And further, what would you say of Moses, who would not consent to take an angel as fellow-traveller and guide from Egypt to the land of promise when God offered him this? He said, "If you yourself go with us, well; otherwise we will not go up." And the godly love for mankind of the good Lord of all consented to perform even this service, as his own servant had declared. Consider too the prophet who said, "Not an angel, but the Lord himself saved us." If, on your view, the Lord already thought it beneath him that he, who gains nothing for his own nature, should work our salvation through himself without shame, rather than use some intermediary servant for his kindness toward us, how could the prophet have borne such witness in the oracles? For he who despised the shame of death on the cross was this very one who, according to the God-taught Apostle, "being in the form of God", emptied himself, and not another. But perhaps, piously opening your ears, you will be moved with opened lips to ask how it is that the benefit which has come to us could not otherwise have passed to us through the Lordly man without his union with the Word. With God our Saviour we shall answer. We shall say that there was every need for it, and that our renewal necessarily came about through union with him. Suppose someone stamps a seal from a ring in pure wax, and then the impression falls to the ground and gets caked with dust. On looking at it, he finds that the dust stuck to it from the earth has made the impression of the ring's design, so recently given to the wax, very dim and now unrecognizable. Wishing to make clear and renew the seal that was first impressed, now covered over by the dust mixed into the wax, he takes the very same ring from

which the original image was stamped, sets it in the wax again, and presses it in more firmly. He imprints the recent design on the same wax again by closer application, union and pressing-in of the shaping nature of the iron in which the design is cut. And although the wax has become earthy and does not readily accept reshaping, he will still stamp the former form on it once more. So too did God deal with humanity, created after his own image, which through its entanglement with earthly things had dimmed the beauty of the divine image. By a more intense and more effective giving of himself he stamped it again into the ancient beauty it had from him, that is, the divine likeness. He granted his divine embrace to those caked with the earthly garment, and worked his spiritual union in those who had suffered the mixture of the flesh. For with almighty goodness the Word himself called back to himself those endowed with reason.

The body, joined in essence to the soul, gains life and sensation from it. But the Lord's body, compounded in essence with the Word, as you hold — tell us, what did it acquire from that? Sensation, or motion? But it had these from the soul. Impassibility and incorruption, then? But you say it had this from the resurrection, just as all men will have it. How then is the essence of God not inferior to that of the soul, if the soul imparts many things to the body, while God's essence imparts no higher mark of distinction? Or will you say it is its being formed without seed? But this is a sign of the working of the Holy Spirit, not proof of an essential intertwining of the Word. For "before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit." Signs and mighty works, then? But the apostles did even greater things than these, according to the Lord's own promise to them. Dignity and lordship, then, and the name above every name given to him? And to whom was this given? Was it through essential union with the superior one, God the Word? And to what superior thing was the Word united? Why, to flesh, that is, to the man from among us. So, first of all, you see, when you hear that the name of dignity was given to him, you substitute nature for it. Second, you oppose those who say that the union of the flesh from among us with God the Word is a dignity beyond compare, and not a natural composition. Third, if the dignity and lordship of the man from among us does not belong to him from his own essence, it must be a gift of will, love and good pleasure, not a present conferred by essential union. For none of the things united in essence bestows any dignity and lordship on that to which it is united. Or will they perhaps say that the sinlessness of the Lordly man is proof of his essential union with the Word? Then how does divine Scripture attribute this to the Holy Spirit, saying, "Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God", and "the Spirit of Jesus will cleanse our conscience from dead works", and elsewhere, "He was justified in the Spirit"? Therefore it was by the Spirit, in whom he was justified,

and not by the Word, in whom lies what is by essence. Otherwise his achievement will be a matter not of choice but of essence. Think of people who want to light great bonfires and are beaten by the all-devouring fire. Once the heavier fuel has been consumed, they see the flame already dying down. They do not have enough fuel to keep alive what they are working at, so in desperation they try to revive it with bits of straw, so that the blaze may not go out on them entirely. In just the same way, now that all the worthless rubbish of your propositions has been consumed by the fire of truth, which devours falsehood, you are merely fanning with idle chatter the strife you yourselves had kindled. For what necessity of complete likeness can the comparison you drew, in one respect, from the example of soul and body impose on us? Must we remind you again, as though you did not know it, most learned sirs, that things whose compositions are the same in some respect do not necessarily have all the same activities, or the other consequences? But I do not think you are wholly ignorant of this. A man is united locally to a man in the church, and likewise a mosaic tile is united locally to a tile in it. For the men, the composition or juxtaposition grants both of them a certain companionship, warmth from one another, and the rest; but the composition of the tiles shows nothing of the kind. You ought to have considered this: where the natures are not the same, neither is what they impart. Since their qualities are not the same, neither would their powers or activities be the same, even if their compositions were in some way thought of as the same. So much, then, against your demand that we show vegetative life and local sensation coming to the flesh from the Word, since these naturally come from the soul joined to the body. But even if not the things of the soul, you still insist that we point to something else that the flesh gains from the Word. Otherwise, as you say, the mode of divine composition would be wholly useless to the flesh, granting it nothing of the soul's gifts or anything above them. For this is what your statement means when it says: "If we testify that impassibility and incorruption came from the composition, we lie; for the Lordly man is attested to have had this from the resurrection." On this too you shall hear from us, you who have not considered the divine gifts: the gifts of the Word to the flesh are very many and very great. For even if it received impassibility and incorruption from the resurrection, as all of us men shall have them, yet even before the resurrection it gave all the faithful superhuman, that is, wonder-working, gifts. And sinlessness and great authority are attested of it in many ways. Where shall we say these came to the flesh from? For no one could simply say that this very thing, resurrection, which is observed in a subject and is not thought of as subsisting in itself, is some nature that brings about the raising, impassibility and incorruption of the bo- (1 Tim. 3:16)

-dy of Christ. For it is merely something observed in essences and supervening on them, like reclining, raising up, lowering and the like. An essence might bring these about, and they might be brought about in an essence. But they themselves will never bring about either themselves or anything else in essences by their own power. Neither the resurrection of Lazarus, nor that of Jairus's daughter, nor that of the others, did anything to them of itself. How then do you say that the Lordly man had these things from the resurrection? If they came to him from a thing that does not subsist, then God, who subsists and is, will not be reckoned their cause either for us or for him, nor will God be the one who raised him. But if it is something that subsists, then it is a nature that produced these things and is said to bestow impassibility and incorruption. And no other nature will supply these except God. For it is not within man's power, as it is said: "Who is the man who shall live and not see death, who shall deliver his soul from the hand of Hades?" The true God will be the efficient cause of these things. And from this you may truly see that he himself was their cause and the one who brought them about, namely impassibility and incorruption, since he is said truly to have raised himself — he who also said, "I am the life and the resurrection." You have chosen rather not to hear that voice. And yet "I am he who is speaking to you" points to him plainly. Though, with the sister of Lazarus, you hear in your ears the audible word uttered from an audible body, you deliberately play deaf. As he says, "The Father raises the dead", and so he has also given the Son authority to raise the dead. If, then, this is enough to convince you, well and good; if not, you shall hear still more said to you. For if the Lord had the resurrection just as all men will have it, what need was there for him to rise first? If he rose as we do, and we rise as he did, what need was there for his resurrection to come first, if we do not rise through it and through its coming first? For even if he had not risen, the one who raised him as he raises us would raise us as he raised him, through his activity, which takes place eternally [?] and alike in all. Thus it has been shown that his resurrection is his own act, and that our resurrection comes from the composition of the flesh with the Word. Next, we must consider the other point you made. You attribute the marvel of his God-befitting birth to the Holy Spirit. You take it to be a sign of the Spirit, and not proof of the Word's essential intertwining. Tell us then truly, sirs: why did this happen in the case of his birth alone? And why did it fashion such a sign for this birth of his alone? For we have it from your own premises that things whose natures differ beyond compare cannot share the same composition. Now then, in response to the thesis you have just put forward, we shall state this very axiom against your aim:

things whose births differ beyond compare will never be the same natures. For no one at all would doubt that being conceived in iniquities differs beyond compare from his conception. Again, we shall argue thus. What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit, and flesh and Spirit are not of the same essence. Every man is flesh from flesh, and so is born incarnate from flesh of the same essence. But our Lord Jesus was born incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin, who are of different essences. How then is such a birth not proof of the Word's essential intertwining, rather than merely a sign of the Holy Spirit, as you supposed? So being from the Spirit, and being Spirit as well as flesh — this is what it shows him to be. For God is Spirit, and the Lord is the Spirit; for he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, and it does not say simply "of spirit". So much, then, concerning the divine birth of our Saviour, which to you does not seem marvellous. The other point of your slander, that somehow the divine signs of the Master… to have nothing by way of its own proof… [?] …whence for you this is not of God… [?] We would gladly learn this from you. Suppose a king insults or threatens someone with a word alone, and his bodyguards then and there torture or even kill the man insulted by their lord. Since their blows are greater, are we to say that the king's servants are greater than he, or his equals? Again, we see such things happen in acts of kindness: whomever the king grants only a word and an audience is offered all sorts of gifts and honours by the king's subjects. Are we to say that the subjects are the greater benefactors? Surely those who judge such matters must know where the deed began, whose power was at work in it, and what was its first and enabling cause. If we do not look into these things, we would say that the whip is greater than the charioteer, the arrow than the archer, the disciple than the teacher, and, as the saying goes, we would turn everything head over heels. To put it another way: suppose, as you hold, his apostles, being earthly, had judged him their equal, while he is their Lord and ours. Then how was it that, though commanded to call no one on earth father or rabbi or lord or master, they called him Lord and God and Teacher? And he who gave them these commands accepted these words as rightly spoken of him, saying, "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for so I am." It is clear, then, that even if the same things, and greater ones, were done by them, they confessed that these did not come about in the same way or from equals. They came from him as their Lord, and from them as his servants and ministers. Nevertheless, to refute the rashness of what you have said… [?] we still wish to learn from you where or when these men, even if [they did] the same things… [?] put them forward in the same way as he did, or

were recognized as he was in things beyond human power. For he, by his own sovereign right, his own authority and his own command, said, "I will; be clean." But they said, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk." See how plainly they confessed that the working was his, and that theirs was only the ministry. For the whole of what they ministered through the miracles was faith in their Master, and this alone was what they strove for. Further, where did these men display what is distinctively characteristic of God — I mean the power to create — as he did with the man blind from birth? He formed from clay the most vital and intricate part of the human body, and through this one member showed that he himself was the one who in the beginning took dust from the earth and formed man. Which of the prophets [?] raised others and yet was able to raise himself from the dead? Or whose body among those on earth remained incorrupt in the tomb? Or who is attested to have had authority to lay down his own soul and take it up again? Nor will you ever hear, however long you wait, an answer to the one who says, "Who is the man who shall live and not see death, who shall deliver his soul from the hand of Hades?" Which of them is said to have commanded unclean spirits with authority, or rebuked the winds and the sea with authority? Or whose word besides his amazed people because it came with authority, and not like that of the others? At the death of which apostle or prophet were heaven and earth, sun and moon, day and night, the dead and the living shaken together and driven from their proper bounds and places? At whose birth was there seen a birth without seed, the course of a star from heaven, a choir of angels singing hymns? Which of them, in the fleshly body, displayed spiritual properties, passing through the virginal membrane and walking on the surface of the waters? And in the spiritual body, which of them showed fleshly properties, being touched by hands of flesh, and after the resurrection accepting food from the disciples and eating it, though not nourished by it? By these things he showed that he himself is the maker and fashioner of both the fleshly and the spiritual nature. He makes all things and refashions them, and can always work wonders in every natural state. For only the one who makes a thing can easily refashion it. Who among those who are of human nature alone has ascended into heaven, or is attested to have come down from heaven? So you have not managed, as you intended, to establish this impious claim, that the wonder-working of holy men and that of the Master's authority are the same. Another of your claims is that the dignity and lordship, the name above every name, and the rest were given to the flesh by the Word, who is superior to it, and that these need not be credited to composition. We do indeed agree that the things mentioned are given by the Word. But we shall ask you this: are certain things that belong naturally to one subject ever

imparted to another when the one who does not have them by nature is not compounded with the one who has them, or only when it has been compounded with it? Why else, when there are many things not compounded with the one who naturally possesses these qualities, were they given to this one alone? See what we observe by example. When fire is naturally compounded with iron, the iron is then called fiery, having acquired from the composition the name and, so to speak, the natural dignity of the fire. When light is blended into water and illuminates it by composition, the water is called illuminated. And when a statue is united with gold by gilding, it is then a golden statue. But when the carpenter merely uses the adze to do his work, not united with it by natural composition, he neither imparts his name or dignity to the tool, nor does the worker receive them from it. Nor will a king, or some nobleman, who takes on any one of his own servants and honours him with whatever dignities, grant him either his name, or his royal dignity and lordship, or his nobility, since he is not naturally compounded with him. For it is not possible even if he wished — as we shall show — however much he might adorn one of his own horses, to call it a man… [?] …being truly acknowledged as the name, and not two of the names that are above all natural names. And if someone should speak of three, and not one, of the hypostatic, divine and transcendent [names], what else would this be than "God and Lord" by nature? For by adoption the name is neither granted to him alone nor above every name, since there are many so-called gods and lords in heaven and on earth. If, then, someone other than the one who is truly God by nature should receive this name, then either the giver must remain nameless, or the name must from then on be falsely applied to one of the two. Either it is falsely applied to the one who has newly received it, who is of a different essence and does not properly possess it. Or it is no longer truly said of the one who had it before, since he has newly lost it and has not remained in the proper nature of the name. For every natural proper name belongs to one nature, not to two different natures. So either it is not properly and truly said to have been given to someone, or, if it was truly given, it was imparted to the other through composition with the very one who alone is truly called by it. For in this way, while still belonging to the same one, the name will also be in the other, because of the one who has come to be in it. No name of a nature is truly used once it has departed from its own subject. The same holds for the account of dignity and lordship, and all the rest.

For these reasons, then, we hold that the name of dignity too is given from the nature, and that in God's case the dignity is his nature, not some acquired covering. To you, it seems, things do not appear so. Tell us, then, what exactly you want us to understand by the dignity, lordship and name in Christ as something that truly exists. Let us see whether what you describe is not altogether of our own order, however far it may surpass what belongs to us by degree, since this does not change its kind. For in that way

…every human being would be of a different essence from every other human being. In what respect, then, do you suppose that Christ, whom we confess to be truly God and Son of the living God, is one of the holy men? We have heard how you make this a dignity in Christ, and not a natural composition, saying that a dignity is given by will.
