Since, then, there was good pleasure, and the whole work of the economy, what was given must surely be some kind of dignity. But to this too we reply. Since you think a dignity is a kind of honour because it is given by will, we will tell you that blows and fetters and disgrace are also given by will, by their own rulers and masters, to wicked servants and citizens. By your reasoning, then, since these are given by will, they will be counted dignities and honours. Do not overlook how utterly absurd it is to say this. Besides, if, when we spoke of the natural composition, we had said that it did not come about through the good pleasure and love for humankind of the all-good God himself, you might reasonably have argued that, since the economy was not by good pleasure, it was not a composition. As it is, we proclaim more loudly than you this very point, that such a composition is by good pleasure, because it shows goodness in the highest degree. For this is how we know the Divine to be wholly free of envy: it is pleased to impart to us not merely an accidental and insubstantial dignity, but a natural one, and no ordinary one at that. For he has imparted to us, his own, not some other good but himself. What is left, after this, that would allow anyone to conceive of any nature whatever as more generous or better than God? Tell us yourselves, and on this we will agree with you. But even when you have been thrown down on this point, you are still gasping and writhing like those whose life is being torn from them, and you will not yield to the true word of piety. You go on to insist that in our Master Christ sinlessness is no sign of divine union. So this too we will examine with you. Sinlessness is admired in those in whom sinning is possible; otherwise one could not properly call sinlessness praiseworthy. Let us see, then, whose sin is. Is it not clearly that of each individual human being, acting by free will? Righteousness belongs to this as well. For if sins and righteous deeds were not matters of choice and in our power, then, to pass over everything else, he who punishes one who does not sin of himself, and rewards one who does not do right of himself, would be unjust. It is agreed, then, that sin and righteousness come from what is in our power and from the free will that belongs to our nature. But the Holy Spirit has borne witness that the sinlessness, that is, the righteousness, of our Master Jesus Christ comes from the Holy Spirit. So you too must necessarily hold that this is his free will, by which he was made righteous, just as we are by the free will that is ours. But if we know that what in our nature is free will and the cause of our righteousness is, in Christ's nature, the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit is truly true God, then have you not, even against your will, most clearly granted us that the divine nature is in Christ through the Spirit? You who formerly thought in your wickedness that he was like

you have now been refuted to your face by him, and shown that the one who was seen as one of us was understood to be above us. For what the ruling reason achieves in us in part, the divine Word achieved completely in Christ, governing both this reason of ours and the other ruling faculties. So whether he is the cause as coexisting with the Holy Spirit, or as being called Holy Spirit with respect to his nature, though not his hypostasis, he himself, and no other, is the cause of his own righteousness.

Is the divine Word immutable in hypostasis, as he is in nature, or not? If not, then, they say, he is neither altogether simple nor incorruptible, nor even God. Moreover, the Father and the Holy Spirit will be open to the same charges, unless indeed they subsist in some other way, for they too will be thought potentially mutable in their hypostases. But if everyone, because the impiety of the alternative is evident, confesses that the Word is immutable in hypostasis too, how will he have a composite hypostasis after a simple one? — But how do you understand the simplicity of a hypostasis? Hypostases are natures together with properties. Perhaps you think a hypostasis is simple, without qualification, because it has one nature and one property, or else any number of natures but only one simple property. Then no one will have a simple hypostasis, not even the divine Persons themselves. For the Father is begetter of the Word, unbegotten, and the one from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds; and the Son is begotten, is Word, and is the one through whom the Holy Spirit passes. These are several simple properties of the same hypostasis, and from all of them together the one composite property of the Father's or the Son's hypostasis is understood. Or perhaps you think a hypostasis is simple because it has one nature, though any number of simple properties. Then tell us how a simple hypostasis would differ from a simple nature. If it differs in nothing, then just as we understand an incomposite nature to consist in its not being united with another nature, so we must rightly hold that an incomposite hypostasis consists in its not being united with another hypostasis. But it is not we who say that hypostasis was united to hypostasis. It is you, so that it is you who speak of a composition of hypostases. Consider iron heated in a furnace. We say it does not draw off some partial hypostasis from the form of fire, but only receives the nature into its own hypostasis, for the hypostasis of the fire in the furnace remains just as undiminished even after the iron has been heated. In the same way we say that the Word took into his own hypostasis a particular nature drawn from our nature. The composition, or union, of the natures with each other is therefore according to hypostasis. But no composite nature has come from them, for they were not compounded by confusion. Nor has a composite hypostasis, since it is not made of hypostases. Rather, the hypostasis of the Word has acquired a more composite [?] property, since after the incarnation several simple properties have been accumulated in it. This shows that neither his nature nor his hypostasis is composite or mutable.
Chapter 21. But, they say, those who search out every argument for setting aside the incarnation of the divine Word also argue as follows:

every whole composed of different parts is seen to be something other than the things it is made of, and is named differently from them. If, then, Christ is composite of God and man, he is neither truly God nor truly man. First, this assertion too is false. There are cases in which a whole formed from different parts is not understood or named as something other than each of its parts. This may be because one of the parts predominates in the composition. We call raw greens 'greens', for example, and we call them 'greens' just the same when they have been boiled with a mixture of several seasonings, flour and pulses. Or it may be because no other species at all arises from the parts of the composite, which belong to the same genus but differ in species. For this reason, when an even part of a number and an odd one, say seven and eight, are put together into one whole, they do not make fifteen a species of number other than even and odd. Fifteen is called odd, just like one of its own parts, because nothing outside the definition of odd is seen in it, just as nothing is in seven. It is clear, then, that only where another principle of species appears in the whole, besides the difference of the parts that have come together, must the defining terms, the definitions and the names change. This is what they failed to recognize from the start. Fifteen, then, the composite whole, is truly called odd, just as seven is; and within its own wholeness it contains seven, which is preserved in it as truly odd. Understand, then, I beg you, that the Word is truly God and the flesh truly man, and that Christ, who by definition is not a nature, is truly both God and man.

'If, then,' they say, 'you too confess that the union is natural, how do you differ from the party of Severus, who speak of one nature of Christ? For every natural union produces some one nature besides those united. Man, for instance, is one nature, as man, and not several. He does not have the natural principles of the soul alone, or of the body alone, or merely of both, for "mortal" belongs to man, but not to the soul by itself or to the body by itself.' Well then, sirs, is there not a union of natures in the case of iron, and in blood-dyed wool an interweaving of the substances of bodies? For what else are these, even after the essential union, but heated iron and bloodied wool, and so still two natures? But know, if you are willing to learn and be persuaded, that natural union is understood and spoken of in many senses. In one sense, natural union is the union of things which are not natures, effected by some nature; that nature, by its own essential principle, makes their union subsist. Such is the divine nature in the case of the divine hypostases, the nature of the soul in the case of the soul's powers, and the nature of fire in the case of its essential qualities. In another sense, natural union is the likeness of different hypostases in their natural species, as of angel to angel

and horse to horse. In another sense, natural union is the coming together of different natures to generate a new nature: of soul and body, for example, into the nature of man, of the four elements into the nature of flesh, and of several herbs into the nature of a plaster. This kind is also called 'productive'. In yet another sense, natural union is the concurrence of several natures in one hypostasis, and not [?] into one nature. Examples are the interweaving of the natures of light and air in the daylight of today, and the union of fire and iron, which is called natural because it is a union of these things according to their natures and not according to some accident of theirs. How, then, can they pass over the question and refuse to understand in which sense of natural union we say the incarnation of the Word took place? And how can they take what we say in the sense by which they stitch absurdities onto you as onto the Severians? Yet even when they have been refuted in this way on these points, they raise a still more formidable problem against our faith, as follows:

'Composition according to hypostasis, that is, of God with man, if it really exists, is either above the nature of the Godhead, or contrary to its nature, or according to its nature. If it is above its nature, it is the work of a power greater than that nature; the nature has been raised to what is above itself, and is not truly almighty, nor does it surpass every reason. If it is contrary to its nature, the nature has become worse than itself, has been shown to be mutable, and has been brought down to a lower state. If it is according to its nature, then the incarnation of the Word is not by grace, and is not of the Son alone but also of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. And if it is according to nature, why did it not happen long ago, instead of being accomplished only now? It would be as if the nature had been imperfect then, and has now been brought from potency to act. All these things are absurd when said of God, and without them natures cannot be united. So either the divine nature has been united absurdly to another nature according to hypostasis,' he says, 'or it has not been united at all.' This would follow if nature were the proximate cause of absolutely everything that happens. Take a man who does not swim in the water, or turn somersaults, or walk the tightrope. Would anyone say these things are above nature for him? Yet another man of the same nature does them. Contrary to nature, then? Yet he is no less a man when he does not do them. According to nature, then? But how is he no less within what is according to nature when he does not swim or tumble or walk the rope? Clearly, then, these things depend on the good pleasure of the nature, and their cause does not lie primarily in the nature of the one who is pleased. For the principle and power over certain contrary things is the will, not the nature. 'But this union of God with what is ours,' he says, 'was brought about by a natural composition, and a nature is not subject to its own will.' It is true that many might be pleased to have the nature of their soul compounded with a body of adamant or of air, yet it is not therefore so compounded. But this really holds only in cases where the good pleasure is weaker than the power of the nature of the one who is pleased. We creatures who go on foot cannot give ourselves wings by nature,

however much we wish to fly. In God, however, good pleasure and nature are equal in power and in harmony. Of the things done to his own nature, then, his own good pleasure is the cause, and the cause of that good pleasure is that the nature itself is pleased concerning itself. So in the simple God, good pleasure is neither inferior nor superior in power to the nature. For 'whatever the Lord willed, he did,' and whatever he does not do, he is not primarily pleased to do either. The divine counsel, then, when it is pleased with anything, can accomplish it absolutely, just as the nature can. And things which are neither according to nature nor above nature nor contrary to nature show, by this alone, the God who is pleased to do them.

The Word is true God, having a simple essence in accordance with the essence of the Father. If, then, he has taken the flesh into his essence, as the Egyptian thinks, he has been estranged from the true God both in nature and in name. But he has the flesh, not in the essence of the bare Word, but in an essence that is one of the essences of his hypostasis, the hypostasis of Christ, who is of two essences. Suppose the essence of the Word is estranged, for this reason, from the simple hypostases that are consubstantial with it, because it is now seen in a composite hypostasis together with the essence of the flesh. Then John's soul too was once of a different essence from the soul of his own brother James, whom Herod long ago killed with the sword before him. For James's soul came to be in a simple hypostasis after death, while John's still appeared in a composite hypostasis.

The Word is immeasurable in hypostasis; the flesh is measurable in hypostasis. Whoever teaches the union of God and flesh according to hypostasis either bends God down to the measure of the flesh or stretches the flesh out to the immeasurability of God. Unless one or the other happens, God cannot be united to flesh according to hypostasis. — If you conceive the Word's immeasurability as some continuous quantity, like the measurability of the flesh, your reasoning is correct. But if the Word is immeasurable in another sense, namely in power, while the flesh is measurable, there is nothing absurd in the surpassing power being united to a lesser thing.

The hypostasis of the Word is uncreated; the hypostasis of the flesh is created. The flesh cannot be united to the Word in an uncreated way, nor can the Word be united to the flesh in a created way. According to what kind of hypostasis, then, did the union according to hypostasis take place? — The predicates of the things united are not by any means also predicates of the union. Union in itself is neither uncreated nor created, for neither creation nor union is an essence, whereas created and uncreated things united according to hypostasis would be essences of some kind. Nothing prevents the bodies restored to us at the resurrection from being united to souls that already existed. In the same way, nothing prevents what is newly created of the flesh from being united to the Word, who has existed uncreated for however long, merely because he existed before it.

But if you say that it is because of the difference in nature between the uncreated and the created, then no other hypostasis either will be made of things unlike in nature. Yet every composition according to hypostasis is made of things of different essence, and none of consubstantial things, unless it is some collection of homogeneous parts. So the very unlikeness of nature should rather lead us to suppose that the union of the Word and the flesh is according to hypostasis.

The difference between uncreated and created naturally prevents union according to hypostasis. The union of God and flesh, of uncreated and created, according to hypostasis abolishes the difference. So whoever anathematizes those who do not confess the union according to hypostasis anathematizes those who confess the difference between uncreated and created. — But why does the difference naturally prevent union according to hypostasis in the case of uncreated and created? Perhaps it is because one of them existed first, as though a thing could not be joined to a nature that did not come into being along with it. Then the divine breath was not united according to hypostasis to the first-formed body of Adam either. Or perhaps the mere variation in the principle of nature makes such things incompatible for union. Then no living being will be made of invisible and visible nature, or mortal and immortal, or corruptible and incorruptible: man, for example, who is made of soul and body and is one in hypostasis. Someone might say that what prevents the union of created with uncreated is not difference as such, but excessive difference. Then, conversely, an intensified likeness ought rather to make things united according to hypostasis. Which, then, is more like the body of Ephraim in its natural principle: his soul, or the body of his brother Manasseh? If it is certainly the body, how is Ephraim's body united according to hypostasis with his soul, which is unlike it, and yet separated according to hypostasis from a body like it in nature? Let those who wish to answer tell us.

If the Word does not now have the proper hypostasis that God the Word had apart from the union, then the hypostasis of the Word has changed; and if the hypostasis of the Word has changed, the Word of the Trinity will necessarily be changed too. — But he has the same hypostasis, though with the addition of the hypostatic properties of the flesh, which is in him and is his own, and of his own property of being united to flesh, now that the Word has been united. For in the principle of his hypostasis and in the assumption of the flesh there is a composition of an essence with his own essence, but there is also a hypostatic property. This brings into his person something distinctive which came into being of itself and distinguishes it from the consubstantial Father and from the Holy Spirit, who are like him.

[?] … of the divine hypostases … [?] … but if fleshly … [?] … so that the Word no longer … [?] … the existence of three other hypostases can be believed. But what, then, do we understand by hypostasis? For if by the one single property differ-

LEONTIUS OF BYZANTIUM [?] … ing from those consubstantial with it … [?] would appear simple … [?] by being unbegotten from … [?] but also by being begetter of the Word, and the one from whom the Spirit proceeds, and not proceeding himself. Likewise in the case of the Spirit too, the properties are several. So the multiplication of hypostatic properties does not make a simple hypostasis composite. But someone might suppose that one hypostasis is compounded of several hypostases. We abhor saying this, for we have never thought, as you hold, that the flesh was first formed and then assumed by the Word, but rather that from the very beginning of its existence it received its personhood in the hypostasis of the Word, so as to be Christ. It is you who make him out of two hypostases into a double hypostasis; or else you do not compound them at all and merely pretend there is a union. Then the nature of Christ has nothing more than other men in its relation to God, and you will be unable to say why he alone is called the one mediator between God and men.

If the hypostasis of the Word without flesh was one thing, and the hypostasis of the Word with his own flesh another, then the Word too was necessarily one person once and another afterwards, for a change in the one who has the hypostasis follows a change of hypostasis. — Something is understood to be 'other' through a change of nature, through acquisition, and through some juxtaposition of accidental features. Wool is the same and not other, whether it is naturally white in colour or has become purple through the blood of the murex … [?] seen … [?] as in essence and hypostasis alike … [?] having in relation to the blood … [?] as the whole … [?] form … [?] other then … [?] the incarnate hypostasis would be understood [as other] than the fleshless one. For his incarnation is not a change of the Word; rather [?] … but of his fleshlessness a change … [?] incarnate now … [?] of the Son … [?] the predication would put … [?] but not the fleshlessness … [?] of the hypostasis of the Word. For in that case the Father and the Holy Spirit, and angels and souls, would also be words, like the Son. But 'fleshless' is a negative predicate, primarily of his essence, and secondarily of his hypostasis too, because the essence was formerly so predicated. Now it is still predicated of his essence in the same way, but it will not be predicated of his hypostasis simply, that is, exclusively, because the hypostasis has received into itself another essence, which is said to be fleshly. And just as the nature of the Word secondarily brought onto its hypostasis the proper predicate of fleshlessness, so the nature of his flesh can also secondarily cast its own predicate, namely incarnation, onto that hypostasis, since it has become its own hypostasis too. But the Word was not one person formerly and another afterwards. He is the same Word, appearing in different ways. Formerly this hypostasis was invisible only; now it is also visible, because of the visible nature it has assumed into itself.
If the man is both man and God, just as God the Word is both, it is clear that just as the man is not God by nature, so

Nor is the Word man by nature; and if not by nature, then not by hypostasis either. — Consider, then: if something is not the same by nature, is it not the same by hypostasis either? What then? Since a horse's soul is not the same in nature as its body (the one being able to move, the other unable to move), is it not the same in hypostasis either? And since light and air are not the same in nature, are they not one in hypostasis during the day either, but separated from each other?

"I am, and I have not changed," cries God. "The Word has been united to flesh by hypostasis," cries the Egyptian. Whoever accepts that Cyril spoke the truth makes God a liar. — So then, when the Word is united to flesh, even if he remains the Word, is he changed [?]? Or rather, is it when he does not remain the Word, even if he is not united to flesh, that he has been changed? For if union is simply change, then every soul united to a body has been changed.

"You are the same," cries the prophet about God. The Egyptian answers the prophet back with his doctrines: "You are not the same, for you have become by hypostasis something else, which you were not." — So when many martyrs have had their bodies burned, yet show themselves in their souls and spirits, and even now prove to us by a great many miracles that they are alive, should we say to them, "You are not the same, for you have become fleshless by hypostasis, which you were not"? And you who no longer know Christ himself according to the flesh, even if you once knew him so, is it then not him but someone else that you know? Who would agree to that? So the Word became flesh, and even so he is the same.

If the Word is consubstantial with the Father in his fleshless hypostasis, it is clear that in his incarnate hypostasis the Word is of a different substance from the Father. — If it was by not having flesh united to him by hypostasis that the Word was consubstantial with the Father in hypostasis, then you would be right to raise this difficulty. But if the Word is consubstantial with God the Father by not being flesh by nature but God in essence, then even when united to flesh he was not changed from the nature of God. And it is clear that the hypostasis of the Word has both remained consubstantial with the Father and has truly become of a different substance from him as well, though through another nature that has come to be in it.

If the Word does not have the hypostasis he had, then he is not the same as he was. — But he does have the same hypostasis, lacking none of its former properties, though with other properties added, by which it is now distinguished from those consubstantial with it.
A man can have the dignity, authority and power of God the Word; but to hold the rank of the whole hypostasis of God the Word is impossible.

For the man is created, while God the Word is uncreated. — You are proposing the less credible thing, sir. For if a man can have the dignity, authority and power of the divine Word (the natural kind, you will say, not an acquired one), and can truly hold the rank of the whole God the Word, though he is of another nature, and, though created in nature, can differ in nothing from the uncreated God the Word, the God by nature; while God the Word cannot make the nature of man subsist in his own hypostasis, then is the man able to receive divine things, but God not able to receive human things [?]?
God, soul and body in a natural union are neither God nor man. — Add the word "only," and drop what is required [?].

Chapter 38. The Egyptian lays down as doctrine what is impossible by nature, and anathematizes what is possible by the economy. — But what was done by the economy was precisely what befitted the divine and supremely good nature: to give itself to our nature as a gift to us beyond nature.

If the impossibility of nature does not allow the man to possess the hypostasis of God the Word uncreatedly, and the Egyptian does not allow the man to possess the dignity of God the Word by the economy, then, caught between nature and the Egyptian, the man has nothing of God the Word, neither the hypostasis nor the dignity. — But the man in Christ does have the uncreated hypostasis of the Word, which together with the Word is also the hypostasis of his created nature. For it is possible for him to have a hypostasis that pre-existed uncreatedly and timelessly and belongs to another, and is also his who came to subsist in it in a created way and in time; but for one who is created in nature to acquire it uncreatedly and timelessly as the hypostasis of his own nature is impossible. For a partial nature too, that of the eyes of the man blind from birth, though created after him and not at the same time as him, came to subsist in his pre-existing hypostasis, and from then on is truly regarded as part of it. Yet even before this his hypostasis was regarded as one, whole and lacking nothing, though deficient in a certain sense through the privation of a nature and a natural part. That privation, indeed, rather enriched the definition of his hypostasis, since by this exceptional feature among its properties it was more clearly distinguished from others of the same nature. So when their nature was completed in its parts, the hypostasis lacked nothing in its properties. It is therefore not impossible for pre-existing hypostases to receive something into themselves by way of addition, in whatever manner, whether they pre-existed in a created or an uncreated way.
If by the co-essentiation of Godhead and flesh the Son is one Son, it is clear that before the co-essentiation the Word was not one, neither God nor Son. — But

even before the co-essentiation the Word was God and Son; and in this state likewise he is God and Son and Word. For it was not by the removal of what he had, but by the further acquisition of what was not in him, that God the Word, the Son of the Father, became Christ.

God the Word can be united to created nature by will, but he cannot be so by nature; for he did not create his own nature, nor can he transform it into another essence. — Then is it because his will is capable of more than his nature that he can do by will what he cannot do by nature, or because it is capable of less? If it is capable of more, then having been joined to created nature by the stronger of his faculties, namely the will, he will be bound up with it all the more easily by the lesser, namely the nature. But if it is capable of less, it is again clear that, having very easily accomplished something by the weaker of his faculties, he will prevail with the more effective one, which is greater than it. So much for that. But God neither created nor transforms his own nature: is that because he once had a will for this, or because he never had such a will? For him to create himself is inconceivable, and to transform himself is irrational. For where would his will have subsisted, so as to create the willing faculty? And how would one who is in all blessedness have a will to change himself into something worse? For there is nothing better. So whatever his nature is capable of, his will too can make him do; and whatever the will has, [?] his nature too can do. For in God, the wholly simple and undifferentiated Good, will and nature are not at war; so that if he can be joined to us by will, much more can he be joined by nature. For nature, including ours, is good and blameless, and comes from him; it is our will and our sins that set a division between us and him. Having a will, then, for this very thing, namely to join his own nature to another essence, he will not be unable to do it. So we rightly say that his natural union with us comes from the good pleasure of one who is good by nature.

If, when God wills, his nature receives an addition, then it can also receive a diminution when he wills; but if the second is impossible, then the first is impossible too. — But it was not the nature of the Word but its hypostasis that received an addition; and this was an addition not of hypostasis, but of the properties understood as the elements of a hypostasis, which accrued to it through the union of its essence with another; while it does not admit the removal of its own properties [?], having from of old not admitted this, since they are eternal [?]. And there are other things that admit increase but [not] diminution [?]: for the simplest thing, such as a
point, can be increased by composition, but cannot be diminished, since it is actually without parts, being the last of divisible things.

Christ at once rules and is ruled. But if there is no difference between ruling and being ruled in Christ, then the difference between God and man is also abolished. — For indeed he is ruled at once and in the same person by the natural order until the humiliation of the economy is complete; but the same one is not ruled in the same one of his parts. In the nature of his flesh he is ruled even by Pilate; but in the nature of the Word in him the same Christ is Lord of all things, even heavenly things. And later he says, also with respect to his humanity, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me."

If Christ is at once God and man, then the man is equal in honor to God. If the man is not equal in honor to God, the Egyptian rightly attacks co-worship; but if he is equal in honor, he is necessarily co-worshipped, and the Egyptian is impious. — Just as, when we worship God as a nature worthy of worship, there is no need to worship the three divine hypostases with three acts of worship, but by one worship the whole of God, worshipful by nature, has been worshipped, so it is with the economy. If we offer worship to the hypostasis of the incarnate Word, there is no need to say that in Christ one thing is co-worshipped with another; rather, the one person of the Word, even though incarnate, is honored by the worship of one hypostasis. If, however, you worship the nature of the Word, you also worship the Father and the Spirit in it; and where the Father and the Spirit are contemplated in the Monad that is worshipped, flesh is not included with it, so as to be co-worshipped as belonging to this Monad. We must therefore worship the three divine hypostases with three equally honored acts of worship; but the divine flesh, as a nature deified along with them by hypostasis, inasmuch as it is contained in one of them and from then on receives the sacred honors of the Godhead, must be co-worshipped in the one Son. For at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, since to him too has been granted the name above every name, namely that of the Godhead, which is worshipful by nature. Yet the natural difference is preserved, and so too the difference between the one who granted his own natural properties and the one who receives them, and between the one deified and the one who deified.

If the flesh by nature does not belong to anyone other than God the Word by nature, but to God the Word, it is clear that the flesh belongs to another Word besides the Word who is in natural Godhead. — It is of another nature, but it belongs to the person. For the Word is confessed to have been fleshless of old, but now incarnate. Chapter 46. If you accept at all, O Egyptian, a divine indwelling of God in a man, stop teaching a hypostatic union of God and flesh; for indwelling and natural hypostatic union exclude each other. — If the indwelling too is called hypostatic, that is, as of a hypostasis dwelling in a hypostasis, you speak truly; as is the case with the tablets of the law, which

existed by themselves, each circumscribed in its own right, but were enclosed on every side by the ark. But if we regard the indwelling as an essential union, as when someone says of his own soul that it went out and departed from me like one who strikes the tent he has pitched, what prevents a hypostatic union from being understood in the case of Hezekiah, a nature dwelling in a nature? But how is the Son and Word of God called man and flesh on the mere principle of indwelling? For the one who dwells is not found to be master of the name of the one in whom he dwells.

If the flesh had as partner of its own existence the Word, almighty and sinless by nature, how could it be called sinless? Or what victory over evil is there for it, when it has taken such a helper, one who cannot be defeated? The achievement would be his, not its. — Then you who trust in your own power and boast in the abundance of your wealth, will you not confess with us that a brother does not redeem, nor will a man redeem? And that a mighty man is not mighty by his own strength, but the Lord will make his adversary weak, the Lord who is holy? Listen, you people, to the one who says, "Let not the strong man boast in his strength"; and know that to overcome sin by itself, without help, belongs only to the sinless nature. If we were of that nature, we would long ago have been shown to be gods. But since we are of a fallible nature, and so are easy prey to the tempter, who drags us down into actual sin, we needed some ready [?] power to dwell within the weakness of our nature, so that we might not be overpowered by the treacherous power opposed to us, which goaded us with the sting of death, that is, sin, made us die, and robbed us of immortality. And this was not in some way outside our essence, nor temporary; for this inventor of evil is immortal and makes his way into our very hearts, and the weakness was in our very nature. Fittingly, then, the nature that empowers us for righteousness and saves us was interwoven with our nature, taking us up through the firstfruits into its own one hypostasis. Thus the enemy could no longer penetrate within it into our nature, coming to be present in it somehow by hypostasis, as happens even now with the possessed; nor could he ever find a moment when our nature was laid bare, since it subsists in the very hypostasis of our guardian, which by nature cannot be entered by the devil, by sin or by death. By such supernatural love for humanity, then, he made his own flesh sinless, and counted those consubstantial with it, sinners though they were, worthy of a sinless spiritual existence here, and in the age to come of existence with it without end. So God the Word, having obtained eternal redemption for us, is glorified in this way.

And perhaps those who deny that the union of the Word with the flesh is a true hypostatic union might raise this difficulty against us: [?] that what is infinite by nature, alongside what is [finite] by nature,

cannot be united by hypostasis. For if the hypostasis formed from both is infinite, what is finite by nature, namely the flesh, cannot pervade the whole of it; and if it is finite, it will not be able to contain within itself the whole of what is infinite by nature, namely the Word. — This too must be readily met. First, we say that every hypostasis, being distinguished by its own defining principles from every other hypostasis, whether of the same or of a different essence, is entirely finite. For if something is not bounded by its own limits, neither is it distinguished from others' limits. In that case not even the infinite nature of the Word by itself could be contemplated in a hypostasis, nor that of the Father, nor that of the Spirit; it would at once be wholly infinite and without hypostasis, since a hypostasis finite according to its own principles could not contain a nature infinite according to its own principle.

Beyond this, with God's help, the difficulty of the infinite must also be resolved in another way. We say that "infinite" is used in many senses. Something is called infinite by position, like the circle drawn from a line: the line has no breadth, its length is indeterminate and indiscernible to any sight, and it is uniform along its whole extent, so that no part of it appears to be its beginning, another its end, and another its middle. Also called infinite is what increases by turning back on itself, such as the multiplication of numbers: having counted ten thousand, one can go on to measure ten thousand times ten thousand, and again count ten thousand times ten thousand ten-thousands, and so on to infinity. We also call infinite what is by nature always divisible, such as the point and the unit. For we conceive of these as divided into halves, and half of these into a further half of the half, and that into another half of itself, and so on to infinity, there being no other form that must take the place of the form being divided as the division is pressed further. With a line, by contrast, when it is divided again and again, the limit of its division was reaching a point; and the limit of the division of a number was reaching the unit, for what is then divided is no longer a number. Also called infinite is what receives no spatial limit in some continuous extension of quantity, as we say that the length of the sun's rays is infinite: if no denser body blocks them, they stretch from the farthest east even beyond the western regions of the sky, provided there were something transparent to receive them. In this sense the water of the sea might also be called infinite as it reaches down in depth to the abyss. Also called infinite is what is perpetual and endless in time, like the age to come and the life of the angels. Also called infinite is what is posited only in thought as having or undergoing something without end, such as the line said to be extended or divided to infinity. Also called infinite is what is so relative to something, even if not by nature, such as the height of the sky relative to us. Also called infinite is what is incomplete in contemplation; for example, if every body is in a place, and place is a body, then the place of the body is also in a place, and the place of that place too; and so to infin-

-ity the thought will go on. Further, something is held to be infinite if, in the active power of its nature, it is not bounded by measure, or is not known only in certain particular activities. One man, say, can run two stades, or only ten; another can lift a hundred pounds, or only a thousand; another can only farm and build ships and write and do certain other things. But none of them can run stade after stade without limit, or carry loads beyond measure, or simply do everything, as if the same man could wage war and sing to the cithara and practice medicine and do everything that is done in the world. If such a man were hypothetically seen, we would call him infinite in active power. With these distinctions made, let us ask those who deny the union of the infinite with the finite: what sort of infinite do they take this divine infinity of the Word to be, that they will not allow it to be united to the finite? If they say infinite by position, or by multiplication, or by division, they will rightly seem to be talking nonsense. If they say it is by the spatial extension of its own continuity, then, the divine being infinite in that way, it must be somewhere wholly outside this entire finite world, having no relation to anything here, separated from all of it and in no way united with it. Then these sayings will be false: "In him we live and move and have our being"; and "From whom and in whom are all things"; and "of him who fills all in all"; and "that God may be all in all"; and all such sayings. Or, if these have been said truly, then, though God is infinite and the world finite in place, they are wrong to be suspicious of the union of such an infinite with the finite, since God is united with all things and fills them. But if they say that the infinite which they take not to be united, in the case of God, is what is endless in time, they are easily refuted from their own hypostasis. For their soul has infinite duration in time, if they really believe it to be immortal; yet it is readily [?] united even now to their finite body, and by hypostasis. But if, pressed on every side, they say that by necessity they mean the infinite in power where the divine is concerned, we must tell them that one or the other of their positions will necessarily be overturned. Either, being infinite in power and capable of every activity, it could accomplish all things even through a finite nature, hindered by nothing in anything; and this is the mark of one who gives himself to the other and, through mutual indwelling, displays one hypostasis formed from the union of the two. Or else, being unable to bring forth and display all that belongs to its own power even through the finite, while being wholly one with the finite, it is found in some way not truly infinite in active power, being hindered, namely by the smallness of the other, from bringing forth all its activities through it. So David, naked and stripped of everything foreign to a shepherd's gear, was able to fight and defeat Goliath; but wearing breastplate and helmet and greaves and shield and sword, and in short burden-

…wearing Saul's armour, he was unable to stand in the battle line and slay the foreigner. So it will be clear: either God the Word is not infinite in power, or, if he is infinite, he is not unable to do everything that belongs to him at all times, even through a finite nature. Therefore it is not possible on these grounds to show that the hypostatic union with this nature is impossible.

"The composition you speak of," he says, "either produced a newer nature, and then why do you not accept the Mixophysites? Or it produced a newer hypostasis, and then why do you shake us off? Or it produced neither a nature nor a hypostasis, and then it happened in vain." But, my friends, it is not necessarily true that every composition produces either a newer nature or a newer hypostasis. Iron heated in coals shows neither some foreign nature nor a new hypostasis. The hypostasis of the iron and that of the burning coals remain as they were. But in the hypostasis of the iron, the nature of fire, which has no hypostasis of its own, was compounded with the nature of the iron and came to subsist together with it. What, then, did composition do in the case of Christ? Nothing other than this: things that were previously uncompounded with one another came to be compounded in the one hypostasis of one of the components. And this is enough to enrich our nature with the whole divine nature.

"Either this union of the Word and the flesh that you speak of is natural, and then how do you differ from those who say that the composition of a man and that of Christ are alike in every respect? Or it is hypostatic, and then why do you not speak as we do, who glorify it in a special way as the union of the beloved with the lover? Or it is neither natural nor hypostatic, and then explain clearly what you think it is." But, you sophists, in the sense you give these words it is neither natural nor hypostatic. In the sense in which they are piously understood, however, we could rightly call it both natural and hypostatic. Each of these words has two meanings, and you have slipped one meaning in for the other and stolen away the more pious of them. A union is called natural, first, when it is in keeping with the principle of nature for some particular thing. An example is the falling asleep of Lazarus: unlike his return to life, which went beyond the principle of his nature, this was in keeping with it. A union is also called natural when it is simply a union of certain natures, or of a nature, and not of accidents, as in the mixing of oxymel. We call the oxymel mixture natural, but not because each of these ingredients is naturally and necessarily subject to mixing with the other, as Lazarus was subject to the sleep of death. Honey and vinegar always remain as they are, even if they are never combined into oxymel, whereas Lazarus would not be a mortal living being unless he was going to fall asleep at some point. In the same way, one kind of union is called hypostatic because it is a union of parts according to the principle of a hypostasis, and another because it is a union of hypostases. We, then, call the union in Christ natural in the sense that natures are united in him. For if we called it natural in the sense of the principle of nature, then the Father and the Holy Spirit, being of the same nature as he, would themselves at some point be united to flesh. Indeed, if humanity is united to God by the principle of nature, all human beings will be Christs: Pilate and Herod and Annas and

Caiaphas would necessarily be Christs, just as all alike die by the principle of nature. Moreover, the Word would then appear, at the incarnation, to have advanced from potency to act in his natural properties, and by comparison the Father and the Holy Spirit would be judged still imperfect. What could be more impious than that? We also call the union in Christ hypostatic, but in the opposite sense to the one we meant when we called it natural: not as a union of hypostases, but as belonging to the Word, to his own hypostasis. Generation, being the Word himself, and other such things distinguish the Son in a way peculiar to him from the Father and the Spirit, who are consubstantial with him. In the same way his incarnation necessarily sets him apart from them, and from no others than the fleshless persons who share his nature. It is an acquired property, yet one that can never be separated from him, and it too appears in the hypostasis of the Word. But they put forward another pretext for impiety. They say that they reject the composition of the Word with the flesh in Christ because one of the parts cannot be equal in honour to the whole. These are their very words:

"They must say that their Christ is in some respect either superior or inferior to God alone and to man alone, that is, to his own parts considered separately and by themselves. For when the parts of a resulting whole are considered by themselves, apart from their composition with one another, they are always found to be in some respect either superior or inferior to the whole made from them. Take stones and timbers, the parts of a house or of the temple built by Solomon: plainly each of them by itself is less than the whole house. Again, blue, purple, twisted scarlet and spun fine linen are parts of the veil of the tabernacle, and each of these by itself is plainly less than the veil. So also with man. According to the Christians, man, this whole living being, is superior to both the soul and the body. For after the soul departs from the body, the soul too is incapable of self-moved activity, as if in the deepest sleep, and continues without even knowing itself. And according to divine Scripture it awaits the recompense for the deeds done with the body;

it will not escape that recompense by being separated from the body, nor does it turn to the worse, so that the words of Scripture may not [?]. From this, that it turns neither to the better, I mean, nor to the worse, it follows either that the complete perfection and full blessedness expected at the resurrection are already present in its nature, or that the rational part is entirely at rest, since it is moved by no self-chosen will and has no perception of anything at all. But the first has never been put forward, for God foresaw something better for us, so that those before us should not be made perfect without us. So it is the second. According to us Christians, then, man is shown to be superior [?] to his own parts considered by themselves. But according to the Greeks and the Manichaeans, on this reasoning, man is superior to the body but inferior to the soul. For they hold that the soul

exists before the body, that it has no need of the body's senses, and that before its fall into the body, as they say, it was ignorant of nothing, and likewise after its departure from the body. So they hold that man is inferior to the soul, since they say that the soul became worse than itself through its imprisonment in the body, as they put it. But since the body is seen to be dead after its separation from the soul, it is clear that man is superior to the body. For the body itself is seen to be better than itself before its separation from the soul than after it. It is therefore established that a resulting whole is in some respect either superior or inferior to its own parts considered by themselves. Hence these people too must say that their Christ is in some respect either inferior or superior to his own parts conceived by themselves, if indeed Christ is in their view a single living being made up of God and man. But if they say superior, they have conceded an impiety, for they imagine something more perfect than God, which they must also say is above the Father and the Spirit. For if the living being they say is made of God the Word and flesh is in some respect superior to God the Word conceived by himself, then this same being is clearly superior also to the Father and the Spirit, who are not compounded with flesh. Since the Son is equal to the Father and the Spirit, what is in some respect superior to him is clearly superior also to the Father and the Holy Spirit. And if they say that this living being is inferior to God the Word considered by himself, they are impious in this way too, for they show God the Word to have become inferior to himself, as in the myth of the Greeks and the Manichaeans about the soul. You would not find the living being made of God and flesh inferior to God alone unless God the Word himself had first become inferior to himself." To this we would reply as follows. It is true that wholes made from parts are seen to be either better or worse than each of their components taken separately. But clearly this is not so without qualification. It is so only where the parts differ in nature and the composition produces the resulting whole through some change, confusion and blending. If the composition is not of this kind, that is, if it does not confuse and alter the different things that have come together, and if the natures cannot be confused into one another or changed, how can the whole on that basis be judged worse or better than one of its parts? An example will make the point clearer. Suppose someone melts down a silver vessel weighing a pound and a lead vessel weighing a pound and makes [?] out of both. Clearly the result will turn out inferior to silver but better than lead, something like tin, for these metals naturally pass over into one another through a certain natural pliancy and kinship. But suppose someone joins a gold vessel weighing a pound to a clay vessel weighing a pound, or coats one with the other and fires them together for as long as you like. Since clay is not of a nature to be blended with gold in a mixture, the result made of clay and gold will never be better than gold in its essential quality. For see: the gold remains unchanged, both under the coating and in its union with the clay, and pure

and unadulterated, we shall say, and it will differ in no way in its nature from bare gold. The coating of clay does not persuade a sound mind that the gold has been harmed in its nature, once its nature is recognized as incapable of changing for the worse. Nor, on the other hand, will anyone reckon it better than bare gold because of the clay coating, for what is once better will never appear better than itself by taking on something worse. Indeed, it is pointless even to say so. But enough of this. Your assertion says that the resulting whole is seen to be either better or worse than its own parts, yet your examples mean something other than what you said. For they say that every composite is in every case better than the parts that came together to form it: the house, it says, is better than the stones and timbers, the veil than the purple, scarlet and linen, and man than soul and body. Let us grant you this too, and then say that it is indeed true in some cases. But you do not know how it is true, and I do not know how you came to know even that it is. The whole is better than each of its own parts when, upon composition, some further shape or quality or form accrues to them that was not, and is not, in any of them, but is seen as something added beyond all the forms of the parts. In this, then, the house surpasses the nature of stones and timbers: it has a shape and an arrangement that neither timber nor stone has by itself. Even so, it does not have a different and superior nature. Likewise the veil, through the weaving and combining of these colours with one another, surpasses each of them uncompounded and by itself. It is not better than all its own colours by virtue of a simple colour. And man, too, if we grant you that he is better than the soul (you who concede everything at random to prop up your own doctrines), displays upon composition certain natural properties that are new beyond soul and body. If, then, when the Word and the flesh are compounded, some new natural property can truly be seen in Christ beyond the divine and human ones, shall we then, by your reckoning, properly call the resulting whole in his case better than its parts? But if nothing is seen except the same parts, how can we hold, for those same parts, not equality of honour but the superiority of the whole over its own parts?

CHAPTER 52. But, as is our custom, let us anticipate and work through every other argument that our opponents might perhaps devise, for our desire is always for the truth and not for victory at any cost. So let us not fail to add this as well. A whole made up of dissimilar parts is in a sense other than its own parts. It is more composite, more varied and more perfect, and it differs from each of the parts in more than merely having acquired some difference from them. We see this in a medicine, a house, a red-hot lump of metal, and a man. The compound of chalcitis and oil is attested to have the power of filling up the hollows of wounds, which neither of its

parts had by nature. Likewise the shape and form of the house differ from those of the stones and timbers in it, for this shape has been added to them. And the definition of this particular man shows something more than the definition of the body and that of the soul, such as being mortal, which is not attributed to either of his parts by itself, just as being capable of laughter or of weeping and his other such properties are not. It is also clear that the definition and principle of the whole man must necessarily differ from the things that are individually consubstantial with his parts, that is, from other souls and bodies taken by themselves. Necessarily his number differs too, for what is called a whole is certainly something countable, if it is anything at all. They might say, then: "If you speak of parts and a whole in Christ, as some of you have declared, then, first, since the parts are divinity and humanity, the whole will be shown to us to be something other than these. Then, according to the definition of the whole, it could not be ranked as consubstantial with the things that are consubstantial with the parts. In his whole self the Lord will be like neither the Father nor his Mother in nature. Nor, on the principle that the whole is countable as a whole, could he be counted in the number of the divine Trinity without making it a tetrad, and if he were counted together with it, he would no longer show himself wholly consubstantial with it. Nor, for the same reasons, if he were counted in the roll of the human multitude, would this whole be consubstantial with it." But even if they should draw these conclusions against us, let them know, first, that our fathers used these terms, namely parts and whole, of our Master Christ solely to represent composition and to rule out any suggestion of the unions spoken of in other ways. They used them, further, because each of the things said to be in Christ is a true nature, and because the divine good pleasure has come together in a natural union, so that both substances fill out Christ and give him subsistence, just as parts naturally make up the whole. They used them also so as to give no room for [?] ever to think of one of the things in Christ as bare and apart from the other, just as the parts can never be seen without one another while the whole is preserved. When they speak of composition, whole, blending and the like, they say these things only insofar as each term holds irreproachably in the case of Christ; if some consequence of these terms is incongruous, they refuse to accept it along with them when reasoning about him. When they say blending, they mean only that the whole is predicated of the whole of each of the things united. They do not accept the confusion that follows from it, the mutual resistance of the [?], or the dissolution and alteration of the things mixed by one another. And they reject these things not only in the case of Christ but even in the union of body and soul. So too, knowing that no part compounds itself, they do not therefore suppose that the Word was compounded with the flesh by someone else. When they speak of a composition of parts, they simply set aside everything that does not befit the divine economy and draw only on what is irreproachable in these terms, to clarify the exceedingly hard-to-discern

divine mystery, because we need some outline of the incomprehensible Word. Otherwise our mind, having no support, might imagine things about him on its own authority, often turn aside to ideas wholly incongruous with the economy, and fashion impieties for itself. Even in more ordinary matters we often name things by some metaphor or analogy or partial likeness, and we do not for that reason accept all the consequences along with the name. When we say that the air laughed as it turned from gloomy to clear, we have not thereby concluded that the element is a living being capable of laughter. But even if all the consequences had to follow wherever one of these terms is used, they would not necessarily follow in the case of Christ. His composition is confessed to be from God the Word and human nature, and if the whole in his case is granted to be truly made of such parts and to be composite, this will certainly rule out such consequences. For the Divine admits of no absurdity, and it is acknowledged that even in the very things said of us as well, it is beyond comparison with us. Although generation is also spoken of in his case, the things that follow from our generations are not. In this respect the consubstantiality of his hypostases and the personal perfection of the individual powers are not like ours, and neither are his other special attributes. Beyond this, granting that when whole and parts are spoken of in Christ nothing like what holds for us follows as a consequence, we must also consider the following. First, it is clear that what was said to happen in the case of a whole made from parts happens to that whole even if its parts are dissimilar in species; but such parts are certainly of the same genus, whether proximate or more remote. This is why, when it comes to composition into a common species, they would not be wholly alien to one another, since they share a certain natural communion in some genus. But the union in our Master is made from things that belong to entirely different genera. For what, properly speaking, is the genus of substances? And even if substance has a genus, what genus could be granted to belong to the divine substance itself together with the human one, so that through some natural kinship they might be blended and produce the nature of some whole? How, then, could they bring the composition of things of different genera under what happens in the composition of parts of the same genus? And how could they conclude, as if it were necessary for us to accept, that what is seen to follow for things of the same genus, namely some further wholeness, must certainly follow for these heterogeneous parts of Christ? If you are going to establish this necessarily on other grounds, by showing that no natural composition according to hypostasis took place, then we would answer them [?]. But if you grant us, at least hypothetically, a composition of God with something, you cannot then necessarily attach to it the consequences of composition. Otherwise, because it is not like the composition you know to occur among things that are not like these, that is, not divine and human parts, you will thereby overturn this composition too. For where the natures are not the same in every respect, neither is the natural relation alike in every respect, and clearly the composition will not be the same either. It must further be said that even if every composition, as you have said, introduces into the whole a form different from the forms of the parts, we have already agreed that one part of the composite now under examination is the Divine,

which, being the divine Word, is the maker of every form. If, then, some other form of a whole should accrue to him and to what is with him as parts, either he himself must produce it, since he is granted and commonly agreed to be the universal giver of form, or someone else must. For everything that comes to be clearly does not make itself while it does not yet exist; if it exists, it came to be by someone, and if it did not come to be, it does not exist. It could not come to be by anyone else, for we all agree that the only one who gives being and natural form is the one posited as a part of this whole. But if it came to be in some way by him as a whole, then the product would come to be by its maker as from its own part. For in that case the cause would be contained by the effect as a part in a whole, which is impossible. Since these things are impossible, it is clear that it did not, properly speaking, come to be. So it is clear from this too that, since the divine Word, the part that has been compounded, is confessed to be such a giver of form, the composite whole, named according to a different conception, will be the same as he in nature and in number. This holds even though the Fathers have said that the Word is a part in it. And it will be predicated of the same Christ of whom both the part and the whole are predicated, since he is understood as God, equally perfect, in both ways. It is true that sometimes, in order to signify each of the things in the composite, the two together have been called the whole, and one of them alone a part. So you are wrong to infer against us that the whole is different in substance from the parts because of the composition, and to see [?] a new number. For even if this whole, as something that is said, is countable, being what every composition signifies when some call it a whole, it will not add to the number of the consubstantial and really existing parts. Sometimes, through different conceptions, a single thing comes to have many names, and there is a plurality in the number of names said of one and the same thing: for example Simon, Peter, Cephas, Bar-Jonah, apostle, disciple of the Lord, and teacher of the holy Church of God. But we must not think that for this reason the number of the one man who is the subject so named is multiplied into substances or hypostases, or that he differs from himself in natural or hypostatic number, in the way that the meanings of his names 'disciple' and 'teacher' differed with respect to the different subjects acknowledged in each case. In addition to this, we say also that, as a part,

…compounded, that is, the divine Word. It has been granted that he stands at the very summit of perfection. If he consented to be compounded, then, because of the principle of his own nature, he who has truly been attested to be all-perfect will never form a whole that is greater or more perfect than himself. Nor will he make his own whole something less than himself, because of the principle of all composition: wholes, at least in themselves, are shown to be greater than their parts and never less. Since, then, the whole of the Word must be neither greater than himself, because of the nature of this part, nor less, because of the simple principle of composition, the whole-making part of himself will have himself as the whole. That part will necessarily be equal to its own part, while also being called its own whole. How then could one reason out a difference between the whole and the parts in the one dispensation of our Lord Christ? We say further: if everything simple is in the composite, and every part must be in its own whole, and everything that is and comes to be is in this part, namely the divine Word, how can there be something that is, in itself, a composite other than him, a whole more universal than he? Then the Word himself, who contains all things, would be contained by it. Yet he himself is the fullness that fills all in all.

Refutation of their second impiety, in saying that two [?] are seen in the dispensation of the Word.

“Hypostasis,” they say, “sometimes signifies something substantial, as in ‘Remember what my hypostasis is’ and ‘the express image of his hypostasis.’ Sometimes it signifies something without substance, as in ‘In this hypostasis of my boasting.’ And sometimes it signifies a gathering of people of one mind, as in ‘Men went out from the hypostasis of the foreigners.’ If, then, they take hypostasis in the last sense, to signify the natures’ sameness of will and agreement of mind, they plainly concede that we may speak of the two hypostases of the two natures in the first senses. If they take it in the second sense, wishing to show that what comes from both natures is something without substance, they are not even worth an answer. But if they take it in the first sense, let them say what it is consubstantial with. Is it David’s hypostasis, of which he said, ‘Remember what my hypostasis is’? Or the Father’s, of which it is said, ‘the express image of his hypostasis’? If it is the Father’s, how has it been constituted from two natures, when the Father’s is simple? For

the essences called hypostases must have the same principle of essence and the same conception; otherwise let them say what ‘consubstantial’ means. If it is not consubstantial with the Father’s but with David’s, then since they say it is from two natures, how can they avoid meaning that it is constituted from soul and body? For David’s is of that kind. And if it is neither the one nor the other, the Son you introduce is of a different essence from everything, consubstantial neither with us nor with the Holy Trinity. If you say that he is partly consubstantial with the one and partly with the other, know that consubstantial things are not consubstantial in part. By that reasoning they would be consubstantial in every respect. And in general, what is partly consubstantial with the one and with the other cannot be the Son of either. Show us something that exists partly consubstantial with different things and becomes the son of both the one and the other.”

Since your first hypothesis has already been demolished, it would be superfluous to answer you on what follows. If, as has been shown, the composition was truly one of natures and according to hypostasis, and in our Lord Christ the union is not one of hypostases, it is clear that the composite hypostasis must be altogether one and not two. You yourselves now suppose the same in the case of David’s soul and body. But we do not want to seem to decline the syllogisms of your second hypothesis as though they were stronger. So, with God’s help, we will meet you fittingly on all of them as well.

Those who search for the truth out of love of the truth do not use, in their search, the very instruments that produce error about it, as you do. The undiscriminating use of a single word with many meanings always produces the greatest deception in the matters under inquiry. And see how you have put this forward to us right from the start, even while you seem to avoid it: I mean in your investigation of hypostasis. You seemed to draw distinctions in part, but you did not fully determine how the word hypostasis is meant in each of the things of which it is said. Since the preposition ‘hypo’ is sometimes exchanged for another and sometimes used in its proper sense, we must first carefully determine in how many ways the word hypostasis is said, and how it is used in each of its different senses, and which sense fits the matter at hand. Then we will not slip from one meaning into another. After that we can refute your subsequent absurdities.

[?]

We say, then, that some of the older writers of the Greek tongue use hypostasis for the sediment and lees of wine and similar liquids, because it shows its own standing (stasis) beneath (hypo) the liquid floating on top; so we speak of signs showing a sediment. Hypostasis is also used for movement, that is, the removal of what was once present, as a state away from and without standing, that is, a privation of standing. Here the preposition ‘hypo’ in the word is exchanged and taken in the sense of ‘apo’ (away from). Those in the wrestling school who make [?] from one another named it so. Hypostasis is also used for someone’s possession of certain goods or revenues from certain properties belonging to the owner, since these are preserved for him and subsist for him without failing;

so we say that so-and-so does not have or possess much hypostasis. Hypostasis is also used for what is steadfast, not easily overthrown, and enduring toward what comes against it, as Holy Scripture says: ‘And now what is my patience? Is it not the Lord? And is not my hypostasis from you?’ Hypostasis is also used for the particular, not universal, premise of some narrative or of a discourse in general, as in the saying ‘in this hypostasis of boasting.’ Faith too is called hypostasis, as the knowledge and firm grasp of some apprehension, as it is said: ‘Faith is the hypostasis of things hoped for.’ Hypostasis is used for a promise, as a hope set by someone for someone and subsisting, as it is said: ‘Lest, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we (not to say you) should be put to shame in this hypostasis.’ And what was that, he says? Their blessing announced beforehand. Hypostasis is used for the base that underlies something’s standing, as it is said: ‘I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no hypostasis.’ Hypostasis is also used for resistance, as Moses says about the people in Deuteronomy: ‘How shall I be able to bear your hypostasis and your contradiction?’ Hypostasis is also used for arrangement, as is said about the temple in Ezekiel: ‘And you shall describe the house and its preparation, its entrances and its exits, and its hypostasis.’ Hypostasis is also used for a gathering of certain persons who have come together, whether of the same essence or of different essences, as in the saying ‘Men went out from the hypostasis of the foreigners.’ The sense that you have now passed over, knowingly or in ignorance, is somehow of the same meaning.

Hypostasis is also said when different particular natures come together into the same thing, together with their properties (natures, not persons), and through the union there comes about, at once, the constitution of one single individual. And hypostasis, in the sense acknowledged by all, is also said when it is not different natures that come together but only several partial properties. Out of them all these constitute one comprehensive property in some one subject, that is, in one single nature. Whether in a simple thing or a composite one, whether in a particular nature or a common one such as the divine, whether in one single nature or in several united ones, but in any case in natures that exist, this standing or constitution of the partial properties, that is, of the common property, conceived as being in some subject, is called hypostasis. And hypostasis of this kind is so called most properly and most fittingly of all. Besides constituting the thing, it also shows, by its particular distinguishing mark, that the underlying individual is separate from all things of the same species and of other species. In itself it is a particular ‘this’: a kind of setting apart, a marking off of the undelimited essences into the numbering of each by person. That is why the Fathers both understand it and name it ‘person.’ Hypostasis is also used for essence and nature, which many co-signify under various

names, by virtue of its subsisting. It is not like accidents, which have no existence of their own, in its being and being conceived, but stands by itself, as it is said: ‘Remember what my hypostasis is.’ As for the sense in which the Son is called the express image of the Father’s hypostasis, which you also adduced, that needs a fuller exposition, and this is not the place for a digression. In any case, none of this helps you with the matter at hand.

We have now carefully distinguished these senses of hypostasis. If you speak of two hypostases in the sense of essences, we fully accept it. But we add that from them there is the one person of Christ, so that we may avoid the ambiguity of the word ‘persons.’ By this we show that we have accepted these hypostases in the sense of natures, while from now on we reckon the person, for your sake, as the hypostasis. For hypostasis co-signifies with both person and nature the thing that underlies each of these different names. So, with God’s help, we speak. But you take nature and hypostasis to be the same, as you often say, since in addition to the two natures you also speak of two hypostases of the Lord. You must therefore go on to introduce either one person or two. Otherwise, keeping silent about that, you must have recognized four natures in Christ but no hypostasis, that is, no person: you speak of two natures and, not content with that, add two hypostases of the Lord as well. Or else you must speak of four persons in the Lord, by way of the natures and the two hypostases, and plainly of no essence of them. That would follow if you used the name hypostasis not in the sense of essence but only in the sense of person. As for the remaining meanings, I do not think any rational person investigating such matters would rave so wildly.

What necessary conclusion do you build by demanding to know what we say this hypostasis is consubstantial with, God the Father or David? First, hypostases are not recognized from things consubstantial with them. Nor is the principle of the hypostasis the same as what it has from the nature of the things consubstantial with it. On the contrary, it is what it has in distinction from those consubstantial things. What is more proper to hypostasis is to distinguish individuals from one another by their particular character, even when they are alike in nature, and to show each one by itself. We say further that if, say, a single man or horse came to be in the universe alone, with nothing consubstantial with it, as with Adam the first-formed, its hypostasis could still be recognized as a hypostasis from things of a different essence. Nothing was consubstantial with it in hypostasis from which it could be distinguished. Yet the account of its hypostasis would not therefore fail to hold just because there were no other things consubstantial with it. The reasoning runs the other way. Among consubstantial things, those that have no hypostasis are not distinguished. It does not follow, as you infer, that the hypostases of things with nothing consubstantial to them are not marked off. The hypostases of things of different essences also distinguish them, though in their case the natures do so as well. But where some things have nothing consubstantial with them, there is no need to distinguish them from things of the same nature. The heaven, for instance, is one, the earth is one, and the ether is one. No one would say that, because nothing else is consubstantial with them, they therefore have no hypostasis. Likewise

this whole world, too, is one. Its constitution would not be without hypostasis just because there are not several worlds consubstantial with this one. What, then, persuades you not to accept the hypostasis of Christ, this life-giving, most particular composite living being, unless there is some other hypostasis consubstantial with it in every respect, neither exceeding nor falling short in any natural principle of those in it? Besides, someone seeking a likeness between things in some respect would not use one principle to compare their relation in another respect to something else. He would use the very principle by which the likeness was being sought. So you should not say or ask what this hypostasis is consubstantial with, if you really recognize hypostasis as person to be one thing and hypostasis as essence another. You should ask either with whom Christ is consubstantial according to essence, or with whom he is ‘co-hypostatic’ according to hypostasis, if what you were seeking was his likeness to the Father and to David according to hypostasis rather than essence. Had you asked rightly about this, we would have answered you that Christ is consubstantial with the Father and consubstantial with David, according to each of his natures respectively. But the Word was not co-hypostatic with the Father before the flesh, nor with David before the divine incarnation from the seed of David. Nor, after the holy incarnation of the Word, will his hypostasis rightly be called like that of God the Father or that of the man David.
