It was clumsy of you, then, to say that consubstantial hypostases must have the same principle of essence and the same conception. You should have said consubstantial essences.

The Lord’s hypostasis, being composite, is not like the Father’s, which is simple, nor like David’s, which is composite but made of lesser natures. If for that reason you say it necessarily follows that it is also of a different essence from the essences of the hypostases unlike it, as your conclusion means to show, then something else will follow necessarily too. Since the hypostasis of Paul is unlike that of Peter according to the principle of hypostasis, they too will be of different essences. Or again, by your reasoning, since they are consubstantial, both will have one hypostasis, and the person of Peter will be the same as that of Paul. Indeed, since all humanity is consubstantial, all humanity will have one person. And since the Holy Trinity is consubstantial, one would have to say that the divine nature too has one person and not three. The absurdity of this, so to speak, not only we but even the stones will cry out in rebuke of you. The hypostasis of our Lord Christ, by virtue of the natures in it, is consubstantial with the Father according to the one and with David according to the other. How will you prevent us from saying so by claiming that consubstantial things are not consubstantial in part? Against those who say his nature, or essence, is one, you would have said this well: ‘in part of the one

essence,’ as they would put it, since for them what is consubstantial is called composite. But against us, who proclaim two natures in the one hypostasis of Christ, how can you reasonably put this forward? Look at a robe made of wool and linen. Its hypostasis is one, yet according to the principle of each of the natures in it, it is consubstantial with wool, which comes from animals, and with linen, which comes from plants. We will ask you this as well. Is the soul of righteous Abel, after he laid aside the flesh, truly said to be consubstantial with the soul of righteous Enoch, who has not yet laid aside the flesh, or with that of anyone else still living in the flesh? And is the flesh of a righteous man still in the flesh consubstantial with the flesh of each of the saints who fell asleep before him, or not? If no one will contradict this, it is clear that the hypostasis of Enoch, or of anyone still in the flesh, is in part, by its own parts, consubstantial with the whole hypostasis of Abel’s soul and with the whole hypostasis of the flesh of this holy man who has fallen asleep. So it was in vain that you ruled this out. Things are not called consubstantial with respect to part of an essence, nor yet with respect to a hypostasis that is sometimes constituted for some beings from several natures, that is, essences. That in respect of which their likeness is observed, namely something perfect and whole in each, which is the essence, is no obstacle to recognizing them as consubstantial. So much on this point.

As for your last absurdity, you think that nothing which is partly consubstantial, by its hypostasis, with two beings can be the son of both the one and the other. We will refute you very easily. One man, in part of his own hypostasis, is the son of his mother and of his father. He is also the son of Abraham, the father of those who walk in the footsteps of his faith, and of the Spirit, which begets spirit. And being all these in part of his one hypostasis, he is consubstantial with all of them. It was really superfluous to answer your nonsense on this point even now. It has been shown in what follows that, according to different modes of generation, the same subjects bear several sonships and fatherhoods. Still, a refutation of these arguments of yours, which have come before their proper place, is ready to hand.

“God the Word is either a part of this hypostasis of Christ or the whole of it. If he is a part, and this hypostasis is the Son, then God the Word is part of the Son, and so before the incarnation the Trinity was two and a half. If he is the whole, then God the Word did not exist before the incarnation, since the whole will [not?] come to be before its parts; and the flesh, which came into being recently, is a part of the whole.”

A part, properly speaking, is what is conceived with some imperfection or other, and God the Word is never that. But the natures of the holy hypostasis of Christ are seen as parts by the principle of comparing them, each taken singly, with Christ’s wholeness. Yet he is always a certain whole, and in being the whole Christ he has left behind the otherness partially [?].

“If God the Word is the whole of this hypostasis,” he says, “tell us from what it is completed. God the Word will not be a part of God the Word, since nothing is said to be a part of itself.” First, then, we did not say that the Word simply is the whole of the hypostasis of the Lord Christ. We said it is the Word incarnate. Besides, suppose that because Christ is said to be its whole as hypostasis, it must be completed from something other than the Word, since parts are always other than wholes. Then, since God the Father too is the whole of the paternal hypostasis, tell us from what other thing, as its part, this too is completed. For on your view God the Father will not be a part of God the Father. Who will not weep over this vain talk of yours and your wilful mischief? As was said earlier, it is not only what consists of parts that is called a whole. A thing is also called whole when it has its own principle complete, my friends. In this way we call the point whole and the unit whole, and we do not know them to consist of parts. Moreover, not every whole is different in kind from all its parts considered together. What, after all, is a red-hot lump but [fire?] and iron together? Or what is a purple robe but shellfish blood and silk threads?

“If the hypostasis of Christ is consubstantial by parts with the Father and the Mother, are these parts of it substantial or without substance? If they are without substance, how are they consubstantial with substantial things? And if they are substantial, how are they not parts of an essence? Every part of something substantial is properly a part of an essence, not of a hypostasis. A hypostasis is not characterized as a hypostasis by essential features. Among men it is characterized by whiteness, snub-nosedness and the like. In the divine essence it is characterized by mode of existence: one hypostasis exists by begetting, another by being begotten, another by proceeding. How, then, can you call the essences two and perfect, since you do not call them parts of an essence, and yet say that the hypostasis is from parts?”

We do call the essences parts of the hypostasis, since it is from several essences, and we say that in Christ these parts are substantial, that is, essences. But why do you think that if something partial is substantial, it must also be part of some one single essence? The parts of the foreigners’ ‘hypostasis,’ for instance, are not of one single essence, and yet they are substantial. When there are several essences in the hypostasis, the substantial part must certainly be an essence, but it need not be part of one essence. And how can you say that because some part is called substantial, it must for that very reason, simply because it is called substantial, be part of some numerically single essence? Man is said to be an ensouled and substantial part of the world. Will he then be understood as part of some more universal soul? And the fig tree, being substantial, is a part of the plant kingdom. Will it then be part of one existing essence of [?] simply? If the form of the word persuades you that what is substantial is part of an essence, then, since something is also said to be ‘local,’ it must be part of a place and
…this will be reckoned; and since an animal is called aquatic, then the animal will also be a part of the water.

If your hypostasis is consubstantial with the Father in part and consubstantial with David in part, name these parts by which it is consubstantial with the Father and with David. Are they God and man, or something else? If something else, say what it is. But if they are God and man, will not the man have a particular hypostasis besides David, with whom he is consubstantial, just as God the Word has a particular hypostasis besides the Father, with whom he is consubstantial? For what is without hypostasis could never be called consubstantial with what has a hypostasis. If, then, there is one hypostasis of God the Word, and it is perfect and consubstantial with the Father, the man taken from us is either without hypostasis and spoken of as a bare word, or he has a hypostasis, and he too has a perfect hypostasis insofar as he is man. If he is without hypostasis, it is pointless for him to be consubstantial with David, for nothing without hypostasis is consubstantial with what has a hypostasis. But if he has a hypostasis, he will rightly be called consubstantial with David, since in general a hypostasis is called consubstantial with a hypostasis. And then your sophism is gone: you refuse to speak of two hypostases while wanting to speak of the two natures, that of God the Word and that of the man from us.

But, my friends, once it is granted that this one hypostasis is, in its natures, God and man, as we hold, how will the man in it, who has that nature, have his own hypostasis, any more than God does? For this man has not been given to us, nor has he ever been spoken of, as being not God, so that a hypostasis of the man and another of God should be sought. Look, you yourselves said, "We call the parts of this hypostasis man and God," and no part has a hypostasis of its own. How, then, do you think you can argue against us from our own premises? Having said that we call Godhead and manhood parts of this hypostasis, how can you consistently infer that the part, namely the manhood, must have its own hypostasis? For no part is seen in a hypostasis of its own, but in the hypostasis of the whole. And even if all this were conceded to you, and it were necessary that there be a hypostasis that is called consubstantial with David and one that is consubstantial with the Father, who has a hypostasis, how would it follow from this that there are several hypostases in Christ? For see: in one and the same whole of this hypostasis of Christ, which mediates in its divine and human nature, there is its consubstantiality on each side. Not only that, but its difference in essence from each of its kinds can also be seen, according to the other principle within it. And its being of a different hypostasis from everything besides itself can be seen by the one and the same whole principle of the same hypostasis. For it is not necessary, as you would have it, that for every essential difference of some hypostasis from another hypostasis we introduce a further hypostasis for each of the essences that differ from it. For it is possible for one and the same natural [?]

[?] composite to have, with respect to many things, both essential likeness and unlikeness, and yet, in its singularity, hypostatic unlikeness to all things. For suppose that, on your view, a hypostasis must always be set alongside: one in relation to David, to show the Word's otherness in essence from him, and one in relation to the Father [?], to demonstrate its essential difference from man; and suppose that one and the same hypostasis cannot display, in one way toward one and in another way toward the other, both the difference and the likeness of the natures within it. Then it is time for you to say that each individual man has countless hypostases, so that we may establish the difference in essence of, say, Solomon from this horse, which is of a different essence from him, and from this eagle, and this gnat, and this elephant, and all the other essences in turn. And I suppose it would follow [?] that his likeness to each individual man among those consubstantial with him must be exacted through an equal number of hypostases in order to show Solomon; and that he must of necessity have as many hypostases as there happen to be essences, both consubstantial with him and differing in essence from him, so that by comparing each of his hypostases with every hypostasis like and unlike him, he might be judged consubstantial or differing in essence in each case, and not be defined by one and the same hypostasis over against different essences and persons. But how long will you hinder us with matters so thoroughly agreed? Does it really follow from comparisons with different things that some one thing needs several hypostases in number because of its difference from several things? And who among you will tolerate those who say this? For it would then be shown that a piece of wood which is equal in measure to one or more things, smaller than others and larger than others, needs, for each relation of deficiency, excess and equality, a corresponding number of hypostases: you would set one against this deficiency and one against that, countless ones against countless deficiencies; and again one against this excess and one against that different excess; in short, it would have a hypostasis of its own to be compared with each of the things that differ from it or are equal to it, so that the things compared are always beyond measure and no one thing is ever compared with several. Likewise a grey colour, which differs from white and black and pale and red and yellow and blue and countless others, and is like another grey, would necessarily have to be shown to be two greys, indeed countless greys in number, so that one is compared with the white, one with the black, and one with the other grey. And a garment of linen and wool needs two hypostases, to present the likeness of the wool to wool and of the linen to linen; and a house needs two, so that we may know what is consubstantial with the timbers and the stones in it; and in short, all such things would be like this. But if it is inexcusable even for boys to say such things, then what we say [?] must be rightly understood: that since there is one and the same hypostasis of our Lord Jesus Christ,

in it God the Word is known to be perfect, and the man from us, like us, is known to be perfect according to nature, since its essences are two. Therefore, when it is compared with the hypostasis of David, the comparison shows it to be both other and like, not according to hypostasis but according to essence, [that is,] according to one or the other of its natures. But according to the principle of hypostasis, it is clear that the comparison shows it to be always different from both the Father and David, as is acknowledged, just as every hypostasis distinguishes all things from all others in its own singularity. So the hypostasis of Christ's natures shows him to be, part by part, both of a different essence from such beings and consubstantial with them; but by the one principle of his whole self it presents him as of a different hypostasis from all that exists. For his one and the same person, which has a hypostasis, can declare him consubstantial with two persons that have hypostases, according to each principle, and of a different essence [?]; for a hypostasis is called consubstantial or of a different essence with those with whom it is so called, not as a hypostasis but as possessing an essence. And thus the singularity of the hypostasis has not hindered us in showing the two natures, nor has the duality of the natures become a difficulty for us in speaking of one hypostasis. Nor does that which, in its one hypostasis, is consubstantial with different things have anything without hypostasis; but neither is it of necessity of two hypostases because it is consubstantial with two things. Otherwise, being not only consubstantial with each but still more of a different essence from even a single nature [?], it would need, when there are several natures in the person, an equal number of hypostases.

We ask again: make clear for us what is being said. Tell us what you signify by each nature of the one you call God and man: a particular man and God the Word, or man in general and the holy Trinity, or man in general and God the Word, or a particular man and the holy Trinity? That you do not want to signify the Trinity together with man in general, nor with some particular man, you have made plain by saying that the one who was crucified and suffered is one of the holy Trinity. It remains, then, that you mean God the Word, and that by the one nature you would say you signify either man spoken of in general or some particular man, and not every man. Tell us, then: in what does a particular man differ from every man? Is it not plain that he differs only by hypostasis and person? How, then, do you not speak of two persons and hypostases, when you speak of two natures to signify God the Word and some one particular man? But if you wish to speak of man in general, either you take him in thought, abstracting him by reason from the essence of the individuals and holding him in the mind, and say that God became man in this, apart from any underlying essence; or you gather together all the individuals themselves in their own existence, when you teach that one of the Trinity became incarnate in them all. But if it is the first, how are you not saying that the Lord's incarnation took place

in bare thought, and not in essential existence? And if it is the second, how will God the Word not have become man also in the impious and in sinners, and in men who died before and who are yet to come? That is impious, and fit only for your wisdom to say. And if you wish to posit man in general in some other way, following those who bring in the so-called Ideas, even so there will be no room for the incarnation. For, to pass over everything else, the body from Mary cannot rightly be said to be a part of that. And how will you not appear quite plainly to be fighting against Scripture, which teaches that the Lord's man is one taken from us? For it says, "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham"; and, "It is evident that our Lord sprang from Judah"; and, "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ"; and, "Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs which God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know"; and, "The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead"; and, "For as by a man came death, so by a man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam we all die, so also in Christ we shall all be made alive"; and, "There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Jesus"; and, "Jesus increased in stature and in wisdom and in favour with God and men"; and, "The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him"; and, "The Lord our God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers"; and, "You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." Can you say, then, that all these things, and the countless others like them in holy Scripture, were said of each individual man? And how can one say that all men are of the seed of Abraham, and not of all of it but of the tribe of Judah, and not of the whole of that but of the house of David, and not of all of that but of Mary the Virgin? Would you perhaps say that Caiaphas too was born of Mary the Virgin? For he too is one of the individual men. And would you say that Mary is a human being, or not? If not, tell us what she is in essence. But if she is a human being, how did she give birth to man in general, who had many generations of men before her and many after her? Or how could one of the things that fall under the universal give birth to the universal? Indeed, you cannot even call the whole nature a male, since you cannot call it a woman either; for "human being" is common to both, while "male" and "woman" mark the difference within the common nature. And how is the other point not clear, that just as Adam, one of

all and the first of the mortal condition, through whom we have all likewise become mortal by nature, so too Christ according to the flesh is one of all, and the pioneer of the life of immortality, through whom all, following him, come into possession of immortal life? And that one man is the mediator between men and God? For how can all mediate for themselves? Or how could all advance in grace and wisdom on their own? For many fall asleep untimely, without advancing to full age; and very many others again are full of folly and impiety, not of wisdom and of the grace of God upon them. Nor indeed are all prophets like Moses, nor priests after Melchizedek; otherwise it is time for you to call the priesthood of those who sacrifice to idols and the divinations of the Greeks Mosaic prophecies and Christian priesthoods, which is impious. But why do I prolong my words about these things? Not even all of them hold this view. For one of the leaders of this very doctrine, when asked by someone not unskilled in argument whether the natures they speak of were universal or particular, answered that they could be both the one and the other, but in different respects. "By having in themselves," he said, "the definition of the common essence, they could be called common, since 'rational mortal animal' is the definition of man in general, and the one taken from us evidently had this. And we would say likewise of God the Word," he said. "But because the whole holy Trinity did not become man, nor did it become man in all the individuals that fall under human nature, they would be particular and not common." And when the questioner asked him, "What would particular natures be, if not a hypostasis?", he said that this was a problem of Nestorius. That alone would have sufficed as their defence: it showed that their own doctrine had been overturned [?].

There is no need of further premises, divisions, constructions and discourses. Let it be granted to you that the two so-called essences are particular, although we certainly say nothing of the sort about the divine nature, but know that it is common and also exists in the particular hypostasis of the Word, which became incarnate in a particular way. For since by its own principle it has indivisibility, being without parts, it keeps its commonness free from suffering even while it is distinguished. But what you gather together and strive for with countless labours is this: that hypostases are nothing other than particular natures, and that we, saying that the two natures are particular, or that only one of them is, namely the human, must recognize that they are also two hypostases, since it is agreed that the hypostasis of the divine nature pre-existed. But you, O wise men, err greatly, because you do not first grasp the definition of the matter in question, but turn aside to certain things that accompany it, or to the condition without which it does not occur. For it is not the case that, because a living man is not without the breathing in of air, we must therefore think that the air breathed in is the soul; nor, because it happens that the dead

are heavier, is it reasonable to think that death is heaviness of weight. Rather, one must understand the whole of what the discussion is about and consider what its definition is in itself. For if something is a substance and has something supervening on it from outside, it is not to be thought an accident; and if something is an accident and has the substance as if supervening on it, one must call it first and properly not a substance but an accident, and say that it has been substantified accidentally. However, since you have not given yourselves over to us to learn such things, neither do we press such teaching upon you. Enough of this.

Other things, which are very obvious, will show how utterly absurd your opinions are. For if hypostases are nothing other than particular essences, then in speaking of three hypostases of the holy Trinity you obviously also speak of three essences; and see, you have slipped into tritheism along with your blasphemy concerning the economy. And the absurdity of your position can be recognized in yet another way. If, say, the particular essence of Matthew differs in no way from the particular essence of Mark (for each admits the same definition and term), then neither will the hypostasis, that is, the person, of Matthew differ from the hypostasis, or person, of Mark; but each hypostasis will display the same definition and account, or description. And not only these but every man will be known by the same properties and in the hypostases formed from them, if indeed the particular essence of individuals is the same thing as the hypostasis. Furthermore, sirs, be ashamed to recall your own words. For a little earlier you said that the hypostasis is not constituted from essential things. If, then, it is the same as the particular essence, the particular essence is obviously not constituted from essential things either; but, as you yourselves said in that passage, the particular existence, or essence, will subsist from snub-nosedness and whiteness and the like, or from a mode of existence. So essence will come from what is not essence, and existence from what does not exist. But if the folly of this is quite obvious even to boys, then you have spent this patchwork of a syllogism in vain and gained nothing for yourselves.

If the man has no hypostasis of his own because he subsisted in God the Word, how does the man have a nature of his own, if he came into being in him? And if the man has a nature of his own, how will he not also have a hypostasis? Or suppose he came into being somewhere outside God the Word, and later subsisted in him: how then could there be a nature of the man from us before his own hypostasis?

Natures, both like and unlike, are distinguished and united not by definition but by number of nature, that is, as each is numerically marked off from another, whether like or unlike. The hypostasis, then, by its nature declares to us the composition of unlike things and the distinction of like things among the beings that exist, since it is, properly speaking, a kind of delimitation and separation of one thing from another, whether

they happen to be alike in nature or whether the things that stand apart are unlike one another in their natures; and this not by definition at all, but in their very existence. For hypostases, preserved in that by which they are delimited, cannot be united in that very respect. If, then, the man had a particular hypostasis, how is the man in God the Word through the union, if he truly had the very thing that separates him from him, just as it separates him from all the other men who subsist outside him, namely the hypostasis? Natures, on the other hand, can be united with one another without confusion in some hypostasis, without abolishing each other's own principles. For it is not the definition of nature to subsist distinctly and separately from every other nature, as it is with hypostases. How, then, could the human nature not be united without hindrance to the nature of God the Word, remaining such a nature and displaying what it is by nature even in the union? For a hypostasis cannot be united with a hypostasis while both hypostases, or "apostases", are preserved, since they signify precisely this separation from others through the most particular property of individuals. For we cannot say that what is distinguished is, in its very being distinguished, also united to something; one of the two will necessarily be abolished: either its not being united, or one's not being distinguished from the other. Nor can one say that this hypostasis is in that one while supposing a union in which their properties that distinguish them from each other are preserved. How then shall we say that a human hypostasis came together in the hypostasis of the Word? For even if it had once existed, yet if it came together as a hypostasis with its whole self, and not partially and by juxtaposition, like stones in a house or young men in a chorus, it would no longer have remained apart so as to be still a hypostasis in the same way. For only in bodies is this partial union of hypostasis seen, and it is bare and not union in the proper sense; it is not according to the whole hypostasis, but by juxtaposition of surfaces or of very fine particles, or by the interweaving of parts, or by joining the individual things locally at their limits. That is how stone is joined to stone, oil to water, and thread to thread. So much on this point.

As for your puzzlement over how there could be a nature before its own hypostasis, that was said to us to no purpose. For we never told you that the Master's particular human nature existed before its hypostasis; on the contrary, we said that it came into being and subsisted at the same moment, yet not in some particular hypostasis of its own alone, such as we know that of a mere man to be, but in the pre-existing hypostasis of the Word. He joined to himself what is proper to the human nature and its properties, and in the concurrence of both natures the One of the holy Trinity showed himself to be one person, alike from each nature and from the characteristics gathered from each essence. He is truly one hypostasis only, and that not a human one, for he has the divine nature and the divine properties. Yet he is not in the divine properties only, for he also abounds in characteristics besides the divine.

…brought together by the assumption of the newer nature. This should be clearly observed in the case of red-hot iron as well. The mass of iron first subsists in its own hypostasis. Then, when it is put into the furnace, the nature of fire is generated in it as well. This fire neither existed before nor ever subsisted on its own, but only in the iron. It is born from the furnace, yet it has its hypostasis apart from the furnace, in the [?] form proper to the iron, and it does not diminish the fire in the furnace.

If the man from among us subsisted at all in God, how is it that the hypostasis of the man from among us does not hold firm and exist in the hypostasis of God the Word? And if the hypostasis of the man from among us does not hold firm and exist in God the Word, how has it not perished after it subsisted, or else never subsisted at all from the beginning? — Does everyone who says that a thing is and subsists also thereby say that it exists on its own? Then, since we say that a hand, a foot, a nail and a liver are and subsist in a man, shall we conclude that these already exist on their own, and that each of them has a distinct hypostasis? We also say that the mind is in the soul, and that colour subsists in the body. Shall we then go looking for hypostases of these as well? And how, on your view, is anything said to be "in something"? Perhaps you will explain it to us. But to say such things, and perhaps even to argue against them, bears witness either to great absurdity or to great learning.

If you say that the man from among us subsisted in God the Word, how do you not show, by that very word "subsisted," that the one who subsisted has a hypostasis? — That the man subsisted in God the Word we proclaim more loudly than you do. But it seems you have forgotten what you were disputing with us about, and are now bringing a different charge. What we do not accept is your claim that the man who was united, to put it once and for all, subsisted on his own. Otherwise we would present two hypostases preserved, each in the principle proper to one of the things that came together, and so overturn the union from its foundations. For if each of the things in Christ subsists on its own, do you claim that any union between them is possible? Would it be the kind of union you say David had with his enemy Goliath, in the grappling of battle and the act of killing him? Or the union Joseph had with Benjamin while he was in Egypt? Or the union of the musician's activity with the lyre? Or some union of that sort [?]? We, however, believe that the Word and the flesh are together in one common hypostasis. And you: even if you do not refute our positions, how do you not refute your own, since you yourselves say that the man is in the Word? For to say that something is in something else testifies to its union with it. But to say that the hypostasis of each of the subjects exists on its own clearly confesses that they are separated from one another. To say or think both of these things about the same subject is utterly incompatible.

If the man from among us subsisted, but does not have a hypostasis, how are you not teaching contradictions when you call the one who subsisted anhypostatic? — You neither remember what you say nor refute what we say. We do not mean to show you that the Lord's man is anhypostatic. God forbid! We mean that he is not idiohypostatic, that is, separated from the Word. Who would doubt that "anhypostatic" and "idiohypostatic" do not mean the same thing, since the second indicates how a thing exists in relation to others, while the first indicates that it does not exist at all, most wise sir? CHAPTER 11. If Peter's soul is other than Paul's, and what is other is other either in nature and hypostasis, as heaven is from earth, or in hypostasis alone, as the father is from the son, how does Peter's soul not differ from Paul's in nature and hypostasis, or at any rate in hypostasis? And if so, how does each person's soul not have a hypostasis by which it differs from another's, whether the two are of the same essence or not? — You have plainly said this now in order to show that each man too has two hypostases. Your aim is not to be barred, even by the example of man, from speaking of two hypostases in Christ, since His natures are two, just as we speak of Peter or Paul. Suppose Paul's soul is indeed other in hypostasis, taken by itself alone, though I do not know how you can judge this about it while it still remains in the flesh. Even so, where has it been said that Peter's soul assumed Paul's, or that Peter's soul is in Paul's, as you yourselves said a little earlier when you granted that the man is in the divine Word? For what prevents a pair of hypostases from appearing is the confession that the natures are united. If the Word had not assumed the flesh, just as Peter did not assume Paul, then truly, following the example of Peter and Paul, the Word and the flesh, that is, the man in Christ, would have different hypostases. But if Peter did not assume Paul in the way the Word assumed the flesh, you were wrong to compare the one case with the other. And if the incarnate Word is one Son and not two, while Paul and Peter are not one son but two, you are setting these side by side absurdly. And if Christ, in Godhead and manhood, is one, while Peter and Paul are not one apostle but two, you have compared unlike things in order to show that whatever is other is certainly other in hypostasis, whether or not it is other in nature. If, then, you say these things because you believe in two Christs, two Sons and two Lords, none of them assumed by the other but each distinct, as Paul is from Peter, you have at long last uncovered the hidden abomination of your impiety. Which one, then, do you suppose is God, and by whom was he anointed to be the one Christ? Which one is the man, and by whom is he anointed? Tell us about the other Christ as well! Which one is truly the Son, the one who received testimony at the Jordan, and which is the one who was visibly baptized? For the only one pointed out and attested by

the Father, if there are two and they are different, will rightly lead you to strike out one of your Sons or Christs. You must reject either the one baptized and visible at that time, or the one invisible, from the Father before the ages. For the Father speaks in the singular of only one being His Son. That Son is moreover perceptible, since the Father pointed out His beloved Son to our eyes, and this Son is also confessed to be the invisible Word. So either the Father's testimony is false, or [?] the opinion drawn from the oracle, or the Son attested was the same one, both perceptible and

If Peter's body differs in no way by nature from Paul's body, how would it not differ by hypostasis? [?] If it does not differ by hypostasis either, and what differs neither in nature nor in hypostasis would be the same in every respect, how will Peter and Paul not have one body, the same in every respect? That is impossible. — But first, one body does differ from another by its own particular nature. You now bring the common nature against us, though a little earlier you poured so much abuse on those who introduce the common nature in the case of man. For not every body is the same, either in number or in every natural quality, since not every stone and plant and so on is the same in nature. Many plants and stones destroy one another, and yet they are still stones and plants. Nor is all flesh the same flesh: there is one kind for birds and another for fish and reptiles, and there are earthly bodies and heavenly bodies. So it is not because their nature differs that they need a different hypostasis to be distinguished. Moreover, if this is why hypostases are needed in Christ, namely that the natures are different, then there will necessarily be no difference of hypostases. But let it be granted to you that all bodies differ in hypostasis without exception, whether or not they differ in nature. Clearly, though, this applies only to bodies not united to one another, for in red-hot iron no different hypostases are seen. So too in the Lord's case: if we spoke of what belongs to Him without any union, we would truly have to recognize a difference of both natures and hypostases, or at least of hypostases. And this would hold even if there were no variation of natures. But if we confess a union, though an unconfused one, of things in Him that differ in nature, what need is there for two hypostases? But enough of that. Where has anyone been granted that Paul's body is united with Peter's, so that this case would be like the Lord's union? The one lived among those of the circumcision in Judea and Palestine, the other among the Gentiles in Corinth, Achaia and Macedonia. We do not say that the Word gave the flesh the kind of right hand of fellowship that Peter, set apart for the circumcision, gave to Paul when Paul was sent to the Gentiles. Rather, we believe in a true union, and in their natural coexistence into the ages to come through the hypostatic union, even though you have openly denied this and left yourselves no remnant of the Christians'

Babbling, and wishing to seem to say something to those present, they turn their backs on the questioner when asked to show an anhypostatic nature. Yet they say that there truly is no anhypostatic nature. "For we too," they say, "call the essences enhypostatic. But it does not follow that whatever is enhypostatic is also a hypostasis, just as, of course, it does not follow that whatever is enousios is also an essence. Look: we say that the hypostases of the holy Trinity are three, and that they are enousioi, yet we do not add three essences to the three hypostases, although we know that each of the hypostases is enousios. If, then, we say, one can speak of three enousioi hypostases in one essence, one can clearly also speak of two enhypostatic natures in one hypostasis. In this way we neither call a nature anhypostatic nor teach that the two natures are two hypostases, just as we neither call the hypostases of the holy Trinity without essence nor divide the three hypostases into three essences. Moreover," they say, "to take another example, when we call a body coloured, we do not regard the body as the same thing as the colour, for whatever is coloured is not thereby a colour. In the same way, whatever is enhypostatic is not thereby a hypostasis. The argument, then," they say, "is pointless. It does not compel someone who speaks of two natures either to call them anhypostatic, or to speak of one of them [?], or else to speak of two hypostases, since what is enhypostatic is not a hypostasis, as we have shown." These are the things they said, deceiving those present, with their eyebrows raised, and by these words naming themselves as come from the Cherubim. But see for yourself how by what they said they demolished their own position. Either they did so in ignorance, their own ignorance, or they were mocking simple hearers who had no experience of such matters and misleading them through the similarity of words. For if nature corresponds to the body and hypostasis to the colour, and they call the natures enhypostatic just as bodies are called coloured, then wherever there is an enhypostatic nature there must also be a hypostasis, just as there is colour wherever there is a coloured body. One cannot conceive of an enhypostatic nature without a hypostasis. If, then, whatever differs in nature necessarily differs in hypostasis as well, let them show me something that differs in nature but does not differ in hypostasis. And let them not lead the simpler folk astray by deceiving them with similar phrases, saying that if a hypostasis can be enousios and not heteroousios, a nature can also be enhypostatic and not heterohypostatic. The last claim is false, since whatever is heteroousios is certainly also heterohypostatic. If, then, the natures differ from one another, they differ by nature, and clearly they also differ by hypostasis. And if it is impossible to speak of a difference of natures within one nature, it is likewise impossible for there to be a difference of hypostases within one and the same hypostasis.

The problems set before you are indeed ours. But you did not meet them fittingly, and have persuaded only yourselves of your opinions. In the example, whose words happen to be alike only by chance, hypostasis corresponds to colour and nature to body. From this you say that wherever there is a body there must also be colour, and you conclude that the hypostases are two because the natures are two. Know, then, that we say this too: where a body is said to be coloured, colour necessarily exists, just as a hypostasis exists where a nature is said to be enhypostatic. But you have not yet shown the point in question, the very point you dispute with us. That point is this: where several coloured bodies are said to come together, there must be as many colours as there are bodies. On your view several bodies could not be coloured by one and the same colour, as snow, milk and white lead are by white when mixed, or wool, linen and silk woven into one white robe. Nor could several bodies be blended into a single new colour, as white lead and ochre, copperas and gum are in a grey eye-salve. For we say that the two natures subsist in one and the same hypostasis. We do not mean that one of them could be anhypostatic in it, but that both can subsist in one common hypostasis, and so each is enhypostatic in the same single hypostasis. For it does not follow that because something must exist, it must exist on its own. None of the houses in a city is without an owner, but not every house that has an owner necessarily has only one owner, since many houses in the city are jointly owned. In the same way, since the natures exist, they must both subsist and be enhypostatic. But since they do not exist on their own apart from one another, a union of them having admittedly taken place, it is not necessary for each to subsist on its own. Clearly, then, their being enhypostatic must be understood not as being heterohypostatic, but as both being in one and the same hypostasis. That is why we also accept what you said at the end: that it is impossible to speak of a difference of hypostasis in one and the same hypostasis. For we do not speak at all of a difference of hypostases in the one hypostasis of the Lord. God forbid! We do recognize a difference of particular hypostatic properties. But we do not speak in the Lord's case of a union of different hypostases or of differences, for this was shown earlier to be impossible, unless one were to speak of things that are distinguished as being united in the very respect in which one sees the distinction. Rather, we recognize a composition of different natures in the one, first, original hypostasis of the Word, and not a second hypostasis or one made out of hypostases [?]. But enough of that. As for the other point you declared, that since the natures in the economy are different, the hypostases must be different too, but where hypostases differ in the divine essence the natures need not differ, how is this shown? First, you said earlier that, in the case of Peter's and Paul's bodies, the lack of difference between natures necessarily requires a difference of hypo-

stases. What grounds [?] do you have, then, for saying this now? Be assured that we will certainly demand that you show the converse as well: that just as, on your account, different natures mean different hypostases, so natures without difference mean hypostases without difference. How, then, do we believe that the nature of the holy Trinity is one and without difference, while the hypostases are different? For it will follow that just as things whose natures differ are said by you to have different hypostases, so things whose natures do not differ must be said to have hypostases that do not differ. Moreover, on your account natures and hypostases must always be equal in number. Since, then, the nature of the holy Trinity is not only without difference but also one, let the hypostasis also be one and without difference. But perhaps you will say that wherever there is a difference of nature there is certainly also a difference of hypostasis, but wherever there is a difference of hypostasis there is not necessarily also a difference of nature, because hypostasis is narrower in extent than essence and does not convert with it in its definitions. First, the particular natures would clearly not be understood as wider than the hypostases, but even narrower; only the common natures are wider. But let this too be granted to you. Then the hypostases must also be more numerous, since the nature is one. For narrower things are necessarily more numerous than the more universal ones. So for each nature there will be two hypostases, or more, or one and a fraction. That being so, the Master's natures, being two, will have four hypostases, or three, or two and a half, or some such number, according to this authoritative law of yours. And it will not be enough for you to wrongly divide the composite person into hypostases. You will also have to divide each simple and particular nature, both His and everyone's, into a greater number of hypostases, and show the particular nature of Paul alone as having two hypostases from the nature of the soul and perhaps three gathered from that of the body. In this way reason refutes you for pronouncing so rashly. And this whole world, along with most of what is in it, clearly exposes the incoherence of your opinion by the facts themselves. Consider a plant's body, say, composed from the natures of the four elements; red-hot iron, made of different natures interwoven; a man, made of different natures united; this temple; a medicine; this whole world, made up of different natures. If each of these does not have one hypostasis, we are wrong to call the man or the plant or the world, or anything else

of the kind [?], one. For we would recognize the quantity of natures and an even greater number of hypostases, and things united by nature in any way would have no grounds left for being named in the singular. And you often say that nature and hypostasis are the same. So if you grant that the hypostases of the holy Trinity are different, you must certainly grant that the natures are different too, and if the hypostases are more than one, there must necessarily be as many essences as well.

"But," they say, "look: man is two natures but one hypostasis. From this it is clear that two natures can exist in one hypostasis." Again verbal hair-splitting, again a battle of doctrines, again contradictory words, and the sophistry of a plainly unreasonable soul! They say that the same man is two natures and one hypostasis, and then again that he has no hypostasis. And blessed were we when we heard "two natures, one hypostasis," compared with now being taught to say "two natures, but no hypostasis." Again, they say that Christ is three natures, and also two natures. Having failed to speak rightly of one hypostasis, they now teach three natures in one hypostasis. Hear how. If man is of two natures and one hypostasis, and he has been assumed and united to God the Word, how are there not three natures, two assumed and one assuming? And how are there not two hypostases, the one assuming and the one assumed? But if Christ is of two natures and one hypostasis, how is the man not one nature? And how is the man not anhypostatic, the man they earlier said was two natures? Who will put up with teaching such a contradiction? — But that man is both one nature and two natures, under different aspects, we have shown, with God's help, in our writings against those who say that his nature is only one. So as not to repeat the same things at length, anyone who wishes may be fully informed on this point there. When we say that there are two natures in our Master Jesus Christ, then, it is clear that we count the human nature in Him as one, since the composition of the natures in Him became the cause of a newer kind. So in the manner and sense that presents its own single nature, this is one nature. As for the hypostasis of man, you yourselves, in the first chapter of the present treatise, confessed that it is one and is from two natures. You said to us about the Master's hypostasis: "If we say that it is consubstantial not with the Father's hypostasis but with David's, how, when we say that it is from two natures, do we not mean that it is composed of soul and body?" For David's hypostasis is of that kind. But let this too be conceded to you, even though such things are often said, not out of conviction but as a kind of management and precaution, by people who, when they lie, do not remember well what they have said before, so that their own refutation awaits them from their own mouths. As for us, we recognize one hypostasis in the individual man, and in every other hypostasis made up of distinct natures. Yet in the case of one who is not simply man

[?] …since the Lord's [man] was never distinguished from the hypostasis of the Word, we know of no hypostasis that belongs to it alone. We say that the Saviour's humanity did not subsist in a hypostasis of its own. It subsisted in the hypostasis of the Word from the beginning [?]. Nor do we now know the hypostasis of the Word simply as the hypostasis of the Word alone. Since his ineffable union, the Word co-subsists in it together with the humanity, with what is consubstantial [?]. So we know one and the same hypostasis, common to both. It existed before the substance of the man, and was formerly proper to the Word within the common substance of the Godhead. Then it created for itself the nature of the Lord's man, embraced it, and joined it within itself to its own nature. At the moment it became the hypostasis of the nature of the flesh as well, it began to be common instead of proper, and it became more complex. For the hypostasis of the Word is no longer distinguished from the Father and the Spirit, as before, only by the property of being begotten. It is also distinguished by being made up of several natures and natural properties, and plainly of more personal properties too. How, then, can a hypostasis of something that never subsisted outside the hypostasis of the divine Word be counted alongside it? Suppose the flesh did have a hypostasis before its conception, which no one could say piously. Once it was assumed, that is, once the assumed and the assuming remained in one another, how could the separation of each from the other persist in them and be preserved, when it is that separation which makes a hypostasis? We must therefore rightly understand that the Word's nature is common to him with the Father and the Spirit. His hypostasis is proper to him over against the Father and the Spirit, and over against all human beings not born of the holy Virgin. It is common only with the flesh that the Word took from the Theotokos. Conversely, the flesh from the holy Virgin has a nature common with all who descend from Adam, since it shares in ours. But its hypostasis is proper to it over against us and over against the Father and the Spirit, and common only with the Word. This is the rule of orthodoxy handed down to us by those who spoke of God. We rightly speak of one hypostasis and two natures both in man and in Christ. That you, by contrast, are quite inconsistent with yourselves will be shown next, with God's help, after we have answered all your arguments on this subject. But first we must show that by this very argument you too call man not only one hypostasis but also one nature, as the followers of Eutyches do. You say that in Christ the natures are two in the same way as the hypostases, and you see neither outnumbering the other. You also know Christ as God and man. Then one of two things follows. Either you know two natures and two hypostases belonging to the man in him, and say that the Word has no nature or hypostasis at all, portraying him as without substance and without hypostasis. Or you know one hypostasis and one nature of the Word, and of the man likewise only one: one hypostasis and also one nature in Christ. Either way you stand refuted. So where now is the verbal trickery, the war of words, the self-contradiction, and who knows what else you declaim in your opening speeches? And whose is it?

[?] …of Paul's body, how will the body of the man not also have a hypostasis? If Peter's soul has a hypostasis as Peter's, and a nature, and Peter's body likewise has a hypostasis as Peter's, and a nature, then Peter is two natures because of soul and body. How then is Peter not also two hypostases because of soul and body? And if Peter's soul and body are two natures, and also two hypostases, how is it not false to say that man is two natures and one hypostasis?

You have tangled yourselves in your own nets. You make us ready to cry out at you in David's words: 'The sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands,' and, 'His mischief shall return upon his own head.' You ought to remember what you were saying just now. In trying to establish two hypostases of man, you conclude that we speak of three natures of the Saviour.

First, then, we do not see how the soul and the body of one and the same man, living in the flesh, could have different hypostases. Suppose that while the composite living being is alive and intact you recognize two hypostases of its parts, as in their separation by death. Then one of two things follows. Perhaps you recognize not just two natures and hypostases in him but more, because of the separation and division of the living being. Everything that is divided multiplies its own number, so his natures and hypostases will be four, or eight. Or perhaps you recognize the same natures and hypostases in him even after the living being has been dissolved. Then you hold that the same account applies to the existence of the living and of the dead, of the united and of the separated composite man. On your premises, the same account will cover contraries in his case.

Still, let this too be conceded to you along with everything else. Now hear from us the other point, which we took up from you a little earlier. You recognize one hypostasis of the body in man, and for that reason you think there are two hypostases in him, just as there are two natures. That is why you also rule us out when we draw on the example of man to show two natures and one hypostasis in the Lord. It is clear, then, that you too call Christ man and God, and that you have recognized in him two hypostases of the man and one hypostasis of the Word. So you will plainly be found to recognize three hypostases in Christ, not just two as you have tried to say until now, one of God and one of the man. You hold two of the man and one of the Word. Likewise you must necessarily give him three natures, for two reasons. First, there is no hypostasis without substance (to use your own terms and follow your own notions). Second, you already say outright that the man has two natures and the Word one. So when the whole sum of your doctrine is gathered together, the things conceived in Christ come to six: three natures and three hypostases, my most wise friends!

[?] …if the one is the same as the other, look: you have granted three of each in the Lord. Then how can you say two of each? You have filched half of your own doctrine. And if, as you often like to say, the natures are the same as the hypostases, then on your view there would likewise be six hypostases, since the number of natures is matched to the hypostases. Then either everything is a substance and he has no person left, or everything is taken as a person and no substance remains for the six persons of Christ. If these things move the hearer to both laughter and lament, you should be very clearly persuaded of this: your wicked song will soon come back at you all the more violently, after striking the truth of true religion and the unbreakable rock of orthodoxy. As the saying goes, 'May it pierce their own hearts, and may their bows be broken.'

Since there are, as all agree, three divine persons (prosopa), he asks, which prosopon do you say was struck? If it was the Word's, then since he is consubstantial with the Father, the Father and the Spirit too will be visible, tangible, able to be struck, bound by time and simply passible, no different from us in nature. For such was the prosopon that was struck. But if what was struck, namely the prosopon of Christ, is different from the three of the holy Trinity, how do you too not grant two prosopa, that of the Word, who is one of the Trinity, and that of Christ?

But their sophism, which plays on the double meaning of a word, is obvious. The prosopon that was struck was not the one taken to mean hypostasis. It was the face, the appearance and shape of the part of the human body around the eyes, and that is where it gets its name. That this is different from the prosopon understood as hypostasis can be shown readily. The one is said of the whole hypostasis of Christ, the other only of a part of his body. Further, in the sense of the hypostatic prosopon, no living thing, whether rational [?] or lifeless, that exists as one in reality has two prosopa, for nothing that is one in number has two hypostases. In the other sense, many animals are two-faced, three-headed or many-headed, such as amphisbaenas, hydras and the rest. In the same way the cherubim, those marvels, are four-faced and four-formed, and are shaped in this and other ways. Yet we do not say that their hypostases are four as well. Further, in the first sense the common nature is distinguished in individuals. In the second, even the individual [?] nature itself is divided, as it were, into this member and that. Further, the first sense, the one taken for hypostasis, is said of inanimate and animate things, of bodies and incorporeal beings, of living and non-living things alike. Whatever exists in its own right is also a hypostasis. The second is said properly only of ensouled bodies. When it is used of inanimate things, in most cases it signifies only their surface. Further, the first is often described by certain intelligible properties that belong to the substance, as the Father is by being unbegotten. The second is always

described only by perceptible accidents. A hypostasis, then, and the prosopon that signifies it, is one for each being, whether it has a face to signify it or not. But it does not follow that each being has two prosopa just because it has a prosopon in the sense of a face. So you cannot show from this that there are two prosopa, that is, two hypostases, of the Word and of his incarnate form. The prosopon of the hypostasis of Christ, the Word incarnate, was one thing. The member of his perceptible flesh called a prosopon was another. If you think otherwise, then each of you certainly has two prosopa: he has a face, which is called a prosopon, and he is a hypostasis, which is understood as a prosopon. Further, every hypostatic prosopon contains the whole soul and all the individual parts of the body, and the face itself is one of those parts. So your one prosopon will be contained in your other prosopon. But what is contained is never the same as what contains it. So each of you would have not one and the same prosopon but two, one larger and the other small. Yet where have you heard of a large and a small hypostasis, and of the same person at that? Moreover, on this reasoning many-headed creatures will have perhaps ten hypostases. Indeed, you yourselves have been split in two by your own argument, though you do not split the Word from his own flesh.

But these, sirs, are sophisms of human cunning, crafted to lead others astray, as the one who spoke of God says. For we will put this to you. You too grant that Christ is somehow wholly moved by the divine Word in what he said or did. So what do you say? Did the Word who said to the leper, 'I will it; be clean,' exist yesterday, the day before and before the ages, or not? If he did not, how can God not seem new, even if he works the greatest things through Christ or through any man at all? But if he did exist, how is it that he willed it and yet did not cleanse the leper until then? In this case it is clear that the Word of God, existing before the ages and always living and active, then made known by his spoken word the will that suited the time and the need. How then is it not equally clear that his impassible and invisible prosopon accepted the dishonour of the slaps, for the sake of our freedom, through the face, which is a perceptible part of his body?

Further, you logicians: there are three consubstantial prosopa of the holy Trinity. On your view the prosopon of Christ is of an entirely different substance from them. Do you call it divine, or not? If not, then you cannot call Christ God at all, or not in the same sense. You can only say that the name above every name, that is, 'God', was granted to him, and that this is the great dignity and gift that comes from his relational union with God. But if you call this prosopon divine too, while saying it is of a different substance from the other three consubstantial divine prosopa, then you have three consubstantial prosopa and one of a different substance. How would that not add up to four divine prosopa for you?

If God the Word, he says, fills all things and is invisibly present to all things in his hypostasis, while the visible Christ was confined in his hypostasis by womb, manger and house before his holy resurrection,

and even after it is circumscribed by places, according to the words, 'He went into heaven,' and, 'whom heaven must receive,' and, 'He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven,' how can the one not be a visible and circumscribed hypostasis, and the other an invisible and uncircumscribed one?

But if every circumscription of a hypostasis is made by marking off a place, is the Word then marked off in his hypostasis from the Father and the Holy Spirit by place? If so, and the Word is said by you to be in the universe in a local sense, then the other two hypostases of the Godhead are either each in some other universe and not in this one, or in none at all. In this one they have no room to exist as distinct, since the Word fills everything here. And how can the divine hypostasis of the one who, as Scripture says, fills all in all be in all things? It is impossible for the same thing both to be the place of certain things and to be in them as in a place. If, then, these things do not belong to the Word by a local circumscription of his hypostasis, what prevents him from remaining the divine Word while assuming the nature of flesh? He would keep the distinguishing marks proper to him as the Word of God and acquire fleshly ones in addition, in his one hypostasis.

The Word has properties by which he is distinguished from the hypostasis of the Father and from that of the Holy Spirit. He is begotten, and he does not beget. He is in the Father as the counsel and word of one who counsels and reasons. He does not go forth from him into other things, and so is not proceeding. He creates in a manner proper to him, and he has his other properties as well. None of this makes him several hypostases. In the same way, adding other properties, more numerous and even opposed, does not multiply his hypostasis. The Father's hypostasis is perfectly distinguished from that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit by unbegottenness alone. When it is further distinguished by begetting, it is not a more perfect hypostasis, nor could anyone truly call it two hypostases.

Besides this, what would you say about the hypostasis of a mere man, Paul for instance? Is his whole hypostasis, soul and body together, recognized by all his visible and local boundaries? Or is it clearly recognized by different ones? Yet his hypostases are not different on that account. He was caught up out of the body to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words with his soul. He had the local and visible boundaries of the body and the intelligible ones of the soul alike, setting him apart from Peter and the rest. Even so, he had no further distinction, but even in this way belonged to one and the same hypostasis.

But we confess the goodness of God, who teaches man knowledge and gives understanding to the foolish, and so we will also set out the problem [?] that came to us in a dream. Someone spoke to us. He was rather dark in appearance and devoutly robed. He asked: 'Is the Lord God by nature, or also by hypostasis?' And he argued that if he is God by nature only, then by hypostasis

he is either man, or something else, or entirely without a hypostasis. But if he is God by hypostasis as well, then by a whole and perfect hypostasis; and look, he has two hypostases, just as he has two natures, if indeed his humanity is not without a hypostasis either. Or else he is God in hypostasis only by a part of his one hypostasis. In that case Christ is either imperfect [?] with respect to [?] of the human hypostasis, or the hypostasis of Christ is more than perfect and more than divine, conceived as above the Father, the Spirit and the Word. For its whole is greater than its own part, by which it was perfect God, according to [?]

But after he had said this and thrown us into confusion with the difficulty, he left, leaving us dizzy. At dawn we turned our gaze toward the true light, asking 'what shall be given and what added to us against a deceitful tongue.' Then we considered that 'God' is first of all a name of nature. It signifies primarily a substance, not a person. In the same way 'man' names not the hypostasis of Paul but the nature. It is applied to one and all and to each individual, because it is common to all human beings, which the hypostatic name 'Paul' or 'Peter' is not. How, then, can the same name be predicated of the same subject in two different ways, from the account of the nature and from the account of the hypostasis?

Further, a name of nature sometimes expresses the likeness of one thing to another, but a hypostatic name expresses only otherness. If, then, 'God' is both a natural and a personal name for Christ, the same name would express both his likeness to the other two divine persons and his otherness from them. Further, if the hypostasis is God not only because of its nature but also because of its own proper character, then Christ is God by two godheads, and so are the Father and the Holy Spirit. Further, if the substance and each of the three hypostases of the holy Trinity are each called God in their own right, we clearly end up with four Gods. Besides this, the nature is more inclusive and more common than the hypostases, so the godhead that belongs to the nature will be greater. Christ would then be thought a greater God by his nature and a lesser God by his hypostasis than he himself is.

Above all, suppose the Word, that is, the hypostasis of Christ, were thought to be God simply because he is Word and Son, and did not claim this name only because of the substance seen in him. The Father is plainly neither Word nor Son, so he would not be God either, or not God in this sense, and likewise the Holy Spirit. There would then be one godhead that is alike in all three and three different godheads, and each divine person would be composed of two different godheads, one alike and the other unlike. If all this is absurd, it is clear that the Word, that is, Christ, and the Father and the Holy Spirit are called God from the nature alone, just as David and Solomon are called man. For 'Christ', 'David' or 'prophet' would not simply be names taken from the nature, nor 'man' a name taken from the hypostasis, unless perhaps by [?] of the contemplation in [?]
Every nature, they say, is known through its hypostases. No one knows horseness without knowing individually

this particular horse. The same holds for humanity and for any other kind, common or particular. If, then, you know two natures of Christ, clearly you first came to know their hypostases.

Shall we then say this? When we see the works of Phidias, we understand his nature, since statues of men are not the work of an angel or of a dumb animal. Do we then also recognize his hypostasis? Bravo to the sculptors of arguments, rather than to the sculptor of men! And since we are not ignorant of the substance of Enoch and Noah, shall we confidently claim to know their persons as well? But perhaps you will say: 'We do not even know Noah's particular nature itself. We infer it by analogy from similar things that we do know.' Very well, let that be granted. We readily inferred the nature from similar things. But we did not come to know the hypostasis from a similar hypostasis, since no hypostasis is ever entirely like another. How, then, would we understand Noah's nature through his hypostasis, which is not available to us and, as you say, has nothing like it? But if we did understand his nature, then it is possible to know a nature without its hypostasis, and without also knowing that hypostasis.

'What then?' he says. 'Do you think of Noah's nature as without a hypostasis?' Certainly not. That is not what we were saying. We were saying that the nature need not always and in every case be known through a hypostasis, as you claim, as if someone who has not first gained knowledge of the hypostasis could not know the nature either. And even if knowledge of a nature always does come through a hypostasis, what prevents us from contemplating, in one hypostasis, several of the natures we already know? When we look at Andrew, we do not see separate hypostases of his soul and of his body. We know one hypostasis of Andrew as a whole. Yet we know two natures in him, that of the soul and that of the body.

Perhaps they might also say this: 'Everything natural to us is seen in Christ as well, for he was made like us in every respect apart from sin. In our natural birth, the body is formed first, before it is united with the soul. So the Lord's body must have subsisted before the soul. Then one of two things follows. Perhaps it had its own hypostasis, and once the soul had been breathed into it, it was united as a third step with the Word as well according to hypostasis, so that two hypostases were joined to each other. One would have to ask how that could happen, and by what single means. It could happen in no other way than by good pleasure alone. Or else the Word was united to the body first, and afterwards breathed the living soul into himself and into the flesh. In that case the Word was united to the flesh not through the soul as intermediary, but rather to the soul through the flesh as intermediary, which is impermissible. For a thing is joined to what is more remote through what is more akin and nearer to it.'

But it is agreed that the Lord, even in accepting what is natural to us, does not lack what is above our nature. Far more at odds with our manner of birth than this are his conception without seed and his birth without corruption, and also his forty-day fast without food, and other such things. So in Christ's case we believe that this too was ordered above our nature, so that at the same time the

…his flesh, and that it is ensouled, and that it is the flesh of the divine Word, ensouled with a rational and intellectual soul. For the Almighty needs no time to accomplish what he is pleased to do. Nor was there any reason why the conception and pregnancy of the blessed Virgin, which came by faith in the word [?], should proceed in the same way that bodily seeds come to term. She believed that “there will be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord,” and those things were beyond all hope, thought and nature. Sowing into the flesh comes from the will of the flesh, and the flesh is formed [?] by a natural power. Faith sown into the soul, however, is a glory kindled by God's good pleasure and imparted through the living and abiding Word of God. It begets people whose mind agrees with the inward judgement of him who said to his own Word, “In you I am well pleased.” By this kind of spiritual rebirth, through water and Spirit, all of us who believe in Christ, who was born in this way according to the flesh, are reborn timelessly from the nature of flesh into spirit. This is because the soul, though it is in the flesh, still received this sowing as spiritual, consented spiritually to be united to that judgement, and was counted worthy of a spiritual nature [?]. Hence also by nature [?]: “For your word, O Lord,” or “your fear,” “we conceived in the womb and were in labour” with it by faith, bringing it to completion within ourselves by our deeds, “and we gave birth to the spirit of salvation, which we have wrought upon the earth.” Someone who is in the flesh, yet holds not to what appears according to the flesh but to what belongs to the spirit, in some way changes his own make-up. He cuts himself off from his natural joining with the flesh and enters into a union of will with the Spirit, which is God the Word. So whoever is joined to the Lord in this way is one spirit with him.

Again, then, they say: “If God the Word is distinguished by his properties from the Father and the Spirit, who are consubstantial with him, and is therefore at once understood to be a hypostasis, then his flesh too is distinguished by its own properties from all who are consubstantial with it. Such properties include, for instance, coming forth from a Virgin without sin. So the flesh too would at once be understood to be a hypostasis. Since the properties of the Word and of the flesh are not the same, the hypostases are not the same either. How, then, have you reckoned one hypostasis for the two natures, when they are distinguished in two ways from what shares their nature?” But anyone who looks more carefully can see that all the properties of the Lord's flesh are contained in one more universal property of it, which is the cause of them all. This is simply the fact that it never subsisted on its own, in its own bare nature. That is why all the other properties that appear specially in him, beyond all other men, are fitting to God. Examples are his sinless birth, his wholly blameless course of life, his purpose that was always entirely good, its surpassing power to work wonders, his knowledge beyond all wisdom, his all-perfect and supernatural virtue, and other divine things like these. And if divine things never appear without a divine nature, then the properties of every hypostasis must also properly belong to it. For not…

…[?] would anyone reckon things that appear in one hypostasis to be the properties of another hypostasis. Necessarily, then, the properties of the Lord's flesh itself, since they are divine, testify that this very hypostasis is not without a divine nature. And since a divine nature is never without a hypostasis, it clearly testifies further that there is also a divine hypostasis in this hypostasis of the flesh, whose properties, fitting to God, set it apart from the men consubstantial with it. The divine nature of the Word has properties fitting to the Son that existed before the flesh and distinguish it from the persons consubstantial with it [?]. The flesh has properties fitting to God that set it apart from the men who share its nature. Yet the divine nature does not divide itself into two hypostases. It follows necessarily that the hypostasis of the Word, even together with his flesh, must be understood to be one only, since both these natures have been united in Christ according to his hypostasis.

Chapter 20 [?]. “If,” he says, “you count Christ's human nature alongside the nature of the Godhead because it lacks nothing compared with the nature of individual men, why do you not do the same with his human hypostasis? It too lacks nothing compared with the hypostases of individual men. Why do you not count it alongside the hypostasis of the Word, and say that the Word's hypostases are also two?” We readily reply that what it lacks is demarcation from every other hypostasis, for this alone is what marks out hypostases. That this is so may be seen as follows. Suppose a woman gives birth to an unformed lump of flesh, or to some hardened, lifeless body, as happens in miscarriages and in the case of the so-called mole conceived in the womb. We say that this offspring is the hypostasis of a body, even if a lifeless one, just as we would of the normally formed body of an infant. Now suppose a body that is in its natural state, belonging to hypostases born long before, develops an outgrowth joined to it, perhaps on the crown of the head or somewhere else. It might be a large excrescence or a sizeable callus, as has often been seen with fatty tumours and mulberry-like growths. It might be equal in bulk to the flesh from the miscarriage and like it in shape, colour and everything else. Nevertheless we do not say that it too has its own hypostasis. Instead we count as one the hypostasis of the body that put out the excrescence, which is contrary to its nature, and the hypostasis of the excrescence itself. In Christ too, all his human elements, which are contrary to nature for it [?], never existed on their own. They subsisted in the already existing hypostasis of God the Word, who from the beginning formed the flesh for himself out of the holy Virgin, as if from raw material. So where would we see a demarcation between the Word and his flesh that would let us say the hypostases are two, as the natures are? For the natures are necessarily distinguished into a pair by their difference, but the hypostases are not so distinguished by demarcation [?].
