“A nature within time,” they say, “will not have [?] a hypostasis [?], just as the reverse is not possible either. So either Christ's human nature must be without a hypostasis, or it must have a hypostasis within time. Then he would certainly have two: the eternal hypostasis of the Word and the temporal hypostasis of the flesh.” But even if [?] it is not…

…possible [?] for a nature within time to have a hypostasis [?], it is still possible for it to acquire one in time, and for the nature that is in time to subsist in the eternal hypostasis. That resolves the whole difficulty. In this way too the whole world, though it came into being, subsists in God, the uncreated maker of the world.

Chapter 21. They say: “Either nothing in Christ is composite, or both nature and hypostasis are. Or else the nature is simple and the hypostasis composite, or conversely the nature is composite and the hypostasis simple. If everything in him is simple, you are wrong to speak of composition in his case. If both his nature and his hypostasis are composite, why do you reject the Severians? And suppose you hold that the natures are simple but the hypostasis is composite. Since the hypostasis of the Word is acknowledged to be simple, while you call the hypostasis of Christ composite, there are clearly two hypostases, that of the Word and that of Christ.” But, my friends, first of all, simple things are contained within composite ones. So it must be understood to be the Word's own hypostasis, once simple and now composite in Christ. All the same, we must make clear in what sense “composite” is said of Christ's hypostasis. A composite thing can be made from certain principles of that thing in the same respect, in which case its composition is somehow simpler. It can also be made from things of different kinds. For example, a more complex drug can be compounded from simpler drugs, one body from other bodies, and a compound word from simple words. So too one composite hypostasis can be conceived from several hypostases, as with a choir, a house and the like. And Christ's hypostasis can be made up from the coming together of several properties, not of the Word only but also of the flesh. If you call it a hypostasis composed of natures, we will agree. But if you mean composed of hypostases, God forbid! Consider also that the hypostasis of the Word was composed of properties even before the flesh, though not of so many. What is proper to the Son is not only that he subsists by being begotten. It is also proper to him that he does not beget a consubstantial Word, that he does not send forth the Spirit from himself as the first source, that he does not proceed as the Holy Spirit does, and the other things that belong to him alone. In this sense, then, not only the hypostasis of the Word but also those of the Father and of the Holy Spirit are composite. How, then, can this lead us to count a simple hypostasis and a composite one in the case of the Word? For it is one and the same hypostasis, made up of several properties as regards its hypostatic principle.

Chapter 25. “Whoever does not divide Christ's hypostases cannot say that some of Christ's acts belong to the Godhead and others to the flesh. He must say that all of them belong to the flesh [?], as many as belong to the flesh.” But one can also assign to each nature what is proper to it by distinguishing the natures. For we do not have different hypostases in mind when we say of the thief on the right, on the…

…cross, that his soul passed to life through repentance while his body passed to death through suffering. Nor do we have them in mind when we say that his legs were broken but his head was not broken, or that his colour changed but not his shape. These things belong to different natures, or different parts, or different qualities, but that does not make us think of them as two hypostases of the man who was crucified.

“If the hypostases are not divided according to nature but united according to hypostasis, then when I hear Scripture call Christ ‘one man,’ what am I to understand? One essence and one hypostasis, or half of one essence and of one hypostasis?” But if, as you yourself say, Christ is not only an ordinary, mere man but also God, we say the same to you. When we hear Scripture call Christ one man, what must we understand: one Christ, or half a Christ? It is clear, then, that the whole is named from the name of one of its parts. So it is said, “To you all flesh shall come,” and “Do not forget the souls of your poor for ever.” And…

“If the hypostases of God and of man are not divided according to nature, then clearly God is not God without man, and man is not man without God.” Is that truly so in Christ? It is not [?]. For in this way Emmanuel will also be [?], since from now on he is always with us…

“When things are united and their hypostases do not remain naturally divided in the union, their union is an alteration of nature.” Was the nature of fire altered in the red-hot iron, then, since its hypostasis is not distinguished from that of the iron? And was the essence of the soul altered in the body?

“In things united voluntarily, the division of hypostases is in no way opposed to the mode of union.” Then, even if the mode of union of things voluntarily united were according to one hypostasis, the division of hypostases would not be opposed to it. In that case division is not contrary to union, since both are seen in the same thing in respect of hypostasis. Yet contraries cannot exist together. And if you say, “But none of the things united according to hypostasis is united voluntarily,” then is it false that “No one ever hated his own flesh,” and that “We do not wish to put off the body, in which we groan”? If these sayings are true, then our union [?] has been shown to be voluntary, even though it is according to hypostasis.

Chapter 30. “Whoever does not divide Christ's hypostases according to nature divides the Son's unity from the Trinity. For we confess a Trinity of three simple hypostases, not of two and a half hypostases.” Yet…

…you ought to have drawn the opposite conclusion, sir. Whoever adds something to a simple thing does not take away half of it. Rather, he increases it through the composition. We rightly confess that the Trinity is of one simple nature. Formerly all three hypostases possessed this most simple nature of theirs in themselves without composition or mixture. Now, however, one of them is seen to hold the natural simplicity of its own Godhead in composition with our nature. The Godhead brought us forth by the Word of truth, that is, by the Son. Its own offspring had been cut off far from it, and it wished to gather them back to its bosom. So, through the same one of its three hypostases through which it had brought beings into existence, it took them back into itself. In this way, since they would not tend to depart from the One who Is, they would not go away for ever into non-being. This, then, does not dishonour the one nature or hypostasis. On the contrary, to anyone who attends with understanding, it glorifies it all the more. Through its simple hypostases it showed that it can exist by way of unbegottenness, begetting and procession. In the same way, through hypostatic composition, it showed that it can exist in two natures [?]. It also showed that the powers of all begetting, procession and creative composition among beings come from it. And it showed that it surpasses all things both by the unbegottenness of the greater of the hypostases and by the simplicity of nature in the being of its three persons.

“If the natural union [?] did not preserve the division of the hypostases, then it would not preserve God the Word, nor the man that he became [?].” Then neither would [?] fire be preserved as what it is, nor the dew, nor the [?], since their hypostases are not demarcated, while the union is plainly natural, that is, a union of their natures.

“If the knowledge of the divine hypostasis remains with the Godhead, and the ignorance of the man remains with the flesh, how can the things belonging to the hypostases remain divided while the hypostases themselves do not?” But it is the nature that either knows or does not know, in accordance with the hypostasis. The hypostasis does not simply know. Take all the things that Paul's hypostasis knows: we do not say that his fingernail knows any of them, or any part of his bodily nature. Only his natural power knows them, and only that of the soul, namely the mind. For not even the whole of the soul's nature knows them primarily. How, then, could the principles of the nature be those of the hypostasis?

“There is one face of God, unapproachable by nature, for it says, ‘No one shall see my face and live.’ And there is one face of a man that was spat upon, for it says, ‘And they spat in his face.’ If Christ's person (prosopon) is one as a result of the union, then it has in itself both the unapproachable face and the face that was spat upon.” But the “face” spoken of in connection with the invisible God was not meant as a hypostasis, which is what we are now inquiring about. For God has not only one face…

…but three [?]. It would not have been said [?] by the Godhead. Nor is “invisible” said to contrast one of the divine persons with the others, as though the two other consubstantial divine persons were visible and only the one speaking were invisible. Rather, “face” indicated the beholding of his nature and the natural form of God, which is not understood to be the same as the hypostasis. Moreover, Christ's face that was spat upon is not the same as his hypostasis either. It is a part, not only of Christ but also of the man in him. It is one of that man's bodily parts, namely the head. And it is not even the whole head, but only one side of it, the front, the part where the eyes are. If the principle of Christ's hypostasis were shown by this alone, then chest, hands, feet and the rest of the body would not be included in it, whether the hypostasis of Christ belongs to a mere man or to God. If the hypostasis of Christ is also his face, then all its other members that the face, that is, the visible features, does not take in must lie outside this hypostasis. So what you have said is plainly either childish or sophistical.

“The person of God the Word is one not as a result of the union but by nature. The person of Christ is one as a result of the union.” But suppose the one person of God the Word came from the union, as Christ's does. Then clearly, before God the Word became one person, he did not have the one person, just as Christ did not. Rather, the very person that is one by nature, belonging to the one nature of the Word, is also, once the nature of flesh was added [?] and assumed by it in him, the one person of Christ's two natures. So the person of Christ is one as a result of a union of natures, not of persons, and it is the one person of the Word, which comes from one nature. Tell me [?]: does Christ have a person by nature in addition to this person that comes from the union, or not? If not, then the union is not of person. As we said, the union is of nature, within the natural person of the Word. But suppose Christ has a natural person, just as the Word does, in addition to the person of the union. Since you also say that the Word has a person of union in addition to his person of nature, then plainly each of them has two persons, the Word and the flesh alike. In which of these four persons, then, do you say the union of these natures and persons into one person is seen? If it is in Christ's person that comes from the union, the Word's person is superfluous. If it is in the Word's, Christ's is redundant. And how, or where, does this person from the union subsist? If it is outside the natural persons, it has its own birth, circumscription and movement. If it is in only one of them, it does not unite the one person with the other. If it is in both, it must be divided between the distinct and demarcated persons, half in each. Then, of its perceptible members, one foot perhaps will be thought of as in the Word and the other in the flesh. The one in the invisible person will be an invisible foot, and the one in the visible person a visible foot. So, according to…

…you, the visible Christ is seen to have three feet, and the same goes for his other members. Such things would be loathsome even in old wives' drivel. So, since you say that the person from the union subsists neither outside the two natural persons, nor in both of them, nor in either one alone, you are clearly teaching that the one person from the union of natural persons is something without a hypostasis, a fabrication, one in name only. And since it is not like Christ's natural person, tell us what it will be like, even if we grant for argument's sake that it subsists. But perhaps you will say that Christ's natural person is the one we have described as coming from the union. If it truly came about from the union of the two natural persons, who is the man belonging to the natural person that was united with it? The one besides the… [?] Did it then both exist before itself and come into being after itself, if it existed beforehand as natural but came into being as the product of union after the natural persons came together?

“If the Word is what he was and is what he became, if he was God and became man, he cannot be both in the one person of the Word. For he became wholly man, having the nature and the person of a man.” But the Word was God by the personal nature of God, that is, because his hypostasis was clearly of divine nature. He was God not simply as being a hypostasis, but because his hypostasis was of such a nature. Otherwise the Father would not be God, since his hypostasis is not of the same kind as the Word's. In the same way, then, the Word became man by assuming human nature, even though the same hypostasis of the Word is without a human person. If the hypostasis of the Word had also assumed a hypostasis of flesh, the Word would not have become flesh. He would merely have acquired flesh. And if his nature, like his hypostasis, had become a nature of flesh, he would not have dwelt among us in the things of the flesh, that is, in the flesh. Rather, the Word would have been changed into it. So the Word can bear both natural names in his one person, which is now of two natures but was formerly of one. Someone might say that he cannot bear another nature in himself. In that case, the persons of our present fleshly nature will not receive the spiritual nature in the coming resurrection either. Either they will have other hypostases, or they will not have better natures. And if God alone is the cause of nature and of hypostasis, what prevents him from transferring some nature into another hypostasis, or a foreign hypostasis into another nature, if truly all things are possible for him? We clearly see the natures of animals and plants, which have hypostases, transferred into other hypostases, namely those that feed on them. And we see hypostases transferred into other natures, as with creatures transformed from a worm into a winged thing.

Chapter [?]. “‘Son of God by nature’ and ‘son of man by nature’ are names of a hypostasis. Christianity cannot be rightly confessed without them, and both are confessed in the one Christ, not both in each nature.” Names of a hypostasis, yes, but add “of the same one.” For if both are rightly confessed in the one Christ, the two names apply to the same hypostasis of Christ, just as with things that have two names…

…taken under one aspect and under another. So, for example, Timothy, while being one and the same in his one hypostasis, was the son both of Paul and of a Greek father. But these things are said in another way: even if they are predicated of the hypostasis, they are clearly named from the natures and from the births.

Is "the Word" the name of two hypostases, the uncreated one of the Lord and the created one of the Lord, or of two halves of the one hypostasis of the one Lord? No one becomes by grace what he is by nature. If "Lord" is the name of the hypostasis of the Word and not of the nature, then the Father and the Spirit are not Lords, since they are not of the same hypostasis. But if it is the name of the nature, it is clear that the human nature has become by grace what the Godhead is by nature, namely Lord, as you yourselves have also said, through its supremely close natural union with it in one hypostasis, by which the Godhead bestowed on it its own natural properties. Chapter 38 [?]. If the Word is God by Godhead and man by humanity, then the Word is in two hypostases, Son of God and Son of man, just as he is God and man in two natures. — If he is God and man in two natures, as you said, then in Godhead and humanity, that is, necessarily in two natures and not in two hypostases, the same one will be understood to be Son…

Chapter 39. If the Word has one uncreated hypostasis and one [?] … [?] … he does away with the hypostasis of the Word, either the uncreated or the created. — But none of the orthodox says that the Word really has two hypostases. Rather, they say that his one hypostasis was formerly made known as a whole, and completely, from uncreated properties, but that now it also has, in abundance, its hypostatic distinguishing marks from created words and deeds as well.

Chapter 40. If it is not peculiar to God the Word alone, but belongs to the flesh as well, not to be begotten from any substance or hypostasis other than that of the Father, then the flesh too will be from the substance of the Father alone, just as God the Word is. — This is indeed a property peculiar to the Word. But before he had taken flesh to himself in union, it was seen as a characteristic property of his simple, single-natured hypostasis; once the natural principle of that hypostasis became composite, it will now be understood not as a property of the hypostasis as a whole according to its natural principle, but as a property of one part, one of the realities that have grown together in the hypostasis. Thus, for example, being indicative of mind and knowledge belongs to the soul alone, and yet this does not show that the soul exists on its own, apart from the definition of man. Likewise, perceiving flavours is a property of taste alone, and yet it does not follow from this that taste has a hypostasis of its own.
If, when divine Scripture calls Christ one man, it calls him one man together with God, it is clear that God is half of the one man. And
so, when it calls a man "flesh," as in "To you all flesh shall come," it calls him one flesh together with the soul; it is clear, then, that the [?] is half of the one flesh.

Chapter 42. Whoever confesses Christ to be at once God and man, but does not say that Christ is at once "one and another," destroys his own confession. — And how is it possible to conceive the same whole of Christ as one whole and another whole of the one Christ? It follows, then, that it is in part, and with respect to a part, that the one Christ is one and another.

They say further: if the Word became man, clearly he became a certain man; for there is no man who is not a certain man, and a certain man is the hypostasis of a man. So either Christ has two hypostases, or the hypostasis of the Word has ceased to be. — But this certain man, Christ, is from his first existence God-indwelt in his hypostasis; which is the same as saying that he is God made man in his hypostasis, through the union of the human nature with the divine substance.

Chapter 41. They say again: if God the Word remained what he was and became what he was not, clearly he remained fleshless in substance, which is also what he was. — And indeed he truly is fleshless in substance; but this is not now also a proper predicate of his hypostasis. In the same way the soul, while Basil is still alive on earth, is fleshless in its substance but enfleshed in its hypostasis.

If the flesh does not belong to some man who is by nature other than God the Word, but to God, it is clear that the Creator and God of the flesh is the creator and God of God the Word. — But the flesh is of another nature, not of another person; rather, the Word himself made it his own by assuming it into his own hypostasis. Chapter 46. One who has flesh and a rational soul but does not have a man is simply a man; but one who has flesh and soul, and has the man as well, is other than the man. And so God the Word, if he has flesh ensouled with a rational soul, necessarily has the man as well. — If, then, one who has flesh and also soul, but does not have a man, is a man, one in his one hypostasis, as you say, then God the Word too, having the man, has flesh and soul; necessarily, then, the man together with the Godhead is one in hypostasis and according to [?], if indeed the soul too is so together with the body, as you said.

Chapter 47. If Christ, he says, is only one individual, he is either something of a single species or else certainly one of the things that fall under a species (for there is no other possibility). So tell us either what his species is, or under what species he falls. — Since, then, the minds of the unbelievers have been so hardened that, though they struggle close at hand, the words of the Gospel do not

shine through to them, we too must say to them that every individual which is either of a single species or ranked under one species only has in itself no union of natures more novel than that found in all existing things. If, then, you know this individual too, namely the person of Christ, as truly something common and one among many, knowing of no more novel union of natures in it, you have reasoned well. But if you too have confessed that in the Mediator between God and men there came about a union of natures beyond all existing things, then by the very thing you grant you refute yourselves once again, since you hold that this too is just like one of the individuals in the universe. We, by contrast, have rather reasoned that in the case of Christ there is something beyond reasoning, saying that the principle of everything paradoxical is inaccessible and cannot be demonstrated by syllogisms. For the rare lies beyond the reach of common notions, and the supernatural cannot be grasped by natural ones. Of necessity, then, either you will grant that this individual too is of the same kind as all the others, and you will look in it for the principle that holds in all of them; or, conceding that it has been naturally constituted beyond all existing individuals, you will no longer subject it, too, to the principle of things unlike it. So much for that. Nevertheless, by way of surplus, we can also show you individuals that are neither simply of a single species nor referred to one species only, but fall under different species. For the individual of the fowl-pheasant hybrids and the like cannot be said to be either of a single species or under any one species, since it is ranked neither among the clean nor among the unclean kinds. And again: every species subsists in itself and not in other species; but in this case, if the pheasant species or the fowl species is removed from its make-up, its constitution is removed along with it. It is clear, then, that there are more novel individuals, both one and several alike, without any more novel natural species being constituted in them. Besides these, we should like to hear what you call the individual of Moses' rod that was turned into a serpent. If it is of a single species, what is this species belonging to it alone, which could be defined neither as rod nor as serpent? And if it falls under one species only, which is it? For whichever one you name alone, you will be convicted of having overlooked the other. Does not even the miracle of the Word's incarnation, then, seem to you equal to that of Moses' rod, that you should reckon the rod as more novel but not the incarnation? Alas for the impiety!

If, he says, Christ himself raised himself from the dead and was also raised, he ought to have said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall be raised." — Why then do you not consider the opposite as well, and so be fully enlightened with piety, you [?]? For if it was another who raised up the one being destroyed, who was he in part, namely his body, then the one conversing with them ought to have said, "Destroy this temple" — that is, his body, pointing to it — "and in three days God will raise it up," or simply someone else,

but not "I," the one conversing with you, who was clearly both soul and body. It is clear, then, that the same person signified by the pronoun "I" comprises the body that was destroyed, the soul that conversed through the body, and the God who raised up what had been destroyed.

"For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" — that is, in the Christ named just before — was said by the Apostle. How then is the fullness of the Godhead not other by nature than Christ, since what is in something is other than that in which it is, and what dwells is other than what is dwelt in? Such too is the saying "God was in Christ." — So then, since it is said, "The spirit that he made to dwell in us yearns jealously," are we one thing and the spirit dwelling in us, namely our soul, another? And when it says, "But those who dwell in houses of clay, of which we ourselves too are made, from the same clay," are we then one clay and the house of clay another? Or is it clear that in such cases something is said to be in something as a part in its own whole? In the one Christ, then, completed [?], the Godhead is a part of his hypostasis, understood as being in him after its incarnation; but it is also as what dwells in what is dwelt in, because this which is regarded in him as a part of the person is a complete and entire nature, and of a different substance from the part of him that it dwells in; for such is the principle of houses and their inhabitants. And the indwelling of the Godhead in Christ is "bodily" in that it is in his flesh, which is a part of him and is now [?] called by the name of the whole; it is not that the indwelling is local, by circumscription, as of one thing contained in another, but an indwelling of the powers of the indwelling nature in the nature indwelt. For only in this way is it natural for incorporeal things to dwell in bodies, and this is the bodily dwelling of incorporeal things: not that the incorporeal are enclosed by circumscription in things that have shape, but that by the entry of their own powers they empower for activity what is by nature powerless, and so through the communion of the natures bring about one hypostasis.

Chapter One. If you do not hold, they say, that God the Word is half and incomplete with respect to being Son, and if, moreover, you do not consider the ensouled flesh taken from us to be unfulfilled with respect to being Son, how do you say that only one Son is produced by composition from both of these? For this makes each of them appear deficient with respect to being Son, and the Word appear perfected by the flesh into being Son, while he in turn perfects it for this; so you represent him as needing it for this, and it as needing him for this, in the same way. For a part, as a part, differs in no way from a part; so for you these are also of equal honour, since they clearly need each other equally for the same thing. — But we do not know the Word as incomplete with respect to being Son of God alone; God forbid! Nor, my friends, the flesh with respect to being son of man alone. But for the divine, according to its own good pleasure, to be glorified also as son of man, and for the human to appear as Son of God, we say that both are truly deficient and need the ineffable union with each other according to their natures. Thus, both natures, to which the sonships belong, having come together in one and the same person, no one can know either sonship as complete without contemplating the other nature along with it; so that one sees, not two sons subsisting as a result, but the one Christ in two natures and sonships. For this is the ineffable gift of the union in reality, if indeed we do not call it a union of divine and human nature in name only. For if certain things have truly been united without change and without diminution, everything affirmed of each of them is affirmed also of the one composite outcome of them. Since, then, they are Son of God and son of man — even though the things united did not subsist before the union — the whole that results from the union is also Son of God and son of man; and since Word and flesh are what came together into one, the same one is perfect God and perfect man. For it is not necessary that, because something is perfect in one respect, it cannot also admit perfection in some other respect. For the lawyer was perfect according to the natural definition of man, and yet he was still being taught, since Christ spoke of the perfection of his teaching as spiritual, saying, "If you wish to be perfect, sell all your possessions and give to the poor, and take up your cross and come, follow me." Moreover,

Nicodemus too was a perfect son according to the flesh and a man born long before; but to be not simply a man but a spiritual man, he needed the rebirth and perfection that come through the Spirit. So too the Word always possessed perfectly his being Son of God and God; but with respect to fulfilling his own good pleasure in his own appointed later times — the good pleasure by which, not counting equality with God a thing to be grasped, he was in travail before the ages to take the form of a servant, and predetermined for himself, even before making all things, the recapitulation of all things in Christ and the deification in himself of the natures that are not divine, as the Apostle says — with respect to this he was still lacking the manifestation of the hidden mystery of his own incarnation predetermined by him. There is therefore no charge of incompleteness here, when the sonship of each nature is understood on its own; there is only the need of each nature for the other in order to complete the union with men according to God's good pleasure, with the result that natures and complete sonships, which by nature are seen distinctly in different hypostases, came together into his one person. So much for that. If, then, because both are called parts in relation to the whole end, that is, Christ, you therefore call them simply incomplete and parts of equal honour, then, since in relation to the whole end of a general displaying himself to the army as a soldier in armour he himself is a part and his armour is a part, are both equally incomplete? Will he not be reckoned among men, nor it as armour? And will they not differ from each other, since a part truly differs in no way from a part, as a part? And by your reckoning these too will simply be of equal honour, you most keen-witted men! But, stung by their conscience that the explanations they have given are not sufficient to defend their superstition, they again contrive other pretexts, trying to persuade us that their impiety is a necessity. So they say this too:

Chapter 2. A son in the proper sense is wholly the son of the one who begot him; for nothing that is from someone only in part is called his son. Nor is one a father who is the cause of a part and not of the whole. Certainly, in the case of the whole that is called a son of man, consisting of a rational soul and a living body, if it happens that one part of it comes out of the womb without the other, we are accustomed to call it an abortion and [?], and in such a case to speak of a miscarriage and not a birth. If, then, you say that Christ is son of man in part, it is clear that he is properly the son neither of a father nor of the mother. Whose son by nature is he, then? Tell us. — What then, my friends? Is all holy Scripture lying when it calls the same Christ sometimes Son of God and sometimes son of man? And who will prefer your drivel to the divine words? And what should we say about "Christ" and about "Son"? For if, as you yourselves have often said in your own writings, the holy oracles call the whole man by a part, as in "To you flesh shall come," and "Jacob went down into

Egypt with seventy-five souls," and also call the part alone by the name of the whole, as in "There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife" — for only Abraham's body was buried there — how is it that you now lay down the law that no one may dare to call someone the son of one of his parents on the basis of a part? And indeed, if, as you yourselves have said, the fathers of our flesh are the causes of the body alone for us, the Father of spirits being clearly confessed, according to the Apostle, to be another, how are not all men plainly called sons in part and fathers in part? Moreover, if even of the body itself the whole cause is not from the male, but the female also contributes something — he, as some say, supplying the more solid parts and she the more fluid parts to what comes into being — how would not each parent turn out to be the cause, in part, even of that part, and so parents in the most partial sense? And if, by the laws you dialecticians lay down, it is not truly possible to call them begetters in part, then no one is truly the father of any of the men born in this life; for no one could properly be called father or mother or son of the flesh alone, but all of us who have come into being are self-generated. And what refutation could be plainer to you than this?

And the example of the abortion: what do you mean by it? Is it not called a son simply because it is a part and incomplete, or because it has not yet lived? If because it is deficient and simply a part, how is it that the maimed and the monstrous, often born without hands and feet and other members, are called sons, though they are in such incompleteness [?]? And further, what would you say about Abraham, who departed this life very many years before, being called the father of the people of Israel, and David being called the father of the Lord after his death? For clearly it is the part of him that survives, namely the soul, that is thereafter called father. If, then, a living part alone can be called son and father, what prevents the living part from also being called son? It is clear, then, that what is not called a son is not so called not because it is a part but because it is lifeless. Further, there are the little daughter of the ruler of the synagogue and the widow's son, who died before their parents while these were still alive. If you think they are rightly still called daughter and son in the Gospel by virtue of their living souls, then look: you too confess that the part is son and daughter. So it is clear that it is primarily because it is not living, and not simply because it is a part, that the abortion is not called a son. For many bodies far more incomplete than abortions, if they are ensouled at all, are born and called sons. Besides all this, we do not even say that every part is a son; only that you were wrong to think that no son is ever properly so named on the basis of a part, or that no one is a father on the basis of a part.

But besides this we shall say, by way of surplus, that we say Christ is the Son of each not merely on the basis of a part but also on the basis of the whole, though by different sonships of the parts in him. For of Christ's body the holy Virgin is the cause of its being, in one respect according to nature, having received this from God through her fore-

bears, and in another respect specially, having been empowered by the Holy Spirit. And she is the mother of his soul, since it was escorted from her as a bride into natural union with its own garment, and was appointed by God to come forth into being through birth from her, as from the threshold of a holy bridal chamber. And of his Godhead she is the true bearer, since the Word, fleshless and uncompounded from all ages, began from her his coexistence with ensouled flesh, through hypostatic union, for the fulfilment of his own good pleasure. Therefore, even if not in the same way, the holy Virgin is nevertheless the mother of all the parts of Christ, and hence of the whole. For whoever is truly said, in whatever way, to have begotten someone is certainly the cause of some beginning for the one begotten, though not necessarily of a beginning of being out of non-being. Otherwise not even the Word, considered in himself, would be Son of the Father by nature; for the one who is coeternal with him was not brought by him into being out of non-being.

They say further: if your Christ is Son of God in part, then clearly he is also God in part and not wholly — a demigod, then. — But for us the one Christ is wholly God, to be worshipped: of the parts in the one whole, one is perfectly divine by substance, the other divine by participation in the part united to it that is divine by substance. But if you conclude that our Christ is a demigod because only one part of him possesses what is divine by nature, then you yourselves, who know neither the whole nor any part in him to be divine by nature at all, clearly know him to be not God at all, but a mere man, in every respect like us.

But, rolling on to other ready pretexts for their impiety, they say that they do not call him one and the same living being, a single whole of a son, from divine and human nature at once, for this reason: everything [?] must be seen to be consubstantial with those who bear it, and must have a likeness of substance to those who begot it, without deficiency or excess. "But your Christ, the Son of God and of man, has something more than God and something in excess of man; how then will he truly be the Son of these, when he is not wholly like them in nature?" — But, my friends, in the first place Christ does have consubstantiality, when compared with both his parents together. For each of us too, compared with both parents together, would rightly be judged to be of the same nature as his own causes, since he has some features from his mother that cannot be seen in his father, and often some from his father that are not in his mother. And if, when judged part by part, he is shown to be a man like each of them, this is seen because he happened to be born of parents both of the same species. For this is not seen in the same way where the causes of what is begotten are of unlike species. For how could the offspring of a cock and a pheasant be judged to be of the same nature, taken separately, with

…the offspring? Yet tell us, you natural philosophers: do you call this little one the son of these parents, and do you recognize it as a single whole living creature, or not? If you cannot deny this, how can you speak of things that exist as though they did not? "But in such cases," he says, "there is a blending and confusion of form in the generation, so that one cannot even tell that this part of them comes from the horse and that part from the ass. All their members are altered and cannot be told apart. If, then, you say that the mingling of the essences in Christ is of this kind, tell us so," they say. But we have not brought in these examples to show a similar union, my friends. We use them only to overturn the pronouncements you have made on the present question, where you proclaim that what is begotten must be fully consubstantial with both of those who produced it, or else it is not to be called a son. In these cases, this very confusion and indistinctness of form will overturn your assertion all the more. For mules are called the sons of horses, and hinnies the offspring of asses, even though they keep no likeness whatever, not even member by member, to either parent. How, then, can you say that because of a partial unlikeness one cannot call a son someone who is not in every respect like those who begot him? You might perhaps have rightly said this against those who hold that Christ is like both his parents in a single essence of his own. You cannot say it against us, who confess that his hypostasis is constituted of different natures. These matters must, however, be examined still more precisely. Does likeness of the whole seem to you to be in every case indicative of sonship, or not? If not, you seek from us in vain, as a proof of sonship, something that is not its cause. For proofs proceed through causes. [?] you are persuaded only that this sonship subsists through these causes. Was Abel, then, because he was like Cain in the whole of his essence, also his son? Was Cain then a son-slayer and not a brother-slayer? Since the relation between like things is mutual, Cain would also be the son of Abel [?], and so he would rather be a father-slayer as well. So at one and the same time Abel, who was slain by Cain, was son and father and brother of the one who killed him, and Cain was son-slayer, father-slayer and brother-slayer. And who will not laugh at these elegant doctrines of yours? We must therefore see clearly what Luke the evangelist did. He considered only this partial cause and partial likeness, which was also present in Adam in relation to God, the Father of spirits. God was the proximate cause of Adam only with respect to the soul, when he breathed into him the breath of life so that he became a living soul, since he had first formed his body from the earth. And Luke knew that only in this respect is the "image and likeness of God" preserved in man. On the basis of this partial cause and likeness, then, he clearly traced Adam's genealogy too as son of God, the Father of spirits. He set it out in this way and said that Adam was "of God," just as he had said, "of Seth, of Adam," meaning the one who came from
Adam. And just as he said "of Isaac," which Matthew expressed as "Abraham begot Isaac," so he said, "of Adam, of God." Let this suffice on these matters. Now we must hear the rest.

"If Christ is Son of God by nature," they say, "and was not granted this by the grace of adoption, how is it said, 'Much more did the grace and the gift of God, in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound for the many'? And, 'God granted him the name that is above every name'? And, 'He did not take the honor upon himself, but was called by God, just as Aaron was'? Tell us, what is this Christ?" Again they twist the meaning, again they shift the sense, again they bring out the usual metonymies! And it is remarkable that you are so forgetful even of what you yourselves have often said, unless you are suffering from lethargy. You know very well that what belongs to one of the parts is predicated of that part, as in: "They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth." You also know that what belongs to a part is said of the whole, as in: "There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife." And conversely, what belongs to the whole is said of the part, as in: "And Jacob went into Egypt with seventy-five souls." You admit further that what belongs to the whole is sometimes said of one part of it alone, as in: "My soul slumbered from weariness." For neither the body nor the soul would slumber on its own. Another example is: "I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh," for he does not mean soulless flesh. And that what belongs to the whole is said of the whole is beyond dispute for everyone, as in: "Isaac was going through the wilderness by the well of the vision." We will mention one more case, a surprising one. In natural unions, because of the sympathy that the union creates among parts united in their experiences of whatever kind, one can see that what belongs to one part of the whole is predicated of its other part. Thus the soul of the murderer is said to be killed in return for the soul of the one murdered, although those who kill kill the body, and after that have nothing more they can do. Of this kind too is: "I humbled my soul with fasting." For it is primarily and really the body that is humbled by fasting, while the soul grows more sober and is exalted the more the outer man is humbled. Another example is: "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me." According to the Apostle, Abel, though dead, still speaks as one living, not with his blood but with his soul. It is clear, then, that everything you have cited is said of the human part of Christ. One of the natures in him is God and Son of God, and is called so, by reason of its essence. The other has truly been granted divine honor and that name by grace and gift. Yet it is not simply a bare name, as if this nature had no underlying reality

properly named by this name, as they say of the "goat-stag" and the like. Rather, through its hypostatic union with him who is God by nature, the honor of the name "Son of God" and "God" is imparted to it. In this way the gifts, the honor and the great name of what was deified are shown in reality to come from the true God, who truly deified it by the gift of himself, unless he is said to grant it his own name falsely. "He did not take the honor upon himself," that is, of himself. Christ did not glorify himself (here "Christ" means the man that he is). It was God who spoke to him in reality, and said to him by the act of making him a son, and not by a bare word, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." That is, by grace: "by which I have united you to my Son by nature in one hypostasis." For whatever he said came to be, and we have learned from him that it is impossible for God to lie. These words therefore show that the Son of Man does not of his own choice boast of God as his Father. He was called by God to the dignity of this divine sonship and of his everlasting priesthood, and this priesthood too is understood not in name only but in reality. For the Lord who swore to him and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek," was himself the one of whom it is said, "The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son.'" So the phrase "just as Aaron" signifies a similar manner in which God gave gifts and called, both in Aaron and in Christ, but not similar gifts. Otherwise it would also have been said to Aaron, "You are my Son," and the rest. It is obvious that Aaron cannot reasonably be compared with Christ as equal in the honor of priesthood. Christ was counted worthy of so much more glory even than Moses, who was greater than Aaron, as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. Moreover, to speak in the words of the Apostle: "If perfection came through a similar priesthood, what need would there be for another priest to arise and [?] be said to be according to the order of Aaron?" Besides, if the priesthood had not been changed, there would not of necessity have been a change of the law either, as the same Paul the apostle says, but only a succession. In the same way let us understand "He will be called Son of God," and "He will be called Son of the Most High," and the rest. For what was born was holy. It was not only sanctified because of the unbegotten Holy Spirit that came together with it, who is also the Word born of the Virgin. For "what was conceived in her," says the angel, "is of the Holy Spirit," and so it is Holy Spirit, just as what is born of the flesh is said to be flesh. God is Spirit, and Christ was God. What was conceived is the same as what was born. So the titles given to Christ (God, Son of God, Only-begotten, Lord of glory and the rest) are not gifts of empty names. They are names of realities. If this were not so, the gift of the name of God in Christ would be a false name,

the kind that idols and heroes and demons once received. Yet it was to destroy such false names that the true Son of God came among us and, having come, carried out so many works of his plan of salvation. And no one would say that he heals evil with evil. Moreover, angels and men have often been called sons of God and sons of the Most High. What more, then, is there in this Christ, the only-begotten Son of God? And how is he even Only-begotten, if the grace of deification or sonship given to him is like theirs? Clearly, then, it is by the grace that comes through hypostatic union with the Son by nature that the Only-begotten is called Son of the living God. "But," they say, "these things must be said in view of the economy, as you would put it, to escape a precise examination of what is meant. Otherwise what is said has no proper outcome: it is parable or allegory or fantasy or mere appearance, and lies empty, meant only to create an impression in the hearers. So who is the son who 'learned obedience from what he suffered,' who 'offered prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears, and was heard because of his reverence,' who was made perfect, was crucified and buried, whom God raised from the dead, who was exalted and glorified, and so on? No one who is not possessed would dare to claim that these things belong to the Word, nor to him as he exists together with another." But we have often told you already that the whole is often predicated on the basis of a part. This is both by the common law of logic and by the particular usage of Holy Scripture. These things, therefore, are not said by mere appearance or parable or in any such way. They are to be taken as true, though with the fitting mental qualifications. And to put it simply, what about you? Suppose you do not understand the Word, the Son of God by nature, to be present in this very Christ of whom such things are affirmed. He is present impassibly, yet in respect of the nature he is himself subject to these things, by means of the principle of his hypostasis [?]. If not, where are we to look for that other Son of God, of whom it is said, "Being in the form of God, he emptied himself, and despised the shame of the death of the cross"? And where is the only-begotten Son of God, who was himself handed over for us by the Father? "For God so loved the world," it says, "that he gave his only-begotten Son." And who is the only-begotten son of the lord of the vineyard? He was sent to the wicked tenants after the servants who had gone before, all of them servants, in the hope that they would perhaps respect him. And whose glory did the disciples behold, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father? Further, who is the one designated Son of God according to the Spirit of holiness? Who is the one who came down and entered like rain upon the fleece, whose name endures before the sun, and whose throne is before the moon? Who is the one who says, "But a body you have prepared for me"? Unless, that is, you are also dreaming of a pre-existence of the soul of Jesus. And how is the one in whom all things were created also called firstborn from the

dead, he who holds first place in all things, the firstborn of all creation? And who is the second man, the Lord from heaven? Who is the one of whom John says, "He who comes from above is above all"? Who is the one who says he had glory with the Father before the world existed, and confesses that he and the Father are one? And who has authority to lay down his own soul and to take it up again? Who is able to raise up in three days his own temple when it has been destroyed, a temple called divine and not a private house? And how does the righteousness that comes from faith say, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down)," unless it is saying that he is heavenly and not merely earthly? And who is the Lord of glory whom they crucified in ignorance? You yourselves do not reject the faith of Nicaea. How, then, do you confess that the one begotten of the Father before all ages is the same Christ who came down from heaven, was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin, and became man? And how do you understand the other passages from the sacred Oracles that we cited earlier about Christ as Son of God? They present him as Son of God by nature as well as by grace. None of these passages in divine Scripture is spoken by mere appearance or fantasy, or to create an impression, or in any of the other ways you mentioned. Nor is Christ himself falsely called God and Son of God and Lord. How then will the same one not be both, since both are said of the same subject? And how will the Son of God by nature and the Son by grace not be glorified as one: the impassible and the passible, the one who raises and the one who is raised, and so on? You are truly unreasonable, you inventors of words! Out of a scruple about mere appearance and fantasy, you take the sufferings and the names that belong to the passible properly, naturally and in reality. But impassibility, glory and honor, and the name of Godhead and of divine sonship, you take as not belonging to Christ by nature at all, nor in reality, nor truly. For you they are a false name, a semblance, a fantasy and an empty title. Even granting that human things are truly said and done by him, consider this with a love of truth. Suppose a king says to his own subjects, "I am one of you and like you," and in time of battle does the work of a soldier out of zeal for the common safety of his own state. This is not only blameless but most glorious. But a soldier who gives orders like a king, or is called king, will bring no small charge upon himself. If, then, being a son of man and only a man, he accepts being called the only-begotten Son of God, firstborn of all creation, God over all and so on, and gives commands with authority as Lord, he stands convicted of impiety toward God. But if he is truly Son of God and God, and sometimes uses human words and deeds, it is plain that besides his natural majesty he also shows a condescension that comes from his goodness.

But suppose you understand these different things to be said not of the same Son or person, but of one son and of another. How then are you not clearly holding two sons? On your view, the one is God, in no way emptied toward men in his essence, and he manages our salvation through another only by his eternal providential activity. Then, by your account, the saying "Not an elder nor an angel, but the Lord himself saved us" is no longer true. And the other son you hold to be a mere man, in no way sharing in God or united to him, neither by nature nor by hypostasis, except, as you say, by name alone. This follows the definition of homonyms, where the name is common but the account of the essence that goes with the name is always different. An example is a real man and a man in a painting: some people, without looking carefully, call both alike "man." How, then, can you avoid saying all this? So this too has been demonstrated by us. But to drag them out and refute the rest of their impiety, let them tell us this. On their view, Christ is the other of the two sons, not compounded with the Word. To whom do they say he is consubstantial? If to no one, then let them tell us whose son he is at all, since he would not be consubstantial with his parents. Then he cannot even be thought of as begotten, nor as a living being, as they themselves granted earlier. But if he is consubstantial with God alone, then there are two divine sons, and the holy Trinity is a tetrad. Moreover, in saying this, either they deny that this son is the one born of the Virgin, or they hold that the Virgin too is God by nature, if he who is consubstantial with God is also consubstantial with her. In that case they would reasonably call all of us gods too, since we are consubstantial with her, and they quite plainly bring in an infinity of gods. But suppose they say that Christ, who is called Son of God, is consubstantial with us only. Then let them tell us how he would differ from the others who are called sons of God. Of these God has said, "And they shall be my sons and daughters," and, "I said, 'You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High,'" and the like.

"We say," he says, "that only God the Word, who is consubstantial with the Father, is Son of God by nature. Christ, we say, is called Son of God by grace, but is like us in nature. Yet we do not therefore present him as a Son of equal honor with us. For we too have received the gift of adoption from God. By grace we are children of God, heirs of God, and fellow heirs with Christ himself. Yet an inexpressible difference is often found among things that are called by the same name. Both the gnat and the angel are properly called creatures alike, yet they are not therefore alike, for there is a great difference between them. So too must we understand the sons of God who differ in adoption and grace. For Christ has been counted worthy of more honor even than Moses, the great one among the prophets, as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself." If, then, you are not pretending in this too, and you truly recognize in Christ at least a precedence of honor and dignity

over other men, even if not of essence, how could you insist a little earlier that his calling, and the honor he received from God, were like Aaron's, because it was said that Christ was called "just as Aaron"? But let this be set aside for now. Concerning your example we will say this, you sophists, if only you will consider it. Creation brings forth and creates things that differ in essence. Moreover, as you said, it makes them be from non-being, both the angel and the gnat, things that differ in nature and came to be in this way by divine creation. What, then, do you say? Did the grace given to Christ make him different in essence from anything, or not? If not, how can the difference made by grace be seen as like the difference among creatures? The one makes differences of essence and the other does not, and truly great is this difference between the two kinds of difference. But if it did, then clearly it made the one to whom it was granted superior in his nature. Grace, then, was given to something already existing in essence. (For grace is not given to what does not exist, nor does it make what is wholly non-existent come to be from non-being; then it too would be creation and not grace.) So what was this Christ in essence beforehand, to whom this grace was given? And what did the grace make him to be in nature, when it came upon him and made him superior in essence? If it was given to a mere man, first tell us where and when this man existed. Next, suppose this grace is truly a grace that makes the one who receives it superior in nature. If he was a man, it plainly shows that he must by nature be an angel or something of that kind, or God. For nothing besides these is superior to man in essence. But if the grace, making him superior in essence, made him precisely this, a man, then plainly the one to whom it was granted was, before the grace, some bird, beast, fish or reptile. Does it seem fitting, then, to say such things about Christ? Besides, on this view all men, before him, with him and after him, will share in the same grace. Indeed they would share in it more than he does, since they have from their original nature the dignity of humanity [?], to which he was raised by grace through an improvement of his nature.

"What then?" he says. "Is there no difference among things that are consubstantial? Say, between gold, the metal, and lead or earthenware, or between John the Baptist and Judas the traitor?" But the difference between these, my good sirs, is of two kinds. In the first case it rests on an inseparable accident, such as a fine color perhaps, or other features of quality, and it depends on opinion. One does not surpass the other absolutely, nor always, nor in every respect. Gold does not seem better to a bull, nor is it more precious to God. Moreover, for some people, at some times, in some circumstances and for some purposes, lead and earthenware are more necessary and more useful. The other difference, in turn, lies in virtue, and is seen in one person compared with another on the basis of their deeds and will. How, then, can the difference in Christ be one of grace, if his superiority over us lies only in one of these?

For to the one who works, wages are indeed given, not as a matter of grace, but as a debt. But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works, since then grace would no longer be grace, as has been said. Put another way: if this grace and the honor that Christ was found worthy of make a difference even compared with Moses, the outstanding one among the prophets, inasmuch as the one who built the house has more honor than the house, and that is clearly the difference between creator and creature, then the difference that this grace produces in those who share in it, compared with those who were formerly like them, is just as great. So not even the natural difference between an angel and a gnat, or between gold and a potsherd, is enough to illustrate how Christ's grace differs from ours. Both of those are created things, even if one surpasses the other somewhat. For if the honor and grace that God gives us do not make us like him, and the divine graces preserve between us and him a difference as great as that between creator and creature, then the grace that comes to be in Christ shows that he alone is truly creator and not creature. It shows him to be neither one of us nor merely on the level of the great Moses, but clearly God. For only God creates and fashions all things out of nothing. All things that come after God have it as their property to be created, some directly by God and others through some intermediary from among the things God created earlier. So clearly the one found worthy of such grace and honor is both creator and God, and Christ of all things, even if you do not want it. But you do not see the force or the aim of the sayings you quote, you who think yourselves precise judges of intelligible things. Now, however, these clever men want to show from Holy Scripture differences among adoptions, just as among kinds of grace and honor. That way, even though they say the same things of us and of Christ, they may seem to give him something more than us and not to think him in every way like everyone else. For our part, we will not deny that there are differences among things that are spoken of in the same way. But we say that unless the difference ascribed to Christ in relation to us turns out, according to the saying, to be that of a creator to his creature, it is not really the one by which he was found worthy of honor above Moses. We set this down as a kind of gauge and rule that shows his superiority over us. With sophistic cleverness they have drawn out the premises of this argument into a long and tangled web, so that its impiety is not obvious to hearers and its refutation is not easy for opponents. They insert their defenses against the charges brought against them and build their case in a transposed and confused order. So we have gathered the whole aim of their argument and set it out in sequence, and we have also laid out the difference they want there to be among the adoptions in Holy Scripture, stating it in order. For all men, they say, were called sons of God, in the words "I said, You are gods, and sons of the Most High

all of you," because they were called in the image of God; [?] in a sinless life they were called sons of God. Even so, they were still capable of sinning again, since their nature was still changeable. They were often shown to be so by their deeds, as the saying goes: "But they have rejected me." And for this reason they were clearly subject to death, blows and punishments: "For the sting of death is sin" and "Many are the scourges of the sinner." So much for them. But we Christians too were called sons of God, according to the words "For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus." Besides being trained in sinlessness through the sacred sayings, we are also taught through the Spirit the righteousness of God that goes beyond the letter. We have been called to freedom and immortality, and to unchangeableness through the resurrection of the dead. We no longer fear punishment, or any change in the blessed life that follows. We will be free of toils and of the rulers of the age of darkness, and we will live in a heavenly commonwealth. For we were predestined in love to adoption by God, to be holy and blameless before him and to have likeness to our heavenly Father. This will come when we receive the adoption we await, that is, the redemption of our body. Then we will no longer sin in any way, and so we will no longer be mortal by nature. We will be raised so high that our nature cannot even potentially receive evil. It is clear, then, how much more we are made like God in these respects than Israel of old, which was also called a son. Our adoption surpasses theirs so far, and in so many respects, that theirs is called a spirit of slavery leading to fear and to subjection under the yoke of slavery, while ours is called a spirit of adoption, by which we can cry "Abba, Father," something theirs never dared to say. Indeed, ours is properly called freedom: "Christ has set us free." So much for this adoption. But, they say, the Lordly man too was called Son of God, according to the words "And he will be called Son of the Most High." In addition to all our privileges, in which he is like us and is said to be the firstborn among many brothers before God, the common Father of all, he also has other things:

[?] of God, far above every authority and dominion and power, having received a name greater than every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, "so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth." For he has subjected all things without exception under his feet. Through him they are subjected to the divine Word, whose person he represents, and through the Word to the Father, from whom the Word is inseparable, together with the Holy Spirit. In this way he is mediator between God and men. Those who say that Christ subsists through a composition of the Word and the man will never give him anything more than these things. If, then, the adoptions cannot even be compared with these, how can they say that we make Christ equal in honor to us because we hold that he is not Son of God by nature but was adopted by grace? It has been shown that neither being called sons nor being adopted by grace involves only a slight difference, or one merely of more and less, between all men, the Jews, the Christians and Christ. To all this, with God's help, we reply that there really is a difference among these adoptions given by grace. What, then, do you say? Our Christian adoption will transform us in the age to come from a fleshly nature into spiritual beings. It will show us immortal instead of mortal and free in nature instead of slaves. Those who were always in affliction and pain it makes fearless for the whole of their life, and those who were distracted it sets at ease. It makes us sinless in our way of life instead of sinners, and unchangeable in substance instead of changeable, so that we no longer have even the potential to fall, which is what makes one answerable to punishment. Does this adoption make those who share in it different in substance from those who share in the Jewish adoption, or not? That adoption shows those adopted under it as still mortal, prone to stumble, slaves, fearful, punished and under blows. But if a living being that is immortal and unchangeable and so on is entirely different in substance from one shown to be mortal, changeable and the like, we must next consider Christ's adoption. Would you not say that it surpasses the adoption of us other human Christians at least as much as ours surpasses the Jewish one, not to say more?

For if it does not surpass it, then look: among us Christ ranks only as a Christian. But if you say that it certainly does surpass it, as you have already granted, then it has made him superior to our substance as much as our adoption will make us believers superior to unbelievers. If Christ is superior in substance to us human beings, even to spiritual Christians, what then will he be in nature? Of necessity he will be either a cherub, or an angel, or one of the intermediate orders, or truly God. Now, everyone without exception rejects the idea that he became an angel in substance, and so do you yourselves. Otherwise the incarnation of the Word would be false, and so would the deification of the flesh and all the other sayings about the economy. So he must be God in substance, deified, as you say, by the grace of this adoption. But everything that makes something is greater than what it makes. So this grace is greater than the divine substance it produces. It is therefore also greater than the divine substance that bestowed the grace, if indeed it was bestowed by God. For whatever proves better and greater than one of two like and equal things must, by geometrical necessity, also be greater than the other. In the same way we too, who are sons of God by grace and not by nature, would be greater than God in substance, because the grace would be greater than the substance. Why, then, do you shrink from saying that Christ shares in the divine substance, [?] my good sirs, when you have no qualms about giving him the grace of adoption, which on your account produces, causes and surpasses the divine nature that exists and comes upon natures? But truly, among evils you have been caught contriving the worse, indeed the worst. For your only concern is not to seem impious, though you are impious by choice. You do not recognize that Christ really surpasses you at all. You reckon him a mere man like yourselves, even if you attach grace and honor and glory to him in name only. You hold in vain the teachings about the union of the divine and the human nature, that is, about the incarnation of the Word and the deification of the flesh.

Let this too now be examined. How do you explain this union of the Word, which you pretend to confess, with the one you take to be the man Christ? You say, with a show of piety, that it took place from the very beginning of his conception, yet you do not accept that a composition of the Word with the flesh took place. A union that is not by composition must be seen in one of these ways. It may be a local juxtaposition, like a stone and gold in a ring, or the border of Judea against the border of neighboring Samaria, and the like. It may be a relation of choice, like the lover of gold to gold, the lover of horses to horses, the lover of pleasure to pleasure, the lover of God to God, and the like. It may be some natural relation, such as parents have to children of the same nature as themselves. Or it may be the union of consubstantial men,

or horses, or all eagles, which by natural likeness makes all the individuals under the species eagle one through its definition. Or it may be the union of an image with its archetype, which the form present in each likewise joins by likeness. If you say that the union of the Word with Christ is by local juxtaposition, then the divine Word is a body, visible, tangible, located in a place and circumscribed, with all the other absurdities that follow. If it is by a relation of choice, then union with God belongs not to Christ alone but also to Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Samuel, David and Jeremiah. It belongs to the rest of the fathers, patriarchs and prophets up to John the Baptist, and to all who have pleased God from John until now. For it is not said of one person only, but: "The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, in all who hope in his mercy." And: "There is no partiality with God, but in every nation the one who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him." It is clear, then, that this union gives Christ nothing more than the God-fearing men of all ages and the angels. So you cannot say that God chose him alone out of all things visible and invisible, or that this kind of union made him worthy, above all others, of some honor or union or sonship or grace. But suppose you speak not of this union but of a union of the Word with Christ by natural relation. This is seen either in things of the same substance (for every animal loves its like, not what is unlike it) or according to likenesses in certain accidents. In the second case, you clearly say that the Word is like Christ by some accident. Then the Word will not be God but a substance subsisting with accidents in a person of its own. In the first case, the likeness is by substance. Then either you take the Word to be flesh, of the same nature as the flesh, and your divine Trinity is one person short. Or you think the flesh is God, consubstantial with the Word, and your Holy Trinity has one hypostasis too many. Of necessity, then, you worship a dyad or a tetrad and utterly counterfeit the Holy Trinity. Suppose you refuse to speak of any of these unions because of their absurdities, and refuse the union by composition because of your doctrines. If so, how do you claim to speak of a union of the Word and the flesh, as you confess, while among yourselves you deny every mode of union? It has become clear, then, that you merely put on a form of godliness, having denied its power altogether. Indeed, in what follows you are exposed as such. You say that this union serves the manifestation of the Word, and you call it, I do not know how, a union "into a person." For, he says, we recognize it in this, that Christ represents the person of the Word. But, you sophists and not wise men, perhaps unqualified even for this, union into a person is not like that.

[?] For union into a mixture produces a mixture, as in vinegar mixed with water. Union into some structure produces a structure, as in a choir. Union by juxtaposition produces juxtaposition, as in a house. Union into some nature produces a nature, as when the body is formed from the elements. In the same way, union into a person will reveal, in a new way, some new person. It certainly does not display some other person in its own place, as you say. Union into a person is not the manifestation of another, unknown person. On the contrary, what you describe is the concealment of a person behind a stand-in, and merely the display of a name. That could have been proclaimed without any person at all, through an interpreter. For by what are things that stand in for one another like this held together? In what do they share, or in what are they united? If by likeness, then again the flesh is God, or the Word is flesh. And if there was likeness, what need was there for the true person not to appear, but only its likeness, if he did not wish to deceive? But if they are unlike, in what does the union of the persons consist? And how will it not simply be a device for deception, to show one thing as another and not as what it is? "Yes," he says, "both are united by the divine name, for what is not divine by nature was found worthy of the divine name." Do you not see that, for you, Christ's great dignities have clearly come down, after a long process of division, to an empty naming? There is nothing else in which he shares with God except the name alone. So how will Christ not have communion with God by the union of homonyms, which is a union in name only, rather than by the reality that underlies the name? Of this, as has been said already, angels of old and holy men were found worthy by God. Demons, carved images, birds, reptiles and stones were likewise found worthy of it by men, being called gods and lords and sons of God and of gods. Is this, then, what makes Christ blessed beyond all? Is this his supremely exalting gift, a falsely named title of God? What shameful doctrines! What nonsensical propositions! So let them tell us further. Homonyms may be things of the same substance that share a name because each bears it as a proper name, such as Judas Iscariot and Judas the brother of the Lord. They may be things of different substances that share a common name, such as the "star" of the sea and the star of heaven. They may be things of different substances where one bears the name as a common name and the other as a proper name, such as "angel," meaning both the spirit and the prophet called Malachi. Or one may be a substance and the other not, such as "wolf," meaning both the animal and the disease. Which of these kinds of union by name describes the union of the name of Christ with the name of God, the Word and the Son of God? And how will that union either make him better in substance, or exalt him, or benefit him at all? For no homonym will enjoy any of the properties of the thing that shares its name, unless this is exactly what they mean: to snatch

the divine glory by a false name, and carry it off before those who do not know the difference between the one who is God by nature and those falsely so named. But if this is Christ's great glory, then the devil and the demons, who desired it long before Christ, have enjoyed it, and so, as has been said, have animals and reptiles been found worthy of it. From all this it has been clearly shown that one of two things is true. Either Christ has not really and in fact been found worthy of honor or glory or any of the lofty and divine things. Or, if he truly shares in the divine titles, it is because he first has in himself God the Word, to whom these truly and by nature belong. For through him Christ is truly rich in all the distinctive properties that belong to God alone and accompany him, and displays them in himself. Moreover, since they say that he has received some dignity, however great, let them answer us. What kind of dignity is this? Is it natural, like man's superiority in substance over the beasts, according to the words "You have put all things under his feet, sheep and all oxen"? Or is it accidental, like Saul's elevation over his kinsmen? If it is accidental, then it is at once neither divine nor worth mentioning. If it is natural, then clearly no one can share in it truly and not merely in name without first having obtained the nature to which it belongs. If, then, Christ has received the natural dignity of God, and "God" is properly the name of a nature, then clearly he first acquired the divine nature itself, to which the dignity and the name belong, and inherited these along with it. Therefore we rightly hold that there is a composition of the divine and the human nature. If that is not so, then the man himself was changed into such a divine nature and was found worthy of the natural divine dignity and name. In that case the one found worthy of the dignity will no longer be preserved, and the one who received the grace will not remain. There will not be two underlying natures at all, and they will not keep the human element in Christ at all. Yet they, on the contrary, are fighting rather to strip the divine from him. I would gladly ask them this too: do they in any way call the Word "Christ"? And do they call Christ "Word," in addition to "Son" and "God," or not? If not, look: they have overturned everything they granted in Christ's honor. They do not even grant the bare communion of name that they pretend to. For if he is not the Word, then he is not the natural [?] of God either, not even in name. But suppose that, having seen this, they call Christ "Word" as well, and the Word "Christ," so that each person indicates the other and their names are exchanged. Then they are saying that the Word himself has also taken on the title of the flesh.
