So insofar as they want the flesh to represent his own person and display it, he will be found representing the flesh's person. And this exchange [?]

[?]…what exchange of persons and names will there be, and for what purpose in the divine plan? If all that was needed was to raise the lesser person by the greater name, why was it necessary to lower the greater person by the lesser name? The one who is glorified gains nothing from the dishonour of the one who glorified him. Nor did the Word, who glorified the flesh with his own name, take a share in its name because he needed glory from it. Let them tell us, then: what is the reason for the exchange of names between the parts, if not the principle of the composition of the whole? And when they say carelessly, "Yes, everything that God the Word is, the man united to him also is," while granting nothing of the Word to Christ, whom they separate from him, how will they not be ashamed of themselves? If God the Word is something besides his essence, something he imparts to Christ, then Christ would share in that alone, and it would be an accident. I do not mean the Word himself. But if any accident at all is conceived in him, he will no longer be God. Suppose instead that the Word is, besides the essence, simply a hypostasis of God, and suppose they also say that the man Christ now exists together with the Word. How then is he not united to him in hypostasis [?]? Either they say that the hypostasis given to the man is another one, similar to the Word's. Then there would be two Words, and these would be two gods and two sons, and the holy Trinity would be a quaternity. Or else this one hypostasis has been imparted to the human nature, that is, has taken it up along with itself. Then it is the common hypostasis of the Word and of Christ's flesh, and we are right to venerate in Christ the union of the Word and the flesh in hypostasis. So much for that. But even if there were no refutation of these plausible arguments they make on behalf of their impiety, would not the absurdity that follows from their own premises be enough by itself to turn people away from their superstition? According to them, there is one Son on his own, wholly Son of God by nature, conceived as being without flesh both before Christ and after Christ. That is one hypostasis. There is another hypostasis, that of Christ, which is known to be wholly son of man by nature and in the flesh, but is called Son of God by grace and by bare honour only. How would these two hypostases not be two sons, when they are different, have different sonships and different parents, and are separated in existence and in place [?]? Suppose they worship the one that is divine by nature and disown the other as being of one substance with themselves. Then they would plainly be Hebrews and antichrists, who also say, "It is not for a good work that we are stoning you, but because you, being a man, make yourself the Son of God." Suppose instead they also venerate as God this other one, which they know to be human nature only. Then they are plainly pagans, who worship the creature rather than the Creator. They are truly worshippers of a man, and they set up a tetrad of divine hypostases, three of one substance and one of a different substance. And let them not say, "But we worship the man Christ by the will of God." Where have the divine oracles told us to worship a man as God? On the contrary, there is no place where holy Scripture does not condemn such people. It commands, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him

alone you shall serve." But let us see next what these excellent people have to say in their defence against this. CHAPTER [?]. "If we said that the two sons were from God by nature, or that both were sons by grace," he says, "you would really be right to conclude that we speak of two sons of God. Holy Scripture speaks of two or more sons only when all those counted together come from the same parent, in the same respect and in the same manner. Either all were begotten by him by nature, or all by adoption, so that they can also be called brothers of one another. So it is said, 'the mother of the two sons of Zebedee.' In Genesis it says, 'To Joseph were born two sons.' And: 'Reuben said to his father, Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you,' meaning Benjamin. Again, it is written in the Apostle that 'Abraham had two sons.' Wherever there are two or many sons, they are also called brothers, and people speak of a firstborn and of those born later, as with Esau and Jacob. So if we said that both the Word and Christ were from God by nature, or that both were from him by grace, you would be right in your reckoning against us. Being two, they would then have to be called brothers, and one of them would be the firstborn and the elder, unless they were twins. But if one is a son by adoption and the other by nature, and Christ is Son of one parent by nature and of another by adoption, then clearly there is no room for counting them together as two sons." That is what they say, these truly are the moulders and inventors of paradoxical doctrines! They refuse to compose the two natures, the divine and the human, into one son and one hypostasis, as though this were impossible. Yet now they decree that two persons, two complete sons, each distinct on its own, are to be joined into one son. Let us say to them, then: My excellent friends, do not let your thoughts reel about like drunkards. There are three possibilities. Either the unlike manner of begetting is what keeps a pair of sons from being counted together, even when they have the same father. Or the cause is that each son comes from different parents. Or both together cause the pair of sons to be abolished, that is, the difference of sonship and the difference of parents. Suppose it is the different manner of birth that makes the two sons be counted as one. Then, first, how could you say that a different birth divides even the one Son? You said it when we shamed you into calling the holy Virgin Theotokos. You claimed that if he was born by another birth, he would not remain the same timeless Son of God, the Word. For you declared absolutely that whatever is begotten in any way at all is other than what already existed before. Besides, if a different manner simply cancels the number of sons, consider John the evangelist. He gained a new sonship and became the Lady's son by adoption, because of what the Master said on the cross: "Behold your mother," and "Behold your son." The Lord, meanwhile, was her son by nature.

Then both of them would be one son, because their sonships were different! Suppose instead it is not the difference of birth but the difference of the parents that shows several children to be one. Since Simon was born to Jonah and John to Zebedee, were the two of them one son? Or suppose that the different manner of birth and the parents' being different persons, taken together, present as one son those who were born as different people, from different parents and in different ways. Since John was son of the Lady by adoption and Simon was son of Jonah by nature, were they then one son, because of the different manner and the different parents? If all this is plainly false, it is clear that this is true only where a single hypostasis underlies the sonships. John alone was truly one and the same son: of Zebedee by nature and of the Lady by adoption. For one hypostasis can be subject to different sonships. But you loudly proclaim two hypostases, of Christ and of the Word, and two complete persons. How then will Christ and the Word be one Son because of a different birth, you tellers of wonders? On your view, difference would be the cause of union among things, and likeness the cause of distinction. From the beginning of the ages this was revealed to no one before you! And if they say that the two are one because their parents differ, that is laughable nonsense. On that view, being born of like parents makes children two, while being born of different parents makes all who are born one son. Are Hophni and Phinehas then two sons, because they are from the same Eli, while Jonathan and David are not two sons but only one, because one is from Saul and the other from Jesse? If this is the cause, then the descendants of Cain and of Seth, who are different, are not two sons either, and all human beings are one son. And if a mere difference in the species of the parents is the cause, then all horses and fish are one son. Who will put up with such absurdities? For this is simply the conclusion: if the parents are different, many sons are one son, but if the parents are not different, they are many. Difference will then be the cause of union and unity, and likeness the cause of distinction and multitude, which is [?]

"But look," he says. "On both grounds, the sons who were Bilhah the maidservant's by nature are Rachel's sons by adoption, and they did not add to the number. As she said to Jacob, 'Go in to my maid, and she will bear upon my knees, and I too shall have children through her.' And again: 'God has judged me, and has heard my voice, and has given me a son; therefore she called his name Dan.' Rachel herself bore Joseph and Benjamin by nature. Yet that does not make four of the twelve patriarchs Rachel's sons, for the sons by adoption are not counted." Yet we would reply: if they are not counted at all, how are there twelve patriarchs, when Dan and Naphtali are not included in the reckoning? It is clear, though, that those by adoption are not counted together with those by nature. Even if they are not counted as Rachel's, look, they are still counted as the sons of Bilhah, who is a different woman,

and among the twelve two are said to be Rachel's and two others Bilhah's. They are sons of different mothers and of the same father. So children are counted as several sons whether they come from different parents or from entirely the same parents, provided they are several in hypostasis. Several sons are not counted only when there are several modes of sonship in the same hypostases. That is why Bilhah's sons, who are the very same persons, sons of Bilhah by nature and of Rachel by adoption, are not each reckoned as two sons because of their two sonships. Otherwise the patriarchs would have been fourteen. Each is one son, standing in different relations to his parents through different sonships, but not measured by different numbers and hypostases. Now consider what they say: that because the man is Son of God by adoption, Christ the Son is not counted together with the Word, the Son of God by nature, to make a pair, since number applies only to those who are sons by nature. This shows that the son by adoption will not enter the number of sons for one of two reasons: either because he is superior, or because he is nothing at all. If it is because he is superior, then among the sons of the Lady John is greater than the Master, and the man is simply greater than the Word in the eyes of God the Father. If he is inferior, how can the inferior one be one son together with the better one? They will not say that things that differ are one. And if they say it is because he is nothing, their notion of Christ's sonship is refuted. To show that they are lying in this too: look, in the Lord's genealogy Joseph, the Lady's betrothed, is called the son of Eli. Yet by nature he was the firstborn of Jacob, Eli's brother. According to the law, however, he was declared to be the offspring of Eli, the brother who had died childless before him. To lay bare their twofold impiety even more plainly, let us say this. Even if, as you hold, Christ, the Son of God by adoption, is not counted together with the Son and Word of God by nature, are you not still caught upholding two sons? On your own view he too is certainly someone's son by nature, namely a man's, for he did not come into being by chance. So it is clear that he is a son, if not of God, then at any rate of some person by nature, even on your view. Do you, then, call this one and the Word two sons? On your view this one is not God, nor Son of God by nature, but son of a man by nature, while the Word is the Son of God by nature. Or will you deny that Seth, the son of Adam, and the Word of God are two sons, though they are sons of different fathers? If you call them two, it is entirely clear that you recognize two sons, the Word and the Christ, just as you speak of two persons. You hold Christ to be neither God nor Son of God, but only the mere son of a man, as we human beings are. These are the very things we have long accused you of. You slipped out one way here and another way there and contrived to escape notice. And look, you have exposed one of your errors by means of the other. The divine power has often shown this even among the demon-possessed. Through the saints it has forced the demons themselves to tell, against their will, of their own assaults, plots and wicked deeds

against those they possess. In this way they parade their own foulness with their own mouths, and cannot seem to be slandered by others out of hatred. These men have been unable to show, either by syllogism or by arguing from causes, how the different persons are not two sons, as they claim. So now they want to present it to us by examples, and they say:

"Things that differ in nature are often called by one name and given one honour, and yet they are not thought of as two at all. We believe that the Church, the holy bread, and what was crucified are each a body. Each of these is a different thing, and yet we are not required on that account to speak of three bodies of Christ." But it is clear that as bodies of Christ they are not two or three. Each of them partakes of the same Spirit. He anointed what was crucified, he sanctifies this bread, and through partaking of the bread he again sanctifies the whole Church. For this reason they are all understood as the body of Christ. As Christ's, then, they are one. If, however, we judge them simply as bodies, they are three: Christ's own body, the bread, and the Church. So if in the same way the Word and Christ are both made sons of the same God by partaking of some other thing they have in common, let them tell us what this is. And let them say what the Word was on his own, apart from it, if the Word became Son through it. For if one and the same thing, given to different natures, made both the Word and Christ Son of God, then it will make [Christ] Son of God by nature, [or ?] by adoption, and the Word to be by [?]…

"But neither do we speak of two seals, the archetype and the impression," he says, "but of one, although we know that they are different in number." But, sirs, by this argument we would not call all humanity two men, or the universal animal, that is, what is common by likeness, two animals. We would name it in the singular. Nor would we recognize that men and animals and plants and seals are many in number, since we say that the form of all of them is alike and one across the whole multitude. Yet we do speak of two and three and ten thousand animals and men. In fact the example means the opposite of what you used to hold. It shows that the sons are two in number but alike in sonship and not different. Yet until just now you were saying that those counted as a pair of sons must both be sons by nature or both by adoption, and alike in the kind of their sonship. So if the kind of their sonship does not differ, as with the seal and its archetype, then on your view they can be thought of as two because of their likeness. And so again: if they are alike to one another in the way things of the same species are, then either the flesh is Son of God by nature, or the Word is Son of God by grace. The Father will also be flesh. For a father by nature begets what is like himself in essence, so if he has begotten flesh by nature, he too is flesh

by nature. And the Word, though God by nature, is not Son of the Father by nature, but by grace along with the flesh. So the Father is not God [?]. So whether the sons are alike or unlike, even then the seals and their archetypes differ in number, even if they do not vary in form. These too, differing in number, could therefore be [two] and be counted together as a pair of sons, like Paul and Peter, or the ring and the wax, or clay and lead bearing an impression. But again they foolishly say that a difference of material cancels the number of the seals and makes the many be thought of as one. Then, we would answer, sameness of material will bring the number back. If opposite follows from opposite, then any seals that happen all to be in wax would be many seals, while those stamped in different materials would be one, on your view. These things call for tears, and yet they force us to laugh.

CHAPTER [?]. "What then?" he says. "Are there two words, the one spoken and the one heard?" But here too, first of all, the inner word is one thing and the word in the mind is another. The uttered word is different again, and below it comes the written word, and after these the word that is heard. What these have in common, as with the seals, is something one by virtue of signifying the same thing. Take a word with several meanings, or a homonym. Even if one person alone speaks it or hears it, it is no longer called one word. Even if it is announced in a single utterance, all dialecticians agree that there are several words. It is clear, then, that a word is properly one by virtue of what it signifies. Someone might say that a word is one in this sense: the same word, one in number, happens to be spoken by the speaker and heard by the one standing by. But then the example would bear no likeness to your case. Here there are not two things in number underlying it, that is, two words called by one name. Yet the person of Christ and the person of the Word are two countable hypostases, and you thought to call them one Son. On the contrary, what you would be showing is that here a single thing in number is called by two names from different relations. The same word, one in number and alone, is called "spoken" from its relation to the speaker and "heard" from its relation to the hearer. So once again, in this way too, your own spittle flows back in your faces.

[?]…hidden [?] of those who say that Christ has one hypostasis and that God the Word is compounded with the flesh. "For what can one find in the word Theotokos, especially when they add 'properly and in truth', but the very thing we found set apart in the composition? Used without qualification, the term Theotokos does in a way admit, through relation, a clarification in a pious sense, since the name 'God' is used in many senses. But now that 'properly and in truth' has been attached to the word, they have filled it with every impiety and with undisguised blasphemy." Even so, we must ask them what such a name means to them and in what sense they have taken it. We call a woman "male-bearing" or "female-bearing" when she usually bears males or females. Do they call holy Mary Theotokos in that way, meaning by such a word that she is naturally inclined to bear gods? Then let them say what gods she bore, and teach us what we do not know. Or is it because she bore God? "Even if they wish to signify this once and for all by naming the Virgin so, we do not know whether a name of this form can convey it." "The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips, the boastful tongue, those who said, 'We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?'" Tell us, you who lay down the law on your own authority that a mother is to be named not from one birth but from several. Isaac was Sarah's only child, Samuel Hannah's, John Elizabeth's, and Mary Anna's. The same goes for all the men and women recorded as having only one son or one daughter. If someone wanted to name these mothers from the birth and from the nature of the child born, would he not dare, on your view, to call them male-bearing or female-bearing? Who, hearing such sophistries of yours, would not spit on them, you wretches? And even if it were as you say, you who claim not to know whether this can be conveyed by such a form, how did you see fit to call her who is truly Theotokos "Christotokos" and "anthropotokos"? If a woman cannot be given such a name from a single birth, then either you think the holy Virgin bore several Christs, or simply several men, or else, you utterly wretched people, you could not use these names of her either. It would also follow on this supposition that the only Father could not be called the begetter of his only Son and Word, God, since he begot only one god and not several. How then do you say that he is properly the one who begets God? "Claiming to be wise, you have become fools, and your senseless heart has been darkened." Number contributes to the proper naming of something only when several things that underlie it in number are signified by the singular form of the name, used as a collective. In this way one vine will not make up a vineyard, nor will anything be vine-bearing [?]…

…anyone would describe a place in this way, nor as fruitful, or as breeding fish, the [?]. But these things belong to your first [?] charge against us. Let the blasphemies you have stated next also be examined, and let them not escape anyone's notice without being publicly exposed.

Since the name "God" is used in many senses in divine Scripture—for example, "Since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith"; and again, "God has stood in the assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods"; and again, "Just as there are many gods and many lords"—in which sense have they taken the name "God" here, in the case of the Theotokos? In the first, which means calling him God by nature; or in the second, that is, God by designation; or in the third, which is the false sense? They would not say the last, not even if they became demons. But if they should say the second, let them know that divine Scripture has never called an angel, or an irrational animal, or any other created thing "God by designation." So do they say that the Virgin is by nature a bearer of a man? But I had forgotten the addition "properly and in truth"; for they have adopted "properly" to indicate that the Virgin gave birth to one who is God by nature. Let us see whether this is possible and does not contradict what we commonly confess. For they confess that God the Word is unchangeable and unalterable, according to the creed of our common Fathers—I mean of the synod at Nicaea. What is unchangeable and unalterable will become neither worse than itself nor better, but always remains the same, unaltered, being eternal: it has never not existed and has received no beginning of being. Let us then consider whether birth from a woman, if predicated of God the Word, will not destroy either his eternity or his unalterability, and in general the attributes that belong to him and that we all confess as belonging to the God of all things.

Now you have dared to overturn the meaning of the word "Theotokos" as applied to the holy Virgin—a word that is properly and truly used—not by arguing that there are not many gods, but by arguing that not even the one who was born is properly God. For by bringing forward the name "God" as used equivocally of things differing in essence, you want to show, in this argument and in the one that follows, as indeed throughout your whole treatise, that when used of Christ it signifies neither the God by nature nor, to be sure, any of those falsely called gods (for this, you admitted, must be refused even by demons), but that by this name the God by designation is signified in Christ. But, as you say, neither an angel nor any other living being except man is called God by designation in holy Scripture. Therefore, according to you, the one who was born must necessarily be called a man, and she who bore him a bearer of a man. But if the one born is a man and God by designation, and the God by nature commands all men

not to serve those who are not gods by nature—for it cries out explicitly, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve"—it follows that you neither worship nor serve Christ, who according to your error is God by designation and not by nature. Rather you are openly Antichrists of a sort, and should not hypocritically pass for Christians. Or if you shrink from this, then by worshipping and serving him you will be caught by us as, properly speaking, worshippers of a creature and worshippers of a man. So do not be aggrieved any longer at being called by such a name, and do not strive to shake off such a reputation; nor stir everything up to prove that you are not such people, as you have already struggled to establish through very many long-winded discourses.

…[?] is the cause of the very existence of what is said to have been begotten, as in "Abraham begot Isaac"; or it is not the cause of its very existence, as when the Apostle begot the Corinthians, according to the saying, "For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the gospel." Of the birth that is a cause of being, one kind makes the begotten coexist with the begetter, the other makes it exist after him. For God the Word, begotten from the Father, coexists with him; but Isaac exists after Abraham, as does anyone else of that kind. Of the birth that is not the cause of the being of the begotten, one kind shows the begotten to be better than himself, the other worse. Better, as in: "But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." Worse, as in: "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" According to which kind of birth, then, do they say that God the Word was born of a woman? According to the one that gives being to the begotten? Then God the Word is not eternal; for no such birth allows the begotten to preexist the begetter, and what does not preexist something that is not eternal is not eternal—which it is impious to say of God the Word. Or do they say he was born according to the birth that does not give being to the begotten? Then God the Word is changeable and not unalterable; for every such birth shows the begotten to be either better or worse, and one who becomes better or worse than himself through such a change is plainly convicted of being changeable and alterable. But if God the Word is neither changeable nor non-eternal, then he was not properly and in truth born of a woman, nor can birth from a woman be predicated of him at all, according to the scriptural

Though you try to escape notice by many insertions of words and alterations of meanings, you are nevertheless very easily caught in your impiety. Granted that these modes of birth are different, and that the things attending them are different, as you have said; still, what we now require from you by way of

proof is whether it is truly impossible, as we say, for one and the same person to undergo two births among these very different births, so that each of the births may be recognized by its consequences. For consider that very many Gentiles among those whom Paul begot in Christ Jesus through the gospel had, admittedly, been born before him according to fleshly birth. Would not then one and the same of his disciples be said both to exist before his own father and teacher Paul and, as is attested, to exist after him? Everyone, I think, would agree; but he will say that the same person both preexists and postexists the same person in different respects. For indeed, as you said, he preexists according to the birth into being, but exists after according to the birth into the gospel. Likewise the brood of vipers, who were of Abraham's nation according to the flesh and were made disciples by their own children, namely the apostles, as the Lord turned the hearts of fathers to their children—how could the same people not be said to preexist according to fleshly birth, but to exist after according to the spiritual rebirth of their own sons? If this is so, what seems incredible to you in the case of the Word too: that according to one birth he is eternal and truly simple, but according to another he begins to exist as composite? For with a certain assumption he comes to be known as new, and is no longer called the simple Word but the composite Christ. Granting that this is so, she who bore the composite certainly also bore the simple, for the simple is in the composite; but he who begot the simple did not also beget the composite, for the composite is not in the simple. Therefore, according to the birth that gives being, and eternal being, to the Word simply as Word, we do not call the Virgin mother. But according to the birth that gives him being in this particular way—that is, incarnate—and being in the flesh that is subject to time, since he had his composition simultaneously with the flesh itself and was born together with it from her, the flesh being temporal in its existence, we know the undefiled one to be truly Mother of the simple as well, though through the composition. For our Master Christ is wholly composed of the eternal Word and of flesh subject to time: the Word was born twice, without flesh from the Father and incarnate from the Mother, while the flesh was born once only, from the Mother without seed. Since, then, the Word is true God both without flesh and with flesh, those who begot him are truly God-bearers according to each birth. So much, then, for the Word's different procession according to his births. But the various kinds of birth that are merely by way of progress and the like are brought forward by you to no purpose in the case of Christ; for no argument ever called the undefiled one Theotokos in that sense, nor has such a thing entered the imagination even of the most irrational.

CHAPTER 4. If properly and in truth the birth from the

[Father] of God the Word is birth, then the birth of God the Word from a woman, as it is called, is not properly and in truth birth, since they are not alike. But if the former, then not the latter.

But if you say that the only birth properly so called is that which is by way of cause alone, timeless and coeternal with the Father—the birth of God the Word, which shows the begotten coexisting with the begetter—then you know that a birth unlike it is not properly birth. You will then no longer recognize as proper birth that of Isaac from Abraham, or of any other human being from a human being, or of animal from animal, or of plant from plant; for these are neither timeless nor coeternal nor simply coexistent with those who bear them, nor do they come about in every way as God the Father begot the Word. But if the birth of Isaac from Abraham is also true, as you yourselves have said elsewhere, as is that of the other animals and plants—though it is in time, shows the begotten existing afterward, and simply differs from the divine birth in countless, indeed almost all, the principles of birth—then according to you the birth of the Word from God the Father, understood as eternal, will not be the only birth properly and in truth. If, then, both that one and these are and are called true births, then those called begetters are also true begetters according to the different principle of each birth. So Paul through the gospel, the Spirit through baptism, Abraham from his loins, Rachel from her womb, and the Father begetting from himself and in himself—all are truly begetters and are called so. If, then, there should be several begetters of one and the same person according to several of these modes, the same one will truly be the son of them all. So the Word was born from the Father by way of cause, and from the mother by way of composition and conception; for what has once conceived does not give birth to the whole from itself, as the very word "con-ception" shows.

If the birth of God the Word from the Father, being true, differs from his birth from a woman that is said to be true, and it is wholly necessary that things whose true births differ should also differ in essence, then it is wholly necessary that God the Word should differ from himself in essence, because the true births ascribed to him differ. But if God the Word differs from himself in essence, he will be like no one in essence, and so not like the Father and the Holy Spirit either—which destroys the homoousion.

You are held fast in impiety by many absurdities of equal weight, and we are at a loss which of them to charge you with first. For we have already shown that even when births differ, all of them are nevertheless truly births, whether they belong to one person or to several of the same kind. And see, you yourselves agreed with us when you said, "whose true births differ"; for you too already know that there are births which differ and yet are true. But what you now say is also false: that where births differ, so do essences. For

those who claim Paul as their father through the gospel, those who claim the fathers of their flesh, those who claim the Father of spirits, those said to have been born of the devil, and those born of vipers—each was born by a different birth, and yet all are of the same essence, namely the like human essence. And the holy Timothy, son both of Paul and of a Greek father, though one in number, was ascribed several such fathers. How then will these facts bear witness for your views? So much for these. But Adam was born in one way, Eve in another, and Seth in another—yet who will deny that they have one nature, the same for all? So it is not true that where births differ, essences differ too. Besides, if the births were taken of different persons, they might perhaps show a difference of essence; but where the same subject has different births predicated of it, how will that same subject not be undifferentiated? Why then, without first showing that one and the same subject cannot subsist according to two different births, or that some things cannot be conceived as consubstantial, do you conclude simply from the difference of births that the one and the same subject born is itself differentiated? For conversely we shall say to you: if where births differ the essence differs, then where birth does not differ, the essences do not differ either. Does not then the birth of asses and dogs and humans and swine and apes—being in time, from seed, through the womb, and alike in manner—present their essence as alike too? And what need have I of other cases or of another birth to show whether the difference or likeness of essences arises from the mode of birth? For of one and the same man the birth is obviously one in number and the same; yet soul and body, the natures born together in it, are different. According to you, then, either we shall say that their essence is not different, since their birth is not; or, saying it is different, we shall believe that one man has two different births at the same time. So much for your clever arguments. Yet no one ever told you that the second birth brought forth the Word as simple in the same way; rather, according to his second birth it brought him forth from his mother together with the fleshly essence, you would-be sages.

If what has come to be cannot, insofar as it has come to be, come to be again, then what exists eternally cannot be born again from a woman. But the former is true; therefore the latter is too.

If you deny to the eternally existing Word every birth, simply as giving being to what is born, then either you will also take away from him, as eternal, his first birth from the Father—for you say that what exists eternally cannot be born—so that he would no longer be Son of the Father (for there is no Son without birth), nor would the Father be Father (for there is no Father without a Son); or, confessing his birth from the Father, you will show that he is no longer eternal, if indeed what exists eternally cannot in any way truly be born, simply because it exists. But if

it is not because it always exists, but simply because something already preexisted and was once born before, how can you say that it is not possible for something to be born once more at all, in any way, or by any other mode whatever? For this is what your word "again" hinted at. Let us examine this too in detail. Had Timothy, then, not yet been born by any birth, nor come forth from other parents, when Paul, who calls him his true child in the faith, begot him in Christ Jesus through the gospel? And who among you does not loathe this obvious falsehood? Understand this case too in the same way, sirs. Of the parts of Christ, we say that one was born both according to his first birth and according to the second; but the other, clearly, neither preexisting nor born before by another birth, we confess came forth together with the [?] of the whole same hypostasis in the one birth common to both. For in the one birth from the Virgin, it is understood to be the second birth of one of Christ's parts, but the first and only birth of the other.

If the essence of God the Word was born in truth from the essence of the Virgin, and things born in this way must be like those who bear them in essence, then either God the Word is man in essence, or the Virgin is God in essence. But each is equally impious and impossible. Therefore the essence of God the Word was not born in truth from the essence of the Virgin.

But first, being born into essence is one thing, and being born according to essence another. Further, among things born from an essence, anyone who examines them precisely will find many differences of likeness and unlikeness, as you too said earlier; for some things give birth to what is like them, others to what is unlike, evidently according to the difference between births of differing natures. For Paul, who effected Timothy's birth, was an essence; Timothy too was an essence, and was improved and born according to essence unto incorruption through faith (for the spiritual rebirth of our nature did not come about by some accident); his father according to the flesh was an essence, and in some way begot according to essence; and the Father, cause of every essence, is himself uncaused by anything. Yet the one begot him like himself by faith, the other by his body, and the Father by his own image. So even if the Father eternally begets the Word from his own essence, and Solomon is said to beget Jeroboam from his essence, it does not follow that each son is exactly the same as his father. For since the mode of births according to essence is understood differently in things of differing nature, even if the births are alike in this very respect, being from the essence nonetheless reasonably shows the likeness to differ too. For see: in the case of one and the same man, a son, a thought, speech, hair, scars, activity and very many other things are said to be begotten from his essence. Must we then think that all of them are like the man in essence, since some of these were born into an essence and according to essence

and from the essence? Or must they not differ from the one who bore them by the difference of their modes, principles and materials, since they are not born from his whole essence or from it alone, nor born alone? So even if God the Word was born from the holy Virgin together with the flesh—not alone, bare in his nature, nor having simple being from her—what necessity is there to demand that the begotten be like in its whole essence to what in any way begot it? For it is agreed that this birth is not the paternal birth, which alone shows the exact likeness of the essence of the offspring to the begetter, that is, of the Father to his own Word without flesh. For the flesh and the preexisting Word were born from the holy Lady; and neither alone, nor from the essence of the holy Virgin alone, as from the Father. For we did not tell you that she alone bore the Word alone, or that she bore him as not preexisting, but as incarnate from her essence. Hence Christ, born according to both his parts, is called both anointing and anointed. But if you insist that we call him consubstantial with one only, and not with two of different essences, then it is time for you to stop saying that Adam, who came to be from earth and from the divine breath, is consubstantial with either of his constituent essences according to the principle of one of his parts; rather, you must either regard his earthly part as divine or suppose his divine part to be earthly. But if in his case these things lead to error, then truly our one [?] Christ too can be, and is said to be, like each of his two begetters by one of the things in him.

If the Virgin is in truth Mother of God, God is in truth Son of the Virgin. If God is in truth Son of the Virgin, he is either like his Mother or not like her. And if he is like her, he is not God; if not like her, he is not her Son.

But we have already said that even a true son is not in all respects like the one who bore him. For light comes from fire, and is not entirely like fire; a thought comes from the soul, and is not [soul]; fish come from water, and are not water. [?] the complete unlikeness of offspring to those who bore them can be seen. And if Christ is in part unlike his Mother and in part like her, what is absurd in that? Since the partridge-pheasant born of a partridge and of pheasants is not wholly like the partridge, will it then not really be its offspring either, O natural philosophers?

The birth of God the Word from the Virgin in truth is either something he undergoes or an activity of his; or both something undergone and an activity; or neither something undergone nor an activity. But if it appears to be something undergone, the impiety is obvious; for what is undergone belongs to what was born, and according to you the essence of God was born; therefore what is undergone belongs to the essence of God. But if it is an activity, and God acts not by his very being,

that is, not by essence, but only by willing. So the generation belongs to the willing of God's essence. If it is both passion and activity, then he has been begotten by being acted upon in his essence and acting by his willing; so both the essence and the willing of God have been begotten, the one being acted upon, the other acting. But if it is neither passion nor activity, then neither the essence nor the willing of God was begotten. Tell us, then, what of God was begotten, such that by its being begotten God was properly and truly begotten.

Alas for your unwise wisdom! May God leave in the world not even a ghost of such eloquence. For what is more wretched than such zeal, which scrapes together every unsuitable explanation so as to give an unsubstantial lie the appearance of the substance of truth? And this for no other gain than to build itself a foundation for blasphemy. First, then, we must hear from you what agreement of thought there is between what you have held about generation and things begotten up to now and what has just been said. Before this you determined that generation in the proper sense is generation from what does not exist, or that which simply gives being to what is begotten; this you put forward both above and below. How, then, do you now say that generation is either a passion or an activity, or both together, observed in the one begotten? For if, according to you, the generation of what is to come into being is its own activity, whether through willing or in any other way, and the one begotten, to whom the willing belongs, has his being from the generation, then before he exists he will both will and bring about his own being, and while not existing he will possess both his own being and his own willing. And if you say that his generation is also a passion, then again, in the same way, he will be found to have been acted upon before he exists. I do not know in what the non-existent, whoever he may be, was acted upon, any more than I know in what he acted, so as to produce his own being. But if you say that the generation proceeds according to both these conditions of the one begotten, all the absurdities of the hypothesis will follow you twice over, in addition to your granting that contraries coexist at the same time and in the same subject. But I forgot: you suppose these things to be in what does not exist; and they do not coexist, for what is in the non-existent does not even exist. So I do not know how there could be beings in what does not exist, when even those that occur in things that exist are not beings in the proper sense. Moreover, one must also attend to this: if generation is an activity or a passion of the one begotten, according to the irrational modes you laid down as necessary, then either, being begotten by himself, he would suffer something in himself; or he would suffer it from the one who bore him, or from someone else. And again, either he will act upon himself, or upon the one who bore him, or upon someone else. And so it will turn out that he has either begotten himself into himself, or into the one who bore him, or into another; or that he has been begotten by himself into himself, or by himself into himself, or by the Father, or by another. Spare us from hearing such things or answering them, you most clever men; we confess that we cannot bear them without indignation. Be silent, then, so that we may speak. For it is said that the corruption of one thing contributes to the generation of another, with one thing acting and another being acted upon,

[?] according to the different modes of the things generated. The form of the bed comes forth by the natural and skilled activity of the carpenter and by the passion of the wood; and again, when the nature of fire acts and destroys, and the tallow is acted upon and destroyed, the form of smoke is generated in the air. Those who conceive and posit nature and matter in different ways, whatever these may be, nevertheless agree that the forms arising from them are generated with the one acting and the other being acted upon. According to your decrees, however, what does not exist generates something; yet no one has ever said that it generates, above all its own being, by passion or by activity. Indeed, no one has ever recognized any passion or activity at all in what does not yet exist. How, then, do you argue against us with such divisions, as though they were natural ones?

But we confess that up to now, by the grace of God, we have neither known nor been taught such things, and we proclaim in an orthodox way the piety taught us by the holy Fathers: the only Son from the only Father, God the Word, existing before the ages by his one, unique, proper begetting. And we confess that in later times, by his own benevolent good pleasure, he brought about his second birth, again most particularly his own, in union with the man who is like us, and was born by coming forth in the flesh from the holy Virgin, sharing likeness of birth with nothing at all, either in his first or in his second birth. For nothing else has been begotten in the manner of his first begetting, which is eternal, unvarying, well-pleasing, unchangeable, undivided, unfailing and never departing from its source. Nor, in the manner of the second, has anything else been born thus, without seed, without corruption and above nature: conceived of the Holy Spirit, perfected without lapse of time, formed, organized and completed in its whole essential principle in the pure womb of the undefiled one, as a temple and tabernacle of the Word, the human flesh being perfected from her alone and joined to him in an instant. Moreover, we believe that, while the virginal gate truly remained closed, his God-receiving flesh, though truly a body by nature, passed through the unbroken body of the Virgin's womb by the supernatural power of the Spirit of the Word that was in it. How, then, shall we not all the more, and still more, for these reasons, recognize this Virgin as truly Theotokos and praise her, in whom and from whom the Word, having betrothed himself to the flesh, came forth like a bridegroom from his holy chamber? From whom Wisdom hewed out her own house and built it around herself? And the marvel is that Wisdom did not draw itself out of the Virgin's womb along with the dwelling by the natural property of the dwelling; on the contrary, by its own natural property, that is, that of the Word who dwelt in it, it spiritually drew the dwelling out with itself from her who bore it. For the Word empowered his flesh to go out spiritually with him and to pass through the unbroken body of the Virgin, just as he himself, without flesh, entering through it, was not constrained. For since, by his own good pleasure,

he gave himself into the Virgin, and from her the fleshless one formed himself in the flesh, he also divinely brought forth with himself the flesh he had taken from her. Let your profane mouth, then, be muzzled until your eyes are opened, so that, having seen the light of the mystery, you may then be able to speak not the fantasies of the idols of the darkness of earthly wisdom, but the mighty works of God.

If God the Word was properly and truly born of the Virgin, and the flesh, mortal and corruptible and animated by a rational and intelligent soul, was properly and truly born of her, then either the flesh exists before the Virgin, or God the Word exists after the Virgin; and either is absurd.

But we have often told you, you natural philosophers, that the birth from the Virgin of both the parts of the one Son is not according to one and the same principle of generation. Yet she is truly mother according to each principle: of the one as having come to exist in the flesh from her, of the other as having come to exist simply as flesh. For in this way one mother of the one who is composed of both has been shown forth. Well then: if Zebedee's sons were properly and truly born of him in the flesh, and properly and truly were the first to beget him anew through the Gospel [?], do they simply exist before him, or does he exist after them? And yet if one exists before, the other certainly exists after. This is mere show of wisdom, and it is not, as you say, either this or that; for by their relation these things are simultaneous and accompany each other, since what exists before exists before what exists after. But it is clear that in one respect and in another the same man, in relation to the same persons, who are both his sons and his fathers, has both the earlier and the later birth.

If the birth of the flesh is truly the birth of God, then its being is also truly the being of God. But if to call this being, and being of this kind, God's is both impious and impossible, then the birth of the flesh is not truly the birth of God.

But your first premise lacks the words "in the same way," and this has been overlooked by you, whether you argue cunningly or ignorantly. For if the birth of the flesh is the birth of God in the same way, that is, according to the same principle of birth as the birth from the Father, then you will indeed grant the same things to both. But if the principles of birth that are spoken of properly and truly are various [?], it will not follow that one should understand the same things from every principle of birth in the case of whatever is said to be born in any way at all. Nor has anyone granted you that the birth of mere, naked flesh is also the birth of God; nor that, God being united to the flesh, the birth of God from the Virgin is nevertheless the same in principle as the birth of the flesh. Rather, it is the same in number, but truly consists in different principles of generation according to both the natures born. For the term "generation," as you yourselves brought forward, is homonymous; and among homonyms there is no more and less, nor

first and second, you most learned men. So all the births are true, but they are not alike. That the birth of the God-filled flesh is also the birth of God incarnate is therefore confessed, but as befits each. For neither flesh nor birth can alter the nature of God. On the contrary, God has been able to alter both the nature of flesh and natural birth, according to the bounds, times and modes of his own economy, whenever he wishes. So it is a birth of God as beginning his incarnation, and of flesh as beginning

If those who give birth differ in essence from one another, then those who are born must necessarily differ in essence from one another. And if this is so, how, since the Father and the Virgin differ in essence, is it not necessary that God the Word, being truly the Son of both, differ in essence from himself? But to say that he who is beyond all simplicity differs in essence from himself is beyond all madness.

But how is it, sirs, that you blurt out whatever happens to occur to you? For fish and other animals, birds and certain reptiles are born from mating with one another, and likewise spontaneously from waters, from earth and from air; and yet they are alike in essence, although those that gave birth to them differ in nature. For the essence of an animal is not the same as that of water and earth; yet the fish born from water and the fish born from a fish are alike and without difference, and so too with snakes and very many others of the kind. Secondly, let us test your thesis by converting it. If things different in nature must give birth to different things, then things not different in nature must give birth to things not different. Since, then, the sun is one, and not many or various suns, and it gives birth to light in the air, to living creatures in water, and to grasses, and these of various kinds, in the earth, must we then consider the essence of all these to be without difference? But no one will say this along with you. Still, let this too be granted you. Yet show us, as has often been said, what prevents the same one from being the son of both. And if those who give birth differ in essence, what will hinder the one who in each birth is born from a different essence, as having been born first from another essence, from being different in the second birth from the one who begot him in the first birth, and from having, out of his whole self, different relations to each of those who gave him birth? Is it as though the first essence were not preserved in the second birth, or as though nothing could be added to a hypostasis begotten beforehand? For in that case none of those born according to the Spirit would have remained flesh in any way, since "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." But if you think that the acquisition of what was assumed by the Word from the second birth does not allow his former simplicity to be seen, you must consider that

you are viewing this difference of essence not within the natural simplicity of the Word, but outside it, that is, in the composite of the hypostasis. So whoever wishes to see that the sameness of essence of the first birth with the one who begot him has been preserved must look at it as in a part of the whole that results from the second birth. And again, one must clearly understand what the Word assumed in the second birth as being in the likeness of the Virgin his mother, since the distinction between the two essences of the composite holds both likenesses in essence. And thus no one would say that the Word departs from his own essence, nor think that the composite one, our Lord Jesus Christ, has left out anything of the difference between the natures of his parents. For we do not say, as you construe it, that both his parents gave birth to the Word simply and naked; rather, we understand that the Father begot him simply and as simple, while the Mother gave birth to the same one in Christ as composite with flesh.

If the essence of God the Word was properly and truly begotten from the essence of the Father, and is consubstantial with him in every respect, and the essence of God the Word was properly and truly born of a woman, and is wholly unlike her in essence, then it is not the fact that an essence is properly and truly begotten from an essence that makes what is born wholly like in essence to those who give it birth, but something else, which cannot even be conceived.

Properly and truly, the essence of God the Word was begotten both from the essence of the Father and from the holy Virgin, but not by a like birth, nor did the one who possesses it receive the same thing from each. For from his first begetting from the Father he has being alone from the Alone, whole from the Whole; and this without beginning, without time, eternally, and in every other way befitting God. From the second, he has being in the flesh, beginning to be composite from a point in time, and the rest of his likeness to us. How then, since he was not begotten into the same thing nor in the same mode of generation, do you demand the same marks of the one birth as true proof of his first and second birth, and in both of them either complete likeness or unlikeness? For it does not follow that, if the same consequences do not attend births that are not the same, they would therefore not be births properly and truly. The land horse is not, because it is not a river horse, therefore not truly a horse; both are truly horses. Nor, because it is not a sea creature, is the land creature therefore not an animal. Being properly and truly begotten, then, will not suffice to show likeness of essence, which you brought forward as the cause of likeness, unless something has been begotten precisely according to that kind of true birth which shows the offspring to be alike. For you yourselves granted at the beginning that some births show the parents to be worse than their offspring, some better, and some alike. Besides, in being begotten in relation to the Father, the Word as God had likeness as a whole; but Christ, begotten

and not simply as Word, has in part a natural likeness to his Mother, but in part also unlikeness [?]. For being one and the same, according to one or the other of the parts in him, he possesses both natural likeness and difference in relation to the Father and to the Mother.

Likewise let us, setting our own examples against yours, demonstrate our position. If Jonathan was properly and truly begotten from Saul, he is like him in essence; and a word was properly and truly begotten from him, and it is utterly unlike him in essence. Clearly, then, it is not being properly begotten that is the cause of likeness, but the particular mode of likeness, whether of whole or of part, in what is understood in the births.

If the Son was begotten from the Father according to his divinity, and preserves likeness in essence to him, and according to you the Son was likewise begotten from the Virgin according to his divinity, then he must preserve likeness in essence to her according to his divinity. And if this is so, the Virgin too will certainly have likeness in essence to God the Father; for things that are like the same thing are also like each other.

But it has been shown and said many times that it is not necessary for everything, nor in every birth, nor in its whole self, that what is begotten from something should preserve the principle of the nature of the one who begot it unaltered. For see: Holy Scripture speaks of "children of wrath by nature," "sons of disobedience" and "of lawlessness," "sons of darkness," "children of the evil one," "sons of this age," and "children of the devil"; but also of "children of God," "offspring of the divine will," "sons of light," "sons of the day," "sons of power," and "sons of the Most High"—according to various births, each true in its own respect, and according to the modes of each birth. And no one would call any of these offspring necessarily consubstantial with what begot it. For the children of wrath are not wrath, nor are the children of the age an age, nor are all the children of God gods in essence, nor are the sons of the Most High consubstantial with the Most High. So, first, it is not necessary that, if something is from something, it should be altogether like the whole principle of its essence. And again we will say that your difficulty would have been reasonable if we had said that the same Christ came forth from each in the same respect and in the same way. For if, because he was begotten from the Father according to his divinity, and the same one was begotten from his Mother according to his divinity—though in another way, namely in that he was made flesh—you demand that he have the same relation in essence to each of his parents, then you ought also to say of Peter that, since he was begotten by Jonah according to essence, and, being filled with the Holy Spirit according to essence and putting it on, was born spiritual, he preserves likeness in essence both to Jonah and to the Holy Spirit, wholly and not in part. And if this is so, Jonah his father too will certainly have likeness in essence to the Holy Spirit;

for things that are like the same thing are also like each other, as you have held. If, then, this conclusion is not prevented by these considerations, but Peter is consubstantial with each in a part of his hypostasis, how shall we not choose to understand Christ in the same way?

Everything that properly and truly gives birth is the cause of what is born; nothing that is the cause of what is born is younger than what is born; nothing that is not younger than what is born is a creation of what is born; therefore nothing that properly and truly gives birth is a creation of what is born.

But you ought to have added to the first premise of the present argument: "in that respect in which it is said to give birth, and in the way in which it gave birth." For it is in this way that what gives birth is the cause of what is born. Thus Paul too, who begot through the Gospel, is truly a parent and a proximate cause, not of the fleshly existence of those he begot, but of their faith through teaching. For many of the sons begotten by him in this birth were older than he in their fleshly age, and he, their proximate cause in respect of faith, was younger than they in time. How, then, could what gave birth not according to being simply, but perhaps only according to being in a certain way—namely, according to the Word's being incarnate—be said to be the cause, and older, not only of the newer state, that is, of his being in this way, but also of any other existence of his whatever, when he had admittedly already been begotten before, and by another birth? And how will it necessarily be granted that Nicodemus, the disciple who came by night, did not exist before the Lord in any respect whatever, since he was urged to be born through water and the Spirit when he was already an old man? Tell us, if you can keep your positions unwounded.

Everything that is properly and truly born has its being from what gives it birth; nothing that has its being from what gives it birth exists before its own birth; therefore nothing that is properly and truly born exists before its own birth.

So then, according to you, if something is said simply to have its being from something, would only that be properly and truly begotten from it and be called its son? And not also if something has a certain kind of being [?] from something? Then how are Seth and those descended from him counted worthy of divine sonship and called sons of God? How are those from among the Jews sons of Israel? How are the children of God's promise children of God? And what of those who have been born anew of imperishable seed, through the living and abiding word of God? How are the apostles sons of the bridal chamber? How is Onesimus the son of Paul, whom he begot in his chains? What reasoning led Holy Scripture to call people "children of wrath by nature" and "sons of lawlessness," or again "sons of light" and "of life," and the like? Or how is the fall or rising that befell them, which came neither together with their being nor from the one who gave them being, nevertheless properly a birth, insofar as

…is said, do we know? For if you recognize their sonship only from what causes their being, you will be forced to hold that Judas and the devil received their very being from perdition, since they are called sons of perdition. But you also say that Judas and the others like him had their being from God, while their being of such a kind they did not have from God, in the sense that some are called sons of darkness and of the curse by an equivocal sonship. So you have recognized that they are called sons in both senses. Among equivocal names, however, neither one is named more properly than the other. Those who are born again through repentance toward virtue and through faith in the Spirit are acknowledged even by you as sons of the bridechamber [?], children of the kingdom and the like. How, then, have you not granted me the point in question? For look: being of such a kind, and having a share in something of such a kind (sometimes something substantial, sometimes something without subsistence), makes a person truly a son of that thing and makes him truly called so. Among equivocal names, as has been said, one is not said more, or more properly, than the other. A living creature does seem to be such-and-such more than a painted one, and to be called so more properly. But in that case the relation is not one of equivocation. It is the relation of what is properly named to what is not properly named. At any rate, when two things are both properly named, the shared name will never admit of more and less: the land dog is not more a dog than the sea dog, nor is it less [?]. The painted thing, then, involves a "more" because of something like a cause or a model. Besides, if the one who is truly said to beget must be the cause of the very being of everything he begets, then no man is the father of a man, and no animal has ever begotten another animal. Seeds do not have an intellective or sensitive soul. Only after the soulless embryo has been shaped and fully organized is the living being given a soul, and this is especially true of man, whose spirit God forms within him. That is why the divine law judges whoever causes a miscarriage after the forming to be the murderer of a living being. Fathers, then, would only, or chiefly, be begetters of flesh, and on your view no one is the begetter of a human being. And since the body flows and changes daily, so that over time no part of the parents remains in it, they would not even be fathers of the flesh. In his old age Isaac would have entirely ceased to be the son of Abraham, and the same would be true of everyone else. How then could God have said, "But you shall go to your fathers, nurtured in a good old age"? These are plain absurdities. The Apostle himself speaks of the fathers of our flesh, whom we also had to discipline us, and calls God the Father of spirits alone, yet he calls Eunice the mother of Timothy, and not just of Timothy's flesh. So it is clear that the Word is truly the Son of the holy Virgin. He did not receive being itself, simply, from her. He received from her his becoming incarnate and his being incarnate. And he will appear younger than she is in his being of such a kind, that is, as composite from simple and embodied from bodiless.

"What is properly and truly born, if it is born in time, exists only potentially in the one who bears it before its own conception, as Levi was in the loins of Abraham. But what exists only potentially in the one who bears it receives the beginning of its being in that one. Therefore what is properly and truly born, if it is born in time, receives the beginning of its being in the one who bears it." To avoid babbling by explaining the same things to you over and over, let us grant your whole aim in the present argument, as it stands. We could say that Timothy was born to Paul both properly and in time, and yet he was not potentially in Paul when Stephen was being stoned, for it is not necessary in every kind of birth that whatever is born should already exist beforehand in those who bear it. What we will say to you is this. In the holy Virgin your Master Christ received, for one of his natures (that of the Word), the beginning not of its coming into substance but only of its union in substance. For the other nature in him, that of the flesh, he received in her the beginning both of its coming into substance and of its union in substance. On either account of each substance of the composite Christ who was born, she who bore him, both natures together, is shown to be truly his mother in time. For those who bear are truly called parents both because they bring a thing forth in time into being and because they bring it forth into being of such a kind. In this case the birth was not natural, so no one could even say that anything was stored up beforehand in potency for this birth, you great experts in nature! Otherwise it would no longer be the working of an astonishing miracle. And if no miracle beyond natural power bears witness to it, then neither will the one born according to natural powers be understood to be God.

"If God the Word was properly and truly born of a woman, then either the one born is subject to time or the woman is above time. But God is not subject to time, and the woman is not above time. Therefore God was not properly and truly born of a woman." But he is said to have been born of a woman and under time not into being but into being of such a kind, you prize babblers!

"If God the Word is truly the Son of the Virgin, he will be so according to substance, and will be what she who bore him is. She is a rational mortal animal. Therefore, on your view, God too will be a rational mortal animal." But a true son is understood in the account of every birth that makes a son, and so is everyone who is begotten as such by any kind of birth. Yet not every birth that shows those begotten to be true sons thereby also shows them to be like their begetters in every respect, as you yourselves said at the outset. If this very thing, likeness, constituted true sonship, then a man's portrait would be his son rather than the child born of his

substance, since the face in the portrait resembles him more than his own child's face does when compared with him. And how is it that a little earlier you said the cause was substance and not likeness? So the truth is this. If something's birth concerns its whole being and comes from the whole of being, then necessarily the whole begetter and the whole offspring will be alike. But if the birth of some composite concerns only its being of such a kind in one part, and its being in another part, then the likeness of the begotten to the begetter will not extend to its whole being. Even so, the one who begot would truly be the parent of its one person, partly as regards being and partly as regards being of such a kind. We see this in the case of man. His body has its birth into being from his parents. His soul has its birth from them not into being simply, for it has that from God, as the first-formed Adam did, but into being together with the body formed for it, without which it is also able to exist. It receives this from those who are, so to speak, causes of the body but only escorts who bring the soul to its bride. And yet the same people are called properly and truly the parents of both natures, as of one man. Why, then, do the mutterings of unbelief so muzzle you [?] that you will not rightly call the incarnate Word who was born God? For you confess without hesitation that the soul too, which was made flesh, was born from the causes of the flesh's being, and together with the body you call the same people its parents.

"But," he says, "we call the woman who bears a human being not 'soul-bearer' but 'human-bearer.' Why then do you not also prefer to say 'Christ-bearer'?" But, you people, "human" is the name of a nature, while "Christ" is the name not of a nature but of a person. How then should we signify the name of the nature of the one born by a personal name?

"But why then," he says, "is she not, in your view, Mother of a Man rather than Mother of God?" We must answer as follows. If, of Christ's two natures, the human prevailed over the divine before his death and after it, and if his birth had to be named after only one of his natures, then you would be right to say "Mother of a Man." But if the immutability of the divine nature always prevailed over the mutability of the human nature, and, changing it for the better, deified it together with itself (as iron is said to be fired, and not fire ironed), then surely the one born, or the birth, or she who bore him should be named after the nature that always remains the same in its own principles and transforms the other into itself, and not after the nature that is being transformed. Isn't that so, my good man?

"If God the Word was born of the Virgin, he was born in time. But everything born in time needs time to reach completion. Therefore, if God was born of the Virgin, he needed time to reach completion."

But, you wise men, not even the soul in itself needs time to reach completion. It is the soul's natural instrument and substantial dwelling that needs it. That is why, after a living being's youth, as time goes on, the instrument once again becomes less fit to serve the soul, for what flourishes with time also declines with time. So, contrary to what you say, the soul over time slackens again in its own activities and perfections: at a hundred, perhaps, it does not see or hear as it did at thirty. This clearly shows that what time made useful or useless for completion belonged not to the soul but to its instrument, and only then to the soul as well, by way of the instrument. How then can you say so carelessly that everything born in time needs time for its own completion? Do you not see that often what needs this is not the thing itself in the first place, but something that has been made its own by what is born in time and naturally united with it in substance? If not even the soul admits this argument of yours, how much less does God, who never even began to be, but only accepted in time being of such a kind? So in babbling these things at us out of an unbridled tongue you will wear yourselves out, and what you propose does not come from a sober mind.

"If the Father and the Holy Spirit are wherever God the Word is, because the substance is indivisible, and if, on your view, God the Word was in the Virgin's womb according to substance, then the Trinity was in the Virgin's womb." You who gather the seeds of every impiety to feed your own blasphemy, what are you saying? Since you are crooked, we must deal crookedly with you, as the Psalmist says. The Son is in the bosom of the Father, and that in which he is belongs to the Father, yet on your reasoning it is the Son himself. Or take it another way. Since the Son and the Spirit are wherever the Father is, and the Son is in the Father's bosom, the Son is also in his own bosom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. And since the Holy Spirit flew down like a dove at the Jordan when the Lord was baptized, the Father flew down too. But if the principle of piety does not force us to transfer these things from the one person to the other consubstantial hypostases, then either you will be required to understand the same about the holy conception of the Word, or you are advancing the argument behind your present difficulty by an arbitrary choice, since it has been agreed that these cases are alike. And so it will be enough for you to be muzzled on this point as well. You act with malice, put forward the inventions of other heresies, and do just what the proverb says, "The asp borrows poison from the viper," as though your own sophisms were not enough to make you completely heterodox. So you had to be refuted by meeting your puzzle with a puzzle, following the method the Lord used against the Pharisees' crafty question, when he asked them in return about the baptism of John.

Chapter 21. "If the Trinity is in the Virgin's womb according to substance, and God the Word was born of the Virgin according to substance, then the Trinity was born of the Virgin." Then, since the Son has been begotten of the Father, and the substance of the holy Trinity is indivisible, on your view the Father himself and the Holy Spirit have also been begotten. Further, since the Father has not been begotten of anyone and has not proceeded, on your view neither the Son nor the Spirit is from the Father, since their substance is indivisible. But we decline to be dragged around any further by your blasphemies, lest, while we are busy refuting you, we too grow used to lawless talk. For the present, then, we must stop you in your twisting this way. As for the doctrine of these matters, how it is to be stated and how it is to be understood, the truth has shown it to its own interpreters. In them it refutes those who wrongly divide and wickedly confuse the doctrine of the holy Trinity, which is beyond being.

"Every birth known to divine Scripture in which wholly unlike parents bring forth unlike offspring shows the one who bears to be worthy of praise or blame. Of praise, as in: 'Because of fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and gave birth.' Of blame, as in: 'Behold, he travailed with iniquity, conceived trouble, and brought forth lawlessness.' But everything that is praised or blamed for bearing bears its offspring by its will and not from its substance. Therefore every birth known to divine Scripture in which wholly unlike parents bring forth unlike offspring brings forth its offspring by will and not from substance." We must examine what kind of unlikeness you are proposing to us, unlikeness in substance or in some accident, and how what you have said could be true. If you mean essential difference, as in a natural quality, look: fire is generated from stones, iron and wood that strike fire. It is unlike them in substance and comes from things unlike it, yet it shows the one who bears to be worthy of neither praise nor blame. Caterpillars come from vegetables, and maggots from mice [?], though their parents are unlike them in substance, and this is neither blameworthy nor praiseworthy. Still, attending to your examples, we will take you to mean unlikeness in existence, and the unlikeness that is praised or blamed to be like lawlessness born from a man, or the Spirit of salvation being born. You hold that whatever bears unlike offspring is always worthy of praise or blame, and from this you infer that such a birth comes from the will. Perhaps your aim, you idle talkers, is to conclude from the unlikeness in the Master's case that his birth from the Mistress is said to be by will. First, remember that we have testified, on the contrary, to Christ's likeness to his mother, even if not in every respect, whereas lawlessness has no essential likeness in existence to the lawless man. Second, even his partial unlikeness to her is not the kind of unlikeness you have now proposed in your examples,

that of something subsistent to something without subsistence. It is rather the unlikeness of a substance of one kind to a substance of another kind. But let us also be carried along with the absurdity of your cleverness.
