If you think that everything in divine Scripture born from things unlike it in existence brings praise or blame on the one who bears it, what do you say about Benjamin, who is called son of pain, Barnabas, who is called son of consolation, and Eli, who is called an elder of years? It would necessarily follow that the years themselves bore Eli and are to be deemed worthy of praise or blame, and the same would hold for pain and consolation. Even if someone conceded these absurdities, how could he listen without tears to what you go on to teach: that years bear by will, or that pain and consolation give birth by will? And how could he hear you teach that the existence of Eli, Barnabas and Benjamin proceeded from something nonexistent, and from parents who bore them by will? Chapter 26. "If God the Word was born of the Virgin, and everything that is born is born either from the substance of the one who bears it or by will, and what is born from the substance always has its being from the one who bears it, while what is born by will sometimes has its being from the one who bears it and sometimes its being of such a kind, then tell us: from which do you claim God was born, from the substance of the Virgin, or by will? For whichever you say, the conclusion is clear." At long last, and against your will, you agree with us that there is a birth that brings something forth into being, and likewise a birth that brings something forth only into being of such a kind. But suppose you say that birth from substance causes only being, and not also being of such a kind [?], that is, the natural distinctness of what is begotten. Then, when a pine is born from a cone, is this very thing, a pine, born into being by will and not from the substance of the cone? Or is it born from the cone's substance and is simply a being, neither a pine nor any other species, unless it is also handed over to another begetter who bears by will for some further birth? What could be more foolish than that?

"If God the Word was begotten properly and truly of the Father and is like him in substance, and if the same Word was born properly and truly of a mother and is unlike her in substance, then it makes no difference whether one is begotten by those like one [in substance] or by those unlike one. If so, then neither will unlike things differ from one another in substance, and it would have been possible for God the Word, though truly begotten of the Father, to be unlike him in substance." All of this is impossible and worthy of the premise it rests on. "They were troubled, they reeled like a drunkard, and all their wisdom was swallowed up." We fittingly chant these words over you, as the divine power shows against you too the force of the rebuke it once delivered to those

who, like you, took up a purpose of fighting against God and set about building the tower in Babylon. "Come," he said then as well about them, "let us go down and confuse their tongues." This is truly why your present muddled, quibbling and piled-up patchwork babblings are contrived to hide the shame of your impiety. First, then, let us find out what you mean by birth from like or unlike parents. How is the likeness or unlikeness of the offspring to those who bear them to be understood? What has not yet come to subsist, and is not said to exist, cannot be said to have its birth from like or unlike parents, since by its own definition its likeness or unlikeness to them comes after its birth. Still, I will let this pass, since perhaps you said it judging from the outcome. What then? Is it impossible for one who was begotten by different births, from begetters of different natures, and who is himself different in his natures, to be truly born by each birth? Is it impossible for him to be shown like one of his parents in something of his own, and unlike the other, because his births are different and so are the substances of his that were begotten? We showed in the first part that even from the same substance, undifferentiated in every genus, species and number, what is born often turns out both like and unlike those who bear it, because the manner of birth differs. So those who rightly divide the truth say this. The Word was truly begotten of the Father, by the birth and substance proper to the Father alone, and is like him in substance as the Word of God. He was also truly born of a Mother, by the birth from her that is proper to her alone, and he is like his Mother in his substance as man, but unlike her as Word. Yet the Word is truly the Son both of the Father who is like him and of the Mother who is unlike him, for each manner of his births has been shown to be true, the birth into being and the birth into being of such a kind. Likeness alone does not constitute sonship, as has often been said. Otherwise all men, since they are like one another in substance, would be sons and fathers at once, begetters would be children of their own children, and brothers would be thought to be sons of their own brothers, because they are like them in substance.

"If what exists eternally is later truly begotten, then what does not exist at all, not existing in actuality, truly comes to be. But the second is impossible, and therefore so is the first." But even if what exists does not come to be insofar as it exists, what exists in a certain way can be born into existing in another way, if not by change then by a new assumption. No one has told you that something both exists eternally and begins in time in the same respect. So what prevents him who is understood to be without beginning in his being from having begun to be in another way, that is, incarnate? For his being in another way does not come about by ch-
…[?] or an outflow of what is its own, but, we say, by the assumption and essential union of something else that had formerly been separate from it.

“If it is impossible for heaven and earth and everything in them, which already exist, to come into being now, then it is utterly impossible for their Creator, begotten of the Father before the ages, to be born in the last times.” But no one says that what exists comes into being in the simple sense, sirs, or that heaven is simply begotten into existence. Rather, it is made new out of old, transformed, clothed in incorruption along with the rest of creation, and set free from its bondage to corruption. In the same way, all who are nurtured in true religion agree that our bodies too will put on life over what is mortal and rise incorruptible. So consider where your view leads. Since the world already exists in some way, namely as corruptible, we could no longer say that it comes to be incorruptible, or is born again. “What exists,” you say, “does not come into being.” You do not add the proviso that a thing does not become what it already is. Instead you refuse to allow even that something which in any way exists can become what it is not. By these decrees of yours, then, no one may any longer say that anything corruptible becomes incorruptible in accordance with our saving hope. Yet since man was born clothed in what is corruptible, we are born again clothed in what is incorruptible.

“If yesterday can become tomorrow, then let it also be possible for the one who exists eternally to be born in the last times. But the first is impossible, and the second even more so.” If we were saying that the same one came under time by a change in what is eternal, you would indeed have spoken well. But suppose he kept what he was, and by taking on something other than himself he gained in addition what he was not. Then what is now seen as the two together has come about through the joining of the new to what always exists, and formerly it was not conceived as it has now become: one and the same subject. How then can you reasonably object to us? Take the day you call “yesterday.” It never becomes “tomorrow” by a change, that is, it never stops being yesterday in relation to today and turns into the next day. But once tomorrow has come in turn after today, it will also acquire the status of “the day before yesterday,” while still remaining “yesterday” in relation to the day that follows it, just as it is “the day before yesterday” in relation to the third day after it.

“If what formerly did not exist can later exist without being begotten or made, then let it also be possible for what exists eternally to be truly begotten later. But the former is impossible, and so, therefore, is the latter.” Look, then: what the Word was, namely without flesh, we do not say came to be. What he was not, namely flesh and incarnate, we believe came to be. Up to this point [?] to be entangled in your tautologies.

“What is born from above, that is, by a second birth, is born of water and the Spirit, or else through teaching. What is born in this way is born into adoption, and what is born into adoption is not born from the essence of the one who begets it. Therefore what is born from above is not born from the essence of the one who begets it.” Tell us, then, what you mean by “birth from above.” Suppose you mean it in terms of place, as a birth above the earth and above those who are from the earth, and you understand it simply as some heavenly birth. Then, to pass over most of what could be said against you, the following must hold. More than any other birth, the birth of the Word from the Father is above the heavens, for “his life is taken away from the earth.” So you must regard this above all as the birth from above. It follows that the one born by this birth, namely the bare Word, must be thought of as born into adoption. On your view, then, he will not be the Son and Word of the Father by nature, of the same kind as the Father [?]. The further consequence of your premise is even plainer and even more impious. It follows that what is born in this way was not born from the essence. So on your view the Son is not from the essence of the Father either, and on top of your own false doctrine you have ratified the madness of Arius.

But perhaps you do not understand it in this way. Perhaps you take “birth from above” to be a kind of repetition of the first birth, and by “from above” you mean the same birth of the same subject happening twice, in the sense of “over again,” so that you understand it simply as rebirth or second birth. Here again you have strayed far from orthodoxy, for you apply and attribute rebirth to Christ. Rebirth is spoken of in the case of those who have suffered some aging, filth or disease, which has somehow debased, corrupted or withered the being they received from their first birth, though it was once undefiled. So it was with us: our being in the image of God, which comes from our first birth, was damaged by the first transgression and by later attachments to worse things. But no one, not even the most lawless, has ever thought that God the Word, through some carelessness or plot, grew old in sin in his first birth, so that he now needed a rebirth to renew him and underwent the second birth for that reason. No one says or thinks that he had a rebirth, or birth from above. Instead, all the holy confess his second birth together with his first. How then have you transferred rebirth to God the Word, in place of a true birth that is second in order, so that you could draw your conclusion against us from it?

Furthermore, we do not understand how you came to think that what is born of the Spirit is not from the essence. Either it is like the activity in a piece of wood, which comes from the nature of the carpenter, or it is like fire kindled from fire in wood, which comes from the essence. If it is like the first, then clearly the one begotten will be unable to do anything, just as this activity

in the wood cannot do the carpenter's work. If it is like the second, then clearly the fire begotten in the wood will also be able to do the work of fire. And if so, the one begotten has received a share in the essence that bore it. Its natural activity, which follows from that essence in this case too, plainly bears witness to this. And if it has received a share of the essence, but the birth is not from the essence and comes instead from an activity without essence, then things without essence will prevail over essence and be the causes of essences, which [?]

“If God the Word was properly and truly born of the Virgin and is unlike her, and the same one was properly and truly born of the Father, what prevents him from being unlike the Father as well, since neither the births differ in kind nor does the one born differ at all?” Now if the births really did not differ in kind, and the offspring were wholly the same in each birth, your argument would have force for you. But the difference between the births is great. One is understood as eternal, the other as having a beginning. One is bodiless, the other in a body. One involves no interval, the other involves interval. In short, one is the birth of the Word bare and simple, the other the birth of Christ who is composite. One takes place without gestation, the other through gestation. And they differ in countless other incomparable ways. How then, tell us, do you conclude that in each birth of the one and the same Son he must be unlike those who bore him, as though his births were of the same kind? Learn where you are stumbling without noticing it, sirs, if you do not want to keep fighting against the truth forever. Because each birth is called a birth properly and truly, you think the one is the same as the other and take both births to be of the same kind. You do not consider that each is a birth properly and truly according to its own definition, not according to the definition of the other. If everything that is said to be such-and-such properly and truly had to be considered of the same kind, then the following would hold. A stone is properly and truly called a body, the sun is properly and truly called a body, and God is properly and truly called bodiless; so you ought to think that the stone, the sun and God are of the same kind. Likewise a man and a frog, since both are living things and each is properly and truly called so. And water, which is truly called lifeless, would have to be thought of the same kind as heaven and millet and all other things, and you would have banished all unlikeness. In fact each thing is properly and truly what it is according to its own definition, even if its name is sometimes used homonymously of something else, as though it were that thing.

“God the Word was truly born of the Virgin. Now every birth that is not blameworthy, whether it gives being to the one born or not, makes what is begotten either equal in essence to the one who begets it, or less. It is equal, as in ‘he begot a son after his own likeness’; and also, ‘In Christ Jesus through the Gospel

I begot you.’ It is less, as in the birth of the faithful from God. In no case is it greater. So God is either equal in essence to the Virgin or less. But both are impious. Therefore God was not truly born of the Virgin.” It is true that every birth that is not blameworthy shows the one born to be equal or inferior to the one who begot it. But you who are blind to the greatness of the divine economy, consider this. That holds for every birth that is not blameworthy and also not marvelled at as something beyond nature. But the case is different with the Word of the economy, which befits God. This, this indeed is the surpassing mystery of his goodness and the proof of God's love for humanity: the Maker of all creation, the cause of every birth, the Master of all nature, the power above the world that rules the whole world, accepted birth, and birth from a nature that is perishable, corruptible and easily harmed; and though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich. If this really were one of the births that are not marvelled at, then this birth, which is not blameworthy, would have to follow that rule. But if it was meant to be marvelled at as well, it must have something beyond the ordinary birth of all beings. Otherwise it could not easily be shown to you to be divine. If you must reason from universal premises and from wholly similar cases, wise men, then show us that every birth marvelled at as this one is, and resembling it, makes the offspring inferior or equal to the one who bore it. Who will not weep over your blindness? The very things that ought to convince you about the divine Birth are the features that are paradoxical, beyond nature and beyond the ordinary. Yet you use them in your rush to establish that the birth is not God's, because it is not like our corruptible, natural births. It is as if, on your view, had he been born by a birth like ours, it would then be credible that the one born is above us. And if not even then, tell us, sirs: by what should God have convinced us about this birth of his, if not by what belongs to our condition, nor by what is above us?

“If birth from wholly like parents is true birth, a birth that truly produces offspring like the parents in essence, then a birth that produces offspring wholly unlike in essence [?] is not truly a birth. For contraries are never true together. But the first holds; therefore the latter is not true birth.” Birth from like parents and birth from unlike ones, birth into being and birth into being of a certain kind, and any other mode of birth there may be, each is a birth and is truly called one in divine Scripture according to its own definition. Even you have often said so up to now. But you grant that it is a birth and still say that a birth not from beings alike in essence is not a birth properly and truly. If so, you must recognize true birth by the likeness of the parents, not by the definition of birth. This was already said to you, as it had to be, a little earlier. How could a frog that is unlike another be born from a like

frog? And yet a frog is never born from a frog at all [?]. But since in your perplexity you keep rolling back to the same arguments, hear this as well, in addition to what we said before. A flame comes from the essence of fire, a grain from the essence of a grain, a man from the essence of a man, and God from the essence of God. All of these are agreed to be from the essence. Yet the offspring do not all have the same pure likeness to those who beget them; God alone has a likeness that is in every way exact. How then can the birth of each of these be called a birth equally, properly and truly, even though it is from the essence? On your view, since the likeness on which you base your claim that a birth is proper and true differs from case to case, you must regard the propriety of birth as differing too. That is obviously ridiculous. What is proper is no longer different, and what differs is never proper in the same respect. Understand this, you natural philosophers, or rather you who are puffed up: stones, iron and wood beget fire, though they are not fire and do not beget it in the way fire does. Yet no one, not even someone like you, would say that what comes forth from natures unlike it is not the birth of true fire. So the whole jumbled mess of your chatter has come to nothing.

We must also hear this argument of theirs. “If the Word is without flesh and immutable according to his natural definition,” they say, “how can the same one become incarnate and remain immutable? For then one could say that he changed and yet still remained immutable. Either God did not become flesh, in which case she who bore the flesh is not Theotokos. Or he himself became flesh, in which case one who is not immutable is no longer God, and the mother of what is mutable is in no way Theotokos.” Why then, since you have gone so completely deaf, do the words of the Son of Thunder not ring in your ears at all: “And the Word became flesh”? Sirs, if you understand the Word made flesh as a change of nature, as when we say the coral plant has turned to stone, or a creature that was formerly alive has died, then you could reasonably be thought to have done away with his immutability. But we say a piece of wood is gilded and a man is armed because of the wood's union with the gold and the man's taking up and putting on of arms. If we understand the Word's assumption of flesh in the same way, how are we introducing a change of nature into him? The wood that is gilded in its subsisting nature is still without gold by nature. The man is still without iron by nature, or to put it better, [still smooth by nature, though grown hairy] [?], whether he is a hoplite clad in iron in his natural hypostasis or a man growing hairy in his prime. Just so the Word remains without flesh by nature, that is, in his essential definition, while he is clothed with flesh that has come upon his natural hypostasis. For immutability of nature is seen in the essential definitions, not in what has come upon the essence. The nature stays the same in its definitions, and what is added is considered in relation to the hypostasis.

Those who know how to say anything at all, so long as they need not agree with the truth, also say the following, and we must also deal with their unwritten arguments. “Look,” they say, “even on your own premises and arguments it is permissible to name someone's mother from a part and in a certain respect. You do not hold that God was born from her without flesh. Why then do you oppose us when we call this Virgin Anthropotokos, ‘mother of a man,’ from a part? You have assigned her the name Theotokos alone as her special title, and you do not even accept those who call her, more fittingly and from the whole, Christotokos.” To this we reply, first: How can you wretches call the holy Virgin Anthropotokos from a part, when you refused to call her Theotokos from a part? The arguments someone uses to reject his opponents' names cannot also serve to put forward his own, unless he does it by sheer authority. Second, you will hear from us that it is quite plainly the custom of divine Scripture to name the whole from those parts that appear to predominate in a composite. It is agreed that all human beings consist of soul and body. Yet when one part of that composite had come to dominate the life and conduct of men, it was said: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” Certainly those who lived carnally at that time were not without souls; the nature of the flesh had simply prevailed. Again, Scripture records that Jacob went down into Egypt with [?] souls. Obviously they did not arrive there without bodies; rather, Jacob's descendants were credited with a way of life that followed the better part of man, until the sons of Israel multiplied and became very numerous. So it is right, and in keeping with piety and the sacred words, that we call the whole Christ God because the divine part predominates. Above all, we see the most distinctive mark of God, which is sinlessness, in him as a whole and not in one part only. Moreover, every action befitting God is in him as a whole

Third, we say to you: All proper names, especially those given for their meaning, signify their bearer by some distinctive mark that sets him apart from others of the same kind, so that the person to whom the name belongs is understood distinctively. How then can you want to call the Virgin who became Mother of God the Word Anthropotokos? Every other woman among human beings who has given birth is called and signified by this name. It is not the name of some particular woman but of every woman. How then can it be a proper name for the Virgin? What belongs to hypostases must be distinctive. And how does someone who calls her by a common name signify her distinctively, as particular names usually indicate a particular individual? Even if it is taken as an epithet, a distinctive

epithet must be convertible with the subject it names. That is how it is with things that have two names, two names properly assigned to one person, such as the sun, which is also Hyperion, and the moon, which is also “the full moon.” These epithets cannot be taken as common to other things as well. To put it more clearly: Anthropotokos and Theotokos are epithets applied to persons. Epithets are either common or distinctive. Common ones are like “Philopator,” “lover of his father,” for one Ptolemy, and “Philadelphus,” “lover of his brother,” for another; for there have been and could be others of the same kind as them who love their fathers and brothers, practically everyone in fact. Distinctive ones are like “motherless” for Adam alone, and “strong in his hair” for Samson alone, as distinct from all who share their nature. Now the epithet Anthropotokos cannot be applied to the immaculate Virgin as a distinctive epithet, since there are countless other women who have borne a human being. And if someone applies it to her as a common epithet, as it applies to others, then, if it is truly common, it must be used in the same way of all to whom it is applied and must signify the same thing in exactly the same way in every respect. Things will not be synonymous unless they share both the name and the thing that is the cause of the name. So either all the other women who are called Anthropotokoi along with her must also have borne some God-men like Christ, so that they too are so called from a part, as she is, and not from the whole. Or else she too did not bear a man united with God, so that she is called Anthropotokos not from a part but from the whole. But she is not called so from the whole, and they are not called Anthropotokoi from a part. She did not bear a mere man, and they never bore one united with God. How then can the name Anthropotokos apply to them in common? Since this name fits the Lady neither distinctively nor in common, it is agreed that the holy Theotokos could not truly be called Anthropotokos on any account. But the name that belongs distinctively to her alone may be applied from a part, how or from where [?], since it does not lead to any homonymy with another woman, as was shown in the case of Anthropotokos. We must also consider this further point. Names of persons signify the particular hypostasis of a certain individual, and so they are meant to be drawn not from common features that others share but from features particular to the named person and belonging to that person alone. Women are without number, those who have borne a human being are countless, virgins are innumerable, and there are a great many Marys. So the only name that is most distinctive, most proper and most significant for the holy, immaculate and ever-glorious Virgin is Theotokos. Her opponents could learn this from themselves, if they have not hardened themselves for nothing but strife. If they themselves simply heard “the woman,” or “the Virgin,” or “the holy one,” their imagination would not yet settle on any one particular person. But if the word “Theotokos” sounded in their ears, since there is no other such woman, they would at once and without doubt look to this Mother of God, convinced that what was said concerned her. And so

…so much for these points. But let them tell us how they themselves mean to call her “mother of a man” in part. Scripture has called a human being by the name of the soul alone, and by the name of the flesh alone, and so does everyone in common usage. Yet if she is not truly Mother of God even in part, and until now she has been called neither “mother of a man” nor “Mother of God” in part, she will be childless or nameless, at least as far as the natural name of the one born is concerned [?]. “Christ” is a personal name, not a natural one, nor the name of a species, so calling her “mother of Christ” does not name her from his nature. It is the name of a person, as if Elizabeth were called “mother of John.” That is not what we are now asking. We are asking how she might be named from the nature of the one born. Someone might say further that “God-bearer” is also a common name, taken from the nature of the one born, and that it applies both to the Father and to the Mother of the Lord. On this view, either his birth must be regarded as alike in both cases, or the name must be assigned to the more proper of the two. Now the Father alone brings forth the Son as God and into being, even if timelessly and eternally. So why would the Father not rather be called “God-begetter” properly and alone, with no one sharing the name with him? But it is quite clear that the Father cannot be called a begetter in respect of the essence. One divine essence did not beget another divine essence that is numerically different, for that would be tritheism. Rather, the one essence has distinct properties, and within it one of these is the cause of another. For example, the capacity for mind and knowledge in David's essence is the cause of his property of being musical. It is not the cause of another, musical essence as an essence, for the unmusical also have an essence. Suppose, then, that you were at some point to say “mother of Christ” instead of “mother of a man,” as though you had all but let go of your impiety. Even so, we shall say that this name does not signify what is most properly hers. In Israel very many were called “christs”: kings and priests anointed with perceptible oil, and prophets anointed by divine operation and by divine appointment, such as Cyrus, king of the Persians. These have many mothers, and so even in this way she will not be distinguished. She will share one common title with all those women under the same epithet. The name “Christ” indicates a composite reality made up of an anointing and the one anointed. It does not indicate of what nature either the anointing or the anointed is. So we cannot name her in this way either, if we want to distinguish her by her proper and particular name from those who share her name, whether in the same sense or in a different one. We must therefore name the immaculate Virgin from what truly belongs to her alone, apart from all other women. This is that she truly gave birth to one who is God by nature, through a birth that was not natural to God but freely undertaken by him. This is why we say that the Virgin is truly Mother of God. We add that the birth was not from seed and not according to nature, and it was like that of no other human being. It was shown to be divine, passing virginally through the unbroken womb. How then could she not be called properly Mother of God from the very manner of the birth? In addition, let us also say

that many parents have often received epithets from how their children turned out. Thus we call a woman “mother of famous children,” “mother of kings,” “mother of fair offspring.” Yet the virtue or worthy deed did not come forth with the infant from the start. It appeared later and conferred the name on the parents. We too, even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now know him so no longer. The Word of God in him is God by nature, and after the resurrection his natural flesh was wholly deified. So we cannot contemplate anything of his, or about him, bare of divinity, either in part or by any line of reasoning. Even what in him is not divine by nature has been granted the name that is above every name, since this Jesus whom the Jews crucified has become Lord and God. Of necessity, then, we no longer name the all-holy one “mother of a man.” We name and venerate her as Mother of God alone. We know that the one who came forth from her is divine partly by essence and partly by participation, and we glorify and worship him whole as perfect God. We also know that the humanity which was deified in the Christ born of her has been preserved, as has that which was ineffably made flesh. The one has been deified by being exalted, not by being abolished; the other has been made flesh by good pleasure, not by change. “But what,” they say, “if some names are used as if in part?” We, however, do not name Christ God as if in part. Even if the divinity is called a part of Christ in order to make his composition clear, the Word is understood to be more perfect than every part and than the whole. We do not say that the Word is less than Christ, but that he is simpler. Consider what is called a part but is seen to be the cause of the other part combined with it. It also holds that other part together and governs it, and it governs their union with itself and the manner of their composition. It leads its own whole rather than being led by that whole as a part, as nature does in other composites. How then would it not properly and truly, more than the other part, and more than what is thought of as the whole formed in respect of it, [?] from itself the name of the person and of the entire compound subsisting around it? [?] Now you too, when you name Christ, know that the Lord and God himself is signified, and by either of the names you think of him no less in terms of divinity. Why then are you displeased with the word “Mother of God” instead of “mother of Christ”? And why do you want to call her rather “mother of Christ,” as if from the whole? If Christ is the same as God, then the name “mother of Christ” is the same as “Mother of God.” But if you know God to be something other than Christ, you are confessing this first blasphemy of yours. Then we would no longer debate the second with you as Christians, as you would be like Jews, utterly faithless and impious once for all. But since, with God's help, these things have been rightly confessed and demonstrated to you, it is holy, just and true that the holy Virgin Mary be hymned as truly Mother of God in

heaven and venerated on earth, with sober reasoning, an undefiled mind and pure lips. She is called blessed by all, now and to all the generations of the ages. Amen. This, then, is our answer to you who reject the true, fitting and most proper name of the holy Virgin, Mother of God.

CHAPTER [?]. They dare to argue that Christ is not reasonably called God either. “The Word was God; he became man. If the Virgin is Mother of God, clearly the Virgin is Mother of what the Word was, not of what he became. But if it is on account of the man that he has a mother, and the man does not have a Mother, then neither can the Word have a mother.” But the Virgin is mother both of what the Word was and of what he became. She is mother of both at once, though not in the same way. She is mother of the Word because he began his incarnation from her, and mother of the flesh because it began its existence from her.

“According to the prophet, the name Emmanuel is the name of a sign: the one born of the Virgin and given to the house of David. But according to the Egyptian, Emmanuel is the name of God, the giver of the sign.” But Emmanuel is not a sign. It is a name signifying a certain subsistence, the one in which God has come to be with us human beings. And how has he come to be with us, unless he was formerly separated from us? Yet God was never separated from us by operation, by relation or by place. It was by nature, then. So he has now been united to our nature by nature, and is truly with us. A sign, however, has not come to be “with us.” Even if someone were to say that the sign is “in us,” it is not “with us.” Everyone agrees that “Emmanu” signifies “with us” in Hebrew. Where have they ever heard that “El” signifies a sign, rather than plainly meaning “God”?

“The nature of those who are born is nowhere indicated by the names given to them. Given names signify what is accidental to the nature, and the name Emmanuel is such a name, since it was given. Therefore, against the Egyptian, the title Emmanuel does not show the nature of the one who received it. It shows that God's alliance is with those who received Emmanuel as a sign of it.” But no other proper name either, not even “Lord” as some say [?], simply indicates a nature. By a proper name I mean one applied to the subsistence of a single person. Such a name does not direct the mind to the essence, either by definition or by signification, as do the names that some call common names and appellatives. Nor does it signify something shared by many in some way. For on hearing “Xanthus” one can picture a horse, a river or a man. Personal names always indicate hypostases through certain features that are given to the essences and accidental to them. So Emmanuel too is applied to a person, the person through whom it has come about that we have communion with God, since he is the mediator between God and

human beings. If the name is applied to the alliance, then the thing named, the subject of “Emmanuel,” is the alliance. In that case, if the prophet says that what the Virgin will bear shall be called by the name Emmanuel, the maiden who conceived in her womb gave birth to an alliance, not to a nature or a hypostasis. But since this is absurd, we shall understand that what the name signifies is some self-subsistent existence.

“If the Virgin is Mother of God because she gave birth to the true God, then the true God is also true God because he was born of a virgin.” This does not follow. Suppose something is named derivatively, or by a name that describes it. Suppose too that its participation in, or connection with, the cause of the name has already been acknowledged as true. The name from which the participation or derivation comes may be applied to what participates or is derivatively named either absolutely or relatively. Even so, it does not follow that this absolute or relative name must be convertible with the name taken from elsewhere. One who loves justice is truly called a lover of justice. That does not mean that justice is in turn called justice because it is loved by man, for injustice too is loved by man. What is just is just for a different reason: in itself and in its own right. The lover of justice is so called for another reason, as standing in a certain relation, namely to justice. So she is aptly named Mother of God as having borne God. But he is God neither by a descriptive name nor from something else, for his name comes to him from his own nature.

“If the Word became flesh by changing into flesh, clearly the Word has a Creator and a Mother. But if the Word became flesh without change, how can the Word, who does not change, be acted upon and born as though he changed?” He is indeed born by a certain kind of birth, but he is not refashioned. Nor does he simply remain bare, and he is not born into being. Nor does he remain such that he is described in every respect exactly as before. Rather, he is enfleshed and is henceforth of this kind. His hypostasis has in some way been altered, if I may dare to say so. This is not by a change in the Word's properties, nor in those that are his as God. It is by the reception and co-assumption of other properties, those of Jesus, the properties of a man. This happens in the one and same hypostasis of the Word himself. That hypostasis has been increased and enriched with natural and hypostatic properties beyond all the persons consubstantial with it on either side. So he is also fashioned, though not at all as Word, but as the Word who is also Christ. And this is in respect of a part of himself, namely the flesh alone.

“What does not belong to the divinity of the Word does not belong to the Word either. How then can the Egyptian deny a second beginning of birth to the Word's divinity, yet grant it to God the Word?” Because his hypostasis has a second beginning. It is the hypostasis in which he is understood as the Word, being God by nature. It is no longer understood as simple and of one nature among the divine persons, but as composite, of two natures, and

“The Egyptian separates God the Word from the divinity and teaches that he is born of the Virgin in the flesh. Yet he says it is the height of madness to subject his divinity to the same fleshly birth to which he subjected God the Word.” It is not to birth simply that God must not be subjected, but to fleshly birth: that is, a birth involving flux, which brings something wholly into being.

“If the Word is God by his divinity and man by his humanity, how is the Word born not as what he is in the flesh, but as what he is in his divinity? For the Egyptian teaches the term ‘Mother of God’ and anathematizes those who say ‘mother of a man.’” The Word is indeed born as what he is in the flesh. But the woman who bore him cannot be properly named by the other of these names, the lesser one. That is a common name belonging to all women, and under it she would be just like all of them.

“Read the ordinance of the law about the purification of women who give birth, which the Virgin fulfilled, and learn. When the law commanded what it said, and the Virgin fulfilled these commands, was it God that the law purified, or a man? For the law says: ‘If a woman conceives and bears a male, she shall be unclean seven days, as in the separation of her blood; and for thirty-three days she shall remain in her pure blood. She shall touch nothing holy and shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification are fulfilled. When the days of her purification are fulfilled, she shall bring an unblemished lamb or two young pigeons to the door of the tent of witness, and the priest shall offer one for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering, and he shall cleanse her from the flow of her blood; and after that she shall enter the holy place.’ Luke the evangelist testifies that the Virgin fulfilled this ordinance, saying: ‘And when they had fulfilled the days of their purification, they brought him up to the temple to present him to the Lord, and to give two young pigeons.’” Many impieties follow from this objection. Unless the legal purifications of the flesh are types of spiritual things, they cannot have been imposed on others until the coming of Christ himself, the true purifier of all; and they were not imposed on Christ. Otherwise, by purifying Christ himself, who made purification for our sins, they present the law as stronger and holier than Christ, who abolished the law of commandments. Why then did he need to come and abolish the law himself? Yet what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. He not only purified sin but also condemned it in his flesh. So Christ, having the power of all purification in his God-woven flesh, fulfils

all the ordinances of the law in the flesh. He does this to free the root of the flesh from the law's condemnation and curse, and to make it worthy of the spiritual way of life he purposed to grant it. But if he needed these things as the offspring of a man, then he also needed circumcision, John's baptism of repentance and the rest. And if he truly needed the baptism of repentance, it was certainly as a sinner, for repentance is not for the righteous who deserve praise. But if Christ performs certain things without needing them, clearly he does this to fulfil all righteousness in his economy according to the flesh. He also does it to show his own divinity by the very fulfilment of the law, since all fleshly nature was too weak to fulfil it and the divine essence alone accomplished it.

“In every case, conception and birth bring into being one who did not exist. But according to the Egyptian, the Virgin gave birth not to the man but to the true God. Clearly, then, she gave birth to one who did not exist. And if the one who was newly formed, newly born and newly named is also himself God, then of necessity he is also a new God. Divine Scripture cries out, ‘Let there be no new god among you,’ but the Egyptian cries back, ‘Let there be!’ and anathematizes those who do not say there is a new God.” Consider the one who says, “My children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you,” and “Through the gospel I begot you.” Consider also the covenant from Mount Sinai that bears children for slavery. Do these signify that some who did not exist at all were born? Or that those who already existed were born so as to exist in another way? He is speaking not of essence, but of the Spirit added to it. If so, it is clear that not every birth simply brings the nonexistent into being. Some can also be born into a new way of being.

“Whoever does not confess the Virgin as mother of Christ does not confess Christ to be what he is either. For the birth from the Virgin is the opening of what is told about Christ.” But “mother of Christ” is not a title that properly marks out the holy Virgin. The mothers of David and Samuel and of the priests could rightly be called mothers of christs, and so could the mothers of all the prophets, especially Jeremiah's. For it was said to him, “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you.” And John leapt in Elizabeth's womb, rejoicing in the Lord. Clearly these were anointed and shared in the sanctifying Spirit while they were still in the womb. So the prophets were the Lord's anointed from the time they were conceived and born. But she alone is properly Mother of God who gave birth to the very Spirit that overshadowed her and dwelt in her, and that was conceived with the flesh taken from her into the hypostasis of one such [?Son]. For she gave birth not merely to one who was sanctified, but to the Holy One born of her, who also sanctifies. That is why he was called the Son not of her alone, but also of God. CHAPTER [?]. “We will not take it upon ourselves to call the mother of Jesus Mother of God, since holy Scripture nowhere [?]

calls her that, nor do any of the Fathers. Instead we follow the voice of the angel, who said to the shepherds, ‘To you is born this day Christ the Lord,’ and the saying, ‘The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ,’ and also, ‘But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth.’ So we call her mother of a man by nature and mother of Christ by dignity. Unlike you, we do not rashly lay down as law what we have not received.” When Scripture expressly and properly calls Christ God, you explain it away and take in another sense what is said word for word. But when Scripture leads to a conclusion by its meaning, without saying it word for word, as in the case of “Mother of God,” you demand the literal wording. Clearly you are trying by every means to flee orthodoxy alone. For if you may not say anything that is not explicitly found in Scripture, then you may not say that the Father begot the Word without flux. Nor may you say that the Holy Spirit is of one nature with the Father and the Son, that God created fire or the air, or that he did not create darkness. Nor may you say that the souls of bloodless ants, crabs, wasps and the like are mortal, along with countless other things, you people. But let us let all that go. You yourselves call her mother of a man or mother of Christ as though by divine oracle. Where will you show us this written in holy Scripture concerning the holy Virgin? If it is nowhere, then clearly you have been caught in the very thing you pretend to avoid while pursuing others. Perhaps you take care not to address her by this or by any other name derived from the birth. Then either you have no idea at all about the one who was born, and how can you lay down doctrine about what you do not know? Or you do have an idea but are ashamed to display your own opinions to us in spoken words. Is that what is happening to you? We, however, following the Apostle, pray with God's help to speak boldly in the gospel, as we ought to speak. For we are not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.

CHAPTER 1. “When, then,” they say, “do you consider the whole of Christ to be God? Immediately from his birth, or after the resurrection? If immediately from his birth, do you then consider Christ to have always been impassible and immortal? Who then suffered and died, was buried and [?] the rest of what is human? Unless what is said about Christ was an illusion. But if the whole of Christ was not God from the beginning, from his birth, then on your view there was a time when the Word was not wholly God [?] whole [?]…”

LEONTIUS OF BYZANTIUM

[?] ...of Christ, we know him to be always God, because of the Word in him, and also man; but of the Word simply and alone, we know the whole to be always God, as being the Word's. When, then, do they themselves say that Christ, whom they call a man by nature, received such [?] glory and grace, adoption and the dignity of divine honour, and "the name that is above every name"? For they confess that he had these from the very beginning, straight from his conception. And what is the benefit of these great gifts if they did not deliver him from suffering, or dishonour, or death? For he would still be subject to suffering if he has acquired nothing more now; or else, having then suffered for someone else and through someone else, he has become free of sufferings. Let them tell us, then, who it was that suffered on behalf of Christ and of us. But if he obtained these things after the resurrection, then there was a time when he was not even in the adoption by grace, and the honour and dignity, that they speak of; and at that time they show him to be in every way a mere man like us. So then what was done to him at that time does not redound to the Word by any appropriation or reference whatsoever. How, then, is it said of the Word that "he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant," and that he "despised the shame" of death? How, too, can it be said, "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory"? And how at that time was "You are the Son of the living God" confessed by Peter, and "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" attested by the Father? So they themselves are not free of their own difficulty. We, however, say that although the hypostatic union of the Word and the flesh took place from the beginning in the holy womb of the Virgin, it was nevertheless the good pleasure of the Word himself that his natural majesty should share the poverty of the flesh throughout its whole life. He did this so that the Word, who does all things with reason, and not by seizure or injustice, might himself, justly, through the whole of his spotless life, exalt together with himself the humanity united to him, which after the death of the flesh became the firstfruits of spiritual immortality and of everlasting honour and blessedness. That is why Christ, asking glory from the Father in the person of his humanity, and saying in the person of the Word that it was such glory as he had before the foundation of the world, and proclaiming himself, the glorious one, to be at the same time without glory, heard: "I have glorified" already—that is, through the wondrous birth from the Virgin and the other divine signs—"and I will glorify again"—that is, through the resurrection after death, and incorruption, and mastery over the world, and authority over all things and supreme exaltation, in short through a like deification, and through the glory before the world of the Word who is in him.

But again they say: How, if the living Word of God is in Christ, does the Apostle say of Christ that he both died and was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures? And how is he again compared with us in the words, "For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised"? For it is clear that he too became dead as we do; and the other things

attested of him show the same. But they themselves know, though they now wilfully forget their own distinctions, that often [?] but only the body. These things, then, are clearly said of the human element in Christ; otherwise how could the words "free among the dead" also be said of the same one? And how, if as you say he became dead in no way differently from us, did he himself raise his own temple in three days—he who, as they say, became entirely inactive in body and soul, like every human being after death? For in their earlier arguments they did not grant human beings any activity of the soul whatever after death until the resurrection, much less divine action. And how, if he himself has authority to lay down his own life and to take it up again, did he become dead as we do? For who among men has ever possessed not merely such dignity but such authority? Moreover, if it was not God who was in Christ, in his death and suffering and in everything else, reconciling the world to himself, as it is written, how did he who was in the form of God humble himself to the point of death—he himself and no other, not through another? And how did they truly crucify the Lord of glory? And how is it said, "God raised the Lord, and will also raise us by his power"—the power, admittedly, of the one who was raised? For since the power of the Lord is clearly able to raise the dead and other bodies, much more did it raise its own body, to which it was united hypostatically; for it is this power, acting more immediately, and no other life-giving power, that would raise it. And how is the Father said not to have spared his own Son, but to have given him up for us all? For if he gave a substitute, these things are not truly said [?] of his love towards us. It is clear, then, that both the [immortality?] and the death are each said of Christ in respect of a part; for both are not said in the same way of the whole, since contraries are never true of the same thing at the same time. If, then, those who hanged Christ on a tree truly crucified the Lord of glory, it is clear that the same one had his being Lord of glory from the divine Word, and his being truly crucified from the human flesh. For by nature, as God, he is owed glory from all, and he alone has authority over it, glorifying whom he will; and by nature, as man, he endured suffering.

CHAPTER [?]

"What then?" he says. "Is it not said most plainly of Christ that he was raised by God and not by himself? And that through his resurrection from the dead, accomplished by the Holy Spirit, he was defined as Son of God? How else has it been said, 'He whom God raised did not see corruption'; and 'who was defined as Son of God according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead'?" But let those who think themselves searchers of the Scriptures tell us: if rising from the dead through the divine Spirit by itself secures the glory of Son of God for the one who rises, how is it that the widow's son in the time of Elijah, and the Shunammite woman's son in the time of Elisha, and Tabitha in the time of Peter, and the others who rose from the dead, were not defined as sons?

For clearly these too rose by the power of God and through the Spirit of holiness, who was at work in those who raised them, since there is no one who has authority over life and death except the Lord, who alone is by nature the life-giving Spirit. For in God alone was life, and he puts to death and gives life, he kills and makes alive, he brings down to Hades and brings up again. It is clear, then, that by raising himself the Lord showed himself to be [the Son?] of God, not dying together with his human part, since he was immortal God, but exercising in respect of a part his properly divine activity and giving life to his part that had died. And this is "the surpassing greatness of God's power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead." For this power, imparted to us as well through partaking of his holy body, also gives life to our mortal bodies after death, through his divine Spirit who dwells in us. So it is clear that the Lord was not glorified as Son of God simply because he rose, but because he rose by his own power. For the Spirit of holiness had already raised very many other dead people, both before and after Christ, and in their case it is not said to have displayed its surpassing greatness as it did in this act of might. It was not, then, without reason, nor from some ordinary glory, nor indeed on the basis of any accidental property, that Christ was defined as Son of God, but from the activity he exercised in the resurrection of his own body, by which he showed that his power is truly divine, and from his power, his essence. For the terms or definitions of the things under discussion are drawn from their essential principles, O you who are wise in your own eyes; and all this ought not to have escaped your ignorant erudition. This very thing, then, proclaims most clearly that Christ, the Son of David, is also the Son of God, because by the very activity he exercised in his resurrection he has been shown to be like God in essence. And we have this as proof that he is the most genuine Son, by nature, of God the Father. In this way, then, he was defined as Son of God according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead.

"But you," he says, "who do not consider the apostle and high priest of our faith, as Paul commands you, tell us: what priest do you know who was ever of the same nature as the one to whom he ministers as priest? Or what apostle who is not subordinate to the one who sent him? Either, then, the one of whom these things are said, being the Word, is himself inferior to God in nature and rank, as Arius holds; or, if he is not, he must be someone other than the Word himself, understood as the minister and servant of God by the working of the Word." But why do you pass over the loftier statements about the Godhead and bring forward to us only these humbler statements about the humanity? For we too say that the same Christ, whom we know to be the Creator of all things, is a creature of God; but not in respect of the same element among those that are in him, since we obviously hold these to be truly unequal. That is why we know the same Christ to be God, priest and sacrifice. For do not suppose that, because he is called a priest,

he is therefore to be understood only as a servant and minister of God, according to the sense that applies to every priest. Rather, listen to the same Apostle speaking again of the same priest: "We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens." Consider among yourselves this very point that you raised against us: it does not belong to a priest to share the throne of the one to whom he ministers [?], and to share his honour and glory, but to someone equal in nature and in power to the glorious God. So it is not as priest that he who became God's priest on earth, offered his own flesh to God, and brought it up to God, sits with God in heaven, but because he, the same one, is also truly God.

We must also examine the argument that they attempt in many places, though obscurely and timidly. "Let it be granted," they say, "that on your view the same Christ is also God by a coming together. But what do you take Jesus to be? For surely you will not say that he too is Word and flesh. For if he too is likewise God, clearly Christ is not always God. For it is plainly said that this Jesus, whom you call God, God made both Lord and Christ. So Jesus did not become, by being made Christ and Lord, what he already was, namely Lord; for no one becomes what he is. Therefore Jesus is not always God either, since he is not always Lord. But if you understand Jesus to be man and Christ to be God, then either Christ will be God only, like the Word, and the Word will be Christ even before the incarnation; or he will be God and some other man besides Jesus, and there will be two men appearing in him after Jesus was made Christ: one of them composite in hypostasis, as you say, and the other, Jesus, a Christ who was made. But if Christ is understood to be truly God and man, then Jesus, having taken on an acquired humanity and the Godhead of Christ, would show himself, on becoming Christ, to be three men and two gods; or else Jesus will be reckoned to have been divided into God and man when he was made Christ." To this we too reply, with the Theologian, that "every spirit that does not confess that Jesus has come in the flesh is not from God." And if he does not proclaim the Word made flesh and Jesus come in the flesh as two different persons, he clearly knows Jesus to be the same as Christ, and Christ the same as the Word. For he is called Christ for no other reason than that the flesh was anointed and enriched with the Godhead of the Word; and he is called Jesus, which means Saviour, for no other reason than that he has a natural power to save. That is how the angel explained his fitting name, saying, "And they shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." He, then, who has the power not only not to sin but also to redeem from sins—what could he be by nature but God? Not even the Jews were ignorant of this, for they said, "No one can

forgive sins but God alone." And he has been named Jesus because he is himself the God who says, "There is none righteous and saving besides me," and "Salvation belongs to the Lord," and "Not an envoy, nor an angel, but the Lord himself saved us." And if someone else is also called Jesus—such as the son of Nun, or the one called Justus—clearly the shared name comes either from a partial spiritual participation, or by chance, or as a type, as is also the case with the prophets, priests and kings called anointed ones. As for the claim that Jesus is not always Christ because Peter said that God made Jesus both Lord and Christ, that is very foolish. For if "made" always signifies a change or advance in something already existing, then does the one who says, "Is not he himself your Father, who acquired you and made you and formed you?" mean that his people were first God's possession and then became his work? And did the one who said, "Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight," not sin at the very moment he did evil, but sin first and do evil afterwards? And who, granting such things, will not be shown up by the whole of Holy Scripture as a sophistical babbler? And when it is said that God made man in the image of God, shall we understand that he first became man and then became the image of God?

The divine Scriptures call Christ one God, one man and one Christ. But the one God is one by nature, and likewise the one man; whereas the one Christ is one Christ by the voluntary union of God with man. Therefore, they say, the one God differs from the one Christ. But Christ differs from being God alone not by not being God, but by being man as well. According to this syllogism, then, Christ would also differ in nature from man. And if Christ differs in nature both from God and from man, tell us what he would be by nature. But if you say that, for these reasons, Christ need not at all differ in nature from man, then neither, on these grounds, does he necessarily differ from God.

"God made Jesus Lord and Christ." Where do you place God the Word, Egyptian? As the one making him Lord, or as the one made Lord? Answer the question without making your [?] distinctions. As the one making him, certainly—but by imparting his own nature to the nature of the man, and by weaving it into his own single hypostasis, which existed of old.

"If Christ shared in flesh and blood in the same way as we do, clearly Christ is a man of the same nature as ours." If, then, whatever shares in the same things and in the same way is certainly of altogether the same nature, and of that nature alone, as the other things that share in the same thing, then, since the ant and the partridge and the shrimp and the leopard all share in the four elements, are these of the same nature? But consider, sir, that the saying states that the Son of God shared in the same things as the children,

and with a like sharing—namely, in blood and flesh; but it does not say that he who shared these things with us is simply like us. So he is composed of what is like us and what is unlike us. How, then, will he be a man only like us?

If the Father was at one time Father only of God the Word, and at another time both Father and God, then either the Father advanced to something greater, or the Son was brought down to something lesser. But he is always Father of the invisible Word, and God only of the visible flesh of the Word.

"If Christ is at once God and man, and God is not the God of the man, clearly they are not to each other what they are called; that is, neither is God God to the man, nor is the man man [?] to God." The natures in the Lord, then, when compared with each other, are related thus: one of them deified, clearly as divine; the other was deified, admittedly as not divine by nature from of old. But Christ himself, that is, the pairing of Godhead and humanity, is neither simply God of the man and of his whole self, nor man of God and of himself according to the hypostasis; rather, the same one is at once both God and man, differing from God by having put on the human, and differing from men by the indwelling of the divine.

Holy Scripture calls Christ a minister of the holy things, and every minister—of God, that is—ministers to his God. "And if the things of the law are a shadow of the things in grace, and in the shadow the law had a minister, clearly in grace too there is a minister." Since, then, the shadow also had a sacrifice, and on your view Christ is the minister as man, where are we to look for the sacrifice prefigured by the shadow? If, then, we understand the apostolic word that "through the Holy Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God," we shall know that the same one, serving as priest once for all and not many times, one and not several, is both minister of God and sacrifice to God, and likewise God to whom the service is offered. For if, being offered through the Holy Spirit, he is said to have offered [himself?], and not to have been offered by another, clearly the Holy Spirit, which is also God, is of his nature.

"If God the Word is not master of the head, then neither is he master of the whole body; but if God the Word is Lord of the Church, of necessity he is also Lord of the head of the Church." If the head is by nature entirely equal in honour and of the same rank as the whole body, then it is not truly a head [?] understood as a principle and as the part set over the whole body that lies beneath it. But if it truly lies above it by its natural position, and from it the whole body is fitted and joined together and supplied with its powers, clearly this is by participation in some ruling nature of the body, distinct from the nature ruled by it

and consubstantial with it, that of the whole body itself. If it does not participate in this, then it is not a head, since it would not then rule of itself; but if it participates in what moves and leads the body, then it is no longer ruled but rules. Therefore the Word is Lord of his own flesh as one of our members, even though it is also understood to be our head, since it too is said to be under him [?]. For God is said to be the head of Christ too—but not of the whole Christ; for the head of the whole is the Word himself, and he is not master of himself. But if, as you say, what is master of the rest is also master of the head, then, since God was said to be the head of Christ, God is master even of God. For if the body—that is, the whole Christ, as you say—is subject to God, then its head, namely God, must also be subject to the same God.

"If God the Word is not God and master of Christ, clearly Christ is not the temple of God the Word either; but if Jesus is the temple of God the Word, of necessity God the Word is also his God and master." The flesh alone is the temple of the Word; for Christ is at once the temple and the God who dwells in the temple. For Christ is truly neither the anointing alone nor that which was to be anointed alone, but both the anointing and the anointed. What was anointed was the Lord's humanity; the anointing was clearly nothing perceptible at all, but something divine of his. Therefore the same Christ is God and man.

"If all things not only came into being through the Word but also come into being through him, clearly Jesus too, both Lord and Christ, came into being through God the Word; and the Word is God and Master of all things that exist through him." If, then, Jesus was made Lord and Christ by God, as has been said, how is he still mastered by God? For he is then no longer seen to have universal lordship over all being besides his own nature, as we understand of him who is Lord in the proper sense, to whom it is said, "For all things are your servants." But if it is said that he too became Lord in the sense that he is lord over some things, though not over everything besides himself as God is, then [?] Herod too and such as he are lords in part, and have been made so by God. Moreover, if he did not, like these, receive his lordship by some rank and by codicils of appointment when he was made Lord, it is clear that in his making he was made by God, so to speak, lordly in his very nature when he was created, and is Lord of all—apart, obviously, from him who subjected all things to him. But if it is not lawful for anyone to be constituted Lord by nature through a lordship that has no hypostasis, clearly it is through the self-imparting of a lordly nature to the nature that came into being that this Jesus came into being and is Lord. And what is the essence that by nature is lord of all? Plainly the divine. And what of it is imparted to Jesus? The Word, his Creator. For having created him around himself, and having grown together with him from the moment of his making, he truly made him Lord through himself. By participation, then, in the Word himself, and having come to be in him

…and being Lord, Jesus, how could he, as one who came into being through him, be the slave of the one who made him Lord, as if he were thereafter a creature? For if his being Lord is done away with, so is his having been made; for he made him Lord. But if he is both a creature and Lord, and he was made Lord in no other way than through the essential possession of the very one who made him, then either the one who is Lord by nature will be master of himself as well, or he will set free together with himself the one made Lord, that is, his humanity, and give it authority over all things. And so, since in ordinary speech too we say that someone made another person free, shall we reckon that for this very reason the one made free also became a slave?

Apart from being mastered by God, it is impossible for a human being to fulfil obedience or to become sinless by keeping the law. If, then, being mastered is simply the cause of these things, we needed only obedience, and not the economy of Christ, for our justification. For since all of us, and the devil himself, are mastered by God, all things would then be sinless and would have come to keep the law, being subject even without Christ; and even after the incarnation of the Word, one who did not obey [?] would never be justified. So the opposite is shown, you people: that flesh, being by nature flesh of sin and unable to be justified and to be subject to the law of God, could not be justified and fulfil all obedience except by participating in a sinless essence, which is the divine essence alone.

"God, your God, has anointed you": if this does not mean the man honoured by the anointing of the Spirit, but God the Word, then the one who anointed him anointed him to his dishonour, since he had in his own nature greater things than those he received through the anointing. For everyone who is anointed is anointed in order to receive something he cannot have by nature. But what this anointed one became in nature through the anointing by God, the Psalmist goes on to say, and to this we must attend: for he then names the one anointed by him God as well. Yet nothing sensible or intelligible can by nature make anyone truly God except true Godhead itself. It follows, then, that the one who anoints is Godhead, because of "your God," and that the ointment is Godhead, because it deifies and shows the anointed one to be God, and not so called equivocally. Indeed, in the Hebrew each "God" in the passage is written in the same way, with the unpronounceable characters. We must therefore regard the anointed one as both God and man: as the subject that receives the ointment he is man, and in this respect "your God" is also said; but as participating in the deifying ointment, which is substantial in itself and exists essentially in him, he is made complete as God.
Truly, as the saying goes, "When the ungodly man comes into the depth of ungodliness, he is contemptuous." Those who say that God the Word is the God or Master of Christ do not say this of [?]

themselves, but in obedience to the teaching of the Holy Spirit given through the prophets and apostles, and further to that of Christ himself. For David, they say, and Peter the apostle said, "I saw the Lord always before me"; and the Saviour himself said, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me"; and the Prophet, "God, your God, has anointed you." But who among those trained in godliness does not know that holy Scripture says very many things of this kind, and how they are said? The one who says, "Bless the Lord, O my soul," though it is the whole person who speaks, nevertheless exhorts his own soul as from one part of himself only; and the one who says, "I am earth and ashes," though it is the whole person who speaks, nevertheless speaks about one part of himself only, namely the body. So too "I saw the Lord before me" and "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," even if they are spoken by the whole Christ, must be understood as belonging properly to his humanity, and so with similar sayings. It was this humanity that the Spirit anointed, and by its anointing showed it to be Christ. As for "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", if we consider with greater awe the doubling, which is not superfluous, it perhaps hints that what was in some way separated had a twofold relation to what was forsaken: the first "My God" is the possession calling out to its possessor, as in "You, O Lord our God"; the second is the possessor crying out to his own possession, as in "Why are you so sorrowful, O my soul?" We must also reason as follows. If death is the separation of things essentially united, and at his death, as you say, these words were spoken by the man to God, then surely the one said in some way to have forsaken him at that moment was essentially united to him. Therefore one and the same person was both God and man, and it was he who died and suffered, through separating death, the separation of the things in him that by nature are inseparable. But if you say that the separation from the holy man came about through the action of God, we see the opposite happening with all the saints: for we know that the Lord is present with the God-bearers and strengthens them in their contests and sufferings, rather than forsaking them at the hour of death. So much for that. As for "God, your God, has anointed you," it needs no further explanation, since David himself, who knew that the one who anointed was his God, confesses in the next breath that the one anointed is truly God. Whoever anathematizes those who say that Jesus was glorified by the Spirit anathematizes those who say that Jesus was anointed by the Spirit. Is that not so? For the Spirit who anointed would not have been joined directly to the one anointed unless it had found in him some glorious spiritual nature of the same kind as itself. Sensible ointment does not cling to a nature that is not sensible; fire is not smeared on water; nor is air rubbed onto earth. Nor, then, did the Spirit who came down from heaven and remained upon him rest

simply as on flesh upon the humanity of Jesus, since God had once declared that his Spirit would not remain among men, because they were flesh. Rather, recognizing the Word of the Father, who is akin to it, it flew to its own; and what is consubstantial is no glory to the consubstantial. So the very same Jesus was made Lord on account of the divine Word and Christ on account of the anointing of the Spirit. For God made this Jesus, whom the Jews crucified, Lord through the Word and Christ through the Spirit, by the gift of his Word and the investiture of his Spirit, the Father gilding both the inside and the outside of this holy ark with divine radiance. And if from his very birth he is named Christ and Lord in the city of David by the angel, this is by anticipation; for Samuel too, before anointing any of the sons of Jesse, said, "Surely this is the anointed, the Lord?"

If, then, Jesus did not receive from the Spirit the power to act, as the Egyptian teaches, why did the Father give him the Spirit? "For God does not give the Spirit by measure," it says; "the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand." How then is the Spirit given to him by God the Father, if not by measure and according to worth? Jesus did not receive the Spirit as a man too weak for divine action. For if it does not belong to the measure of another nature to receive the Spirit who proceeds from the Father, but it is given only by kinship of nature and by love toward him, and the Son alone is consubstantial with the Father and the Spirit, then clearly it is out of natural love that the Father has given his consubstantial Spirit to the consubstantial Son. For the Father has given all things into his hand, so that the Son says, "All that the Father has is mine." CHAPTER 20. The flesh of the Lord is life-giving when it is believed to have been made alive by God the Word; otherwise it is not life-giving. But it was not now made alive simply by the action of the life-giving Word, as in the creation of Adam; for then man would once again have corruptibility in potency, even now. Rather it was made alive by the indwelling of a life-giving nature in a nature, through a union of two essences that shows forth one hypostasis, so that the corruptibility lying latent in potency in human nature could never again prevail to come forth into act; since no human hypostasis lies latent along with it, but the power that makes incorruptible, life itself by nature, holds the human nature together in the same divine hypostasis [?]. In the same way, some people who administer juices or herbs that are harmful to the bowels for the sake of some other benefit mix them with certain substances that specifically bind the bowels, into the compound of a single drug, and then give it without fear, no longer wary of harm to the bowels because the binding agent is combined in one and the same drug.

"In taking up man, God takes up a certain man, who is man by nature but above man by being taken up." If God took up later someone who was already a man, you speak well. But if it was in the taking up and after the taking up that someone was seen to be a man, how did he take up a certain man, bare and not yet having attained his assumption? And if he is man by nature because of his nature and above man because of the taking up, then nothing other than the nature itself was wholly changed, through the taking up, from being what it was by nature. What, then, came about? Either something else, which is neither God nor man, is what was assumed, or [?]. So, on your view, Christ has one nature, and that divine; and plainly there is one hypostasis in him, and that God's.
