It is written that both the one who sanctifies, namely Christ, and those who are sanctified are all from one, that is, from God; for which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, "I will proclaim your name to my brothers"; and again, "Since, therefore, the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same." But even if all are from one, it is not in the same way. He is from him by begetting, ineffable [?] and without beginning; they by creation alone. The potter's son and the jar are not of the same nature, though both came from him. Otherwise, how are the one who sanctifies by nature and those sanctified by nature of the same nature, if the creator and the created are not? And why is he not ashamed to call them brothers? For what shame could even be suspected among those who are wholly consubstantial and equal in honour? Or what praise for humility is due to one who calls himself what he wholly is by nature, having nothing more than that? For one who is by nature only in the form of a servant does not show himself free of vainglory by calling himself a servant. And what deliberate sympathy toward the children who share by nature in blood and flesh caused the one who is wholly like them by nature likewise to share by nature in flesh and blood? Even if he had not wished it, or rather even if those consubstantial children of his had not shared in them, or had not existed at all, if he shared in blood and flesh by reason of his own nature, he would certainly have shared in them even if he were alone. Here too, then, the transcendence of God is plain to us: he accepted being of one nature with us, became man, and deified man. He also calls these, his brothers according to the flesh, "children," saying, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." For even if according to fleshly birth he is their brother, having come forth from Adam the forefather into this present age, yet having made his own dead body spiritual by resurrection, and giving it to us as food so as to place in us too, through it, a power for resurrection after death that brings about the spiritual revival of bodies, he himself is clearly the cause for us of such a

spiritual nature in the age to come, and of an endless and incorruptible condition for our bodies, which are now corruptible. This is why the one whose children we are is called Father of the age to come. For on account of us, whom he raises incorruptible in spiritual bodies, he also restores as incorruptible bodies the places and everything around us, suited to those who dwell, move about, live and, in short, conduct their life in them; for the creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the glory of the freedom of the children of God, of this one who, as man, is both brother and Father, and who says, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me."

If the very one who was in the form of God "humbled himself, emptying himself into the form of a servant," is the one who was highly exalted and on whom God bestowed "the name that is above every name," then what the Word had by nature he later had by grace. But if it is the same one, emptied in one of his natures into the humanity that is by nature servile, and exalted in the other into the Godhead that by nature rules, is the reward for the humiliation of one then given to another, irrationally and unjustly? Yet the humiliation, even on your view, belongs to the Word; and it is said to have gone as far as death, even death on a cross. So you conclude that the sufferings and the death belong to the Word properly, apart from any natural union with flesh and any co-subsistence whatever of another essence.

"No one has ever seen God." If, then, the one seen on earth, whose glory they beheld as that of the Only-begotten from the Father, is himself God by nature, how is the statement first confessed true? Yet what follows makes clear that he is the same one who is invisible in his own nature and visible to us in his own flesh. For it is said that this very fact, that no one has seen God, the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father has himself made known. When he says that he was seen and that we beheld him, however, he does not mean his nature, for it is clear that the Son is of the same nature as the invisible Father, but his glory, and that not the glory of natural dignity but of his relational order toward his own Father; for he says, "glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father." And does not the one "seen on earth" and speaking, who says without deceit, "I and the Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," clearly show that whoever cannot see the Father cannot see him either? Invisible, then, in Godhead and visible in humanity is Christ, God and not man [?].

If the Word makes his own all the properties of the flesh, and the flesh is granted all the properties of the Word, then coming into being from nothing, which is natural to the flesh, also belongs to the Word, as do being mutable, being visible, and being circumscribed. And if someone were to grant these too, how could the flesh also [?] the opposites? For the visible, not

"If Christ is God by nature, how does he say on the cross, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' For there is no God of one who is understood to be God by nature; so the one who plainly calls God his own God is by nature [?]." Since, then, we too call the God in heaven our Father, are we for this reason, even in what we are according to the flesh, sons of God by nature, or certainly not? For if we do not declare the one we call Father to be by nature the father of the whole of us, neither must the one whom Christ calls his God be the God of his whole nature.

"If the demons knew Jesus to be God by nature," he says, "how could they say, 'I adjure you by God, do not torment us'?" Granted, then, that the unclean spirits did not know him to be God; for no human being can say that Jesus is Lord, that is, God, except by speaking in the Holy Spirit, as it is written. Why, then, do you think trustworthy what is said by the demons, who are always enemies of the truth and friends and teachers of falsehood?

"If the flesh is flesh and not Godhead, since the Godhead was not changed into flesh, nor again helps make up the essence of the flesh, how, for the same reason, is the man not also man and not Godhead?" Indeed, the nature of the flesh is truly a fleshly nature, and that of humanity, as human, is a human nature; but these are not individual hypostases, nor does either of them subsist in Christ cut off from the other. For in all other mere human beings too, it is not the nature of man in general [?] but the nature of each particular individual that is seen to be enhypostatic; and yet neither would the flesh, merely by being called flesh, be distinguished from the soul by a hypostasis of its own, nor the soul from the flesh. This is what the account of the mystery of our Master's incarnation teaches, and it demands our faith on this point: that the Word, who had his own hypostasis and nature, fleshless before the ages and pre-existing the human nature, clothed himself with flesh in the last times and made the human nature subsist in his very own hypostasis, not in that of a mere man.

"If the flesh is flesh and not Godhead, and the man is man and not Godhead, how do you name the man from a part, the flesh?" By the principle of nature, both are understood by us in Christ as differing from the Godhead, whether both signify one thing indifferently, or the flesh is spoken of as a part and the man as the whole. By the principle of hypostasis, the flesh, understood as a part, will again be reckoned as having the same meaning in relation to the Godhead of Christ, and for us it is anhypostatic; for neither in the Word nor outside the Word has it been allotted a hypostasis of its own, but it is always regarded as part of the living being. But the one called man in Christ, since he is not simply part of a whole hypostasis except in Christ alone, no longer keeps in Christ the same hypostatic principle as in all other human beings. For if he were considered by himself, he would show in Christ a principle of hypostatic as well as natural otherness, which is not the case; for then the whole composition of the totality of Christ's person would be disjointed, divided by natures and by hypostases, and the confession of the union of the natures, which we piously hold concerning Christ, would be false. For the one called man in Christ is made new beyond all human beings, compared with his former state, into glory [?] through the ineffable union with God: unlike us, he does not have his own human hypostasis, peculiar to him and distinguished from every nature of the same or of a different kind, but the hypostasis of the Word, which is common to and undivided between his own nature and the nature above him. Therefore, if the human nature is named from the flesh as from a natural part, with nothing suspect arising to lead us into knavery, we know both to be the same. But if you wish to introduce his humanity as having a hypostasis of its own, as though it were one of the hypostases making up the whole Christ, like members of a chorus, and you do not say that it is composite with the divine nature, we will accept neither the term man used barely, nor the term flesh used in place of a complete, bare man.

"If the flesh is flesh and not Godhead, but the man is no longer man and not Godhead [?], tell me: in what sense does the Godhead belong to the flesh, and in what sense to the man?" With the flesh, which is the same as saying with the man too, the Godhead is co-enhypostatic in Christ. But with the flesh, as has been said, which remains unchanged by the principle of both nature and hypostasis, and is regarded in him, as in others, as a part and as different in relation to the whole; whereas with the man the Godhead is co-enhypostatic as with one made new beyond the many in respect of hypostasis: for instead of an individual hypostasis he has acquired a common one, instead of a human hypostasis a divine one, and instead of being a hypostatic whole he is regarded as a part within it. For this truly serves him for the completion of perfect blessedness. It must also be observed that the flesh does not always signify for us the man as a part, nor the man the flesh, but only when the discussion concerns nature alone; and even then, not because the whole man is flesh, but because in

…of Christ, the whole humanity is distinguished, as one nature according to the flesh, over against the divinity: as created over against the uncreated, and as admitting one definition of its own, distinct from that of the divinity.

If the divinity of the flesh is the same as the divinity of the man, yet the flesh is other than the divinity (for it is flesh and not divinity), how is the man not also other than the divinity, since it is man and not divinity? — Truly the divinity of the flesh, even if it is called only flesh and not man, is the same as the divinity of the man. And it is other than them, being only co-subsistent with them through the hypostatic union, whether both terms signify the man, or one says that it co-subsists with the one as with a part and with the other as with the natural whole. But again, how are the flesh and the man truly other than the divinity in Christ, if not [?]? Since they are flesh and man, and not divinity, as you yourselves say. But they are other according to a different nature: clearly they are other in this way, and not according to hypostasis, since the divinity is a nature and the humanity is another nature.

If God the Word was not part of the flesh but was part of the man, how are you not taking the side of Arius or Apollinaris? — But the Word is part neither of the flesh nor of the man, God forbid! For even if someone were lawlessly to give the Word to the flesh in place of a soul, as did the blasphemers of God whom you have mentioned, still not even so would he present him as part of a man. For such a whole, made up of soulless flesh and the divine Word, will no longer be a man, since the account and definition of man is a body animated by a rational soul, not one animated by the divine Word. And if someone should in some way call the Word a part of Christ, he clearly means a part of a whole, and not of a man simply; and he says this only to signify that his person is one, composed of different natures.

If, just as God the Word is not part of the flesh, so he is not part of the man either, how is the man not other than God the Word, just as God the Word is other than the flesh? For the Word is God and not flesh, just as the flesh is flesh and not divinity. — God the Word is part neither of the flesh nor of the man, whether by nature or by hypostasis, but of Christ, since the hypostasis of our Lord Christ was not that of a mere man. So the Word in Christ would be understood to be other than the flesh and the man, that is, the humanity, only according to nature, and not also according to hypostasis. You, however, being treacherous about the subject, keep silent about the othernesses and identities, about what they are of and how each is spoken of, so that by means of the acknowledged otherness of one thing, namely nature, you may covertly bring in the otherness of another thing as well, namely hypostasis; and so that you may establish what has been your concern from the beginning, two hypostases, and sever the union
of our Lord Christ, which you pretend to accept in word only. For whoever distinguishes something both by nature and by hypostasis thinks of its conjunction as nothing more than accidental.

[?] Demonstration of the impiety of those who call our Lord Jesus Christ a God-bearing man, and not God made man. CHAPTER ONE. If the Word has the flesh as a garment, according to what he said about himself in his own words, "He will wash his garment in wine," then clearly whoever anathematizes the one who calls Christ a God-bearing man anathematizes the wearer before he anathematizes the speaker. — But if the flesh is the garment of the Word, and the Word is God, and the flesh is the man, it would be more consistent to call Christ a man-bearing God. His apostles, on the other hand, who were clothed with power from on high when the Holy Spirit of God came upon them — these, and those like them, it is fitting to call God-bearers, so that the divine nature may be understood as something acquired by a human hypostasis. In the Lord, conversely, the human nature is glorified as something acquired by the divine hypostasis. For he himself put on what belongs to our nature, he who clothed all of us with what belongs to his own nature, taking flesh and giving the Spirit.

"God was in the Son," according to the saying; [so one must] [?] say that the Word is in a man as the wearer is in what is worn; nor, then, can God be in Christ in any other way. — If, then, God was in Christ in this undifferentiated way, as the wearer in what is worn, then the Word is in the flesh by way of circumscription and enclosure, as under a covering and a veil; and they are united to one another by the local juxtaposition of the boundary of the one to that of the other, just as the husk or the shell is a covering around the almond. So the Word is circumscribed by the flesh, either wholly or for the most part. Moreover, in that case he will have devised the incarnation for himself not so that the Word might be made manifest to the world, but so that he might be covered over and not laid bare to anyone's understanding. Otherwise, the Word would be thought to be a body even before the flesh, if he has a surface in this way. And even if we are allowed to say every absurdity, even so the God from God would be not God-bearing but rather man-bearing. Or if, according to you, Christ himself was the one worn and also the God-bearer, Christ stands in the middle between two Gods: one contained within him, because

The mode of a voluntary union does not abolish existence within; for if one thing does not exist within the other, neither is it united to it. — But existence within, according to the voluntary union of the natures with one another, never exists in a pair of hypostases, as of an indweller and that which is indwelt.

If the Word does not have the man as a temple or a garment, he necessarily has him as part of his essence; and whoever takes the flesh into the essence of Christ makes an increase of the essence of the Son, turning and altering it into something else. — But the Word is in the flesh as in a temple, as in a tent, and as in a garment, by a certain analogy; yet not without any difference, as he would be in any one of these. For if being in all these things is not the same, nor in the same manner, much more will his not being wholly as in any of them mark the difference in Christ between what is possessed and the one who possesses it. But if what exists apart from these shows at once that it has been assumed into essence, and not rather into hypostasis, through the coming together of essence with essence, then so it is with the fire in the red-hot iron with respect to the iron, and with the soul with respect to the body in man. For here the entry is not as into a temple, nor the indwelling as in a tent, nor the clothing as with a garment; for what is in these is not of a nature to cover over the surface of the houses or garments that carry it, and as it were to become itself their garment. Nor, simply because one thing suffers along with the other, must one suppose a change of the essence of the fire into the essence of iron in the red-hot iron, or an exchange of the soul into body in man. And indeed, even if there were a change, as you say, there would be no increase; and if there were an increase, no change has taken place. For increase comes about while the underlying subject remains, but change does not in the same way.

If it is absurd to call Christ a God-bearing man, teach us how one must name Christ as man: a God-fleshed man, or a man-fleshed God? But if Christ is such a man, it is clear that Christ is a man other than the nature of Adam. — "The word is near you, on your lips and in your mind," that is, God incarnate, who truly has something beyond the nature of Adam, while preserving everything that belongs to it.

If, just as the Word was one God and one Son before he became flesh, so he is also after the incarnation, it is clear that he has the flesh as a garment and a temple, and not as part of his essence. — But now the same one is also one man, for he was counted among us; that is why he is also called Emmanuel. Yet no one who lives in a temple or wears a garment is counted together with temples or garments.

CHAPTER 7. If Christ is not a God-bearing man, then neither is Christ a man who hears the truth from God: "For why," he says, "do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from the Father?" — But he is a God-borne man, and not a God-bearer; for the flesh did not dwell in the Word, but the Word in the flesh.

Whoever prevents God the Word from acting in Jesus prevents the man from being seen as God the Word. — You have spoken well, if you will confess it clearly. For the Word alone, by himself, works in the flesh its deification, primarily as God, but through his natural interweaving with it; in the way that the soul properly works in its own body, in man, its vivification, and fire in iron, in the red-hot iron, its burning. And this is shown when the work of one of the things that have come together into the other has truly gone forth, through the display of the outward activities of the one that acted upon it, which from then on always proceed from what was acted upon. CHAPTER [?].

If Christ is not both the one who acts, as God, and the one acted upon, as man, then Christ is either only the one who acts or only what is acted upon. — The Word brought about the assumption of the flesh to himself, and he works its resurrection from the dead; yet the whole Christ is not acted upon by another in these things, nor does he act upon someone else. For they belong to the same Christ, on whose account are the Word and the flesh [?]. But in the activities that Christ performs on others, the Word often acts properly through his flesh when working miracles, the flesh being understood from then on to be joined to him as a natural instrument.

"But Athanasius too," he says, "whom you do not reject, says in his work On the Incarnation: 'He prepares the body for himself as a temple, and makes it his own as an instrument, being made known and dwelling in it'; and again: 'offering his own temple and saving instrument as a ransom for all.'" — Understand, then, that it is called an instrument naturally united, as a body is to a soul, and a house in the same sense. For it is said that "the Word became flesh," not merely that he dwelt in flesh.

…to have suffered in the flesh? For if you speak not of three gods but of three hypostases, it would be consistent to say "one" in the neuter or in the feminine of the Trinity, looking to the hypostasis or the person, and not "one" in the masculine; for this, said in the masculine, is applied to gods or fathers or sons. This is why you do not even tolerate speaking carelessly of the Christ whom you confess as "one and another" in the masculine, but only as "one thing and another thing." — It is astonishing that you have not blushed to try to show us impious by means of the very opinions you put forward as your own when you were examining what concerns the Lord's hypostasis. For you taught that the essences of the Holy Trinity are particular and three, and that one of them is the one said to have become man; and you said that this alone, the particular essence, is a hypostasis. Yet the accused would not be free of the charge simply because they had their accusers as fellow sinners. Let that pass, then. On these matters, at any rate, we can say this to you now: when we call the Word "one" of the Holy Trinity in the masculine, using this term that signifies number, it is not only him that we call God; we also call the Father himself and the Holy Spirit "God" in the masculine, and we do not on that account think them three gods. For neither our holy Fathers nor holy Scripture have anywhere taken care to avoid speaking in this way about each one of the three persons of the divine nature. Indeed, they have called the Father and the Son by masculine terms in very many places, because the complete perfection of each, both essentially according to what is common and hypostatically according to what is particular, makes known the same perfection of divinity and lordship in all three. For this is how the God-gathered assembly of the synod at Nicaea says one is to believe: "in one God, the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ"; and yet they always speak of the hypostases and the persons in the feminine and the neuter. And in setting forth this very creed about them, as a rule and standard of orthodoxy concerning God and the divine Trinity, they did not say to believe "in one" in the neuter, but proclaimed both in the masculine, both in the word that signifies number, namely "one," and in the absolute and particular names, namely "God" and "Lord." And the sacred Oracles often speak of two in the masculine, even dividing the activity concerned with a single matter; and yet, contrary to what you hold, this does not necessarily introduce any intention of polytheism. Examples are: "The Lord rained fire from the Lord"; and "The Lord said to my Lord"; and "God, your God, has anointed you"; and very many others, none of which has shown that there are three gods, or done away with the oneness of the divinity and lordship in the three. For elsewhere it is said: "The Lord your God is one Lord"; and "Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth"; and other such things from his Holy Spirit. Was the Spirit then obliged to say "one" in the feminine or the neuter, or "holy," "lord" or "divine" in the feminine, so as not to be liable to your accusations? And how, then, do you yourselves address the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit? If

neither as Lord nor as God (for these are said in the masculine), how are you not utterly godless? But if you too say the very things for which you accuse us, how will you not be judged utterly shameless?

If the Holy Trinity is impassible, and Christ is passible, and Christ is one of the Holy Trinity, then either the Holy Trinity too is passible, or Christ is not one of the Holy Trinity. And if you add "he suffered in the flesh," suffering in such a way does not free him from suffering; just as, if someone were to say that a person was strangled in such and such a way, that does not free the one spoken of from suffering or from being strangled. — But Christ is not only one of the Holy Trinity; he is also one of humanity, in one and the same hypostasis of his. For God the Word took up into his own person something in addition to his own nature, namely the creature he himself had fashioned; and what was taken was taken not as a hypostasis but as a nature, co-subsisting with the nature of the Word in his own hypostasis. It has often been shown, in the appropriate place, that it is possible for even several natures to exist in one hypostasis. Let us see by an example how this is so in the case of our Lord Christ. Suppose Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, after their departure from this life, are now defined by the definition of immortality, each of them being in this respect an immortal rational living being rather than [like] the rest [?]; while Joseph, who is one with them in nature and truly consubstantial with them, but is still ruler of Egypt and living in the flesh, is defined as mortal, since he is understood still to be living the present life with corruptible flesh. Must those men then, according to you, still be defined as mortal and die twice, so that Joseph's definition may not be false? Or must Joseph too be immortal and be so defined even before his departure from this life, so that they may not falsely be called immortal? But if these things are absurd, it is clear that Joseph, even before laying aside the flesh, is truly consubstantial with those persons who are understood to be immortal in their whole selves, according to that part of himself by which he will never die, namely the soul; and he is mortal and numbered with mortals according to what he had for the time being in addition to those consubstantial with him in immortality, namely the body that he bore. In the same way, then, we too say that Christ, who is of flesh and divinity, is passible in the flesh and not in the divinity. But since you say that "in the flesh" signifies only a different cause and mode of the predicate that befell the subject, Christ — namely the suffering — and is not said, as we hold, with reference to one of the different essences existing in him, his same hypostasis suffering this partially, then by your reasoning, whenever someone says that a man was cut in the flesh, we must always think that he was divided wholly, soul and all, and imagine only this about what was said: that the whole man was cut, not perhaps by a sword or a stone, but by flesh, being divided in soul and body through this as a cutting instrument. Consistently,

on hearing that he was stripped of hair, covered in sores and bitten in the flesh, you will think that the man suffered in both, that is, that these things befell the man in soul and body, but through flesh having the power of a depilatory [?]. Furthermore, in the case of those whose flesh is spared torture though they suffered something, if we say that so-and-so remained unharmed in the flesh, through the flesh, then once this is granted, according to you it will equally be said that his soul remained unharmed through the flesh, since nothing else is left to him besides the flesh. But what fool is so insensible to these things? So it is clear that "in the flesh" is said neither as through an instrument that produces suffering, nor as though the flesh were a part of God the Word considered by himself, when it is said, "God the Word suffered in the flesh," in the way we say that so-and-so stumbled with his foot or was hung up by his hand. For when we say "God the Word," we always understand Christ after the union of the natures; and we speak of the flesh as a part of Christ, according to which we say that God the Word too suffered, as Christ. So too in the case of a man we speak in terms of a part, saying that Paul was weak in the flesh but healthy in the spirit, and absent from some people in the flesh but with them in the spirit. In the same way we also call the Jews God-slayers, and use similar expressions, since Christ is God and Word. Since, then, Christ suffered for us in the flesh, according to the apostle Peter, it is clear that God the Word too would be said to have suffered, not as the part, but as Christ. For the whole Job is said to have suffered, although only his flesh suffered: "But his soul," the Lord says to the devil, "do not touch."

If they should claim that "he suffered in the flesh" means "not in his own essence," they contradict themselves in saying so. For they say that the essence in which, according to them, God the Word suffered is not his own, so as not to confess him passible in his essence. But what is not one's own is another's, and what is another's belongs to someone other than the one whose own it is not; so they speak not only of two essences but also of two persons: one, that of God the Word, and one, that of the one whose essence it is in which God the Word suffered. And whose is it, if not clearly a man's? And a particular man is a person. — But the mind is the soul's own, as a power; its thoughts are its own, as activity; the body is its own, as an instrument; a man's son is his own, as coming from him; and his field is his own, as a possession. And although all of these are truly his own, none of them is his own in the sense in which another is, even though all are said of the one man. Clearly this happens because "own" has many meanings. Since, then, the field is truly this man's own in its proper sense, while the other things are not his own in the same way in the sense that applies to the field, and since, according to you, everything that is not in some way one's own will at once simply be another's, then the field will be this man's own, but the mind and the body

of this man, and the rest, will not be his own. And how would thinking this way not be plainly out of one's mind? Moreover, both the Christ whom we glorify as God to be worshipped, and the one whom you understand as a mere man — or even something more than a man, though not God, if you take pride in granting him something else besides — behold, he presents the flesh and body that endured the nails and the lance as truly his own; for these were its members. Concerning these he says: "They pierced my hands and my feet." And again he shows that the mystical partaking of the bread of the eucharist is the giving of his own flesh, when he says, "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood," and elsewhere, "This is my body." And further, he regards the Church as his own flesh; for the Apostle teaches this when he says, "For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church"; and in another place, "You are the body of Christ, and members in part." Since, then, the Church is his own flesh and body, will what is not his Church not be reckoned his own, according to you? And since he was not crucified in this flesh but on its behalf, he will necessarily have suffered in alien flesh. For if, according to you, what is not in some way one's own is at once another's, and the Church is his own, then what is not his own in the way the Church is will be wholly alien to him. Likewise, if you were to say that the flesh that was nailed is properly his own, the Church will not be his own, since it was not nailed. For you have decided that whatever is said not to be one's own in some respect is at once another's as well. But, my friends, the flesh was not proper to the nature of the Word; it truly became proper to his hypostasis in the last times. We also say that the upright posture belongs to man, being proper [?] to the nature of the soul, yet observed in its hypostasis in the body. If you had understood how this is said about it, you would not have woven for us your syllogisms of shadows and dreams. But enough about these matters. At the end of your argument, apparently overcome by the affliction of lethargy through inattention, you would have moved us to no small laughter, had we not been restrained beforehand and held to reverence by the awesomeness of the questions under inquiry. For although absolutely everything you have said is false, still we see that you now wish to reach this very conclusion: that we speak of two essences and two persons, that is, hypostases, in the case of the Word and the flesh. And you strive to refute us as though we held this as an absurd conclusion and an unlawful opinion — the very thing that yesterday and the day before, and may it not be so tomorrow, has been the chief point of your religion alone. Above all, the absurdity of such an opinion is your distinguishing mark; to us it is truly utterly hateful and hostile. Indeed, it is for this very reason that, with God, we contend against you on so many points.

If the “one of the Trinity” that is spoken of is common to the divinity and the humanity of Christ, is it common to the Father and the Spirit in the same respect, or in one respect and another, as if the one Word were somehow made up of both? If the communion is in the same respect, first, how is the flesh not consubstantial with the Word? Then, how is the Godhead not a tetrad rather than a Triad? But if the Word shares with the Father and the Spirit in one respect and the flesh in another, how are you not bringing two natures into the holy Trinity? And if you call the “one of the Trinity” a whole made of parts, then God the Word by himself will be half of one of the holy Trinity. And if one must also call him consubstantial [?] from two, then by saying this of the Father and the Spirit as well, you have made the Word one of a holy Trinity of six units. — But you who are thin in understanding, yet clever, as you suppose, at reasoning precisely about such things: first, it is not at all necessary that whatever makes a thing one, and one of many, must also be something it has in common with the many. Rather, it is because it is said to be one that it is also said to be with many. The Word, then, has been called one of the holy Trinity by hypostasis. In essence he is not one out of three; the Word is glorified as one together with the two. By his own hypostasis he has no communion with the Father or the Spirit, neither before the flesh nor after the flesh, since the Word is not these; nor will a hypostasis, simply as hypostasis, ever have communion with a hypostasis. How then can you ask what communion the one of the holy Trinity has with the other two persons, whether as the Word simply or as the incarnate Word, that is, Christ, in the very respect in which he is one out of the three who are unlike? For they are not one in the principle or the number of hypostasis. What is one in them is truly the essence and the number of the essence, and in that respect they are never three, so that we could call Christ one of the three and consider how his likeness to the others stands. For it is clear that the hypostases have one unvarying nature, not by hypostasis but by the essence that is in them; and because they have in every way one existence, we also speak of their identity. The Son is said to be like the Father, and to be the image of the Father, when his property is understood together with the nature, namely his being from a cause. For in this way the notion of an image includes, along with the common element of likeness, its own proper element as well: not being the archetype but being from a pattern. But when we consider both hypostases in terms of the essence itself, we no longer add “likeness,” since it is not one essence [?] set against another. No otherness at all will be seen there; we know only its identity, in unity. So although you have not put your question reasonably, if you ask these things with the proper communion of our Lord Jesus Christ in mind, you will receive this answer from us: the Word, being one whole person and one hypostasis of the holy Trinity (for the Triad is made up of hypostases, not of natures),

he who was formerly without flesh became flesh and is Christ. By a part of himself, that is, by one of the natures in him, he is common with, consubstantial with, and one in nature with his good Father and his Holy Spirit, united to them in essence. He brings neither an excess nor a shortfall of hypostases into the holy Trinity, since the Word was one hypostasis both before the flesh and after the flesh. Nor is he shown to have been less than one hypostasis before the flesh, in the holy Trinity, that is. For the perfection of hypostasis he now has does not come from receiving an added hypostasis. He possesses only the one he had, even after the addition of the [?] nature which he did not have. And so your whole reckoning of doublings into triplings dissolves into nothing, and every item in your unreasonable list is reasonably reckoned false by us. For Christ is wholly one out of three, you who are wise in your own eyes, but not by communion. He is one together with the other two persons by the communion of one of the natures in him, not of both the natures in him. And it does not follow that if something does not share with another in everything that belongs to it, it will have nothing in common with it.

If the “one of the Trinity” means one made of divinity and flesh, how will the flesh not also belong to the Trinity? And if the holy Trinity is in some respect a monad, will the flesh not also belong to the monad? And if the flesh belongs to the monad, and the flesh is created, how is the monad uncreated? — But what argument could you have to show that whatever shares in some respect must necessarily share in every respect? Suppose the flesh has shared with the divinity in the hypostasis of the Word, so that for this reason it truly belongs, together with him, to one of the units of the holy Trinity, that is, of the numbering of hypostases. What argument compels it to share also in the essential principle of the divinity, that is, in the principle of nature, and so be included with it in the oneness of the divine existence? For this very reason we say the opposite of what you say. By the good pleasure of the economy, the divinity was united to the flesh in that principle in which it somehow differs from itself, namely in hypostasis. Admittedly, then, it will not share with the flesh in the principle of essence, in which it does not differ from itself. Even considered in itself, the divinity is not shown to share in both its principles, that of essence and that of hypostasis, for it is one in one respect and three in another. How then will you have it share in both with what is other than itself, namely the flesh? If that were so, the divinity would in truth have testified that the flesh alone is somehow above God, incomparably simpler than itself and superior to itself. So much for that. But if, because of the subtlety of the argument, what has been said is perhaps not easy for you to understand,

you must be refuted more crudely, by an example. In a particular hypostasis of a red-hot lump, a part of fire has been joined to a part of iron, and its being is made up of common fire and of iron. Since fire is wholly present in it by nature, how could one not say, on your reasoning, that the iron is also consubstantial with the fire? But if this is plainly refuted, it is admitted that the different bodies in the lump are one with each other in the hypostasis by one kind of communion. By another kind of union, each of them is again understood as one with the things consubstantial with it, in a common nature. So you were right to say that the flesh also belongs to the Trinity, because it belongs to one of the three hypostases. But it does not also belong to the monad, my friends, in the primary sense, that is, by its own principle. “But the Trinity is in some respect also a monad.” [?] … so that the flesh, together with them, is likewise also a monad, just as it belongs to the Trinity, you thoughtless people!

If the “one of the Trinity” is made up of divinity and flesh, and the Trinity is confessed to be impassible, how will both the divinity and the flesh not be impassible? And if they are impassible, who is it that suffered for us? And what does “passible before the resurrection” mean? — But no one has granted you that the one of the Trinity is made up of divinity and flesh in the sense you take it. The Word of the divinity in the Son was not deficient in nature or in hypostasis. Nor was the flesh added to him and taken on because the Word alone, by himself and without flesh, did not count toward the number of the Trinity of persons or of the monad of nature, the passible thus subsisting in him, the impassible. God has no need to acquire suffering and passibility in order to be perfected and made complete. So the Word, one and the same, truly displays both his impassibility, before the flesh and after the flesh, and the sufferings of his flesh. But do not try to trap us with what is confessed about the time before the Word's incarnation or after the resurrection of his flesh, by simply saying that the holy Trinity is impassible. We openly confess this to you: during the time of the Word's sojourn on earth in the flesh, just as the whole holy Trinity of hypostases was not without flesh, so not every one of its hypostases was impassible, if, as the saint said, “the Christ is subject to suffering” and “the first to rise from the dead.” For he is the very Word who was in the beginning. But the divine nature, his own and that of the good Father and of his Holy Spirit, is impassible, and it is always in the same hypostasis of the Word of truth, whether without flesh or incarnate.
If the “one of the Trinity” is made up of divinity and flesh, how will the one of the Trinity not be man as well as God, and consubstantial also

with his Mother? And if so, how will the one of the Trinity not truly be one of human nature, just as he is one of the Trinity, and moreover belong to the Trinity both by divinity and by flesh? How then will he not also belong to human nature both by divinity and by flesh? — But it has already been said that the Word was not completed by the flesh, as though he lacked something needed for perfection or for being what he was [?]. Even before the flesh he was perfect, one of the holy Trinity. It was the opposite: he took flesh in order to make the flesh, which is imperfect compared with God, belong to one of the perfect members of the holy Trinity, that is, to himself, and share in his own perfection. And so after taking on the flesh the Word, together with it, is likewise again one of the holy Trinity. Yet as God he is truly one, and just as he is consubstantial with the Father, he is consubstantial with his mother, by a consubstantiality corresponding to each, and this not by the same one of the natures in him. So much for that. But what follows, on your part, clumsily slips in nature for us in place of hypostasis. To avoid any absurdity, you ought to have drawn the consequence like this: “If, just as he is one, that is, one hypostasis, of the three hypostases of the divine nature, so he is also one, that is, one hypostasis, of the many hypostases of human nature; and if he is one of the hypostases of the Trinity by a hypostasis that is both divine and human, then he will also be one of the hypostases of humanity by a hypostasis that is both divine and human.” Among the divine hypostases he exceeds them by what is human … [?] … exceeding in nature; and among the human hypostases he surpasses them by the divine property. But you kept silent about … [?] … the name of hypostasis, so that you could charge us, who say that the unconfused union of the natures is hypostatic, with a natural change and overturning, as if we were among those who say that the union came about in one nature.

By the same line of reasoning, “God suffered in the flesh” must also be examined, and likewise “the Word,” “the Christ,” and “the Son.” Either these names include the two in their meaning, or they do not. If they do not, our opponents will make either the flesh or the Word without essence, or make one of the two an instrument or a worker. But if each of the names includes the two, the absurdities already mentioned will follow for them. — But, my friends, each of these names does include the two in one hypostasis. The names “Christ,” “God,” and “Son” include them not as one nature but as two. “Word” and “God,” however, can also be used of the one nature alone, the one that existed before the flesh, and so “in the flesh” is added to them, that is, the other nature in the composite Christ. That is why, when we predicate suffering of the Word or of God, as of the whole person of Christ, we add, from one of the parts in him, through which of his natures he suffered.

They say further: “If the Word did not suffer in the flesh in essence, clearly he suffered without essence; and if without essence, he did not suffer at all, for sufferings belong properly to an essence.” — But the Word is said to have suffered by hypostasis. He took a passible essence into his own hypostasis together with his own impassible one, and what is predicated of an essence is customarily, and rightly, predicated of the hypostasis.

“Look,” they say, “your father Cyril says that God the Word suffered in the flesh, and when he is asked how he says this is possible, he defends it again and again by the Word's appropriation of his own flesh, which by nature suffered. If, then, God, who truly remains in himself, is passible by appropriating what suffered at the hands of the Jews, then God in him is born of a woman only by appropriating what was born of her. So the Jews are not truly understood to be God-killers, even if they are called that, and the Virgin is not the Mother of God, even if she is called that. For to appropriate what suffers or what is born is not yet to suffer or to be born.” — But we say that the Word truly suffered and was born, not simply by appropriating the flesh. When certain things are united into one hypostatic whole, the names of each of its parts can be applied to the whole. So it is said of human beings, “and all flesh shall see the salvation of the Lord,” and to Lot, “Save, save your own soul.” Sometimes what belongs to the whole is applied to the parts, as when we say that a man was broken, though only a limb of his body was, or that someone is a proud man, though he is proud only in his soul. And sometimes what belongs to one of the parts of the one whole is applied to the other part joined with it. We say, “How many souls were cut down at the capture of Jerusalem!” though only the bodies were, and that a free body does not endure insult, though only the soul feels the shame. It is clear, then, that when Christ's flesh suffered, one can say that the impassible Word himself suffered, because of the union and not only by appropriation. For the same reason he was also born, since he himself underwent his own birth together with the flesh. He was not born into being, as the flesh was, but into being in the flesh, and his own invisible hypostasis took on form when the flesh received its being in it. “It is not possible,” he says, “for anything that is passible by nature to suffer through another that has suffered. For the suffering itself is seen only in the one in which it took place, and not in the one through which [?] it came to it, nor as present in it. How much less, then, could the pious rightly say that the impassible Word suffered in the flesh?” Let them know, then, that those whose piety is more fitting to God would rather say that the Word suffered in the flesh in Christ

than that he did not suffer. For we know the divine not simply as impassible, but also as making impassible the things it is joined to. We glorify it not only as immortal, but also as making immortal whatever comes to be in it. The flesh, then, was united to the Word by a union so close that, even by our opponents' own reckoning, no closer unconfused blending of things of different natures could be conceived. It is not that whatever the flesh suffered the Word is also simply said to have suffered, and to be passible by nature, except as Christ. Rather, because the flesh suffered by his economy while united to the one who makes things impassible, it lets us see an interruption of the Word's natural activity, which is the definition of a certain kind of suffering. And this is accomplished with great power and surpassing wisdom by the immeasurable goodness of God. Through the suffering, in a part of humanity, of the very one who makes impassible, he brings about impassibility for the whole of human nature forever. For this was the goal set before him. And a suffering that comes about in accordance with the purpose and good pleasure of the one who suffered would rather count as a natural activity, for he takes pleasure in what is according to nature, not in what is contrary to nature. And nothing according to nature, not even suffering, is blameworthy in any way. — I think the refutation of their eighth impiety is missing; look for it. This book was copied by me, Cornelius of Nauplia, of the Mourmoureis family, son of Andrew, living in Venice, in the year 1552 from the birth of God.
